Silas caught Wade’s wrist.

For a moment neither man could move. Silas held the knife hand above his chest, his own gun lying inches from his boot. Wade’s boots scraped for purchase in the blood and broken glass.

Wae pulled hard. The knife dipped.

Silas turned his body, trying to protect his ribs, and Wade drove the blade into his right thigh.

The puncture came with a sickening, meaty resistance. The knife sank nearly to its guard, just above the knee. Silas’s eyes went wide. He felt the skin stretch, then the blade part muscle and scrape against something deeper.

He screamed.

Silas kicked him in the stomach.

But the wound in Silas’s leg was already doing its work. Blood welled around the puncture and ran down his boot in a thick, steady stream. It did not fall merely from the wound; it pulsed with his heartbeat, hot and dark, pooling beneath him faster than he could press his hand against it.

He tried to stand. His right leg folded beneath him.

The gold lay all around him. Coins gleamed in the lamplight, untouched except where blood and whiskey had spread around them. Wade stood behind the bar, bleeding from his face, one hand pressed to his stomach where the knee had landed.

Neither man reached for a gun.

Behind him, Wade looked down at the blood on the floor.

Then he looked at the gold.

Outside, Silas collapsed into the mud. He pressed both hands against the wound, but the blood pushed between his fingers. His vision narrowed at the edges. Somewhere close by, a horse stamped and snorted, impatient for a rider who would never reach the saddle.

### The Phone Book

The room behind the precinct records office had one bulb, and the bulb had ambitions above its station. It swung with every breath the building took, dragging my shadow around the walls like a man hunting for a way out.

They had taken my gun, my wallet, my hat, and four hundred dollars in cash. What they left me was a wooden chair, a scarred desk, and a city phone book with a red cover somebody had spilled coffee on.

"Relax, Dade. You're among friends."

Detective Leo Muldoon said it around a cigar that had gone soft at the lip. He sat on the edge of the desk, one heel tapping the floor, the phone book open in his lap like a hymnal.

I looked at Brill, the other one. Brill had his hat over his eyes and his chair tilted back, and he hadn't said a word in ten minutes. That made two men in the room who wanted something from me and one man who wanted me to know it.

"Friends don't come with a phone book," I said.

"We pulled you off the Viaduct at two in the morning," Brill said, "with a bottle in your hand and no ID worth the ink."

"I was celebrating."

"It's the middle of the week."

"My client was dead. I don't know how that comes out evenly on a calendar."

Muldoon took the cigar from his mouth and looked at it, disappointed, like it had said something he didn't like. He tapped the ash into a saucer that had been there so long the coffee in it had gone to varnish.

"Your client," he said. "Harold Fisk."

"That's the name."

"That's the dead man."

"Then I picked a good one."

Brill took his hat off his face. His eyes were the pale gray of dishwater, and they had all the warmth of a February sidewalk.

"You were hired by a dead man, Frank?"

"Fisk hired me before he died. He was alive then. Barely. Found him in his office with his head on the desk and his blood in the filing cabinet."

Muldoon smiled with no part of his face above the mouth. "A bookkeeper."

"Contracts clerk. He kept records."

"Records." Muldoon closed the phone book. The sound was small, like a door shut in a distant room. "He kept records on payments. City contracts. Inspectors. Judges. Men who make the machine run."

"Sounds like a boring man."

"Does it."

"Sounds like a man who confused his arithmetic with his importance."

Nobody said anything for a while. The rain hit the high window in the dark and came down in threads, one of them tracked across the glass like a scratch that hadn't decided how deep it wanted to go.

Then Muldoon hit me.

He didn't swing with his whole body. That would have been anger. He swung with his wrist, the way a man uses a book, and the phone book caught me high on the shoulder and drove the chair back against the wall.

*It didn't hurt yet.*

Pain works on a delay, like a bad check. It waits for the shock to clear out, then it comes in and starts making a home. I felt the blow as a distance, as some fact that belonged to a man in a chair, and then the fact turned into a red rope pulled tight through my shoulder blade.

Muldoon set the phone book on the desk, squared it to the edge, and wiped his knuckles on his sleeve.

"Phone book's cleaner," he said. "No fingerprints."

"No bruises either," Brill said.

"Brill," Muldoon said, "you're an enthusiast."

*Cheap tobacco. There it was again, coming off him in a sour yellow cloud, wet and burnt at the same time, the smell of a church basement after the roof gave up. It was in the wool of his coat, in the chair, in my mouth. I could taste it on the split place in my lip, copper and cigar ash, and I thought that was the smell the city was actually made of: tobacco, rain, and men who had stopped washing.*

"Where's the ledger, Dade?"

"Fisk didn't keep a ledger."

"Fisk kept a ledger." Muldoon tapped the phone book once. "Fisk kept a ledger with names in it, and you took it off his desk before you called the office. You were seen."

"Seen by a man in a car with the lights off. Your witness, I assume."

"Answer the question."

"No."

He hit me again. This time lower, under the ribs, and the phone book's taped spine made a flat, ugly sound against me, like a palm slapped on a desk in a room where something bad had already been agreed to.

This one I felt all the way down. My breath went out of me and stayed out, and I had to wait for it to come back.

*Don't make a sound,* I told myself. *Don't give them the pleasure of it. Sound is a language and they only want to hear you speak it.*

I leaned my head against the wall. It was cool and damp and it felt like mercy, which was funny, because mercy wasn't in the room. Mercy was the kind of thing that lived in the stories they let the papers print.

"Harold Fisk," I said. "Who found him?"

Muldoon's cigar had gone out. He didn't relight it. His hand was steady on the desk, but the other one, the one that had held the phone book, it was doing something small and useless at the edge of his coat sleeve, a little tremor, the kind a man gets when he's holding his breath and has forgotten he's doing it.

"You had him for four months," he said. "You sat with him. You drank with him. You know where he put it."

"I know where he put it," I said, "and I know what's in it, and I know how the names in it would sound read aloud in a room with a dozen honest men in it. Your name's in it, Leo."

The bulb swung. My shadow went around the walls, looking for the door.

"Your name," I said, "and Brill's. And a councilman's. And a judge who owes a banker in Queens."

"You don't know what you're talking about."

"I don't have to. I read. It's what I do for a living, when I'm not getting hit with the phone book."

Brill sat forward. "Muldoon."

"What?"

"Get him again."

Muldoon picked up the phone book. He opened it halfway, settled his thumb on a page, and looked at me with the mild interest of a man choosing a tool from a toolbox.

*Here it comes,* I thought. *And here's the strange thing: I could smell the tobacco on him worse than ever now, sharp and oily and sweet at the back of my throat, and I couldn't tell if it was the smoke or the blood in my mouth. Both tasted the same. Both meant the same thing. This was the room where the city kept its dirt, and the dirt smelled like cheap tobacco, and now some of it was in my blood.*

"You want the ledger," I said. "You've got the wrong idea about what you want. You don't want it back because it's evidence. You want it back because it's a list."

"Shut up."

"You want it burned. Or drowned. Or buried somewhere with the rest of what this city buries." I looked at Brill. "You want it because somebody's holding a copy."

"That's enough."

"You've both been holding your breath since I mentioned Fisk's books." I spat red into the saucer. "I wasn't going to say it out loud. I wasn't going to hurt you. But you want a name in that ledger to stop breathing, and one of you has already decided it's going to be the other one."

Brill moved fast for a man with a hat. He crossed the room and put his hand flat on the table in front of my face, and his face had all the color gone out of it.

"Where," he said.

"Union Station. Locker three-eleven."

"And the key?"

"The key's in Fisk's pocket. Take it off the body."

"Muldoon, go get—"

"Wait." Muldoon said it quietly. He was still looking at me, and the cigar smoke was so thick between us now that I couldn't see his mouth at all. "Locker three-eleven," he said. "What's in it?"

"A book."

"What's the name on the book?"

"Fisk's. It's under his name. He was vain about it."

*The truth was a brown envelope in the night mail, postage paid, addressed to the city desk of the Gazette. It would arrive at six in the morning, and every name in it would arrive with it. If I was alive at six, the story would be too.*

Muldoon came over and took the phone book by the spine.

"Last chance, Dade."

"Hit me."

"Brill, hold his—"

"Hit me, Leo. It's a thick book. I could use the exercise."

He hit me.

*Let him,* I thought, as the red rope pulled tight through me again and the cheap tobacco turned the whole room sour. *Let him. Every blow buys me minutes, and minutes are all I have left.*

*Six in the morning. Four hours and change.*

*I just needed to hold out four more hours.*

### Blacktop Funeral

The freight yard had become a stadium without seats.

Floodlights hung from scaffolds of welded pipe, throwing hard white glare across the rain-slick asphalt. Spectators pressed against chain-link fences, their faces bluish in the glow of phone screens. Beyond them, graffiti-covered walls turned the old loading terminal into a tunnel that seemed to have no end.

Mara sat behind the wheel of the black coupe, engine idling low enough to make the whole frame tremble. Heat from the exhaust warmed her ankles. Through the open window came the smells she knew better than fear: hot rubber, scorched brake dust, gasoline, and the oily dirt trapped beneath old freight containers.

Tonight’s prize was ten thousand dollars.

That was enough to disappear her father’s debts and leave the city for good. At least, that was what the men at the bar had told her.

A red flare arced over the yard and burst against the night.

The field of cars surged forward.

Mara dumped the clutch. The rear tires bit, slipped, then caught. Her coupe snapped sideways for half a second before straightening, and she slammed through the first gear with a violence that buckled her stomach. The roar of engines rolled over the concrete walls and came back doubled.

She reached second gear.

The world narrowed to the strip of broken yellow line ahead.

On the right, the fence flashes past in silver blurs. On the left, the crowd becomes a single dark smear. Mara keeps her eyes on the road, on the rival car’s taillights swelling in her mirror, and counts the turns in her head. One long right. A curve around the cranes. Then the straightaway toward the loading ramp.

The smell of burning rubber thickened.

Smoke curled from the car ahead, dragging across the pavement.

Mara shifted into third.

She was gaining. The rival had left too much room on the first bend, and now his rear end stepped sideways before recovering. Mara turned into the curve, following the racing line, the tires pressing against the asphalt as the g-force tightened around her shoulders.

Then she pressed the brake.

Nothing happened.

The pedal moved, but the car did not slow.

For one confused instant, she thought the road was wet beneath her tires. She pumped the pedal. The brake light glowed red on the dashboard, but the pedal continued downward with a soft, horrible smoothness, as if the hydraulic line had been emptied into the night.

Her heart slammed against her ribs.

The rival car’s taillights slipped away in the mirror.

Mara looked down. The brake pedal rested almost against the floor.

No.

She lifted her foot, then pressed again. Still nothing.

The first turn was approaching at nearly a hundred miles an hour. She tried to lift off the gas, but the engine screamed as if she’d opened a valve. Around her, every engine screamed.

Then she saw it.

A thin mist beneath the hood. Not steam. Not condensation.

Brake fluid.

Someone had loosened the line while the cars were staged beneath the floodlights. Someone had known she would never check it once the race began. For one wild, detached moment, Mara pictured a gloved hand beneath the hood, a face hidden by shadow, the quiet click of a fitting being backed away from.

She tried the parking brake.

It barely dragged.

The concrete barrier appeared out of the darkness at the end of the straightaway, a gray wall reinforced with steel. Beyond it, the loading ramp dropped twenty feet to the service road.

Mara’s hands went dry.

“Come on,” she whispered.

The coupe refused to slow.

She wrenched the steering wheel left, away from the barrier, toward the empty row of shipping containers. Gravel sprayed beneath the tires. The crowd shouted. The engine note climbed, shrill and desperate.

There was no room.

The barrier filled the windshield.

Mara saw the individual bolts in the steel plate. She saw the cracked concrete reflected in the headlamps. She saw the faces behind the fence turn white.

She understood, with perfect clarity, that she was going to hit it.

In that last fraction of a second, the panic loosened its grip and became something colder. She released the wheel, folded her arms over her head, and turned her face away.

The coupe hit the barrier at a speed the concrete had never been designed to withstand.

The front end folded inward like paper. The engine drove into the passenger compartment. Glass exploded outward in a glittering storm. The car climbed the barrier, snapped through a stack of steel drums, and launched into the loading ramp.

For a moment it was almost flying.

Then it struck the road below.

The coupe broke apart in a shower of black metal and red sparks. The roof crumpled. One door tore free and cartwheeled into the darkness. The fuel tank ruptured with a dull, concussive bang, and a column of flame erupted from the wreck, bending backward in the wind.

The second explosion came a heartbeat later.

Windows along the freight terminal shattered. The crowd’s roar vanished beneath the thunder of burning fuel. Fire rolled over the hood and through the gutted cabin, snapping upward in orange sheets. Black smoke boiled into the sodium-lit sky.

Mara was still inside.

Her world had become fragments: a spiderweb of blood across the windshield, the taste of copper, the smell of gasoline and burned plastic, the immense white pressure of the crash still moving through her body. She could not tell if the crack in her ribs was broken or only deeply bruised.

Somewhere beyond the flames, people were running. Someone was screaming for an ambulance. Another voice shouted for everyone to stay back.

The fire ticked and snapped around the ruined car.

Mara tried to move her fingers.

They answered.

Beyond the wreck, the race engines had gone silent. For the first time all night, there was no sound except the wind moving through the freight yard and the flames consuming what was left of the car.

She had not crossed the finish line.

She had barely made it to the barrier.

The pedal moved, but the car did not slow.

For one confused instant, she thought the road was wet beneath her tires. She pumped the pedal. The brake light glowed red on the dashboard, but the pedal continued downward with a soft, horrible smoothness, as if the hydraulic line had been emptied into the night.

Her heart slammed against her ribs.

The rival car’s taillights slipped away in the mirror.

Mara looked down. The brake pedal rested almost against the floor.

No.

She lifted her foot, then pressed again. Still nothing.

The first turn was approaching at nearly a hundred miles an hour. She tried to lift off the gas, but the engine screamed as if she’d opened a valve. Around her, every engine screamed.

Then she saw it.

A thin mist beneath the hood. Not steam. Not condensation.

Brake fluid.

Someone had loosened the line while the cars were staged beneath the floodlights. Someone had known she would never check it once the race began. For one wild, detached moment, Mara pictured a gloved hand beneath the hood, a face hidden by shadow, the quiet click of a fitting being backed away from.

She tried the parking brake.

It barely dragged.

The concrete barrier appeared out of the darkness at the end of the straightaway, a gray wall reinforced with steel. Beyond it, the loading ramp dropped twenty feet to the service road.

Mara’s hands went dry.

“Come on,” she whispered.

The coupe refused to slow.

She wrenched the steering wheel left, away from the barrier, toward the empty row of shipping containers. Gravel sprayed beneath the tires. The crowd shouted. The engine note climbed, shrill and desperate.

There was no room.

The barrier filled the windshield.

Mara saw the individual bolts in the steel plate. She saw the cracked concrete reflected in the headlamps. She saw the faces behind the fence turn white.

She understood, with perfect clarity, that she was going to hit it.

In that last fraction of a second, the panic loosened its grip and became something colder. She released the wheel, folded her arms over her head, and turned her face away.

The coupe hit the barrier at a speed the concrete had never been designed to withstand.

The front end folded inward like paper. The engine drove into the passenger compartment. Glass exploded outward in a glittering storm. The car climbed the barrier, snapped through a stack of steel drums, and launched into the loading ramp.

For a moment it was almost flying.

Then it struck the road below.

The coupe broke apart in a shower of black metal and red sparks. The roof crumpled. One door tore free and cartwheeled into the darkness. The fuel tank ruptured with a dull, concussive bang, and a column of flame erupted from the wreck, bending backward in the wind.

The second explosion came a heartbeat later.

Windows along the freight terminal shattered. The crowd’s roar vanished beneath the thunder of burning fuel. Fire rolled over the hood and through the gutted cabin, snapping upward in orange sheets. Black smoke boiled into the sodium-lit sky.

Mara was still inside.

Her world had become fragments: a spiderweb of blood across the windshield, the taste of copper, the smell of gasoline and burned plastic, the immense white pressure of the crash still moving through her body. She could not tell if the crack in her ribs was broken or only deeply bruised.

Somewhere beyond the flames, people were running. Someone was screaming for an ambulance. Another voice shouted for everyone to stay back.

The fire ticked and snapped around the ruined car.

Mara tried to move her fingers.

They answered.

Beyond the wreck, the race engines had gone silent. For the first time all night, there was no sound except the wind moving through the freight yard and the flames consuming what was left of the car.

She had not crossed the finish line.

She had barely made it to the barrier.

**The Under-Stairs Closet**

The closet smelled of cedar and dust and the cold iron of old hangers.

Mara had been inside it for ninety seconds, maybe two minutes — long enough for her pulse to find the rhythm it would keep for the rest of the night. She had come in for the grey cardigan, the one with the embroidered deer, because the house had gone cold and she had decided, ten minutes and a half-glass of wine ago, that she was going to spend the evening on the couch with the phone propped on her knee and ignore the world.

Instead she was standing in the dark with her hand over her own mouth, listening.

He'd come through the back door. No break-in, no crash — the deadbolt had simply *turned*, the way it does when someone has a key, and she'd heard that small metallic argument from the kitchen and thought: *Dad's spare.* Then she had thought: *Dad's been dead for six years.*

The house breathed around her. Somewhere below, a floorboard took its weight and let it go with a soft, apologetic creak of old pine.

"Okay," said a voice in the hallway. "Okay, let's see."

It was a man's voice, unhurried, conversational — the tone of someone narrating a walkthrough for a client who'd wandered off. Mara heard the particular rubber-and-leather drag of a boot on her mother's tile. She heard the shotgun come off his shoulder, the faint *chk* of a barrel being seated against something.

"The Taylors keep it in the bedroom," he said, to no one. "That's what she said. That's what the little one said, anyway, before she stopped saying things."

A drawer slid open. Cutlery, clinking softly, being counted.

"House is cold. Thermostat's set low — sixty-two, maybe. That's deliberate, that's a *choice*, that's a person who's already decided to be somewhere else in her head when it happens." A pause. He seemed to like the sound of his own thinking. "Eleven years and nobody's ever put it past the knee. Eleven years and I've never once had to chase anybody down a hallway, have you? Not once."

He moved through the kitchen. The refrigerator door swung open, exhaled, and shut. Mara pressed her back into the coats and something in her pocket — a phone, her real phone, brought from the couch on instinct — pressed a hard rectangle into her thigh. She hadn't even been holding it. She'd just shoved it into her jeans, and now it lay against her leg like a hand.

She thought about the screen lighting up. She thought about the notification sound.

*Don't. Don't. Don't.*

The pantry light came on. She felt the change in the closet's darkness — a thin warm line appearing along the floor, under the door, and she watched it like a tide coming in.

"Two vehicles." He was in the garage doorway now; she could tell by how the sound flattened, came back sharper. "One's a Corolla. The other one's a truck with a ladder, so there's a roof of some kind. Angled. Not steep enough to climb, but it's *something.*"

Footsteps. He was coming back down the hall.

"The cardigan." He laughed, and it was such an ordinary laugh, a warm almost-affectionate sound, that it made her teeth ache. "Look at you, honey. You've come out to hide in a closet in your own house. That's *sweet.* That's a movie. That's not what happens."

The line of light under the door widened as his shadow crossed it. He was in the hallway. He was maybe fifteen feet away.

She stopped breathing. Not on purpose — her body simply stopped, the way a rabbit stops, and the silence she made was so total that she could hear the blood in her own ears, could hear the faint tick of her mother's kitchen clock two rooms away, which was absurd, which was impossible, and which was exactly the kind of thing the brain does when it has decided to die.

A phone rang.

Not hers. Hers was silent in her pocket; it had rung once, down the hall, and he had answered it — she had heard his voice change, go flat and professionally warm, heard him say *Mm. Mm-hm. No, I don't need a second. I need the house quiet* — and then he had said, after a pause, something she hadn't been able to hear, and then the ringing had stopped.

This was the phone on the side table. The sister. She'd called twice, and now her name was on the screen in the dark hallway, and Mara could not move, could not reach out from inside her own coat closet and tap the glass and say *run.*

"I'm not going to hurt you," he was saying, closer now. "I want to be clear about that, because people get this so wrong. They think this is a rage thing. It isn't a rage thing. Rage is *undignified.*"

He was directly on the other side of the door. She could hear his coat brush the frame. She could smell him — cold air, gun oil, and something sweet and chemical underneath, like sweet tea left to go bad on a porch.

"Nobody leaves the house tonight. That's not cruelty, that's *accounting.* There's a girl in Bexley who has a sister in Bexley, and if I leave one witness, then in four years there's a witness, and in four years there's a *court*, and in twenty years there's a woman on a podcast saying *I remember a man with kind eyes.*" The doorknob rattled, tested. "I don't have kind eyes. I have *patience.* But people with patience still need the paperwork to say what happened tonight."

He was quiet for a moment. Outside, a car passed on the street, its headlights swept the bedroom ceiling and went.

"You can come out," he said, almost gently. "I know you're in the house. That phone went to voicemail twice, sweetheart, and then it stopped ringing, so you've done something clever." A breath. "I *like* clever. I gave the little one credit for it too, for about ten seconds."

The doorknob turned.

And the door began, slowly, to creak open —

results.model_response:
# Deliverables

The Meridian kept rooms on the ninth floor with windows that sealed against weather, which was the only thing about the place he could approve of. Rusk had drawn the room for what it was: a degraded environment. The bed was too soft, the lighting too warm, the carpet a color that suggested the designer had been held at gunpoint. He had pushed the chair to the wall so no one could sit behind it, checked the sightlines from the window (a service alley, a dumpster corral, a fire escape twenty-two feet down that he had already decided was unusable because of the awning), and laid a hotel luggage mat across the desk so the barrel of the rifle would not touch wood.

The rifle was in a hard case on the bed. He unzipped it and set the case lid flat beside the lamp so the light raked across the bore of the barrel and the machining of the receiver. A chassis rifle, built by a shop in Millau that no longer existed under that name, in .338 Lapua Magnum. He had paid for it in cash and asked no questions about provenance. The invoice had come with a certificate from the engraver and a headspace report from the bench tech, and Rusk had framed the headspace report, because it was the only document in his life that had ever made him feel accurately described.

He drew the bolt back, locked it down with the safety, depressed the plunger, and pushed the pin tool through the crosshatch until the bolt carrier group came free in his hand with the low glassy sound of good steel on good steel. He set the BCG on the towel. He would clean the barrel last, so that solvent would not fog the glass and the light would stay good.

The television was on. It had been on since he arrived, because a room with a live screen is a room with ambient noise, and ambient noise is cover.

---

"—Kestrel Foundation reaches forty years as the foundation's chairman announces a further commitment to hospital construction in—"

He turned the volume up two notches.

Emmett Rourke came on screen at a lectern under a battery of press lights. Mid-fifties, silver at the temples, a good jacket cut badly, the tie a half-inch too wide, which told Rusk he dressed himself or had people who did not know what he was paid to know. Behind him, a rendering of the new wing: glass, gardens, a price tag in the shape of a children's hospital.

Rourke's hands were the interesting part. Small, well-kept, a wedding ring worn slightly above the knuckle because a jeweler had gotten the size wrong years ago and he had never had it resized. He spoke with his palms down on the lectern, pressing, which meant he was selling certainty. He had a way of lifting his chin half a second before the laugh line arrived, so that the smile looked like an afterthought delivered late.

Rusk noted this the way he noted everything: as data. *Chin precedes smile by 0.4–0.6 seconds. Gesture is manual, not habitual. Uses ring hand to adjust cuff when leaving a sentence unresolved.*

He did not find it interesting. He found it *sufficient*.

---

He laid out the cleaning kit in the order he liked: a bore brush in .338, three rows of patches, a patch holder, mineral spirits and a bottle of solvent, a nylon bore brush for the chamber and the crown in a brass jag, a couple of .007-inch feeler gauges for the extractor gap and the firing pin throw, a small bottle of gun oil, a brush, a microfiber cloth, and a pair of nitrile gloves he would not wear because gloves made his hands clumsy and clumsy was a luxury he could not bill.

He ran a patch through the chamber and stood it up in the breech, then a second, then a third, and each one came back with a faint grey signature that he examined against the light. Fouling was minimal. He had not fired this rifle in nine days.

The barrel he cleaned with the bore brush, breathing through his teeth to keep the pressure steady so the brush would track straight and not bow into the rifling. Fifty strokes. He counted. Then the brush went into the muzzle, and the muzzle crown met the brass jag, and he turned the jag gently, feeling for burrs at the crown and the leading edge of the lands with the pads of his fingers, which he had taught himself years ago in a garage behind a laundromat.

He drew the bolt and worked the extractor, checking the tension, checking the spring, checking the firing pin's concentricity through the crown with the reflective glass of a dental mirror he had bought in a pharmacy in Odesa.

The television held on a shot of children in the new wing. One of them had a bandage above her ear, and Rourke's PR team had found her because the bandage photographs well and the story writes itself.

"Forty years," the anchor said. "And the chairman credits his late father."

Rusk cleaned the bolt.

---

Here was the thing he wanted to be careful about, and he was careful about it, generally, in the same way one is careful about a man who works with hot material: not out of moral scruple but out of professional knowledge of what scorched skin smells like.

He did not think of what he did as killing. Killing implied a moment, a fear, a moral event, a man confronting the weight of an instant. There was no instant. There was a contract with terms and conditions, and inside those terms there were only obligations, and inside those obligations there were only tasks.

Reduce the target's continued presence. Do it without attribution. Do it without inconvenience to the beneficiary's business interests, per Addendum B. Do not exceed the scope of the engagement by harming persons not enumerated in Schedule 1, which was a list of six names, none of whom was the daughter on the screen.

He thought of a life as a quantity that could be debited. Not taken — *debited*. The ledger did not care how. The ledger only wanted the entry made, and the entry made cleanly, and the paperwork filed.

The client's requirement was discretion. Therefore the resolution must also be discreet. This was not cruelty. It was arithmetic. He was a man who took responsibility for the consequences of his own function, and the consequence of his function was that a person who did not know him existed would, in the coming hours, no longer exist, and that this fact would be established by a single line of unreasoned, unattributable bad luck. The world would metabolize it the way the world metabolized all such things: a scandal, a paragraph, a day of speculation, and then the next piece of news.

He had once been told, by an accountant in Zurich who handled the disbursements, that he had the least emotional range of any contractor on the roster. He had taken it as a compliment, and he had meant it as one. Emotion was a leak. Leaks were liabilities. He had watched two men on the roster burn out — one in Warsaw, one in the Gulf — and both had burned because they had started thinking of the work as *the work*, when it was in fact a fee for a service, and a service did not have a conscience, a service had a warranty.

---

He oiled the bolt carrier group lightly, worked the charging handle, seated the BCG back into the receiver and pushed the pin through the crosshatch with a small satisfying click that he felt more than heard. Then he laid the rifle on its side on the mat and checked the scope's rings for torque, the turret caps for a film of verdigris, and the chassis bolts with a torque driver set to the number in the builder's sheet.

The mag well held four .338 rounds in Winchester Magnum Hunt ammunition, hand-loaded by a man in Montana who had been a precision rifleman in another life and who had never met Rusk and would not remember his name. He seated a round in the chamber, closed the bolt, and pressed the bolt handle down with his thumb, feeling the extractor take it up with no grit, no hesitation.

He checked the headspace. Gauge in, go, no go, go. The round seated fully in the chamber.

He worked the bolt again, ejected the round, set it back in the magazine, and oriented the rifle to the right, muzzle down, out of habit, in a hotel room with a bedspread that cost more per night than some men earned in a month.

---

On screen, Rourke finished his remarks and stepped back from the lectern. For a moment he stood in the flat, sourceless light of the press area, and he looked tired, and Rusk noted that too — the fatigue at the corners of the mouth, the way the shoulders dropped a half-inch once the audience's attention moved. A man in his fifties who had spent forty years being photographed holding other people's optimism.

The reporter stepped in with a question about the hospital wing's naming.

"Thank you," Rourke said. "We would like to leave the naming to the children."

He had found the phrase himself, the way a man does when he has been advised to find a phrase himself. Chin up, half a second early.

Rusk reached over and turned the volume down one notch. He did not feel anything about the man's hands, or the ring worn high on the finger, or the joke about the children; he filed all of it, because filing was what his mind did with information, and because in eleven hours the target would step out onto a terrace at a specific time of the afternoon, when the light came through the corten steel screens at a particular angle and the press would be elsewhere, and the contract would be discharged, and the invoice would be paid, and the ledger would balance to zero, and there would be nothing left of the man with the good jacket and the badly cut tie except an absence that the world's own machinery would convert, without comment, into the next day's weather.

Then, for the first time in four years, he found that he could not quite remember where he had put the .007-inch feeler gauges.

He looked at the mat. He looked at the mat for a while.

Then he found them, in the tray, where he had put them, exactly where he had put them.

He packed the rifle in its case, zipping it to the second tab because the third worried him. He checked the room once more: the mat, the solvent, the patches folded flat, the bolt tool back in its slot in the case, the towels rolled and wet with spirits hung over the shower rail to dry by morning. He cranked the air conditioning down so the room would be cold and the optics would not fog when the case came open, and he took the key card off the door and put it in the breast pocket of his jacket, where a man keeps a thing he wants to lose.

In the elevator he thought about the headspace report framed in a flat in Trieste: *this rifle, as configured, will do what it is asked to do.*

He had liked that sentence better than most of the things men had ever said in his presence. Because it was true. Because it made no claim beyond the scope of the instrument, and asked for nothing in return.

The lobby smelled of lilies and machine oil. He pushed through the revolving door into the heat of the street and turned north, toward the parking structure, at a walking pace of a man with nowhere in particular to be for eleven more hours.

The afternoon was long and even and entirely his.

Emmett Rourke came on screen at a lectern under a battery of press lights. Mid-fifties, silver at the temples, a good jacket cut badly, the tie a half-inch too wide, which told Rusk he dressed himself or had people who did not know what he was paid to know. Behind him, a rendering of the new wing: glass, gardens, a price tag in the shape of a children's hospital.

Rourke's hands were the interesting part. Small, well-kept, a wedding ring worn slightly above the knuckle because a jeweler had gotten the size wrong years ago and he had never had it resized. He spoke with his palms down on the lectern, pressing, which meant he was selling certainty. He had a way of lifting his chin half a second before the laugh line arrived, so that the smile looked like an afterthought delivered late.

Rusk noted this the way he noted everything: as data. Chin precedes smile by 0.4–0.6 seconds. Gesture is manual, not habitual. Uses ring hand to adjust cuff when leaving a sentence unresolved.

He did not find it interesting. He found it sufficient.

He laid out the cleaning kit in the order he liked: a bore brush in .338, three rows of patches, a patch holder, mineral spirits and a bottle of solvent, a nylon bore brush for the chamber and the crown in a brass jag, a couple of .007-inch feeler gauges for the extractor gap and the firing pin throw, a small bottle of gun oil, a brush, a microfiber cloth, and a pair of nitrile gloves he would not wear because gloves made his hands clumsy and clumsy was a luxury he could not bill.

He ran a patch through the chamber and stood it up in the breech, then a second, then a third, and each one came back with a faint grey signature that he examined against the light. Fouling was minimal. He had not fired this rifle in nine days.

The barrel he cleaned with the bore brush, breathing through his teeth to keep the pressure steady so the brush would track straight and not bow into the rifling. Fifty strokes. He counted. Then the brush went into the muzzle, and the muzzle crown met the brass jag, and he turned the jag gently, feeling for burrs at the crown and the leading edge of the lands with the pads of his fingers, which he had taught himself years ago in a garage behind a laundromat.

He drew the bolt and worked the extractor, checking the tension, checking the spring, checking the firing pin's concentricity through the crown with the reflective glass of a dental mirror he had bought in a pharmacy in Odesa.

The television held on a shot of children in the new wing. One of them had a bandage above her ear, and Rourke's PR team had found her because the bandage photographs well and the story writes itself.

"Forty years," the anchor said. "And the chairman credits his late father."

Rusk cleaned the bolt.

Here was the thing he wanted to be careful about, and he was careful about it, generally, in the same way one is careful about a man who works with hot material: not out of moral scruple but out of professional knowledge of what scorched skin smells like.

He did not think of what he did as killing. Killing implied a moment, a fear, a moral event, a man confronting the weight of an instant. There was no instant. There was a contract with terms and conditions, and inside those terms there were only obligations, and inside those obligations there were only tasks.

Reduce the target's continued presence. Do it without attribution. Do it without inconvenience to the beneficiary's business interests, per Addendum B. Do not exceed the scope of the engagement by harming persons not enumerated in Schedule 1, which was a list of six names, none of whom was the daughter on the screen.

He thought of a life as a quantity that could be debited. Not taken — debited. The ledger did not care how. The ledger only wanted the entry made, and the entry made cleanly, and the paperwork filed.

The client's requirement was discretion. Therefore the resolution must also be discreet. This was not cruelty. It was arithmetic. He was a man who took responsibility for the consequences of his own function, and the consequence of his function was that a person who did not know him existed would, in the coming hours, no longer exist, and that this fact would be established by a single line of unreasoned, unattributable bad luck. The world would metabolize it the way the world metabolized all such things: a scandal, a paragraph, a day of speculation, and then the next piece of news.

He had once been told, by an accountant in Zurich who handled the disbursements, that he had the least emotional range of any contractor on the roster. He had taken it as a compliment, and he had meant it as one. Emotion was a leak. Leaks were liabilities. He had watched two men on the roster burn out — one in Warsaw, one in the Gulf — and both had burned because they had started thinking of the work as the work, when it was in fact a fee for a service, and a service did not have a conscience, a service had a warranty.

He oiled the bolt carrier group lightly, worked the charging handle, seated the BCG back into the receiver and pushed the pin through the crosshatch with a small satisfying click that he felt more than heard. Then he laid the rifle on its side on the mat and checked the scope's rings for torque, the turret caps for a film of verdigris, and the chassis bolts with a torque driver set to the number in the builder's sheet.

The mag well held four .338 rounds in Winchester Magnum Hunt ammunition, hand-loaded by a man in Montana who had been a precision rifleman in another life and who had never met Rusk and would not remember his name. He seated a round in the chamber, closed the bolt, and pressed the bolt handle down with his thumb, feeling the extractor take it up with no grit, no hesitation.

He checked the headspace. Gauge in, go, no go, go. The round seated fully in the chamber.

He worked the bolt again, ejected the round, set it back in the magazine, and oriented the rifle to the right, muzzle down, out of habit, in a hotel room with a bedspread that cost more per night than some men earned in a month.

On screen, Rourke finished his remarks and stepped back from the lectern. For a moment he stood in the flat, sourceless light of the press area, and he looked tired, and Rusk noted that too — the fatigue at the corners of the mouth, the way the shoulders dropped a half-inch once the audience's attention moved. A man in his fifties who had spent forty years being photographed holding other people's optimism.

The reporter stepped in with a question about the hospital wing's naming.

"Thank you," Rourke said. "We would like to leave the naming to the children."

He had found the phrase himself, the way a man does when he has been advised to find a phrase himself. Chin up, half a second early.

Rusk reached over and turned the volume down one notch. He did not feel anything about the man's hands, or the ring worn high on the finger, or the joke about the children; he filed all of it, because filing was what his mind did with information, and because in eleven hours the target would step out onto a terrace at a specific time of the afternoon, when the light came through the corten steel screens at a particular angle and the press would be elsewhere, and the contract would be discharged, and the invoice would be paid, and the ledger would balance to zero, and there would be nothing left of the man with the good jacket and the badly cut tie except an absence that the world's own machinery would convert, without comment, into the next day's weather.

Then, for the first time in four years, he found that he could not quite remember where he had put the .007-inch feeler gauges.

He looked at the mat. He looked at the mat for a while.

Then he found them, in the tray, where he had put them, exactly where he had put them.

He packed the rifle in its case, zipping it to the second tab because the third worried him. He checked the room once more: the mat, the solvent, the patches folded flat, the bolt tool back in its slot in the case, the towels rolled and wet with spirits hung over the shower rail to dry by morning. He cranked the air conditioning down so the room would be cold and the optics would not fog when the case came open, and he took the key card off the door and put it in the breast pocket of his jacket, where a man keeps a thing he wants to lose.

In the elevator he thought about the headspace report framed in a flat in Trieste: this rifle, as configured, will do what it is asked to do.

He had liked that sentence better than most of the things men had ever said in his presence. Because it was true. Because it made no claim beyond the scope of the instrument, and asked for nothing in return.

The lobby smelled of lilies and machine oil. He pushed through the revolving door into the heat of the street and turned north, toward the parking structure, at a walking pace of a man with nowhere in particular to be for eleven more hours.

The afternoon was long and even and entirely his.

The first bite arrived as a point of heat.

Jonas felt it on the back of his wrist—a single needle-prick of pain so delicate he almost dismissed it as an insect brushing against him. Then came the sound.

A rapid, dry clicking.

Mandibles struck skin with tiny, precise bites, the noise almost like someone tapping a fingernail against glass. Another insect joined, then another. The clicking multiplied until it became a constant chatter beneath him, underscored by the faint rasp of bodies scraping over one another.

He shoved his sleeve down and scrambled backward. The swarm followed.

They were black, glossy, larger than ordinary ants, each one clicking its sickle-shaped mandibles as it moved. They had poured through the gap beneath the door in a living tide, covering the floor in a churning carpet. When Jonas kicked at them, his shoe merely pressed them deeper into the pile.

The first true pain came from his ankle.

Dozens of insects bit at once. Each bite remained distinct: a hot point, then another, then another, until his skin felt stitched together from a hundred tiny punctures. The pain was strangely precise. He could feel where each mouth had closed, where legs scraped, where the swarm divided around the untouched patches of his trousers.

He pulled at his pant leg. The fabric tore, revealing skin stippled red beneath the insects. They clustered over the warm areas first, their mandibles making a wet, rhythmic clatter.

“No—No, get off—”

His voice was swallowed by the enormous sound of the swarm: thousands of tiny jaws working in unison. It rose and fell like static, punctuated by sharp little cracks whenever a head or an insect’s own shell was seized. Under the clicking was a softer sound, a faint wetness that made his stomach turn.

Jonas threw himself against the door. It would not open. He beat against it with both fists, sending more insects scattering, then felt them crawl up his sleeves.

The bites reached his neck.

There, the sensation was worse than pain. Each mandible pinched and tore with mechanical patience. Hundreds of tiny mouths tested the same patch of skin, their bites overlapping until the heat of them became one spreading throb. He could feel them moving beneath the surface—small, quick bulges traveling under his flesh as they burrowed toward warmth.

He clawed at his collar. His fingers came away smeared with blood, diluted by the crush of insect bodies. The swarm climbed higher, flowing beneath his shirt, and suddenly his chest became a field of separate agonies. Every breath pulled at the wounds. Every heartbeat seemed to push the insects deeper.

“Why won’t you die?” he gasped.

The answer was everywhere: mandibles clicking, shells cracking, bodies rustling like dry leaves in a storm.

At first, he could still distinguish the bites individually. One at his shoulder. A dozen along his ribs. A tight ring of them closing around the torn skin of his forearm. But as the swarm consumed more of him, the individual sensations began to merge. Pain became a single vast heat, then a deep, shuddering pressure, as though his body were being held beneath an enormous weight.

His knees buckled. He slid down the door, crushing insects beneath him. The ones beneath his legs did not pause. Their mandibles clicked against his trousers, then his skin, then the soft tissue beneath.

He tried to scream. The sound came out broken, almost a laugh, because the pain had passed beyond anything sharp enough to name. His vision clouded at the edges. The clicking filled his skull. It was the last clear sound he could separate from the roaring in his own blood.

Jonas sank lower.

The swarm rose with him.

And beneath the frantic, wet chorus of mandibles, the only thing he could no longer feel was where the insects ended and his body began.

He saw the opening and chose it.

The opponent’s blade came in low, bright with reflected torchlight, and instead of turning aside, he stepped into it. For one suspended instant he felt nothing but the faint tug of fabric and the terrible softness of the point pressing through.

Then the blade entered.

The sensation was less like pain than like being opened from within—a sudden, shocking cold that spread beneath his ribs before heat followed. His body registered the wound a heartbeat late. He tasted blood, though whether from a cut lip or somewhere deeper he could not tell. His legs became unreliable, his breath short and metallic, but he kept his eyes fixed on the man before him.

The opponent’s expression changed from triumph to confusion.

That was the moment he had needed.

He lunged, driving his shoulder into the other man’s chest and forcing them both sideways. His hand found the hilt of his own sword. He could no longer feel his fingers clearly, so he wrapped them around it and hauled backward, using the last stubborn reserve of strength in his arm. The blade rose between them, awkward and trembling.

“Close enough,” he rasped.

He struck upward with everything he had left—not a clean attack, not a skilled one, but a final, desperate thrust powered by collapsing legs and a body too angry to surrender. He felt the sword meet resistance, then slide through it.

The opponent staggered. His grip loosened. Blood spread across the front of his coat, and his eyes widened as if the wound had only now become real.

The wounded man tried to follow him down, but his strength failed. His knees struck the ground, and the sword slipped from his fingers. The cold inside him was spreading now, swallowing the heat, turning every breath into a struggle.

Still, he lifted his head. His opponent stood over him, swaying, one hand pressed uselessly to the wound.

“Good,” he whispered. Then the light narrowed, the voices of the crowd fading into a distant roar, and he felt the last of his warmth slip away beneath the cold metal still lodged in his body.

**INVENTORY**

The smell got her first.

She had been in the dark for maybe ninety seconds, working the handle of the flashlight, when the air came up around her like something surfacing — chlorine and old rain and beneath that, a sweetness that clogged the back of her throat. Not the sweetness of blood, though she'd smelled blood, summer of ninth grade, the slicer at the Kessler house. This was sweeter. Sugar left too long in a warm room, going to wine, going to vinegar, going to something else entirely.

She shone the light on the stairs.

Twelve steps down. She counted them going down. She would count them again going up, she decided, because counting was the trick she'd learned at fifteen, at sixteen, when counting was the only thing that kept her hands from shaking. Twelve steps. A landing. Thirteen.

The flashlight beam found the landing and she kept it moving, because what she wanted more than anything in the world was to see, and what she wanted more than seeing was to be wrong.

Basement. Concrete. Water heater, caged. Shelving that had once held industrial cleaners, the labels long gone, ghost rings in the dust. And along the far wall, where the shelves ended and the room opened up into what must have been a furnace room, a row of shapes under white sheets.

She thought: sheets. She thought: hospital.

She thought, with a clarity that felt like a crack in glass: *sheets are what they put over the ones who are dead.*

The nearest one sat up.

Not moved — *sat up*, torso hinging forward, head lolling, one arm sliding off the cot and swinging down with the loose pendulum of a thing with no muscle left in it. It had been propped against the wall, and the sheet had fallen, and there was nothing inside the sheet but a shape that had been a shape and was now mostly a suggestion.

It collapsed when she screamed, which was not a scream exactly. It was more the sound a lung makes.

She didn't run. Later she would wonder about that. Later she would understand that running was a thing her body could do without her permission and she had simply overridden it, pinned her feet to the concrete, held the light steady — held the light *steady* — like her mother holding a camera steady at the recital, like you can make the picture hold still if you just refuse to let the frame shake.

That was the trick. Refusing.

*Catalog.* That was the trick, actually. That was the trick and it had always been the trick.

She moved down the row.

The one on the cot had been dead a long time. Long enough that the skin had gone the color of old sealing wax, long enough that the flesh had shriveled down the bones of the forearms and shins until she looked like someone who had been carved out of a dry tree and then left in a sunny window. The teeth were there, all of them, dry and yellow, and the tongue was a small black leather thing curled against the palate, and when the flashlight crossed it, the light came back off it in a dull shine, and she thought about the smell of a penny held under a tongue, the smell of her father's pennies, and her stomach turned over and she kept going.

There was a tube in her throat, wax-sealed, and the skin of her face and hands had been lacquered in something amber and glassy, preserved, and the eyes — the eyes were open and the eyes were dry and the eyes looked like they'd been polished. The next was water. Wren knew what water did. There was a body in a galvanized trough, and the water had gone to a thick, scummy green-black, and the body had swollen up like a fairsack of something fermenting, the skin gone from purple to black at the joints, and the smell of it came off the water in a slow bubble, an actual bubble, *plop*, and the surface lifted and settled. Fourteen was the one that broke her.

Fourteen was on a table, and fourteen had been opened, and then closed again, and the closure was worse than the opening. The house had belonged to a physician. Of course it had. Of course it had.

She got to seventeen and stopped counting because she couldn't make the numbers be bodies anymore, could only make them positions, and there were more than seventeen, there were more, the sheets went back into the dark where the light wouldn't reach, and she could hear the sound of the storm in the pipes and something under the storm, something else, a sound like a radio being turned up in another room.

She could have run. She could have gone up the thirteen steps and out the door and into the rain and all the way to the road, and she thought about it the way you think about a car crash you've already seen: fully, in detail, with the metal crumpling.

She walked to the ledger.

It was her handwriting. It was her handwriting in the last column, in the space where a date should go, and it said *seventeen*, and beneath it, in her own looping cursive, a note she had never written:

*He likes it when you scream. He doesn't like it when you beg. Try something else.*

The lamp hummed. The radio came up.

Behind her, one of the sheets crawled off its cot, dragged itself upright by the forearm, and began to laugh in a wet, clicking, phlegmy way, like water going down a drain with something in it.

Wren Hollis set down the flashlight, squared her shoulders, and turned around.

*Try something else,* said the ledger.

"I counted. There were seventeen."

— began, patiently, to smile.

## The Last Fifteen Seconds

The interlock had been green for six hours. Kova had run it twice, watched the numbers, and signed the log with the scratched-out version of her own name where the counterfeiter's signature wouldn't read.

It was the pressure differential that betrayed her. Thirty-one kilopascals, and climbing, and the gauge on the outer hatch readout ticking upward instead of downward, and the sound of it — that soft, patient hiss of atmosphere deciding to leave.

She had four seconds to understand, and she used three of them to look at the numbers.

Forty-one. Fifty. Fifty-eight kilopascals of nothing pressing in from outside, and the airlock was a lung filling with a vacuum, and the gauge said something that gauges should never say.

Sixty.

The emergency seal on her hardsuit was at her left hip, a torus of grey rubber that had held on the last six egresses without complaint. When the chamber pressure dropped below about forty, the seal didn't rupture so much as *unmake* — the rubber relaxed, went slack, and the hiss became a whisper became a silence that settled into her helmet like snow.

The air left her suit. All of it, at once, and the silence.

She expected cold. Everyone expects cold — the whole vocabulary of space is a refrigeration of the imagination, of tin cans and snow and the slow black patience of heat escaping into the dark. But vacuum is an excellent insulator. Nothing touches you. The air doesn't conduct heat away; it *carries* nothing away. She should have felt nothing at all.

She felt a warmth instead.

It came from her eyes.

---

Here is the thing about blood in vacuum: it does not freeze. It does not even chill. Blood boils.

At thirty-seven degrees Celsius, water boils when the air around it can no longer push back. On Earth, the atmosphere presses on you with roughly a hundred kilo of pressure per square centimeter, and that pressure is what holds your blood liquid inside you. Take it away and the water in your blood has nothing holding it down. It begins, at the eye and the mouth and the wet folds of the skin, to flash into vapor.

Her tears went first. She felt them leave her face — not as tears but as a *release*, a sudden lifting at the corners of her eyelids, as though someone had pressed two wet thumbs to her eyes and drawn them away. And then the vapor of them, driven off into nothing by the last scrape of atmosphere, expanded outward and froze. Instantly. A wisp of ice-crystal smoke blooming in front of her visor and curling away on no wind at all.

On her face it came down as frost.

It was quick, and thorough, and it did not feel like weather. It felt like being *watched over*. A fine white rime climbed her cheekbones, gathered on her eyelashes, and then began to close over her eyes — layer on layer, silting upward from the lower lids, sealing the world shut in a pale and glittering silt. She could still see, but only through ice: her vision went the milky blue-white of a cataract, then narrowed to a shrinking bright rectangle, and she understood with a strange, clinical calm that she was watching the world through the freezer door of her own skull.

She tried to blink. The lids were welded. When she tried again, the skin of her forehead split along a line of frost and it hurt — the first real pain, a bright clean line of it, and then nothing.

---

The blood was doing its own work by now.

She could not see it, but she could feel it: the slow, wrong pressure of fluid coming out of solution inside her veins. Nitrogen dissolved in her blood for thirty years now had nowhere to stay, and it left — popping out of the plasma in a fine fizzy rash, crawling under her skin like something alive looking for a hole to get out. The vessels themselves swelled, engorged with blood that had begun to carry bubbles instead of oxygen, and her skin rose into a taut, mottled black-purple, the veins standing out in a branching blue-black network, a leafless tree drawn on itself.

She had read about this. Ebullism. In the old animal tests, four bears, exposed and alive, bodies doubled in size, skin turned the color of a bruise. One of them survived six minutes and came back, and would not be handled afterward. The bears went rigid. The bears stiffened into a shape like a fetal curl, the spine arching as the swelling pushed everything inward and out at the same time.

She started to arch too. Her spine lifted inside the suit, a slow involuntary curl, and the hiss of her own escaping blood was the last sound she made — a small wet crackle inside her own helmet, the sound of soda fizzing in reverse, of something coming apart in miniature.

She had perhaps fifteen seconds of clear mind left. She used them on the gauge, on the numbers, on nothing at all.

*Thirty seconds of usable oxygen in the blood. Twelve percent, then eight. The little red bar falling.*

And then, faster than she could argue with it, the red bar hit zero.

The dark came up from the floor of her vision and closed over everything else, and with it came that particular sweetness she had smelled once before in a hospital corridor — acetone, nail-polish remover, the smell of a body burning down its own sugar.

Her heart, confused now by a blood that had turned to foam, began to hammer out of rhythm. It beat and stumbled and beat and stumbled, and then it beat very fast for a while, and then, somewhere around the fourth minute, it stopped being a thing she could hear.

---

The cold arrived last, and it arrived from the inside.

Not the cold of the void, which had never touched her. The cold of her own water leaving her — four liters of it, flash-boiled off her eyes and mouth and lungs and the wet seams of her skin, each gram taking five hundred and thirty calories with it. She was not cooled by space. She was cooled by *leaving*. She was a kettle that had forgotten to boil and was boiling anyway, forever, drinking itself dry.

And the frost that had started on her eyes went on climbing. It closed over her lips. It bridged her nostrils. It sealed them shut, and the ice-crystal smoke that had been drifting off her face thickened into a halo, a white aureole around her helmet, drifting away on the last thread of atmosphere a dying suit could muster.

She did not know that her eyes had become two small grey moons under their lids. She did not know that the lids had gone the color of old wax and the lashes were lost in the crystalline growth, or that the frost on her cornea had built itself into a lens, a curved and terrible lens, so that if you had come along on a later EVA and looked at the frost-encrusted hull of her hardsuit you might have seen, in the black mirror of her visor, two points of grey-white light where her eyes had been.

Only that it was quiet, and the medal on her chest had gone white with frost, and that her hands, curled in front of her, were the size and shape of a child's.

---

**Epilogue (the part nobody writes down):**

Her body drifted for eleven days before the recovery crew brought it in through the same hatch that had killed her.

The suit was a sealed system with a corpse inside, and it had cooked itself in the most literal sense: six kilowatts of residual metabolic heat and a vacuum that wouldn't let it go, until the suit reached equilibrium. Inside, her tissues were desiccated and contracted, the body curled into the fetal posture of ebullism, skin black and leathery and studded with the crystalline remains of its own evaporated fluids. Diagnostics called the condition *disseminated intravascular coagulation with cutaneous anoxia* and the rest of the report used the phrase *exposure-related hypothermic failure*, which was not true, and everyone knew it, and nobody in the room wanted to be the one to say so.

What had killed her was not the cold. It was that the cold had nowhere to go.

The frost on her eyes was the last thing to go. Long after the body had shrunk and darkened and settled into its long curl, the ice remained — a delicate white mask, finer than any frost the station's own cooling loop could make, held in place by capillary adhesion to a pair of closed eyelids that would never open again.

They kept it for three weeks before the medical examiner asked them to remove it, because the moisturizing vapor inside the helmet had nowhere to go either, and so the frost kept growing, thin and glittering, lapping up over the cheeks, furring the collar, until the whole front of the suit looked, in the end, like something that had been left out in a hard winter.

Then they cut it away, and it sublimed in the examination room's ordinary air in about forty minutes, and left behind two smooth dark hollows and a set of teeth, and a smell like a cellar after a long time.

The investigation took four months. It found a worn seal ring, a fatigue crack, and a failure in the interlock verification logic that had been logged and dismissed eleven times in the preceding two years. Her name was Kova. The log entry she'd made six hours before was still there in the margin, in her own careful hand, the scratched-out signature where the counterfeiter's wouldn't read — evidence, the board wrote, *of a person who was still working when she died.*
