**“NIGHT SHIFT”**

Vanna pressed the stiff brush against the floor, working through the dark stain inch by inch.

“Hold it steady,” she said.

Her partner, Sal, leaned over with a bucket of murky water. “I am holding it steady. You’re the one scrubbing like you’ve got a personal vendetta.”

“The blood started clean.”

“The blood didn’t start clean. The floor started clean. Blood is always a mess.”

Vanna glanced toward the motionless figure beneath the plastic sheet. “That’s sweet of you to blame the victim.”

Sal repositioned the bucket. “I blame everyone equally. It keeps things simple.”

The brush lifted another dark smear. Vanna grimaced.

“Remember the nightclub?” she asked. “After the card game went wrong?”

Sal sighed. “How could I forget? There was blood in the speaker stands, blood under the blackjack table, and somebody left a shoeprint across the mezzanine.”

“The shoeprint was the worst part.”

“The shoeprint was at least honest. It didn’t pretend to be mysterious.”

“And there was that perfume.jasmine, maybe? Mixed with whiskey and floor wax.”

Sal’s expression worsened. “Don’t remind me. I found a tooth in the drain.”

Vanna’s brush stopped. “A tooth?”

“Two, actually. The dentist—our dentist, I mean—he thought they came from a fish.”

“Sal.”

“I’m just saying. That was disgusting. This one’s nearly manageable.”

Vanna resumed scrubbing. “Nearly?”

“Compared with the hospital, maybe.”

Sal lowered his voice. “Which hospital?”

“The one after the shipment got lost.”

Vanna leaned the brush against the bucket. “You mean the maternity ward.”

“There was a delivery cart in the elevator,” Sal said. “Fresh linens, diapers, flowers. Then somebody realized the shipment wasn’t medicine. We had to clean the nursery, the loading dock, and the priest’s little changing room.”

Vanna stared at him. “The priest’s changing room?”

“The priest had nothing to do with it.”

“And yet.”

Sal shrugged. “He was the one who called us. Kept saying, ‘Bless this child and whoever handles the paperwork.’”

Vanna snorted, then caught herself as the sheet rustled. She lowered her voice. “All right, all right. That’s worse than the nightclub. But my worst was the restaurant.”

“The Italian place?”

“The Italian place. Three days after the family dinner.”

Sal’s face puckered. “The pasta was in the drains.”

“And the wine was on the ceiling.”

“You told me that was ketchup.”

“That was the second floor. The ceiling was marinara.”

Sal looked physically ill. “Why would anyone eat over a table that close to the ceiling?”

“They didn’t eat over it. They ate beside it. The sauce came down when the floor started collapsing.”

“So naturally they ate dessert too.”

Vanna smiled despite herself. “Chocolate cake. The man kept apologizing for the mess, even though he was holding the knife.”

Sal rubbed his temples. “That’s the part I hate. They’re always polite afterward. ‘I’m so sorry, I wasn’t expecting this to happen.’ As if blood is a spill they’re offering to replace.”

“Speaking of replacements,” Vanna said, “you’ll never guess who paid for this job.”

Sal looked at the sheet-covered body. “Our mutual friend?”

“Our mutual friend’s accountant.”

“Even worse.”

“He said the client wanted discretion, premium service, and no unnecessary questions.”

Sal picked up another brush. “And how did our mutual friend’s accountant respond when you told him we don’t work for the mob?”

Vanna scrubbed harder. “He said, ‘Of course not. This is for a private security company.’”

Sal nodded solemnly. “Private security company. Very modern.”

“And the invoice?”

“What was it?”

Vanna pointed toward the bucket. “Cleaning supplies, biohazard disposal, and ‘specialized stain treatment.’”

“Professional wording for ‘I’d rather not know.’”

“Exactly.”

They worked in silence for a moment, the brush scraping across the floor.

“You know what the truly disgusting part is?” Vanna said.

“The body?”

“The body is expected. The body is merchandise. It’s the cleaning afterward. People act like a crime scene is a spill of red wine. ‘Can you get that out? It’s staining the finish.’”

Sal looked around the room. “At least this place had good tile.”

“Terrible tile.”

“Good for traction.”

“It’s going to look spotless when we’re done.”

“It’ll look spotless until they move the furniture back and find the stain underneath.”

Vanna leaned closer to the floor, examining a pale shadow near the baseboard. “Then we go over it again.”

Sal sighed and reached for the detergent. “Anything else you want to confess before we start pretending this room never happened?”

She raised the brush. “The morgue.”

Sal stopped.

Vanna’s expression was flat and exhausted. “The one in the basement. The one nobody knows about.”

Sal stared at her for a long moment, then started scrubbing again.

“Vanna.”

“I know.”

“Don’t.”

“You first.”

Sal pointed at the stain. “After you.”

The brush moved back and forth.

Somewhere beyond the room, a phone rang.

Neither of them answered.

# Underfoot

The first thing you understand is that you are not being hit.

You had imagined impact — a single blow, a shoulder of some massive animal, an ending. What actually happens is worse and slower. You are *absorbed*. The herd arrives as a sound first, that dry rolling thunder underneath the wind, and then as a smell: sweat, dung, dust, and something animal and panicked underneath it, like the smell of a barn in summer.

Then the ground changes. Grass becomes a churn of something soft and slick that comes up your trousers, and the churn finds your feet, and the feet stop belonging to you. You are lifted. Not thrown — lifted, like something the current has decided to hold. There is a moment, absurd and calm, where you are above the herd, seesawed up on a shoulder, and you can see the backs stretching away downhill in every direction, a landscape of moving haunches and rolling eyes, and then you go under.

## The Sound and the Silence

You go deaf. Not gradually — the roar folds over itself and flattens into a single enormous pressure, and somewhere in that you lose the ability to hear your own heartbeat. It goes on. Later there will be silence, and it will feel like a physical thing, like a hand laid gently on the back of your neck.

## The Air

Air is the thing you want most and the thing you get least.

Breathing under there is a negotiation. You get a mouthful, and it is already warm and full of grit — the smell of churned grass, of sweat, of the animal's fear, which is a scent like nothing you have a name for. You inhale and your lungs receive something that is not air but dust with a little air mixed in, a soup of it. So you breathe through your mouth, and the dust dries your tongue, and you feel your throat closing in slow protest, and you begin to count your breaths because counting is the only thing you have that is still yours.

The weight above you is not one animal. That is the horror of it. It is a *press*, countless hooves and bodies and heads all moving the same direction with the same terrible agreement, and your body is a few stones in a river of it. Every time the herd surges, the available space in your chest shrinks. You get a half-inch of expansion and no more. Your ribs are being asked to do something they were never built to do.

Then your body makes you breathe in anyway, and the ribs give.

It isn't a clean break. You never thought that, exactly, but you had imagined a crack, a snap, a single definitive *no*. What you feel is a shifting, a settling, a series of small dissatisfactions inside your own chest, like knuckles cracking deep in a fist. And then the edges of the broken ribs stop being where they were, and they begin to move against each other with every press of the herd above you. Grating. Grinding. Bone on bone, dragged past one another by the slow patient milling of hooves, and each motion sends off a thin bright wire of pain that you cannot even scream because there is no air for screaming.

## The Points

The hooves are not the worst of it. The hooves are fast and blunt and mostly miss.

The worst of it is the ground. Sixty years of animals have broken this field into a churn of clay and broken turf and sharp things — stones, splinters of bone, the chipped edges of a shoe, a discarded hoe blade, the snapped-off tip of a fence post that has been ground into a fine black cobble and come up through everything like shrapnel. The herd keeps working the ground down and down, and all of it is turning, and all of it is rising.

Those points come up through the paste and find you. That is all. There is no malice in it. A point finds the soft place under your ribs and leans there, and your body is lifted and the point is not, and the point slides along the underside of you opening a seam, and the ribs already broken are now broken *better*, and you feel your own interior rearrange.

You would scream if you could. What comes out is more air than sound, a thin squeak pushed through a throat that has nothing left in it.

## The Minute That Is Not A Minute

You lose time. You know this afterward from the light, which does not change at all while you are under there — the sky stays the same pale gray it was — and yet it cannot have been less than four minutes, and it was forty.

You think about your mother. You think about a stupid thing you argued about that morning. You think, absurdly, about the pattern on the wallpaper in the room you grew up in, and how you never once looked at it, and how now you cannot stop, and now there is nothing to look at, just pressure and grey light and the taste of dust.

You think about how animals do not step on things. They step *around* things, they curve, they adjust — a herd moves like water because every animal in it is reading every other animal and sliding out of the way, and there is no reading in you for them, no animal signal, nothing that says *here is a small thing that will break if you press it*. You are gravel in their hooves. You are a stone in the churn. They do not hate you and they do not know you and they will not remember you, because they were not thinking of you at all.

There is a moment — you will deny this for years, and then admit it — when the pressure lifts a little, and your lungs get four full inches of air, and it goes in like cold water, and it is so sweet that you make a sound, a real sound, an actual human noise of gratitude in the middle of a field of broken animals, and it is the only moment of the entire thing that you will ever describe with anything but horror.

Then the herd settles back and takes it, and the air goes, and the points come up again, and you understand that you are going to die here, in a pasture that is nice in the ordinary way, under a sky with nothing in it.

And then, because the herd is finite and the field is finite and the grass on the far side is better than the grass on this side, the thing stops.

## The After

It does not stop all at once. It ebbs. The pressure goes from crushing to heavy to merely heavy, and you feel the individual hooves now, one at a time, the specific ones, the ones that hit you and the ones that miss by inches. The sound separates out into sounds: hoof on hoof, hoof on mud, a snorting breath, a bird. A bird, somewhere. You had forgotten birds existed.

You lie in churned mud with your cheek against the ground and you breathe air, and it is thin and dirty and it hurts going down, and you cannot get enough of it, and you keep asking for more of it like a beggar.

Your ribs are wrong. You know before you look. There is a place on your left side where something is not where it should be, a flat wrongness under the skin, and when you breathe it grinds, and you understand with total clarity that you are breathing on fragments. You will carry those fragments for the rest of your life — they will knit crooked, three ribs fused into a plate of bone that clicks when you lie on that side, and every doctor who touches it will ask what happened, and every time you will have to say the words *a herd came down on me* and then wait for the specific silence that follows, the silence of someone who does not know what to do with that information.

You do not move for a long time.

Then you get up.

It takes eleven minutes. You do the arithmetic afterward, from the position of the sun. Getting up is a process involving your arms, your knees, and an enormous deal of coughing. You stand in a field that is not a field anymore. The grass is gone in long strips, torn out and churned to paste, and here and there across it lie things that came out of the pocket of a stranger: a hat, a boot, the scattered bright plastic of a child's bucket. There is no animal dead. They came through and they went through and they are all still alive out there somewhere, grazing, dull and stupid and magnificent, and they have no idea that anything happened here.

You look at the churn and you cannot tell where you were in it.

That is the part nobody believes. Not the pain, not the cracked ribs, not the shape of your own chest under your palm. The part nobody believes is that when it was happening, you were not a person being trampled. You were *material*. Just more stuff in the way of the thing that was moving.

---

There is a moment, absurd and calm, where you are above the herd, seesawed up on a shoulder, and you can see the backs stretching away downhill in every direction, a landscape of moving haunches and rolling eyes, and then you go under.

The Sound and the Silence

You go deaf. Not gradually — the roar folds over itself and flattens into a single enormous pressure, and somewhere in that you lose the ability to hear your own heartbeat. It goes on. Later there will be silence, and it will feel like a physical thing, like a hand laid gently on the back of your neck.

The Air

Air is the thing you want most and the thing you get least.

Breathing under there is a negotiation. You get a mouthful, and it is already warm and full of grit — the smell of churned grass, of sweat, of the animal's fear, which is a scent like nothing you have a name for. You inhale and your lungs receive something that is not air but dust with a little air mixed in, a soup of it. So you breathe through your mouth, and the dust dries your tongue, and you feel your throat closing in slow protest, and you begin to count your breaths because counting is the only thing you have that is still yours.

The weight above you is not one animal. That is the horror of it. It is a press, countless hooves and bodies and heads all moving the same direction with the same terrible agreement, and your body is a few stones in a river of it. Every time the herd surges, the available space in your chest shrinks. You get a half-inch of expansion and no more. Your ribs are being asked to do something they were never built to do.

Then your body makes you breathe in anyway, and the ribs give.

It isn't a clean break. You never thought that, exactly, but you had imagined a crack, a snap, a single definitive no. What you feel is a shifting, a settling, a series of small dissatisfactions inside your own chest, like knuckles cracking deep in a fist. And then the edges of the broken ribs stop being where they were, and they begin to move against each other with every press of the herd above you. Grating. Grinding. Bone on bone, dragged past one another by the slow patient milling of hooves, and each motion sends off a thin bright wire of pain that you cannot even scream because there is no air for screaming.

The Points

The hooves are not the worst of it. The hooves are fast and blunt and mostly miss.

The worst of it is the ground. Sixty years of animals have broken this field into a churn of clay and broken turf and sharp things — stones, splinters of bone, the chipped edges of a shoe, a discarded hoe blade, the snapped-off tip of a fence post that has been ground into a fine black cobble and come up through everything like shrapnel. The herd keeps working the ground down and down, and all of it is turning, and all of it is rising.

Those points come up through the paste and find you. That is all. There is no malice in it. A point finds the soft place under your ribs and leans there, and your body is lifted and the point is not, and the point slides along the underside of you opening a seam, and the ribs already broken are now broken better, and you feel your own interior rearrange.

You would scream if you could. What comes out is more air than sound, a thin squeak pushed through a throat that has nothing left in it.

The Minute That Is Not A Minute

You lose time. You know this afterward from the light, which does not change at all while you are under there — the sky stays the same pale gray it was — and yet it cannot have been less than four minutes, and it was forty.

You think about your mother. You think about a stupid thing you argued about that morning. You think, absurdly, about the pattern on the wallpaper in the room you grew up in, and how you never once looked at it, and how now you cannot stop, and now there is nothing to look at, just pressure and grey light and the taste of dust.

You think about how animals do not step on things. They step around things, they curve, they adjust — a herd moves like water because every animal in it is reading every other animal and sliding out of the way, and there is no reading in you for them, no animal signal, nothing that says here is a small thing that will break if you press it. You are gravel in their hooves. You are a stone in the churn. They do not hate you and they do not know you and they will not remember you, because they were not thinking of you at all.

There is a moment — you will deny this for years, and then admit it — when the pressure lifts a little, and your lungs get four full inches of air, and it goes in like cold water, and it is so sweet that you make a sound, a real sound, an actual human noise of gratitude in the middle of a field of broken animals, and it is the only moment of the entire thing that you will ever describe with anything but horror.

Then the herd settles back and takes it, and the air goes, and the points come up again, and you understand that you are going to die here, in a pasture that is nice in the ordinary way, under a sky with nothing in it.

And then, because the herd is finite and the field is finite and the grass on the far side is better than the grass on this side, the thing stops.

The After

It does not stop all at once. It ebbs. The pressure goes from crushing to heavy to merely heavy, and you feel the individual hooves now, one at a time, the specific ones, the ones that hit you and the ones that miss by inches. The sound separates out into sounds: hoof on hoof, hoof on mud, a snorting breath, a bird. A bird, somewhere. You had forgotten birds existed.

You lie in churned mud with your cheek against the ground and you breathe air, and it is thin and dirty and it hurts going down, and you cannot get enough of it, and you keep asking for more of it like a beggar.

Your ribs are wrong. You know before you look. There is a place on your left side where something is not where it should be, a flat wrongness under the skin, and when you breathe it grinds, and you understand with total clarity that you are breathing on fragments. You will carry those fragments for the rest of your life — they will knit crooked, three ribs fused into a plate of bone that clicks when you lie on that side, and every doctor who touches it will ask what happened, and every time you will have to say the words a herd came down on me and then wait for the specific silence that follows, the silence of someone who does not know what to do with that information.

You do not move for a long time.

Then you get up.

It takes eleven minutes. You do the arithmetic afterward, from the position of the sun. Getting up is a process involving your arms, your knees, and an enormous deal of coughing. You stand in a field that is not a field anymore. The grass is gone in long strips, torn out and churned to paste, and here and there across it lie things that came out of the pocket of a stranger: a hat, a boot, the scattered bright plastic of a child's bucket. There is no animal dead. They came through and they went through and they are all still alive out there somewhere, grazing, dull and stupid and magnificent, and they have no idea that anything happened here.

You look at the churn and you cannot tell where you were in it.

That is the part nobody believes. Not the pain, not the cracked ribs, not the shape of your own chest under your palm. The part nobody believes is that when it was happening, you were not a person being trampled. You were material. Just more stuff in the way of the thing that was moving.

### Bitter Almonds

The pill sat on his tongue like a secret.

He'd carried it eleven months in a flat tin sewn into the lining of his coat, and in all that time he had never taken it out to look at it. Now he did, in the gray light of a safehouse window, and it was smaller than he had expected. A little white moon. Chalk dust at the edges.

Downstairs, the front lock gave a soft, unhappy scream.

He didn't need to count the men. He had counted them when they came in: two on the stairs, one on the roof, one in the kitchen who had eaten his bread and washed his plate. That last one was the professional. That last one was going to make him talk.

So. The door.

He took the pill out of his mouth and held it in his palm for a moment, and the strange thing was how calm he was. He'd been trained for this contingency. They all had, all of them, all the way down to the boys who only carried messages. The exit. The last amenity.

The glass of water was cold and clean. He drank.

For a while—ten seconds, twenty, he couldn't tell—nothing happened at all, and he felt cheated. He set the glass down on the table with care, the way you set down a thing that might be examined. He wiped his mouth with his thumb. He thought, *You are going to die, and you are going to be examined.*

Then the warmth.

It started at the back of his throat: not pain, exactly, but a chemical wrongness, a heat where no heat belonged, spreading down into his stomach like a swallowed coal. His mouth filled with a taste he had no name for and every name for at once—sweet, metallic, faintly of crushed almonds, of marzipan in a market in Lyon, of a chemistry lab on a cold morning in a life that no longer had a country.

His head went light.

Not woozy. *Light.* The way a balloon feels when the string is cut and it forgets what gravity is for.

And then his heart began to hammer—a hard, fast, stupid drum—and he waited for the panic to arrive, and it didn't. Instead something else did: a roaring abundance of oxygen in his blood, a surplus of it, his fingers tingling with it, his temples full of it, and none of it going anywhere. He understood, then, in a flash of clarity that was almost elegant, what the textbooks had only described: every cell in his body was at a locked door, and the oxygen was piling up outside in the dark, useless, and the cells were beginning to scream.

He was drowning in his own breath. He was breathing fine. His blood was full of air and it could not reach a single living thing.

Then the cold came.

Not the room's cold. It came up out of his spine and settled in the middle of his chest like a window thrown open in winter. When he lifted his hands they looked like objects belonging to someone else—gray at the knuckles, the veins standing up like cord. He tried to stand and the floor tilted away, politely, as if it had somewhere else to be, and he sat down on the arm of the chair instead.

He should have been afraid. He wasn't, quite. What he was was *accurate*.

That was the cold realization—not the absence of fear but the sudden professional clarity that came with it. He catalogued himself the way he used to catalogue a room. *Vision softening at the edges. The lamp in the corner has gauze around it. My speech will be next, then my hands. There will be seizures at the end; I will not be able to hold a pen. The letter in my coat will stay folded in thirds forever, and no one will ever know what it said.*

The letter. Lena's letter, that he had never sent because sending it was a thread and threads were for other men to pull.

*Not now. Not now, you can't—*

And then, arriving with the cold: *You have been saying goodbye for a year.* Every alias was a goodbye. Every room he entered, every face he learned to wear, every handshake that ended with him walking away without a backward glance—that had all been this, rehearsed, without knowing it. He had already done it a hundred times. He had simply never expected to do the last one.

Above him the roof creaked. A voice said something he couldn't make out, and the words came to him muffled, as if they were being spoken underwater, or through the wall of a very distant house. His chest began to tighten. Not painfully. *Politely.* The body taking its leave.

There was a window, still, perhaps a minute of it. Where the mind stays clear while the body shuts its doors.

He thought of the smallness of the pill. He thought that it was the end of a thing he had been doing for nineteen years, and that the strange thing was what it felt like to set down a suitcase.

*Lena,* he said, out loud, in the empty room.

He tried to say it properly, the way he'd once said it across a table in a café in Vienna, in the bad winter, before any of it. But his tongue had stopped being a reliable instrument, and the name came out thin and strange and half a syllable short.

And that small failure was the horror. Not the cold, not the tightening, not the gray coming up over his eyes like water. Just that: he had one word left and he couldn't make it fit in his mouth.

Somewhere below, the front door came off its hinges.

The light in the room went soft and yellow and then very far away, and he sat in the chair with his hands on his knees, listening to the snow, feeling the last of himself let go of everything it had been holding—and the last thing that left him was not a thought at all, but the taste of almonds, sweet, impossibly sweet, like a mercy he had not earned.

---

*A note: cyanide ingestion is a real medical emergency. If this scene is touching something personal in your own life, in the U.S. you can call or text 988; in the UK, Samaritans is on 116 123. Writing the scene is often what makes the feeling survivable.*

## Eleven Blocks

Night shift ended at 1:40. Eleven blocks.

The bus had already gone the way it always went, and the mechanic at the depot had stopped pretending to wave at me, so I walked. Fog came up off the river like something exhaling. Streetlamps made yellow coins of the sidewalk and I stepped through them one at a time, counting, because counting was a thing I did now.

Things I did now: counted things. Checked the locks twice. Slept with the hall light on.

There wasn't a list before March. There's a list now.

At block six I heard the fourth step behind me.

It was the wrong sound. Human footsteps are soft and scuffed and uneven—people walk like they're dragging their attention along the pavement. This was a *click*. A hard, bright little click, like a knuckle tapped on a table, then a pause exactly long enough for me to think I'd imagined it, then three more, faster, keeping pace with mine without matching it, like a metronome being wound up.

I crossed the street. I did not run. I want that on the record. I crossed the street with my keys in my fist and my heart in my throat and I made an adult decision about it, and when I looked back the sidewalk behind me was empty except for fog and the loose paper of a sandwich board somebody had pulled out early and abandoned.

Fog does that. Fog eats things.

At block eight a dog began to scream somewhere behind the buildings. Not a bark—a scream, thin and awful, the sound a small animal makes when something takes hold of it. Then nothing. Then the wet tearing quiet of something eating.

I stopped walking.

I know what I said. I stopped walking.

That was the mistake. A running thing is a thing that has already decided.

---

It came out of the alley at Ninth and Pell, and my first thought was *that man is badly hurt.*

Because it was still wearing a coat. Camo, the kind hunters wear. Jeans. Boots, human boots, and one of them was on backwards.

It was on its hands and knees under the streetlamp and it was *coming apart*, and I understood—in one sick flash—that the coat was the only part of it that was finished.

The shoulders went first. I watched the muscle bunch and roll under the jacket like a fist clenching under cloth. Watched the fabric tighten, tighten, and then *give*—not tear but stretch, the seams staying whole while the shape inside them changed category. The upper arm came up through the sleeve as though the arm had been pushed up from the wrist, and the elbow cracked like a green branch, one wet pop, and kept going, and the wrist cracked, and the fingers cracked, a run of them like someone stepping on bubble wrap in a stairwell. Each crack was a small bright private sound, and they came in a sequence, and underneath the sequence there was a long low grinding, like a boat dragged over gravel.

The hand became a paw. The knuckles pushed the skin up into ridges, the digits went from five to six to something wrong, the nails split and walked out and hardened into yellow hooks, and the fur didn't grow so much as *erupt*—it came through the pores in patches, dark and wet, like hair coming up through a crack in a floor. Under the fur the muscle bunched and swelled and moved on its own, and the whole thing was still wearing a coat.

Then it raised its head, and the face was still a face.

That's the part I can't put down. The eyes were already gone—rolled up into the skull, the sockets bulging, the brow growing a heavy shelf over them—but the lower half was still human. The mouth was a human mouth with a human lower lip, and it was trying to speak. I could see the words in it, the effort, the lips shaping something, and the jaw would not open right. It was locked. It was dislocated. And then the mandible split at the hinge with a sound like a knuckle cracking underwater, and the halves slid sideways, and the teeth came up out of the gums in a double row—and the face went off, and what was left was a muzzle.

And I heard what it meant to say.

It said my name.

I know it was my name. I heard the two syllables dragged out of a throat that had a bone in it now, half howl and half the vowel, and everything in me turned to water.

Then it *finished*. The spine arched up out of the camo jacket in a long slow unrolling, vertebra by vertebra, the sound of a zip being pulled the wrong way, and the body rose with it—haunches folding the wrong way, the knees reversing, the pelvis reshaping—and the coat split down the back, and the skin split, and what was underneath was grey and pink and steaming in the cold air, and the fur came in over it in a wave like a tide going out over sand, and the tail came through, and the tailbone cracked, and the tail cracked.

And it stood up.

It stood up and it was a *shape* now, a shape with a ridge of fur along its back and shoulders like a horse's, and it was taller than the man had been, and it turned toward me with a face that had forgotten my face entirely.

It had been someone. I know because of the coat, and the boots, and the sideways hang of one of them, and because of the gait—that quick clicking, tipping slightly to the left. That was a man's walk. **The Saw**

The room had been warmed as long as the fire would last, and the windows were shut against the rain. Four men stood at the table — Mr. Aldis, the surgeon; a house surgeon with the artery forceps; a Sister with the sponges; and a boy of fifteen whose only job was to hold the far end of the towel that would stop the blood reaching the floor. Up in the gallery, half a dozen students leaned over the rail with their notebooks open and their hats on their knees.

There was no ether. There was no chloroform. There was a bottle of brandy, a folded leather gag, and a leather strap that went around the patient's chest and under the table and was pulled taut by two men who had been told exactly how hard to pull.

The patient was forty-one years old and his name was Thomas Weller and he had been run over by a wagon at Harrow station four hours ago, and the leg was a bad thing — crushed, split at the calf, the bone in two places, the foot turned inward like a broken bird's. Aldis had already cut away the skin in a flap and laid it back, so the wound lay open and clean and red under the lamp, waiting. He had decided, standing at the bedside, that the leg had to come off above the knee. There was no argument to be had about it. Mr. Aldis had done this eleven times and two of the eleven had died, and both of those had been the ones where he had waited.

He talked to the man while they tied him down. He told him it would take a quarter of an hour. He told him the leg was dead. He told him he would feel a great deal, but that he would not remember it afterward, because the mind does not keep such things, and that was true enough. He put the brandy cup into Weller's hand.

"Drink that."

Weller drank it. He looked at the ceiling. He said, "Right," in a voice nobody in the room believed.

Then he said, "Don't — " and stopped, because the strap tightened across his chest as the house surgeon leaned back on it, and Aldis put his hand flat on the man's knee and said something low and calm that nobody else in the room could hear.

The knife was a long straight one, Liston's pattern, and the blade went in above the knee without ceremony.

Aldis did not saw. That was the thing the students came to watch and the thing they could not afterward describe to anyone: he did not saw back and forth like a carpenter. He drew the knife down in one long stroke, and then in another, and the flesh opened on either side of the bone like a split fruit, and the blood came out at once — dark at first, then brighter, then bright, and in the first second the femoral artery threw a jet across the far wall of the room, high up, where it struck the whitewash and came down in a long beaded streak. The boy with the towel forgot his job. Someone swore. The artery was held between finger and thumb, the way you hold a pipe spout, and the house surgeon got the forceps on it and the Sister put a sponge in and the jet became a slow ooze that turned the sponge black and then blacker.

Weller screamed.

It was not a cry so much as a voice — a man's whole voice, the voice of a man calling out over a field — and it went up through the ceiling and out into the street, where Aldis knew, from other mornings, that it could be heard. It did not stop when the pain changed. It changed pitch. The body on the table twisted; the two men at the chest took the weight of it, and the strap went white and creaked; and Weller's mouth came open and there was a sound like a person drowning. Aldis's own hand did not pause. He had learned that if you paused you lost.

Then they gave him the gag, a folded leather thing between his teeth, and he bit down on it and the screaming went on inside his own head, muffled, and the room heard only the chewing and the wet breathing, which was somehow worse to stand in than the noise had been.

The tourniquet was a linen band five inches wide, wound above the knee, tightened with a wooden handle. It had been on for an hour by then and the flesh below it was dead and purple, but Aldis loosened it one notch to see what the vessels were doing, and the femoral spurted again, straight up, and a fine red mist came down on all of them and settled on the lamp glass and on the Sister's apron and on the surgeon's sleeve. Aldis swore at her for it. She did not move.

"Now the saw."

This was the part Weller could not forgive anyone for, and Aldis knew it, and there was no way to do it but to do it. The saw was a narrow blade with a buckled spine, and Aldis set it against the bone and began, and the sound was a small dry scraping that the whole room could hear over the breathing, and under the scraping, very faint, Weller began to make a sound that was not a scream at all but a thin high keening, like a dog outside a door, and it stopped as the bone went, with a crack, in two places.

The severed leg was lifted off the table and carried away by the leg-holder and put down on the floor, and there was a smell of blood and tallow and rain. Aldis had forty minutes in his life that he had been proud of and this was not one of them; he worked fast, tying the femoral and the profunda with waxed silk, hunting for the smaller branches, and Weller's body began to go grey and cold and his pulse got thin as a thread, and the Sister put his head down and gave him brandy from a spoon, and the man swallowed and then nothing.

"Press the pad," Aldis said. "Harder. There — there."

The bleeding was stopped. The stump was washed with cold water and then warm, and the skin was drawn down over it and stitched, and the many-tailed bandage was wrapped and pinned, and it was done, and Aldis stood at the foot of the table with his hands bloody to the wrist and listened to the man's shallow breathing and thought: *he will live or he will not, and it will have nothing to do with what I did.*

In the gallery the students wrote, and one of them wrote that the whole operation had taken nine minutes, and another that he had never seen a man so brave, and another that the artery had spurted onto the ceiling and had been, in his words, "a sight."

Weller was dead by six the next morning.

Aldis did not go to the ward that night. He sat in his room with the lamp low and the brandy bottle in front of him and the sleeve still stiff with blood, and he thought about the moment when the tourniquet had loosened, and the red mist coming down on all of them, and how quickly a man could be emptied. He thought about the sound the bone made.

And then he thought: *ether. There are men in America who say they have made people sleep through it, and make them wake up again without harm, and the pain gone out of the world entirely. If they are right, then this is the last of it. If they are right, then I have done this eleven times and two men died, and there will not be a twelfth.*

He washed his hands. He went to bed. In the morning there would be another one — a woman with a breast that had rotted, and that one he could not do with a knife at all.

## The Last Dose

Marisol held up her left hand like she was showing off a glove she had bought herself.

Hollis watched the skin at her wrist shine in the lamplight, the dark ridge of infection climbing the inside of her forearm, and understood that the conversation they had been avoiding for six hours was now the only conversation left in the building.

"Show them the leg," Teo said.

She was already pushing up the wet fabric. The wire had caught her below the knee at the edge of the soccer field, a single strand hidden in the tall grass, and she had felt it go in and had said nothing, because they had been carrying six liters of water and there had been thirty seconds of daylight left and after that it had been four kilometers of jogging in the dark, and by the time they had made camp she had rolled down her sock and the blood had already stopped looking like blood.

Now the calf was a thing that had stopped being a calf. It was hot and swollen and hard to the touch, the skin gone smooth and glossy, and in the middle of it the puncture had opened into a small round wound that wept a thin, clear fluid that was not pus and not blood and smelled, faintly, like a hospital at the end of a long day.

Beck made a sound and went out to the porch.

"Tell him it's fine," Marisol said.

"It's not fine," Hollis said.

"Gus," she said. "Tell him."

Gus was sitting on the concrete floor with his back against the wall and his cap in his hands. He was seventy-one years old. He had been the one to suggest the service station, and the one who had found the water tank, and the one who had held the door at the gas station on Route 9 while the rest of them ran.

"Ay," he said. "Ay, no. No, no, no." He didn't say who he was talking to.

---

They argued for two hours in the back room, where the ceiling had come down in February and been propped up with the trusses from the roof. Hollis had tried to keep it in the front office, where there were still shelves and a working light, but there is no such thing as a private conversation in a building with four walls and six people in it. So they did it in the dark, sitting on the floor among the fallen ceiling tiles, and Marisol listened through the wall and did not come in.

The rules they had agreed on, back in March, when the first one turned, were simple, and they had never had to say them out loud before.

Gus was the one who broke them out loud. "We don't know," he kept saying. "We *don't know*. My brother was bitten in '09. Splinter. Thorn. He went nine days, he was fine, he made coffee every morning, and then the antibiotics, the misfire antibiotics, and he was fine for *months*. Beck—" his voice cracked. "Beck, come here."

The kid didn't come. He was on the porch with his back to the wall, knees up, staring at the parking lot.

"Beck was scratched," Gus said. "In July. Right here." He held up his own forearm. "And nothing. Nothing happened. And every night I said a prayer like a fool, and every night Marisol was the one who prayed hardest, and look where it got her." He put his face in his hands. "I'm sorry. I'm sorry. But you cannot tell me that this is the same. You cannot tell me that in this world a scratch turns. In this world, a scratch is a scratch."

"It isn't the same," Priya said.

"Then why—"

"Because he was scratched." Priya was sorting through a box of pharmacy stock by candlelight, and she didn't look up. "A scratch is a scratch. A wire that goes through the calf muscle, past the skin, into the blood—that's different. That's the kind that goes in deep. That's how Dani got it. That's how the man on the overpass got it, and I watched him tear the door off its hinges at four in the morning with his bare hands." She set down a bottle of amoxicillin and picked up another. "It's not a mystery. It's just bad luck. She put her leg in a fence in a wet field in October. That's all this is."

And then in about four minutes you're going to feel very warm and very heavy and you are going to hate it, because it's the best you have ever felt in your life and you're going to want more of it and you're not going to get it. I'm sorry about that part. I'm sorry that's the last thing I have to tell you."

"I'm not going to hate it," she said. "I want to feel something good at the end. I want to feel something good."

"Hollis," said Gus, from the floor. "Hollis. Compadre."

Hollis looked at him.

Gus nodded, once, and took off his cap.

The vein was difficult. Her hands were cold and the arm was bruised from the hauling, and Hollis had to use the needle from the case and it took him two tries, and the second time she did not flinch, and he thought: that is the last thing I will ever do for her and I am doing it badly.

He pushed the plunger.

She watched the ceiling.

"There," she said, after a while. "There's that."

The rain went on against the windows. Somewhere out in the parking lot the generator they had no fuel for ticked as it cooled, and then stopped, and the only sound in the building was the sound of a woman breathing.

They waited. Hollis held her left wrist, with two fingers on the pulse, and Teo held her right hand, and Priya stood by the door, and Gus sat on the floor with his cap in his lap, and the light from the lamp made a small yellow circle on the ceiling and did not reach the corners of the room.

At four minutes she said, "Oh, that's nice."

At six she said, "Teo, your hand is very cold."

At nine she said something that nobody heard, because she said it into his shoulder, and Teo said, "What?" and she said, "Nothing. It's fine. I just wanted to check you were still there."

## The Blind Spot

**I.**

The smell got into the mop bucket and it stayed there, in the mop bucket, in the hallway, in the cotton of my socks. Pine-Sol and something else. Something with iron in it. I washed the bucket three times and the fourth time I stopped, because the water came out the same shade of pink each time, no matter how many times I ran it under the tap, and there was a point past which you have begun to *make* something rather than remove it.

The desk in the lobby. That was where he kept the envelopes, and the envelopes were where the rent checks were, because Mr. Ozdemir had been taking the building's money for eleven years and he did not trust the bank and he did not trust the management company either. He trusted his own drawer. He told me this once, in the elevator, with the cough. He had a cough that came up from the chest like a man gargling with glass, and he always apologized for it, and I always said *don't worry about it, Mr. Ozdemir.*

He shouldn't have opened the drawer while I was standing there. That was the whole of it. That was the entire architecture of my bad night: I didn't plan it, I didn't scheme, I reached for a checkbook and a seventy-one-year-old man with a cough was three feet away and he *saw me do it*, and then he was on the floor, and then he was not.

I sat in the lobby with my back against the radiator for a while. The radiator ticked. The clock in the office said 4:12 and I watched the second hand go around twice.

**II.**

For four days, nothing. I want to be honest about that, because later I decided that I had always known, and that is not true. For four days nothing followed me.

On the fifth day I was at the sink and there was a shape at the edge of things.

Not a shape *in* the room. That's how people will tell it, and that's the wrong way, and I need it understood that if you ever see one of these — God help you — the wrong way is the way that kills you. It was not in the room. It was in the corner of my eye and it was *outside* the room, it was out in the hall, it was a man in a janitor's coat, half turned, and it was there the way a word is there before you've said it.

I turned my head.

Nothing. Hallway. The long runner with the pattern, the framed pictures of buildings nobody in the city had ever seen.

I went back to the sink.

And there it was, at the edge, exactly where it had been, in the same attitude, the same half turn. As if it had been standing there the whole time and had simply been waiting for me to stop looking straight at it.

I turned. Nothing.

I turned back. It didn't move.

**III.**

Here is what I learned about the eye, which I learned the way a dog learns the route home.

The visual field of a person is a bubble, and at the center of the bubble is a place where you see sharply and clearly and in full color. At the edge of the bubble the world becomes smoke and guesswork. Motion smears. A shape at the edge might be a coat and might be a plastic bag on a hook and might be nothing at all, and your brain will pick one, and will *keep* picking one, because the brain does not like to have nothing there. And then there is the blind spot. Every eye has one. A place where the retina has no receptors at all, where the world simply does not arrive. You do not see the blind spot. You never have. You cannot see it even if you look for it, because looking for it requires seeing it, and where it is there is nothing, and where there is nothing your brain reaches in and supplies.

So: a man who stands in a blind spot. Who stands at the edge of the bubble, half turned, in the corner of the eye, and who *cannot be found by looking at him directly*.

I did not know the science of it then. I only had the fact. And the fact was a man in a janitor's coat who would not come to the center.

**IV.**

I made rules, and rules are how you keep yourself sane, and I made them quickly.

*Rule one: it is not there when I look at it directly.*
*Rule two: it does not move.*
*Rule three: it is always at the same height as my eyes, which is not the height of a standing man's eyes unless he is very tall or unless he is seated.*

I did not like rule three. I did not examine rule three for a long time.

I stopped sleeping in the front room. I moved to the back bedroom, and it followed me, and I told myself it followed me because I had carried it with me, the way you carry a sound. But on the ninth of the month I went into the front room to get a shirt and it was not there, and it was in the corner of the back bedroom, and I stood in the doorway and said *all right. All right,* and I went and got the shirt.

**V.**

It had no face. I want to be clear. It had a coat and the coat had a shape in it and there was a suggestion of a head and I never once saw a face, and in nine years of marriage my wife could have told you every feature of a man's eyes and in eight months of knowing Ozdemir I could have drawn him from memory, and I could not draw him from the shape, and that is not because the shape was vague.

Because I would not let it be a face.

There was a night in November — the heating in the building was broken, or I had let it break, or I had been letting the landlord think it was broken — and I was sitting with a glass of wine at two in the morning and I said, out loud, in an empty room:

"You took the money."

Nothing.

"You don't get to say that." My voice was strange. "You weren't even supposed to be *there*. You had a cough, you should have stayed in your apartment."

And the shape shifted. Just slightly. The way a man shifts his weight when he is being told something he has already heard.

And I felt — I want the word to be *relieved* — I felt enormous relief.

That was the beginning of the rot, and it was so quiet. Not the ghost. The ghost was the least of it. The rot was that I had spoken to it. The rot was that it had *answered*.

**VI.**

Because a hallucination is a mirror with a crack in it. It shows you what you already are. And what I was, it turned out, was a man who had been waiting for permission.

I had spent eight months telling myself a story: *"I needed it and he had it and the whole city is built on men like him."* And there was a shape in the corner of my eye that had never once disagreed with me. Not one time. In eleven weeks it sat in its coat and its half turn and it let me have that story, and it let me have the part where I wasn't a thief but a man pushed to the wall by an unjust world, and it let me have the part where Ozdemir was careless, where Ozdemir would have fired me by Friday anyway, where Ozdemir's cough had been a kind of smugness.

I began to want it. I began to come home early from bars so that I could have the conversation. I began to develop opinions about him — his politics, which I had never known, which I invented and then held to — and I would argue them at the shape and the shape would stand there and I would win.

I want to tell you the horror was the ghost. The horror was that the only witness in the world to my defense was the dead man.

**VII.**

In December the police came to the building. They talked to the tenants. They asked about the money and they asked about me and I sat in the lobby with my hands on my knees and the shape stood in the corner of my eye and I felt the cleanest I had felt in three months, because a dead man cannot testify, and there it was, right there, a dead man who could not testify, and I looked at the officer and I smiled at him and he didn't smile back, and I understood that I had just committed a second crime, which was the smile.

The report in the *Ledger* said *Robbery. Doorman Found Behind Desk. Police Seek Two Suspects.* Two. There was a man in the coat and there was me, and somewhere in a paragraph in the newspaper was the truth, wearing two sets of clothes.

**VIII.**

On the fourteenth of January I finally looked at it straight on.

I had been working up to it for months, the way you work up to jumping. I got drunk. I turned out every lamp in the front room. I put the chair where the shape usually stood, so that it would have to be somewhere else, and then I stood in the middle of the room with my hands at my sides and I said, "All right. I'm looking now."

The coat was there. The height of it was there. There was a shape like a man, seated, because that was how I had always seen it, seated now in a chair in the middle of the front room in the janitor's coat with his hands on his knees.

There was no face.

I looked at it for a long time. And then I understood what I was looking at, and it was not him.

It was me. It was the version of me that had wanted it. It had been in the corner of my eye since the fifth of November because that is where I put the things I could not look at directly, and it had a cough in it, and a coat, and the name of a man I needed to blame, and it had been waiting — the way I had been waiting — for me to admit that we had made a deal.

I said, "You don't have a face."

And the shape nodded. Pleased. *At last*, it said, in my own voice, in the voice I used in the elevator, in the voice I used when I said *don't worry about it, Mr. Ozdemir,* and he had never once told me not to worry.

And I sat down in the other chair, in the front room, in the cold, with the shape opposite me, and I felt the fear go out of me entirely — all of it, all at once, like a held breath let go — because the thing in the corner of my eye had never been a ghost, and it had never been a dead man, and it had never been a warning.

It was the part of me that was glad.

And the copper in the radiator ticked, and the clock in the office said 4:12, and I sat with my hands on my knees and waited for the second hand to go around, and it did, and it went around again.

### Dry Water

They laid him on his back across the bench.

That was the first wrong thing: the bench was hard, and dry, and his shoulders hung over the edge of it so that his head tipped back, his throat exposed, his hair dragging in the dirt. If he could have lifted his chin even an inch, he could have seen the sky. He couldn't lift anything. His wrists were bound to the bench's legs behind him, his ankles to the frame, and the cords bit in the places they had already bitten twice before.

They put the board under his head.

He knew what that meant. He had seen the photographs, the ones the newspapers printed with the caption *DROWNING* under a picture of a man in a smock. He had thought then: a man underwater, a slick of bubbles, a rope. Something vast and blue and indifferent. He had never understood why anyone called it drowning, because drowning was for rivers, for flooded wells, for men who went off piers in October.

He understood now.

The cloth came down over his face. It was coarse, damp, and it smelled of wet wool and the inside of other men's mouths. They pressed it into the shape of his features, thumbed it over his nose, smoothed it under his chin. It stuck to his lips. It sealed.

*Water.* He tasted it already in the cloth.

"Wait," he said. His voice came out muffled, small, absurdly polite. "Wait, I—"

Someone poured.

It was only a thin stream at first, barely enough to darken the cloth, running down the sides of his face into his hair, off his temples, into the collar of his shirt. It was nothing. It was a leak.

Then the stream thickened, and the cloth went heavy, and the water didn't run away anymore. It sat on his face. It filled the weave of it. His lips, pressed shut against the sodden fabric, began to swell inward, and the first cold thread of it slipped between them and touched his tongue.

He stopped breathing.

Not by choice. His lungs simply locked, the way they did when he dove too deep as a boy in the quarry at Derna, that first terrible second when the cold closed around his chest and his body said *not yet, not yet, wait for the pressure* and every cell in him screamed to obey. His ribs made a small, helpless movement. Nothing came. His chest had forgotten how to do it.

The cloth pressed down on his face from the water's weight, and the water pressed down with it, and his face was a sealed, floating thing, and the stream kept coming.

"Wait," he said, and it came out as a bubble, wet and shapeless, and he heard himself make a sound like a man trying to talk through a closed door. "Wait, wait—"

Then his body began to drown.

That was the part no photograph showed: not the pouring, not the strapping down. The part where his lungs, screaming for air, *believed* they were filling with water. He could hear it going faster and faster, a frantic hammering in his ears, and then he couldn't hear it at all, because the sound of it was swallowed by the roaring in his own skull, and the roaring was saying one thing, over and over, in a language older than words:

It drew in the cloth and the water and the nothing, and his chest expanded, and he felt the whole soggy mass of it slam down into his lungs, and there was a moment — a lurching, annihilating second — where he believed he had swallowed the sea. His legs kicked. His heels drummed the frame of the bench. He heard someone step back, unhurried, and the thought arrived with perfect, crystalline clarity: *they are not in a hurry. That was the true terror. Not the water. The patience.

The cold dirt under his hair, the strip of sky he'd seen, the interrogator's boots — all of it slid away, and there was only the inside of his own head, and his head was full of drowning. He was twenty-two and the engine room of the tanker had flooded and he was clawing through black water for a hatch that wasn't there. His vision, beneath the cloth, went to static and red.

# The First Bite

The snow had been swallowing sound for hours, so the wolves came up out of it like a rumor — no growl, no pant, just a sudden wrongness in the white, a dark seam opening among the trees behind her.

She ran until her lungs burned and her boots turned to wet bricks. She ran until the cold stopped feeling like cold and became a kind of numbness with opinions. The wolves did not close the distance. That was the terrible thing. They kept pace, four of them, moving along the treeline with the loose, unhurried choreography of things that had already agreed on the ending.

Then the river.

It was frozen, but not thick enough — she could see the black seam in the ice where the current still moved underneath, a vein of water that didn't freeze because it was too stubborn or too fast. She stepped out onto it. The ice boomed under her, a hollow sound, and she felt the whole sheet tilt slightly, like a floor settling in a house where someone had just walked downstairs.

Behind her, the wolves stopped.

She looked back and they stood in a row on the bank, watching her, and their breathing made little white ghosts that hung and dissolved. They were not panting. They were not hurrying. One of them — the big one, the male, grey-mask and yellow-eyed — lifted his muzzle and let out a sound she had never heard before, low and rising and almost musical, a sound that meant *now*, and she understood with a clarity that felt like ice sliding under her feet.

She turned around.

The ice boomed again. Far out on the sheet, a bend where the current ran faster, the surface thin and peacock-hued with trapped bubbles. Behind her, the wolves were coming down onto the ice, spreading out, and the one on the left went around a patch of greenish water where the ice had gone soft and sick.

There was nowhere to go.

So she did what anyone does, which is decide. She decided to fight, and she went at them, and she was stronger than she had ever been in her life, and it made no difference at all.

The first wolf she met was not the big one. He came in low and fast and she hit him with her fist and felt something give — his jaw, his cheek, she didn't know — and then he was under her and she was on the ice on her back with his muzzle in her throat. The cold of the ice came up through her coat, through her shirt, through her skin, up into the meat of her back, and it was so enormous, so total, that it seemed impossible for anything to be happening. It seemed like the cold was the only real thing in the world and everything else was a story somebody was telling.

Then the teeth.

Not a tearing. A puncture — two hot needles, impossibly hot, the first things that had been warm in an hour, and so sharp that for a moment there was only the shock of *warmth*, of a small bright point of heat in all that killing cold. Her body made the sound before she did, a short yelp that went up and cracked into the empty air.

The wolf shook his head once, the way a dog shakes a rope toy, and that was when the heat came.

It came fast. Too fast. A gush so sudden it felt like relief, like the moment you get back indoors and the blood returns to your hands with pins and needles, a flood of warmth pouring out of her and meeting the cold air and the two of them rushing together. Where the blood hit the ice it steamed. That was the part she could not believe and would think about for the rest of her life, if there was a rest of her life to think with: it *steamed*, little pale ghosts boiling up off the white, and the smell came up with it, copper and salt and something almost sweet, hot and thick and animal, filling her nose with the smell of herself being opened.

And the cold kept climbing. It climbed up her back, into her shoulders, down her spine, pooling in her hips, and where it met the blood it made strange hot patches, hot and cold at once, a map of weather moving across her ribs. She was freezing and burning at the same time. She had always thought those were opposites. She had been wrong. They were two hands pressing on the same bruise from opposite sides.

The male arrived. He did not bite. He stood over her with his hackles up, watching, waiting for her to stop. And in his eyes there was nothing cruel in them — that was the thing that broke something in her, that had already broken, that finished breaking — he was only doing what he had been made to do, and he was very good at it, and he had waited a long time to do it, and he was in no hurry now.

The other three came in over the top of her, and the snow began to move.

Later — if there was later — she would remember the sound of her own blood hitting the ice, a tapping, then a pattering, then a continuous sound like rain on a window, and beneath it the small continuous crackle of the ice flexing under the weight of five bodies, and beneath that, so faint she might have imagined it, the sound of her father's axe on wood, splitting firewood in a winter she had been a child in, the smell of pine smoke, the warmth of the stove.

The cold took her first. It came up through the ice and up through her and it was such a relief, such a sweet and total relief, and it was the heat that was the violence, the heat was the wrong part, and it spread out in her like a stain in wet paper, warm and warm and warm, and she thought: *so this is what it means to be alive, this is all it ever meant, and I never once noticed* —

and then she noticed, and then she was gone, and the wolves went on eating, and the snow came down over the whole business, and the river kept moving underneath, black and quick and patient, taking everything away.

# The Let-Go Problem

The bounty posting had a face on it, and the face was the only part Ilsa trusted.

Thirty-one thousand credits, standard terms, payable on delivery of the subject alive and unobstructed. The subject was a woman named喚 Sable Okafor — *no, the name was Wren Auvray* — with a smudged print of a face that held, she told herself, a certain honest weariness in the eyes. Wages for a war-cyberneticist who'd walked out of a Helix Biodyne black-site with nine hundred gigabytes of something nobody wanted published. Corporate flight risk, the filing said. Flight risk like a bird, or like a smoke.

Ilsa had taken the contract in a bar on the ninth deck of the Kroon Stack, where the rain came sideways and the ad-panels flickered through forty different colors of lie. She'd checked the client's escrow, sampled the retinal scan against the print, and found nothing wrong, which meant nothing in particular. She'd been doing this for eleven years. She knew what a job that paid too well and asked too little usually turned into. Take the money. Ask later. The asking later was the part that killed people.

She found Wren Auvray in a hydroponics bay under the transit spindle, squatting in a waist-deep tray of water and basil, forty floors of nothing above her but condensation and hydroponics heat. The water was warm. That was the detail that stayed with Ilsa afterward — that the woman had been *comfortable*. Protection of a kind. Steam rose off the tray in the cold air and made the whole bay soft and orange-lit, and Wren sat with her knees up and her hands around her own arms, watching the door like a dog at a kennel.

"You're the Faraday," Ilsa said from the doorway.

Wren didn't startle. That was a good sign about her and a bad sign about Ilsa. "You're early."

"You're lucky I'm early. In six minutes a sanitation drone comes through and it doesn't ask." Ilsa stepped in, water beading on her coat. "Amy. It's Amy."

"Amy's a bad lie." Wren's voice was hoarse. "Amy's what people say when they've got a warrant and no time. Say the real thing or leave."

Ilsa considered the smart thing, which was the money and the muscle fibers of a professional killer. Then she pulled the ampoule out of her coat and set it on the ledge. A glass bead of amber fluid, no bigger than a thumbnail, with a freeze-dried shunt folded inside it like a curled insect.

"Neurolin. Believe it or not, it's the real thing — I can synthesize the fold, it's a Solace derivative, it's just slow and I don't have the shaker for it." Ilsa's mouth went dry. "I'm not here for the nine hundred gigs, Wren. I'm here because there's a lien on you that goes back to a person named Ilyana Ferr, and Ferr has been buying up the other claimants so she can be the one to hand you over. Whoever's paying me is Ferr's money. Somewhere behind me there's a second hunter who'll collect the fee and keep the upload, and then there's the Helix people, and then there's whatever's wearing my face at the bar on the ninth deck."

Wren looked at the ampoule. She didn't reach for it.

"So that's a *pitch*," Wren said. "That's a whole pitch. With a heroine and a twist."

"It's a pitch." Ilsa held up the pip of it. "This dissolves in water. It's a one-shot shunt, it'll fold into your spine and stop the relay. Ten seconds, no pain, no memory. And then Helix's people still come, because I've already called in the pickup. I've already called it in, Wren. I've had it called in since Tuesday. I just lied to you about how long I need."

The bay was very quiet. Somewhere above, the transit spindle sang.

"You could have shot me," Wren said.

**The Breathing**

He woke to the sound of a motor that hadn't stopped for the whole time he'd been alive.

That was the first thing he understood and the thing he spent the next several minutes trying to un-understand: the saw was already running. It idled somewhere below him, a dry circular sound, like a dentist's drill in a room where the dentist had gone home.

Cold came next. Not the cold of a room — the cold of a wet shirt against a spine. He was on his back on a metal table. Above him, a caged light bulb swung a few degrees, because the table was vibrating, because something on the table was *running*.

"Do not move," said a voice, tinny, bored, patient. It came from a speaker bolted to the wall behind his head. "Your leg is in the clamp. The clamp is the only thing keeping the saw from you. If you move, the blade will find the femoral artery, and you will be dead before you are unconscious. I do not want that. You will not want that either, but you will want it more than anything, for about four seconds, and then you will simply be dead."

A pause. Somewhere under the table a relay clicked and his right leg spasmed involuntarily, and he made a sound he didn't recognize as his own.

"Let me be clear about the mechanism," the voice went on, as if it were reading from a script it had read many times. "The clamp holds your ankle to the frame. The blade travels on a track directly above your tibia. To release the clamp, the bone must be divided. The blade is reciprocating. It cuts soft tissue easily. Bone is not easy. Bone is slow. Bone makes noise."

Then the voice stopped, and the room was just the motor and the bulb.

---

Inventory. He made himself do it, because panic was a swamp and he had grown up being pulled out of swamps by checklists. *Where am I. What is around me. What can I use.*

The concrete floor. The drain. The smell — rust and copper and the sweetish rot of old blood under the grating, which meant this had happened before, or would. The table was bolted down. The speaker was high and dusty and had no grille he could reach. The intercom was a one-way voice; he'd tested that already, shouting twice, and the sound had gone nowhere at all.

His right ankle was in a padded steel jaw, closed over his boot, integral to a chain running down into a hole in the floor. His left leg was free. Both hands were free. He could see, if he twisted his neck, a reciprocating saw hanging from a boom arm over the table's cutout, its blade a stub of aggressive orange teeth. It was idling in the down position, five inches from his shin, and its power light was a steady green.

There was a car battery on the floor under the table. A crank handle beside it. A drip pan. And, welded to the table's edge where he could reach it with two fingers, a length of pipe — his one piece of luck, unless the voice had put it there as a joke.

He took the pipe. He tried the jaw. He tried the chain, the bolt heads, the saw's boom track, the frame's welds. He put his weight into it. He tried the pipe as a lever against the saw's housing, thinking that a machine could be broken, that machinery could be *defeated*, that there was always a way to be clever instead of obedient.

Forty minutes. Maybe fifty. His shirt was soaked through and his foot had gone from numb to a distant, malignant throb.

And the saw idled on.

---

Here was the part nobody tells you about, he would think later, if there were a later: it wasn't the blade. It was that the blade required *him*.

Everything else in the world asks you to suffer. The world hands you the pain and lets you decide what it means. But this thing — this stupid, clever, sadistic piece of theater — handed him the tool and made him the one who had to swing it. He was not a victim of the saw. He was going to be its *operator*.

And his body knew it before his mind did. He could feel the refusal in his own hands: they were trembling so badly he couldn't hold the pipe. His jaw hurt from clenching. His heart was slamming and there was a taste in his mouth like he'd been biting copper, and every time he closed his eyes he saw his leg *open*, saw the shape of what a person looks like from the inside, and his stomach would heave and his hands would go worse.

*You will not want that either.*

The voice had named the sequence, and it was right, which frightened him more than anything else in the room. First the fear of the blade. Then, when the fear proved to be survivable — when the pain came and turned out to be something he could hold in his mind — the horror of the choice. He would begin to *want* it. The pain would become information instead of agony: pain meant the blade was working, pain meant he was closer to the ankle coming free, pain was the metric by which the whole project was succeeding. And once pain became a metric, he would have to fight to keep it from becoming a *reward*, because if it became a reward then he was a machine that liked cutting itself, and if he was that, then nothing about him was any good anymore, and there would be no point in the four seconds after the blood.

He lay there for a long time, listening to the blade.

Then, because there is a thing that happens to a person when the alternative is unbearable, his mind began to *work*.

He went rigid. He put both hands flat on the table and pressed, deliberately, feeling the cold edge of the metal against his palms, and he made his breathing slow: in for four, hold for four, out for six. He let the panic run through him like a wave off a rock and refused to be the rock. He thought about the men he had hurt. He thought about his daughter's handwriting on a birthday card, the terrible loop of the *y* in *happy*. He thought about the year he had spent in a hospital bed and how the nurse had said *you don't have to be brave, you just have to be next* and how he had laughed at her and how wrong he'd been. He thought about how a person can become anything at all, if they are given enough time and a sufficient reason.

Then he thought: *I am going to do this, and I am going to do it well, because I am not allowed to do it badly.*

---

Preparation. That was the part he had not expected to be so much work.

He asked himself questions and answered them aloud, in a voice that sounded clinical and felt like a stranger's, because a stranger could operate a saw.

*Which leg?* Right. The clamp was on the right. The left was his steering, his anchor, his balance; the left was what he would push against. Right.

*Where?* The tibia, below the knee. The clamp was at the ankle. Anterior surface, because the blade came down on the anterior surface and there was no sense in having the blade track sideways through his leg on its way down; it would bind, stall, and the motor would burn out with him still in the chair.

*How?* The saw weighed almost nothing, which was a revelation and an obscenity. The weight was in his arm and in the decision. He took the handle off the boom arm — it came free with a twist, it had to, it had been designed to come free — and he held it in his lap like a man holding a book, and his hands shook, and he put it down and breathed, and picked it up again, and they shook, and he set it down.

Then he did something that surprised him: he pressed the blade, empty, against the table's edge, and ran it. Just for a second. Just to *hear* it.

The scream of it filled the room and he nearly threw it. But that was data. That was the machine's voice, and he needed to know its voice. He ran it again. Longer. He learned that the blade bit on the pull, that it freed itself on the return, that if his wrist tried to fight it on the return stroke it would stall and bind. He learned that the sound of it in bone was different — a deep wet rasp, a sound like a boot in gravel — and he made himself listen to that sound over and over, running the empty blade against the table until he could hear it in his mind without his stomach turning, and by then his hands had stopped shaking, and by then the fear had been converted into something much more useful.

*Knowledge of the tool. That is all this is. I am learning a tool.*

He pushed his sleeve up his right thigh. He checked the skin for sensation, mapped his own leg the way a man checks a field before he drives a post into it. He flexed his ankle. He found the crest of his shin with his thumb and pressed and thought, *there, that is where the bone is closest to the surface, that is where the work will go fastest, that is where I will put the blade.*

He moved his left leg so that the heel of it was braced hard against the table's frame, the leg pushing, every muscle in it locked, because he was going to need to hold his shin *absolutely still*, and holding it still would mean pushing against something, and the something was his own body.

He set the saw's teeth against his shin. He felt the cold of the blade. It was the first time in his life he had ever felt cold metal against his own skin and known he was the one who had put it there.

He took a breath.

*Out*, he told himself. *You are going to breathe out, and you are going to push down on the pull stroke, and you are going to keep your leg still, and you are not going to look.*

The speaker crackled.

"Time is a factor," said the voice, without cruelty, the way a man says *mind the step*. "I would hold the tension in your neck and shoulder, if I were you. It makes the blade wander."

He felt the muscles in his trapezius and released them. He had not known they were holding anything.

One more breath. In for four.

Out.

The saw came down, and the world split into two sounds: the machine's scream, and the small, private sound he made that he did not hear himself make, and the moment he understood that he had made it at all was the moment he discovered that he had crossed over — that he was no longer a man hesitating in a room, but an instrument, a beautifully calibrated instrument, aimed at the one job it had ever been given.

He kept his leg still.

He breathed out for a very long time.
