His right ankle was in a padded steel jaw, closed over his boot, integral to a chain running down into a hole in the floor. His left leg was free. Both hands were free. He could see, if he twisted his neck, a reciprocating saw hanging from a boom arm over the table's cutout, its blade a stub of aggressive orange teeth. It was idling in the down position, five inches from his shin, and its power light was a steady green.

There was a car battery on the floor under the table. A crank handle beside it. A drip pan. And, welded to the table's edge where he could reach it with two fingers, a length of pipe — his one piece of luck, unless the voice had put it there as a joke.

He took the pipe. He tried the jaw. He tried the chain, the bolt heads, the saw's boom track, the frame's welds. He put his weight into it. He tried the pipe as a lever against the saw's housing, thinking that a machine could be broken, that machinery could be defeated, that there was always a way to be clever instead of obedient.

Forty minutes. Maybe fifty. His shirt was soaked through and his foot had gone from numb to a distant, malignant throb.

And the saw idled on.

Here was the part nobody tells you about, he would think later, if there were a later: it wasn't the blade. It was that the blade required him.

Everything else in the world asks you to suffer. The world hands you the pain and lets you decide what it means. But this thing — this stupid, clever, sadistic piece of theater — handed him the tool and made him the one who had to swing it. He was not a victim of the saw. He was going to be its operator.

And his body knew it before his mind did. He could feel the refusal in his own hands: they were trembling so badly he couldn't hold the pipe. His jaw hurt from clenching. His heart was slamming and there was a taste in his mouth like he'd been biting copper, and every time he closed his eyes he saw his leg open, saw the shape of what a person looks like from the inside, and his stomach would heave and his hands would go worse.

You will not want that either.

The voice had named the sequence, and it was right, which frightened him more than anything else in the room. First the fear of the blade. Then, when the fear proved to be survivable — when the pain came and turned out to be something he could hold in his mind — the horror of the choice. He would begin to want it. The pain would become information instead of agony: pain meant the blade was working, pain meant he was closer to the ankle coming free, pain was the metric by which the whole project was succeeding. And once pain became a metric, he would have to fight to keep it from becoming a reward, because if it became a reward then he was a machine that liked cutting itself, and if he was that, then nothing about him was any good anymore, and there would be no point in the four seconds after the blood.

He lay there for a long time, listening to the blade.

Then, because there is a thing that happens to a person when the alternative is unbearable, his mind began to work.

He went rigid. He put both hands flat on the table and pressed, deliberately, feeling the cold edge of the metal against his palms, and he made his breathing slow: in for four, hold for four, out for six. He let the panic run through him like a wave off a rock and refused to be the rock. He thought about the men he had hurt. He thought about his daughter's handwriting on a birthday card, the terrible loop of the y in happy. Where? The tibia, below the knee. The clamp was at the ankle. Anterior surface, because the blade came down on the anterior surface and there was no sense in having the blade track sideways through his leg on its way down; it would bind, stall, and the motor would burn out with him still in the chair.

He took the handle off the boom arm — it came free with a twist, it had to, it had been designed to come free — and he held it in his lap like a man holding a book, and his hands shook, and he put it down and breathed, and picked it up again, and they shook, and he set it down.

The scream of it filled the room and he nearly threw it. But that was data. That was the machine's voice, and he needed to know its voice. He ran it again. Longer. results.model_response:
## The Plank

The sea had been flat all morning, glassy and deceitful, the color of a new coin. By noon the wind had come up, and now it worried at the rigging in long, whistling sighs, and the *Kestrel* rolled in a slow, patient rhythm, like a ship walking in its sleep.

Elias Crey had not been born a fool, though he had certainly been born unlucky. He had come aboard the *Kestrel* at nineteen, out of Bristol, with a knife in his belt and a dead brother in his wake. Five years he had sailed under Captain Corvin Ash — five years of hard bread and worse weather and a captain who never once raised his voice, which was how you knew a man was angry — and in all that time Elias had learned exactly how much rope the world gave a sailor who stepped out of line.

So he had not confessed. Not until the third day, when the drink had worn thin and the lies had worn through, and he'd stood in the captain's cabin with his hands shaking and told the truth: the chart, the charts, the ones with the black hand and the safe anchorage, sold to a man in Nassau who had paid in Spanish silver. He'd told it plainly, the way he imagined a man does when he's decided to stop being a liar and start being dead.

Captain Ash had listened without moving. Then he'd said, "Thank you, Elias," and had called for the mate.

That was three days ago. Three days of the hold, of the smell of tar and old bilge water, of the crew passing the hatch and looking away. Three days of listening to the ship's conversation overhead — the boots, the voices, the ordinary business of the world going on, the gulls — and thinking, absurdly, of the woman he'd left in Bristol, and her letter still folded in his sea chest, and how he'd meant to answer it.

Now he stood on the quarterdeck in a canvas shift, bare-footed, and the sun was high and warm and had no idea what was about to happen.

"Bring him up," Ash said.

---

The crew made a space. That was the thing Elias would remember longest, afterward, if there were an afterward: the way they made a space. Two rows of men along the port rail, hats in their hands, faces like weathered timber. No one spoke. Someone near the bow was chewing something — a piece of rope, maybe — and the wet sound of it was the loudest thing on the ship. Nobody looked at Elias. They looked at the plank.

It was a good plank, actually. That was the obscene joke of it. Three boards of seasoned oak, lashed at the seaward end to a spar, projecting out over the water maybe twenty feet. Ash had had it made himself, the first year, when the *Kestrel* had still been a merchantman with a merchantman's mildness about discipline. "A man can walk off a ship or walk off a life," he'd said then, laughing, and the crew had laughed with him, and Elias had thought it a funny thing to say.

Twenty feet. He had measured it with his eyes, and then measured it again, because eyes were what a man had left.

Below the waterline the sea was not the same color as the rest of the sea. It was a paler, colder blue, shot through with moving shadows. Shadows that moved wrong. Shadows that moved *together*, and did not drift with the swell, but circled, the way gulls circle a boat that has found fish — unhurried, delighted, certain.

Elias's stomach went to pieces.

"They're coming up from the deep," said the bosun, quietly, to no one. "Two of the big ones. I seen them off the port quarter an hour back."

"Stand to your stations," said Captain Ash. He was at the rail, six feet away, and he spoke at a normal volume, the way a man speaks to a horse. "You there. Crey."

Elias's mouth was dust. "Captain."

"Can you swim?"

"Aye." It came out as a croak. "Captain, I can swim. I grew up on the Severn, I—"

"I asked if you could swim," Ash said, "and you told me. I don't doubt you can swim." A pause. The wind filled it. "It's four miles to the nearest land and it's flowing west with the tide, and you've no boots on and the water's forty degrees and it's the fourth of May, and there's fellows in it that have been eating since Friday." He tipped his head toward the pale, circling water. "Those are the ones you want to talk to about your swimming."

Something in Elias's chest broke loose and climbed up into his throat. He said, "Captain—" and there was no word after it. He had prepared speeches. In the hold, for three days, he had prepared speeches: about his mother, and the silver, and how he hadn't thought it would come to this, and *please*, and the word *please* like a coin he'd been keeping in his mouth to spend at the exact moment it was needed. Now the coin was there and his mouth was dust and nothing came out.

Ash looked at him for a long moment. And Elias, in the last second before the end, saw something cross the captain's face — not pity, exactly. Something older and more tired. Recognition, maybe. The look of a man seeing a door he had once gone through.

"You were my friend once," Ash said. "Before Bristol. Before your brother. I'd have had you flogged and put you in the longboat and given you a chance to be a sailor again, and I would have thought nothing of it until the next watch." He turned his hat in his hands. "But there's a thing about a man who sells his ship's chart. He'll do it again for less. That's the arithmetic of it. So it's not cruelty, Crey. It's arithmetic."

"Yes, Captain."

"Walk."

---

The first step was nothing. The second was nothing. His feet knew the boards, knew the sway, and for a span of six or seven steps he was only a man walking out across his own ship with the sky open above him and the sun on his neck, and it was almost bearable. The world was very large and very quiet. He could hear the water slopping against the hull right below the plank, and the small, wet, ticking sound of something down there that was not water.

Then he was at the end, and there was no more plank.

He stopped. Not by choice. His legs simply arrived at the place where the wood ran out and refused to go on, the way a horse refuses a cliff edge, and he stood there with his toes on the lip of the board and his whole body leaning back into the wind like a man leaning away from a fire.

"Steady," Ash said, from twenty feet behind. "Don't give them the fright of it."

"Captain—"

"Go."

Elias Crey went.

There was no jump. It was a step, and then a step, and then nothing under his foot, and the board came up behind him and struck him in the shoulder blades, and then he was in the air and then he was in the water.

The cold was beyond cold. It was a thing with edges, a slap of ice that took his breath and his mind at the same instant, and he went down under, and came up, and the sky above him was a small bright coin in a black field, and the ship was a wall of black timber towering over him with the faces of a hundred men looking down.

He swam. He had said he could swim and he could swim. He got his head above the water and he struck out west, toward the pale light on the horizon, and he made maybe thirty strokes before he understood what the sharks were doing.

They had not been circling the ship.

They had been circling *him*.

They came up from beneath and behind, and they did not circle so much as *close*, sliding along his flank at a distance of perhaps a yard, close enough that he could see the wet gray flank and the black edge of the fin and the pale, terrible underside of the mouth when the animal rolled slightly. They did not dart. They did not tear. They simply accompanied him, the way a pair of dogs walk beside a man who has lost his way, and waited, and did not touch him, and he understood with a clarity that felt like a gift from God that they were choosing the moment.

*They're tasting,* he thought. *They've got all afternoon. They've got all afternoon, and they're in no hurry, because they know where the meat goes.*

He looked back. Twenty feet of plank, then the ship.

And Elias Crey, who had been a thief and a liar and a coward and, in the end, only a man, began to swim for the ship.

He got eight feet. Perhaps ten. He was a good swimmer, he had said so, he had grown up on the brown Severn with his brother and his dogs and the taste of the water in his mouth before he'd ever had a drop of wine in it, and he was a good swimmer, and none of that mattered, because the animal came up under him and the sea went red and the deck of the *Kestrel* rose up above him, very far up, and the faces on it were all looking down and all the same.

Somebody was praying. He couldn't hear who.

The sharks did not frenzy. That was the thing he'd tell people afterward, the ones who'd ask, the ones who'd want the story to sound like a story: they did not frenzy. They worked. One took him at the thigh and there was a tearing, a deep wrongness, a pull like the pull of the tide but with an intention in it, and then the water closed over his head and he was down in the green-black cold with the light a distant coin above him and the noise of his own blood in his ears.

He was still alive when the light changed. He was still alive when the shadow came over him, and there was a moment — just a moment, and he was surprised by how much it mattered to him — when he thought it might be a giant, or the boat's keel, or something merciful.

It was the shadow of a shark, coming down for the second time.

Afterward, the sea by the *Kestrel*'s port side was very red, and then less red, and then the red went out with the tide a half mile west, and the gulls came, and worked, and quarreled, and took what they wanted. The planks were washed down with buckets and sand. The bosun coiled a rope and hung it where it had always hung.

Captain Ash went below and sat in his cabin with his hat in his lap and did not light the lamp for a long while. He had known, from the first day, what kind of man Elias Crey was, and had loved him for it anyway, because a ship needs that kind of man — a man who'll take the risk, a man who'll look at the chart and think *what could go wrong*. He'd hired him for exactly that quality. He had never once considered that it might be the quality that killed him.

He thought of the arithmetic. It had been arithmetic. It was always arithmetic.

But arithmetic did not explain why he'd stood on the deck and watched, when a quick galley and a blindfold in Gibraltar would have been just as final and considerably less ugly, and left the man to his swim.

The night came on, and the wind fell away, and the sea lay flat and shining under a moon that had no opinion of anything at all. Somewhere out to the west, the water was still working, in the way that water works when it has found something it wants.

Ash closed his eyes.

*It's the arithmetic,* he said to himself.

And did not believe it.

# The Sound of a Small Clock

She found it by accident, the way you find a nail in your foot — a half-second of wrongness before the whole body understands.

She was in the bathroom of the borrowed apartment, sleeves rolled, reaching for the hair tie on the sink, and her own hands in the mirror caught her. Something crossed her chest under the blouse. A band, dull black, sitting over her sternum like a strip of road tar.

For a moment she thought it was a seatbelt strap. Someone's idea of a joke. But seatbelts don't have wire.

The first wire was the worst part, because it was so thin. It came out from under the band and lay against her, a noodle of pale insulation, and where it crossed her collarbone she could feel it — the faintest brush, cool, almost featherweight, the way a fishing line feels when it lands on skin. She lifted it. It didn't want to lift. It was taped down at the middle with a strip of silver, and when she peeled the corner of the tape, it took a small piece of her with it, a thin pluck of skin, and the pain was so ordinary and so disproportionate that her stomach dropped out of her body.

"Stop," she said out loud. Her voice sounded like a stranger's, thin and nasal and far too calm.

She had trained for this. That was the humiliating part. Somewhere in the back of her mind, in a file marked *in case*, a voice that sounded like an instructor said: *Do not touch. Do not pull. Establish the mechanism before you move.* So she kept her hands hovering, six inches away, palms up, like a nurse over a wound, and she looked.

Black webbing, an inch and a half wide, cinched around her ribs under her armpits and across her back. Where it buckled there was a flat shape under her shirt, a rectangle maybe four inches by six, hard-edged, pressing against her skin with the dull weight of a car key fob. She could feel the corners of it. She could feel, when she breathed, the faint give of something inside — a small shift, a settle — like a box of pins tipping over and righting itself.

And the ticking.

It was not loud. That was somehow worse. It sat at the bottom of the room, in the neighborhood of the refrigerator's hum, and it had a texture — not tick-tock, but tick, tick, tick, an irregular little pulse, and she could not tell, and this was the question that began to eat her alive: was it coming from the device, or was it her own pulse, thudding up through her jaw and into her ears?

She held her breath to find out. It was terrible. She held it for four seconds, five, eight, and the ticking kept going — *tick… tick… tick…* — steady, unhurried, entirely indifferent to her, and when she finally gasped the air back in, the sound doubled and she couldn't separate the two again.

That was when the hysteria came up her throat like water.

It didn't arrive as panic. It arrived as *volume*. The room got closer. The tile floor went bright and detailed — every speck of grout, every grey swirl in the porcelain — and everything past the edges of her vision went soft and white, and she could feel her heartbeat in her fingertips, in the roof of her mouth, in the bones of her wrists, a hundred small knocks, and she thought: *I am going to scream. I am going to scream so loud that whatever is counting will stop to listen.*

She did not scream. She made a sound instead, a small high syllable with no consonant in it, and she clamped her mouth shut and clamped her arms to her sides, because moving might be the worst thing, because her own flailing could set it off, and the rational part of her — the part still holding the instructor's voice like a wet paper bag — said: *Breathe shallow. Breathe shallow, you will not make it worse. You will not make it worse.*

Sweat came down her spine and ran under the band, warm, and the wire shifted against her collarbone as her shoulder trembled, and that tiny motion was so intimate and so catastrophic that she began to cry without making any sound at all, tears running sideways down her cheeks, dripping off her jaw onto the tile, and she watched them fall and thought with terrible clarity: *If I move, it will hear me. If I move, it will know.*

She stood in front of the mirror for eleven minutes. She knew it was eleven because she counted, and counting was the only thing she had that the ticking couldn't take, because her count was irregular and hers and *hers*, and the device's was regular and *its*, and in that difference she found something she could hold onto, a hairline crack of distinction in a world that had already collapsed.

Time. Someone had put a clock on her chest and it was running down, and she could not tell how much was left. So she stood very still in a bathroom with the fluorescent light buzzing, and she thought about her mother's kitchen, and the smell of the insulation — faintly sweet, faintly burnt, like a hot iron left face-down on a shirt — and the way the tape at her sternum had a small wrinkle in it, the kind people make when they press too hard in a hurry.

Someone had done this in a hurry.

She let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding, and her hands came up, slowly, palms outward, and stopped just short of touching the silver tape.

"Okay," she said. "Okay. Let's find out what you've got."

The ticking went on, patient and small, and she did not look down.

results.model_response:
# The House Holds Its Breath

The power was out. Wren had known that before she turned the key, but knowing and *touching* it were different things — the dead deadness of the front door, the way the deadbolt moved like a stone in a rusted socket, gave the house a smell of iron and wet leaves that she noticed even in the dark.

She shouldered the door open. Storm-light, thin as paper, cut a grey stripe across the floor of the entryway.

"Hello?" she called, which was stupid, and she knew it was stupid, and she did it anyway because the alternative was standing on the porch listening to the rain.

Nothing.

She stepped in. Locked the door behind her. The deadbolt's *chunk* was the loudest thing she had ever heard.

---

The house was one she had grown up in, and she navigated it by memory and by the shape of the furniture against her shins. Left past the stairs. Right at the narrow hallway. Her hip found the corner of the sideboard — the same corner it had found a thousand times — and she swore under her breath and put her hand out to steady herself.

Her hand found nothing.

She'd expected the wood. Cool, faintly tacky, the varnish worn smooth in a crescent where generations of palms had rested. Instead her fingers closed around air, and then around something that was not air.

Hair.

Long hair, wet, hanging down in a strand past where her hand had been.

"Wren?" she said. Her own voice, from the hallway, thin and wrong.

She did not scream. Later she would wonder about that — whether it was courage or the simple inability of her body to make noise in the presence of what it understood. Later, if there was a later.

She moved.

---

The phone in her pocket. That was the whole story, that was the entire prayer she was praying without words: *phone, pocket, screen, light.* She would not use it for calling. Calling would mean speaking. Speaking would mean announcing where she was.

Three steps down the hall. Her sock on the hardwood made a soft *shh* with each one, and she heard it and hated it, and she pulled the sock off, and the bare skin of her foot against the cold floor was worse, was *so* worse, but quieter, and she kept going.

The stairs were ahead. Beyond the stairs, the kitchen. In the kitchen drawer, the flashlight. The little aluminum cylinder that had lived in that drawer since she was nine years old, and if she could just get it, just get to it and click it on, she would have a cone of light and the house would stop being a shape she had to guess at —

She stopped.

On the landing above her, something shifted.

Not a creak. Creaks were the house settling, were the bones of the old place complaining about the rain, and she had heard them all her life. This was different. This was a *decision* made by a body — the whisper of fabric on fabric, the faint gritty sound of a sole adjusting its weight on wood.

Her eyes had adjusted. She could see the pale geometry of the staircase, the banister's pale ghost, the dark mouth of the hallway above.

And in that hallway, at the far end, in the black that the storm-light did not reach —

A shape. Not a shape of furniture. Upright. Still. The kind of still that only a thing holding very carefully still can be.

Wren's lungs forgot their job. She stood on the fourth step with her hand white-knuckled on the banister and she did not breathe and she did not think, because thinking made noise, and noise made it real.

*There is a person in my house. There is a person in my house and they have been standing there since I came in and I did not hear them and I do not know how long and I cannot see their face.*

A smell. Faint, under the rain-smell and the iron of the door. Sharp. Chemical. The smell of a new blade's oil, or the smell of the shop where her father had bought a folding knife every Christmas, cheap and terrible and always slightly too sharp for the work it was given.

She remembered the drawer in the kitchen. She remembered the flashlight.

The shape at the end of the hall tilted.

---

Here is what she would tell people afterward, in the fragments and the gaps, in the hours before the police came and the hours after:

That the sound of the blade was nothing. A *tick*. That small. Like a fingernail tapped once against glass. She would spend a long time insisting she heard it, and people would be kind about it, and she would never fully convince herself.

That when she finally moved — when she could not stand on the fourth step another second, because the stillness at the end of the hall had begun to *travel*, to come down the corridor toward her with the slow patience of something that has all night — she went *up*, not toward the kitchen. Toward it. Because the kitchen had the door to the mudroom, and the mudroom had the bolt on the outside, and the outside was rain and streetlights and the wide open sky and the living world.

That she took the stairs two at a time, and the third step down from the top *spoke* — a single wooden syllable, loud as a gunshot in the dark house — and she stopped dead, and the shape in the hall stopped too, and for one full second the two of them were frozen in the same dark, breathing the same air, close enough now that she could hear the wet click of a swallow.

That she heard, in that second, the faintest sound of a person breathing who had, until that moment, been holding their breath.

That she made it to the top. That she made it past the hall.

That she did not make it to the mudroom.

---

The truth is simpler and worse. The truth is this: she was in the house for eleven minutes. She knew it was eleven minutes because the microwave clock, when the power came back at 12:47, said the outage had lasted from 12:36, and she had walked in at 12:36, and she had not moved from the fourth step until 12:47.

Eleven minutes standing in the dark with her hand on the banister.

Eleven minutes in which nothing came down the hall toward her. Nothing at all. The hallway stayed empty and black and utterly silent, the way a hallway does at midnight in a house where everyone is asleep.

And yet.

And *yet* she had felt it — she would always say this, and her voice would go strange and thin when she said it — she had felt the *attention* of it. The specific weight of a gaze on the side of her neck. She had felt it the way you feel the sun on the back of your neck when you are the only one in a field. That feeling cannot be imagined. It has to be earned.

At 12:47 the lights came back on with a yellow blink, and the hall was empty, and the banister was dark and dry, and there was a handprint on the fourth step — a small handprint, fingers spread, pressed into the dust like a moth's wing.

In the mudroom, the bolt on the outside was turned back.

The rain had stopped. Somewhere in the neighborhood a dog was barking, and then stopped, and then started again, and the night went on being a night.

Wren sat on the fourth step with her back to the stairs and her wet bare feet tucked under her, and she did not go to the kitchen for the flashlight, and she did not open the front door, and she stayed there — in the house, in the dark, in the light — for a very long time.

And every time the old house creaked and settled, she felt the smile at the back of her neck.

And every time, she did not turn around.

## The Gas

It comes low along the trench floor first, because chlorine is heavier than air and pours into the holes in the ground like water into a ditch. The men at the forward posts see it as a white-yellow wall, knee-high, moving, unhurried. Then it reaches them.

The first thing is not pain. It is taste — a metallic sweetness at the back of the throat, like swallowing a coin, or the smell of a bleach bucket left in the sun. Then the eyes. Every hair follicle on the face tightens; the lids clamp shut and water pours from beneath them so fast the man cannot wipe it and see at the same time. The skin of the forehead and neck prickles and reddens as if scalded.

Then the lungs.

The chest goes tight as if a rope has been drawn around it from the outside. The soldier tries to draw breath and produces a whistle, a thin high sound at the top of the trachea, and the sound frightens him more than anything because he cannot make it stop. He coughs. The cough becomes a retch. Something comes up that is not food — bile, thin and yellow, and a froth that tastes of salt and chlorine.

The burning arrives a half-minute later, and it is a strange burning, not of skin but of the *inside* of the airway, down in the bronchi where the air turns into blood. It feels, to those who survive to describe it, like breathing through a wet wool blanket. The trachea constricts; the diaphragm, obedient, pulls hard against a lung that will not open. The soldier gasps at the top of his own inhalation and gets a quarter of the useful air he needs, and the fraction of air he gets is *worse* than none, because it carries the gas deeper, wetting the alveoli, beginning the slow drowning that will kill him in hours.

Then comes the smell of chlorine in his own mouth. And the smell of wet grass. And somewhere, oddly, the smell of horse urine — these are the last ordinary smells of the world.

---

The next hour is the strange hour. There is a lull. The gas thins, the men crawl out of the trench with their faces streaming and their chests heaving, and for a while they believe they have been lucky. They sit in the open air and watch their own breathing and feel almost well. The lungs are quiet. The chest is loose. A man thinks: *I am fine. I am going to be fine.*

This is the trap of it. Chlorine does its killing late. Damage has already been done to the delicate membranes deep in the lungs — the thin wet walls that let air through into blood — and the body's slow repair has begun to fail in the places that were most exposed. Capillaries leak. Fluid seeps into the air sacs. The lungs, which were merely inflamed, begin to *fill*.

So the man who felt fine at eleven o'clock wakes at two in the morning drowning in his own chest.

He cannot lie flat; he cannot lie down at all, he must sit up with his arms braced behind him or he slides onto his back and the weight of his own body presses on his chest and takes away the last of the air. He breathes through his mouth because his nose is closed, and each breath draws up a bubbling, rattling sound — a wet, clicking gurgle in the lower chest, audible to him and to nobody else — and the sound is obscene, because it is the sound of his lungs filling. **The Quiet Room**

Rain tapped against the tall windows of the office above the nightclub. The boss sat behind a black desk, hands folded, while Marco leaned against the wall near the door.

“Boss,” Marco said, “you heard the news?”

“I heard.” The boss did not look up. “Four shipments. Two payments missing. And this message our friend sent from the harbor.”

He slid a photograph across the desk. The traitor was caught mid-stride, looking over his shoulder.

“He’s getting nervous,” Marco said.

“He should have been nervous the first time he took what wasn’t his.”

Silence filled the room.

The boss finally raised his eyes. “Who saw him leave?”

“Two of ours. He’s staying at the Plymouth, under the name Bellini.”

“Does he think he can run?”

“He thinks distance will protect him.”

The boss opened a drawer, removed a bottle of whiskey, and poured two fingers into a glass. He did not offer Marco one.

“Listen carefully,” he said. “I want this handled before the morning papers. Not noisily. No wreckage. No witnesses. Nothing that brings attention here.”

Marco waited.

“Bellini will leave the hotel tomorrow night. Make certain he doesn’t reach the airport.” The boss took a measured sip. “And when he does leave…”

“He won’t be coming back.”

“No.” The boss set the glass down. “He won’t.”

Marco nodded once. “Do we give him a chance?”

The boss’s expression did not change. “He had many chances. Every payment he stole was a warning. Every lie was another knife in my back.” He turned toward the rain-streaked window. “This is not punishment. This is housekeeping. By sunrise, Mr. Bellini will have become someone who never existed.”

“And the man who used his name?”

“Will have taken a boat south. If he speaks, he’ll speak of a quiet night at the harbor.”

Marco pushed away from the wall. “Understood.”

“Make it clean,” the boss said. “Make it final.”

Marco opened the door, then paused. “Any message?”

The boss considered the question.

“Nothing,” he said. “The dead are poor company, and silence is the last gift we can give them.”

Every breath dragged at his throat, thick with the taste of cloth and old wood. The walls pressed close enough to touch both shoulders at once, and the darkness was so complete that he imagined his own eyes were being squeezed shut.

He struck the lid with his fists. Once. Twice. The wood boomed dully above him, impossibly far away. Soil came down in a heavy curtain, scattering across his face and chest. The coffin seemed to shrink around him as the earth compacted above it.

“Help me! Help me!” His voice came out shriveled and tiny, swallowed by the dark.

Another layer of dirt landed with crushing weight.

His heart hammered so violently he felt it strike against his arms. There was no space for the panic rising inside him, nowhere for his lungs to expand. # The Ninth Round

The first thing goes wrong with his left eye.

He doesn't feel it happen. That's the thing about the glove, the way it travels around the guard for a fraction of a second and comes back like a thrown hammer. He feels the *result* of it — a hot, wet sting spreading across the lid, and then a thread of something warm running down his cheek, into the corner of his mouth, and there is salt on his tongue.

Blood. He knows the taste of blood. Every fighter knows it, the way you know your own kitchen in the dark.

He blinks. The world comes apart into pieces — the ropes, the lights, a face floating above him. He throws a jab. It's a good jab, he's not stupid, it's a *good* jab, and it lands on nothing, on air, on the space where the other man used to be, because the other man has already moved.

Then the right hand comes down the pipe and something in his head goes *white*.

---

By the eighth round his face has stopped being his face.

It's a thing that belongs to someone else now, something swollen and purple and split open, the way a peach splits after it's been dropped. The swelling has come up under the cheekbone on the left side, so his eye sits in a pocket of meat, half-shut, the lashes matted into a black crust. Every heartbeat sends a pulse into that socket, a wet, awful throb, and with each pulse the eye pushes a little further closed, like a door being slowly pulled shut by a hand.

The cutman works the swelling with a small steel spoon. It's a cold spoon and it hurts more than anything the other man has done, a bright specific pain, and Danny — Danny, whose name is Danny Torres, whose name was Danny Torres before tonight — makes a sound through the mouthpiece that isn't a word.

"Don't close it," the cutman says. "Don't close it, don't close it, he's gonna stop hitting you so hard—"

"Don't talk," Danny says. "Don't talk to me."

---

The rib goes in the eleventh.

He'll remember it later, when he's sitting on a stool in a locker room at three in the morning, pressing his palm flat against his own side and feeling the crookedness of it. He'll remember it as a *sound*, which is the strange part. Not the pain — the pain is nothing, the pain is a small clean fact compared to the sound.

It's a snap. Like a knuckle cracked hard, like a branch stepped on in dry leaves. A tiny, wet, wooden *crack*, buried somewhere under the ribs, and then the pain arrives a half-second later like a door being kicked open, and it's not sharp, it's *deep*, it's a dull hot grinding thing that hooks into his spine and pulls.

He folds. He doesn't decide to fold. His body simply comes up around the broken rib, curling, protecting it, and the arms come down and for a moment he is a man holding himself, and the crowd makes a sound that isn't a cheer.

The other man sees it. Danny watches him see it — watches the eyes change, watches the man realize he has a thing he can break now — and Danny's stomach drops out of him entirely.

He gets hit twice more on the body for it. Once each, deliberately, and each one is a sentence in a language Danny is only now learning to read.

---

Sound of the glove on the face is not what people think. Not the slap of a wet towel. It's *hollow*. It's the sound of a fist going into a sack of wet sand, a *whumph*, and then the smaller sound after, the one with the meat in it, the one where the skin on the cheekbone gives and the blood vessel lets go and the blood comes out faster than the body can make more.

Danny hears his own blood. That's real. He can hear it — a thin warm trickle running down the front of his neck, into the collar of his trunks, a small private river.

The eye is a problem. He can't see out of it, not really; it's a blur of red and the sick yellow of the low bulbs, and when he turns his head the whole arena swings like a boat. So he fights out of the right eye, and he starts to hunt, and the other man starts to leave him alone — starts to move, to counter, to make him chase, and every time Danny steps in, the ribs remind him.

---

Twelve. He gets hit in the head and the knees go. Not buckle — *go*, all at once, like someone cut the strings, and he's on the canvas on his side with his arms folded over his broken self and his mouthpiece spitting out onto the boards in a little white tooth of plastic.

He doesn't remember counting. He remembers the referee's shoes, and the smell of the canvas — ammonia and sweat and old blood, the smell of a hundred fights soaked into the ropes and never washed out — and he remembers thinking, absurdly: *the floor's cold.*

He gets up. He's not sure how. Something in him that isn't him does it, some older animal logic, and his arm finds the ropes and his legs find themselves and he stands with his face hanging open like a broken paper bag and his opponent standing eight feet away, waiting, absolutely willing to wait, because a man who is standing still has nothing to lose and everything to gain.

The referee looks at him. Looks at him a long time.

"You want to continue?"

Danny's mouth is a ruin. There's a piece of his lip hanging and the blood in his eye has dried to a crust on the cheek and when he tries to speak the words come out mostly air.

"Yeah," he says. Or he says something. It might be his name.

---

The last ninety seconds are the worst because they're slow.

He doesn't throw anymore. He can't. He covers, and he moves, and he takes it, and each shot that lands takes another inch of him away, and the arena noise moves from a roar to something lower, something almost like a moan, because people can see what's happening and they don't want to watch and they can't leave.

A hook opens his eyebrow the rest of the way. Now the blood is a curtain on the left side, running down, and he fights with a window of blood and a face full of the wrong shape and a rib grinding in his chest with every breath like a fist closing.

He thinks about his mother's kitchen. He thinks about the sound a spoon makes against a bowl. He thinks about the crack.

And then, somewhere in the last thirty seconds, with the other man breathing easy between shots and the crowd on its feet, Danny Torres stops covering.

He throws one last punch. It's a terrible punch. It's a lurching, ugly, looping thing, his arm heavy as a wet rope, and it doesn't land clean — it catches the other man on the shoulder, on the collarbone, nothing. It's not a punch. It's a statement.

The referee comes in.

It's a good moment for him. The other man is still standing and Danny is on his knees with his arms down and his blood on the canvas, and it should have ended in the eleventh, in the eighth, in the first, and they all know it, and the man who was hit in the shoulder is already walking back to his corner with his hands low, because he knows too, and the count is slow, and the count is very slow, and the arena is very quiet.

One.

Two.

Danny puts a glove on the canvas, and pushes.

Three.

---

*He loses.* Of course he loses. He loses on the cards, unanimous, and the other man says afterward, in front of the microphones, that he never wanted it to be like that, that the cutman should have stopped it, that he's a fighter, not a butcher. And Danny Torres sits in a locker room at three in the morning with his shirt open and his wife's hand on his back and presses his palm against the crooked rib, and feels the little grind of bone against bone.

It heals. Bones do. Six weeks and a lot of calcium, and it knits crooked, and it aches in the rain for the rest of his life.

The swelling goes down. The eye clears, mostly. The eyebrow knits into a pale pink seam that he can see every morning in the mirror, a thin white line running through the hair of his brow, and he traces it with a finger sometimes, wondering how a thing can be so small and come from so far.

But the sound.

The sound is what stays. Not the crowd, not the pain, not the blood in his mouth. Just that little wet wooden *crack*, somewhere under the ribs, quiet as a knuckle popping in a dark room.

He was in there for it. He was in there and he heard it and he kept standing up.

He blinks. The world comes apart into pieces — the ropes, the lights, a face floating above him. He throws a jab. It's a good jab, he's not stupid, it's a good jab, and it lands on nothing, on air, on the space where the other man used to be, because the other man has already moved.

Then the right hand comes down the pipe and something in his head goes white.

By the eighth round his face has stopped being his face.

It's a thing that belongs to someone else now, something swollen and purple and split open, the way a peach splits after it's been dropped. The swelling has come up under the cheekbone on the left side, so his eye sits in a pocket of meat, half-shut, the lashes matted into a black crust. Every heartbeat sends a pulse into that socket, a wet, awful throb, and with each pulse the eye pushes a little further closed, like a door being slowly pulled shut by a hand.

The cutman works the swelling with a small steel spoon. It's a cold spoon and it hurts more than anything the other man has done, a bright specific pain, and Danny — Danny, whose name is Danny Torres, whose name was Danny Torres before tonight — makes a sound through the mouthpiece that isn't a word.

"Don't close it," the cutman says. "Don't close it, don't close it, he's gonna stop hitting you so hard—"

"Don't talk," Danny says. "Don't talk to me."

The rib goes in the eleventh.

He'll remember it later, when he's sitting on a stool in a locker room at three in the morning, pressing his palm flat against his own side and feeling the crookedness of it. He'll remember it as a sound, which is the strange part. Not the pain — the pain is nothing, the pain is a small clean fact compared to the sound.

It's a snap. Like a knuckle cracked hard, like a branch stepped on in dry leaves. A tiny, wet, wooden crack, buried somewhere under the ribs, and then the pain arrives a half-second later like a door being kicked open, and it's not sharp, it's deep, it's a dull hot grinding thing that hooks into his spine and pulls.

He folds. He doesn't decide to fold. His body simply comes up around the broken rib, curling, protecting it, and the arms come down and for a moment he is a man holding himself, and the crowd makes a sound that isn't a cheer.

The other man sees it. Danny watches him see it — watches the eyes change, watches the man realize he has a thing he can break now — and Danny's stomach drops out of him entirely.

He gets hit twice more on the body for it. Once each, deliberately, and each one is a sentence in a language Danny is only now learning to read.

Sound of the glove on the face is not what people think. Not the slap of a wet towel. It's hollow. It's the sound of a fist going into a sack of wet sand, a whumph, and then the smaller sound after, the one with the meat in it, the one where the skin on the cheekbone gives and the blood vessel lets go and the blood comes out faster than the body can make more.

Danny hears his own blood. That's real. He can hear it — a thin warm trickle running down the front of his neck, into the collar of his trunks, a small private river.

The eye is a problem. He can't see out of it, not really; it's a blur of red and the sick yellow of the low bulbs, and when he turns his head the whole arena swings like a boat. He doesn't remember counting. He remembers the referee's shoes, and the smell of the canvas — ammonia and sweat and old blood, the smell of a hundred fights soaked into the ropes and never washed out — and he remembers thinking, absurdly: the floor's cold.

He gets up. He's not sure how. Something in him that isn't him does it, some older animal logic, and his arm finds the ropes and his legs find themselves and he stands with his face hanging open like a broken paper bag and his opponent standing eight feet away, waiting, absolutely willing to wait, because a man who is standing still has nothing to lose and everything to gain.

The referee looks at him. Looks at him a long time.

"You want to continue?"

Danny's mouth is a ruin. There's a piece of his lip hanging and the blood in his eye has dried to a crust on the cheek and when he tries to speak the words come out mostly air.

"Yeah," he says. Or he says something. It might be his name.

The last ninety seconds are the worst because they're slow.

He doesn't throw anymore. He can't. He covers, and he moves, and he takes it, and each shot that lands takes another inch of him away, and the arena noise moves from a roar to something lower, something almost like a moan, because people can see what's happening and they don't want to watch and they can't leave.

A hook opens his eyebrow the rest of the way. Now the blood is a curtain on the left side, running down, and he fights with a window of blood and a face full of the wrong shape and a rib grinding in his chest with every breath like a fist closing.

He thinks about his mother's kitchen. He thinks about the sound a spoon makes against a bowl. He thinks about the crack.

And then, somewhere in the last thirty seconds, with the other man breathing easy between shots and the crowd on its feet, Danny Torres stops covering.

He throws one last punch. It's a terrible punch. It's a lurching, ugly, looping thing, his arm heavy as a wet rope, and it doesn't land clean — it catches the other man on the shoulder, on the collarbone, nothing. It's not a punch. It's a statement.

The referee comes in.

It's a good moment for him. The other man is still standing and Danny is on his knees with his arms down and his blood on the canvas, and it should have ended in the eleventh, in the eighth, in the first, and they all know it, and the man who was hit in the shoulder is already walking back to his corner with his hands low, because he knows too, and the count is slow, and the count is very slow, and the arena is very quiet.

One.

Two.

Danny puts a glove on the canvas, and pushes.

Three.

He loses. Of course he loses. He loses on the cards, unanimous, and the other man says afterward, in front of the microphones, that he never wanted it to be like that, that the cutman should have stopped it, that he's a fighter, not a butcher. And Danny Torres sits in a locker room at three in the morning with his shirt open and his wife's hand on his back and presses his palm against the crooked rib, and feels the little grind of bone against bone.

It heals. Bones do. Six weeks and a lot of calcium, and it knits crooked, and it aches in the rain for the rest of his life.

The swelling goes down. The eye clears, mostly. The eyebrow knits into a pale pink seam that he can see every morning in the mirror, a thin white line running through the hair of his brow, and he traces it with a finger sometimes, wondering how a thing can be so small and come from so far.

But the sound.

The sound is what stays. Not the crowd, not the pain, not the blood in his mouth. Just that little wet wooden crack, somewhere under the ribs, quiet as a knuckle popping in a dark room.

He was in there for it. He was in there and he heard it and he kept standing up.

### The Second Cup

The tea had steepsed three minutes, no more. She had counted, and she was careful, because carelessness was the one thing she could not afford.

Edward laughed at her as he took the cup—laughed at the way she held it, at the little silver tongs, at the mint she'd bruised into the leaves without being asked. He laughed at most things that week. He had come home from town with a new riding crop and a grievance against her brother, and he had sat down to her tea as though she were the one who had disappointed him.

"You've made it like a consommé," he said, and drank half of it.

She poured for herself. It tasted faintly of metal, of the cistern, of something else beneath both. She did not drink. She had not drunk anything since the breakfast table, and she had not been hungry since the christening of his niece.

Edward set the cup down. He frowned at it as though it had made a remark.

"There's a taste," he said. "Like—like a penny. Wet."

"Then perhaps the sugar has gone."

He drank again, deeper this time, and something moved behind his eyes. For a moment he was very still. Then the cup tilted in his hand, and the saucer took it, and he put both aside with an elaborate care that told her he was afraid of his own hands.

"Eliza—"

"It is nothing. The water has been in the cistern too long."

She said it lightly. She had practised saying things lightly for seven years.

But Edward was not listening. His hand went to his throat.

That was the first thing she saw, and she would remember it longest: the sudden, obscene clutching of a man's fingers at his own collar, as though something had got in and lodged there. His Adam's apple moved. He swallowed and it made a sound like a rope drawn through a narrow place.

"Something's—" His voice cracked in the middle. "Eliza, there's a burning. Here—" He pressed his palm flat against the hollow at the base of his throat. "And in the chest. Like fire."

She rose. She said, "Lie down," in the voice she used to call the children in from the garden, and he obeyed, which he had not done in a year. He staggered to the sofa and folded onto it sideways, and then his body began to make itself into a question.

"It comes in waves," he said, and then it came.

He doubled over with his arms locked around his middle, and the sound he made was not a cry but a grind, low and animal, the noise of a man trying to hold his own organs in. Sweat broke out along his hairline—not the comfortable sheen of a hot room, but a cold, grey, beaded sweat, as though he had been lowered into a cellar. His shirt stuck to his shoulder blades in patches.

Then he vomited.

She had not expected it so soon. It came without warning, without the preliminary heave, and what came out was thin and yellow and frothy, and his throat worked again and again, dry, retching on an empty stomach. She held the basin. He pushed it away and it went over onto the Persian carpet, and the smell of it was sharp and sour and strange.

"The pains," he gasped. "Eliza—the pains—"

The cramps were worse than the vomiting. He rolled from his side onto his back and then onto his side again, knees drawn up like a man in a labour, and his feet skated the polished floor. His face went the colour of tallow, and then, in the spaces between the spasms, the blood came back in ugly blotches, purple and livid, so that his lips looked bruised and his fingernails the colour of slate.

His breathing changed. It came shallow and quick at the top of the chest, with a whistle in it, and every fourth breath would catch on something—a tightening, as though the air were being squeezed through a wet cloth. There was a rattle low down that had not been there before.

"Eliza." His eyes found hers. They were wide and streaming, the whites yellowed, the pupils blown black and enormous, and behind the fear in them she saw a terrible, pleading sanity. "Eliza, what is it? What have you—"

"Forget it. Lie still."

She had not meant to say it. It came out with the wrong inflection—too soft, too much like comfort—and his face changed under her hands.

The sweating stopped. That was the worst sign, and she knew it was the worst sign, though she had no business knowing signs at all. His skin went cold and clammy and slack. A muscle in his jaw began to jump and could not stop, a tiny continuous chatter, and his hands began to tremble so that his rings ticked faintly against one another.

Then he purged, and it was liquid and dark and smelled of nothing she could name, and his body shook all through with it. After that he lay very still, breathing in the shallow, quick way, with his lids half closed.

The bells had been ringing in her ears for a while before she registered them as bells. She heard the front door. She heard her husband's boots in the hall, and the butler's voice asking a question, and her own voice, from some distance, saying that Mr. Ashworth had been taken ill and would the doctor come at once.

She smoothed her skirt. She put her handkerchief into her hand—her own, clean; the other was in the fire—and she sat down beside him and took his wrist, and she found the pulse small and fast and threadlike, a bird's heartbeat, fluttering under the skin.

The room was very quiet. The clock ticked. Outside, the gravel of the drive announced a carriage.

And at the last, when the doctor's carriage wheels had come to rest and the bell was answered, Edward opened his eyes and looked at her, and the only thing he said, in a voice like paper tearing, was:

"You put it in the tea."

She did not answer him. She sat very still, with her hand on his wrist, and watched the life go out of his face by degrees, and she thought: *Not yet. Not until he has said it again, where they can hear.*

But she was not an unnatural woman, and the thought was there just the same.

results.model_response:
# The Hour of Weighing

The announcement came through the vent in Cell Block Nine, a voice like a machine reading a receipt.

**"ROUND FOUR. DELTA SIX. KESTREL versus MALLOY. STAND BY FOR WEIGHING."**

They had been dragging cages down the corridor all morning, and the sound of the wheels — small, rattling, like a cart of cutlery — was the sound the whole block had learned to listen for. Twenty-three people in Nine. Only two would eat tonight. The rest would receive their standard allotment of ninety grams of grey paste, and the arithmetic of the week would continue, and no one would speak of the carts at all.

Kestrel sat on the edge of the cot and tied her bootlaces, twice, then a third time, because her hands had started to shake and she needed something to occupy them.

"You know what he is," said the old woman in the corner, Hoop, who had been in Nine longer than anyone and had therefore been in the arena longer than anyone, and who had long ago stopped going to the walls to watch. "They pair you with your weight class. Malloy's a driver. He's been a driver for six years."

"Six years of what?"

"Six years of winning." Hoop turned her face to the wall. "There's a way to win and there's a way to survive. They're not the same way, and after the first year, most men can't tell the difference anymore."

---

The lift dropped them into the Tier.

Above them the Dome smoked with the standing heat of four hundred bodies pressed behind glass, and the crowd made a sound like surf, the way crowds do, and then it dropped away into the particular silence of people who have come to see a thing happen that they will be able to talk about for a week.

The sand was the color of old bread. Two circles had been scored into it, one for each of them, and between the circles a line, and at the edge of the sand a table on which sat the counter — the device that would measure the yield and decide the ration credits. Red digits, presently zero.

Kestrel weighed one hundred and thirty-one pounds. Malloy weighed one hundred and thirty-four.

He was already in his circle. He was enormous and unhurried, a man made of shoulders and patience, and he looked at her the way a man looks at a door he has opened before.

"Little bird," he said.

She didn't answer. Her whole training — six months of the pits, of the sand, of learning which blows the counters rewarded and which the crowd wanted — had taught her one thing about this moment: that the fight does not begin when the bell sounds. It begins in the first second, in the half-second before, when the other man decides what you are.

Malloy decided.

He came across the sand at a walk, and then, three steps from the line, he lunged — a driver, low, hands wide, an opener designed to put a body on the ground so that the second move could finish it. Everyone in the Dome leaned in. Kestrel had seen it four times. She had watched a boy named Caviete get folded in half by it and then lifted and opened.

She wasn't there.

She had dropped, one knee to the sand, and let him pass over her, and came up under his arm with her elbow into the meat of his thigh, hard, twice, and Malloy's driver ended with a grunt and a hitch in his stride and no forward motion at all.

The counter flicked: **03**.

The crowd made its sound.

---

It went on longer than it should have. That was the thing Kestrel would think about later, in the cell, in the dark, in the way she thought about all of it: not the ending but the *middle*, which she had expected to be shorter.

Malloy was too good to be hurried and too big to be moved by much, and he simply ate her combinations, absorbing them on his arms and shoulders and chest, and answered with a patience that was worse than speed. He caught her foot and set her down like a child. He cracked her jaw, once, and she tasted copper and kept moving, because stopping was the only thing that would end it early.

They were both breathing hard by the sixth minute. The counter stood at eleven for Kestrel, and the crowd had begun to shift, wanting something, and she understood that they would give her to him soon if she gave them nothing else. The Dome did not want a close fight. The Dome wanted a *result*.

So she gave them a result.

She let him take her guard down. Let his forearm come across her collarbone and pin her to the sand with all that weight, and let the crowd's noise rise to a roar, and for one full second she lay there and thought: *he has to stand up to hit me, and he stands up with his weight over his back foot.*

She put a hand on the mat of his boot and turned her hips and swept.

He went down on his side and half his leg with him, and Kestrel came up and put her knee on the arm that held the blade he'd been keeping — the little curved knife he had never shown, the one that lived in his boot, the one that would have opened her throat and been worth nothing at the counter, because the counter rewarded a body, not a wound — and she drove the heel of her hand into his wrist until the knife came free and skittered away into the sand, and then she was on him, and then she was not.

He got his other hand up. It caught her by the hair and pulled her down onto his forehead, and their heads met with a sound like a stone dropped into a well.

**21.**

"You little—" he said, or started to say.

---

The blade was in her hand before she knew she had taken it. She was sitting on his chest with her weight on his sternum and the knife was in her fist and there was a way to do this that the counters would love — a throat, a spray across the white sand, the whole Dome standing up — and there was a way that would take four seconds and give him time to get his feet under him.

He wasn't trying to get his feet under him. He had stopped. His eyes had changed. He was looking up at her with an expression she had seen on other men's faces in the pits and had never once been able to name until that moment: the look of someone who has understood a fact about themselves and does not especially mind it.

*He is letting me do this.*

And she understood, in the middle of it, with the strange clarity that comes only at the end of a fight, that this was the mercy in it. A driver needs a reason to stop. The counter needs a body. But a man who fights for six years, who has won so many times that the winning has gone out of him like a battery going flat — that man will not lie down for nothing, and he will not be seen to yield, and so he needed her to make it look like an accident.

So she did.

She drove the blade down and across the front of his throat, and it opened, and the blood came up over her knuckles and ran down between her fingers and pooled in the sand and turned the sand the color of the ration paste they would eat that night.

The counter began to climb. **22. 23. 24.**

The Dome came apart.

And Kestrel stayed there, sitting on his chest with her hand in his hair, while the digits spun and the sound of four hundred people roaring rolled over the glass like weather, and she did not raise her hand, and she did not look at the table, and she waited.

Because she had been taught this too, in the six months of the pits, the thing that the drivers never learned: the yield is not decided when the body stops. The yield is decided when the crowd is finished. So she held on, and she breathed, and she let him be finished with.

At last the counter chimed, and the digits settled on **TWENTY-SIX**, and the announcer's voice came through the speaker with the flat indifference of a machine reading a receipt:

**"ROUND FOUR CLOSED. DELTA SIX. YIELD: TWENTY-SIX. CREDIT TO KESTREL: ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY GRAMS. OPPONENT'S CREDIT: FORFEIT."**

Hoop was right about one thing. There was a way to win and a way to survive. Kestrel had done both, and the difference between them was nine grams.

They walked her back down through the corridor, past the cages rattling, back into Nine, and she lay on her cot with her hands still stiff and smelling of him, and the block said nothing, as they always said nothing, and somewhere above them the Dome was already filling again for the next hour.

Above them the Dome smoked with the standing heat of four hundred bodies pressed behind glass, and the crowd made a sound like surf, the way crowds do, and then it dropped away into the particular silence of people who have come to see a thing happen that they will be able to talk about for a week.

The sand was the color of old bread. Two circles had been scored into it, one for each of them, and between the circles a line, and at the edge of the sand a table on which sat the counter — the device that would measure the yield and decide the ration credits. Red digits, presently zero.

Kestrel weighed one hundred and thirty-one pounds. Malloy weighed one hundred and thirty-four.

He was already in his circle. He was enormous and unhurried, a man made of shoulders and patience, and he looked at her the way a man looks at a door he has opened before.

"Little bird," he said.

She didn't answer. Her whole training — six months of the pits, of the sand, of learning which blows the counters rewarded and which the crowd wanted — had taught her one thing about this moment: that the fight does not begin when the bell sounds. It begins in the first second, in the half-second before, when the other man decides what you are.

Malloy decided.

He came across the sand at a walk, and then, three steps from the line, he lunged — a driver, low, hands wide, an opener designed to put a body on the ground so that the second move could finish it. Everyone in the Dome leaned in. Kestrel had seen it four times. She had watched a boy named Caviete get folded in half by it and then lifted and opened.

She wasn't there.

She had dropped, one knee to the sand, and let him pass over her, and came up under his arm with her elbow into the meat of his thigh, hard, twice, and Malloy's driver ended with a grunt and a hitch in his stride and no forward motion at all.

The counter flicked: 03.

The crowd made its sound.

It went on longer than it should have. That was the thing Kestrel would think about later, in the cell, in the dark, in the way she thought about all of it: not the ending but the middle, which she had expected to be shorter.

Malloy was too good to be hurried and too big to be moved by much, and he simply ate her combinations, absorbing them on his arms and shoulders and chest, and answered with a patience that was worse than speed. He caught her foot and set her down like a child. He cracked her jaw, once, and she tasted copper and kept moving, because stopping was the only thing that would end it early.

They were both breathing hard by the sixth minute. The counter stood at eleven for Kestrel, and the crowd had begun to shift, wanting something, and she understood that they would give her to him soon if she gave them nothing else. The Dome did not want a close fight. The Dome wanted a result.

So she gave them a result.

She let him take her guard down. Let his forearm come across her collarbone and pin her to the sand with all that weight, and let the crowd's noise rise to a roar, and for one full second she lay there and thought: he has to stand up to hit me, and he stands up with his weight over his back foot.

She put a hand on the mat of his boot and turned her hips and swept.

He went down on his side and half his leg with him, and Kestrel came up and put her knee on the arm that held the blade he'd been keeping — the little curved knife he had never shown, the one that lived in his boot, the one that would have opened her throat and been worth nothing at the counter, because the counter rewarded a body, not a wound — and she drove the heel of her hand into his wrist until the knife came free and skittered away into the sand, and then she was on him, and then she was not.

He got his other hand up. It caught her by the hair and pulled her down onto his forehead, and their heads met with a sound like a stone dropped into a well.

21.

"You little—" he said, or started to say.

The blade was in her hand before she knew she had taken it. She was sitting on his chest with her weight on his sternum and the knife was in her fist and there was a way to do this that the counters would love — a throat, a spray across the white sand, the whole Dome standing up — and there was a way that would take four seconds and give him time to get his feet under him.

He wasn't trying to get his feet under him. He had stopped. His eyes had changed. He was looking up at her with an expression she had seen on other men's faces in the pits and had never once been able to name until that moment: the look of someone who has understood a fact about themselves and does not especially mind it.

He is letting me do this.

And she understood, in the middle of it, with the strange clarity that comes only at the end of a fight, that this was the mercy in it. A driver needs a reason to stop. The counter needs a body. But a man who fights for six years, who has won so many times that the winning has gone out of him like a battery going flat — that man will not lie down for nothing, and he will not be seen to yield, and so he needed her to make it look like an accident.

So she did.

She drove the blade down and across the front of his throat, and it opened, and the blood came up over her knuckles and ran down between her fingers and pooled in the sand and turned the sand the color of the ration paste they would eat that night.

The counter began to climb. 22. 23. 24.

The Dome came apart.

And Kestrel stayed there, sitting on his chest with her hand in his hair, while the digits spun and the sound of four hundred people roaring rolled over the glass like weather, and she did not raise her hand, and she did not look at the table, and she waited.

Because she had been taught this too, in the six months of the pits, the thing that the drivers never learned: the yield is not decided when the body stops. The yield is decided when the crowd is finished. So she held on, and she breathed, and she let him be finished with.

At last the counter chimed, and the digits settled on TWENTY-SIX, and the announcer's voice came through the speaker with the flat indifference of a machine reading a receipt:

"ROUND FOUR CLOSED. DELTA SIX. YIELD: TWENTY-SIX. CREDIT TO KESTREL: ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY GRAMS. OPPONENT'S CREDIT: FORFEIT."

Hoop was right about one thing. There was a way to win and a way to survive. Kestrel had done both, and the difference between them was nine grams.

They walked her back down through the corridor, past the cages rattling, back into Nine, and she lay on her cot with her hands still stiff and smelling of him, and the block said nothing, as they always said nothing, and somewhere above them the Dome was already filling again for the next hour.

**Mara**

She is thirty-one and she has not slept in two days, and right now she can hear her own blood in her ears like a faucet left running in another room.

The avenue is wet. That's the thing nobody tells you about running for your life through a city at dusk — it isn't the speed, it's that everything reflective turns the world into a mirror. Streetlights smear across the asphalt in long orange tongues. A bus window slides past and she sees herself in it: a woman in a stolen gray coat, hair plastered to one side of her face, holding a pistol low against her hip like something she's already regretting.

Behind her, a black sedan has been gaining for eleven blocks.

She checks the rearview mirror by twisting her neck — no room, no time for the mirror; the sedan is simply *there* in the smear of her peripheral vision, its headlights a pair of animal eyes. It leans as she leans. It has more patience than she does.

There are two ways out of here and she can take neither.

She can pull over and let them take her, and whatever she's carrying goes with her.

Or she can keep going.

Mara rides the yellow line, and the traffic is thick now, the evening crowd all soft faces and glowing phones, and she knows — she *knows* — that she is holding a gun in a space full of people who have no idea they're standing in the middle of something. A man on a bicycle with a crate of bread. A woman lifting a toddler into a booster seat. A bus driver with his elbow out the window, bored, watching the light.

The toddler's shoes are the color of good hamburger buns and Mara thinks, absurdly, *don't you dare*.

She fires once.

The sound is enormous — a flat crack that she feels in her sternum more than she hears. The sedan swerves, its front fender starred with a new dimple, and for three full seconds the road ahead of her is empty and gold and utterly silent, and then the siren comes back, closer, wailing like a kettle.

Her hand is shaking. She folds it into her coat to still it and it shakes anyway, and the shaking goes up her forearm and into her shoulder and she has to breathe through her mouth to keep her teeth from going to pieces.

Two blocks. Three. A green light swells at the intersection and the crosswalk is full — *full*, forty people, a hundred, a crowd waiting for the walk signal with that particular stillness of people who feel safe — and the sedan is already on her bumper, and if she stops she dies here, and if she goes through she might kill all of them.

So she does the only third thing available. She aims low and to the left, at the sedan's front left tire, and fires twice, and the shots go somewhere she can't follow, and the sedan yaws hard right, and its nose swings toward the curb, and for one bright crystalline second the whole world holds still.

Somewhere in that second, a man in a suit on the sidewalk sees it coming. She watches him understand. He moves. He gets a hand on a stranger's arm and *shoves*, and then he is running, and the sedan is a big black animal sliding up onto the sidewalk, and the sound it makes is not a crash so much as a long tearing exhalation — glass, metal, a scream that cuts off short — and Mara is past the intersection before it finishes, and she is still alive, and there are sirens everywhere now, more than one, coming from behind and from ahead and from the side streets like the city has decided to close its fist.

She doesn't look back. Looking back is a luxury she has never once been able to afford, and looking back would mean seeing the man in the suit, and the crowd, and the thing she just did with a nine-round pistol in a public street — the way the bullets don't know the difference between a tire and a person, the way a mistake she makes at sixty miles an hour belongs to somebody else forever.

The gun is warm in her hand. That's the detail that undoes her, later, when it ends however it ends: not the report, not the sirens, but the heat of it, the small ordinary weight of it, the way it sits in her palm like a bird she caught and can't quite bring herself to kill or release.

Her forearm cramps. She shifts the pistol to her other hand, and her other hand is steady, and she thinks: *I have one good hand and one bad hand and I have used up all my chances.*

Ahead: the bridge. Beyond it, the warehouses, the fence, the water on the other side. Everything she's got left is in the next mile.

She takes the river on the west side, where the traffic thins, where the light goes long and orange and the puddles turn the whole world to hammered copper, and the sedan — or whatever's left of the sedan — falls away behind her, and the adrenaline doesn't leave. It just changes shape, becomes something quieter and more permanent, a low hum under her ribs that she will carry for a long time, along with the memory of a little girl in bun-colored shoes being strapped into a car seat two seconds before the world broke open behind her.

She will think about that girl for years.

But right now she leans into the merge, and the tires hiss on wet concrete, and she runs.
