# Possibly Incidental

The body was at the top of a narrow house on Cutler's Row, and the first thing Oriana Vance saw — before the body, before the smell, before anything — was the light.

Two candles on the sill, one guttered into a cold blue puddle of wax, one burned down clean and steady. A cold rectangle of dusk in the window. And on a clamp at the drawing board, a work-lamp, switched off. The room had been lit for work. It had been lit the way you light a room when you intend to spend hours in it and do not intend to be interrupted.

"It's a studio," said DI Priya Raval, on the stairs, not asking.

"It is," said Vance.

Four flights, and the whole house smelled of turpentine, size, and cold ash. Under that, the other smell. Everyone smelled it eventually. Vance had trained herself to smell it last, because it was the one that told you things you could not unsee, and there was no point arriving already defiled.

The door was open. Inside: a narrow room, a sloping ceiling, a plaster wall the color of old milk.

And on the wall, a metre above the floor, a bird.

---

She did not go to the body first. She never did, and she had been asked about it in three separate professional-development reviews, and she had never given a good answer.

"You want to see the composition before the victim," Tomas Ek said once, early in her career, meaning it as a criticism.

"I want to see the light before I decide what it was doing," she said, which was true, and was also a way of not saying: *I want to see the thing he did last, before the thing that killed him.*

Because that was the order of it. Everybody else walked into the room and saw the horror first, the sprawled ugly fact of the body, and everything after that arrived already shaped by horror. Vance came in and saw what had been made. Then she saw what had happened to it.

She stood in the doorway for a long moment.

The bird was painted in blood on lime plaster. A heron, standing, wings half-raised, the head turned back over the shoulder as though something had come up behind it. It was a little under a metre long and it was, without qualification, the most beautiful thing she had ever seen.

"Christ," said Ek, behind her.

"Yes," said Vance.

"It's a bird made of her blood."

"Yes," said Vance. "It is."

---

Later — much later, in a room with a lamp and a wall of her own making — she would take the whole thing apart and lay it out. But then, in the doorway, she just looked.

The long stroke of the neck and back was a single sweep of a loaded brush: forty centimetres, tapering at both ends like a whip laid down by a patient hand. Below it, a shorter, broader stroke for the breast, and where the brush had been lifted and set down again there were small faults, tiny skips in the flow where the bristles had run dry, and Vance's heart did something unpleasant and warm at these, because *nobody* paints like that except people who have had their brush renewed two hundred times.

The head was a dense black-brown bloom of contact stain, three centimetres across, the blood so thick in the middle it had come away from the plaster in a shallow curl and lifted like a piece of scab.

The beak was flicked — a hard thin line of spatter, four centimetres, launched from the brush with a snap of the wrist.

The wing was the piece she would spend the rest of her life thinking about. It was not drawn. It was *thrown*: hundreds of droplets flung off a stiff brush in a single motion, each one with a comma-tail, spreading in a fan that was dense at the shoulder and thinned toward the tip until the wing seemed to come apart into air. Flicked spatter. You could not make that with a brush. You could only make it by throwing something wet and letting physics do the drawing.

And the eye.

The eye was the only place in the entire composition where the wall was allowed to be white. Four millimetres of clean plaster, lifted out of the black with the butt of the handle, and in it, if you craned, a single fleck of red that had run back in. The bird had one eye and it was looking at something out of the room.

The legs were two thin runs of drip, down the plaster and onto the boards, and at the foot of them, where the drips had gathered and stopped, two small clusters of contact stain: the feet.

And below all of it, low on the wall, near the skirting, a small neat mark.

Vance went closer. She crouched, and the cold came up off the boards through her knees.

It was about three centimetres tall. It was a capital letter, formed in blood, in the flat unhurried hand of somebody who had spent a life making letters.

*S.*

She noted it. She wrote it in her notebook, along with a small sketch of the whole thing, and beside the S she wrote the word *mark?* and underlined it.

Then she looked at the rest of the room, and the rest of the room took over, the way it always did.

The body lay on its side at the foot of the drawing board, one arm folded under her face, the other out. She was thirty-one. Her name was Nell Marrable and she was a sign-painter and gilder, and the room was full of her tools: a mahlstick, a gilding tip, a jar of size gone cloudy, a book of gold leaf that somebody had left open and which lay on the table like a small shining door. There was turpentine in a saucer. There was a smell of turpentine. The murder had happened in a room that smelled of *work*.

On the floor by her knees lay the ruined panel. Thirty by sixty centimetres of seasoned wood, cracked through the middle, the raised wing snapped clean off and lying beside it, and the surviving gold leaf of the heron still blazing in the blood, dulled but unmistakably there, ultramarine and gold and a black eye. The panel and the wall bird were the same bird. The same angle of the head. The same doubled feather at the second primary, the little flaw in the wing.

Someone had put a boot through it.

Then there was the pool, and the arcs: twelve of them on the boards, each with a tail, each pointing the same way, describing one swing. They were ugly. They were the only ugly thing in the room.

Vance stood up. She had been in eleven hundred rooms. She knew the statistics of them, the way the ordinary ones announced themselves — the dust, the clutter, the mess of a life interrupted — and the rare ones that had been *composed*, which were always the same: they had a focal point, and a hierarchy, and the hierarchy had been chosen.

This one had a focal point and a hierarchy.

Her job, for the next four hours, would be to explain that hierarchy to a jury in terms that made a man with a knife sound like a curator.

---

"You know what your problem is," Raval said, in the van, on the way back down the hill. "You're going to tell me that bird is a masterpiece."

"I didn't say that."

"You were thinking it. You get a look." Raval was fifty-four and had a way of looking at Vance that made her feel like a specimen with a pin through it. "There's a difference between noticing and enjoying, Oriana."

"I know."

"Twelve years I've worked with you. You've never once walked into a scene and seen a person."

"That's not true."

"You saw her on the floor."

"I saw her *work*," said Vance, and then heard herself, and looked out of the window at the wet street going past. "That's not fair."

"No," Raval agreed. "It's not."

---

They called her back to the house three times in that first week, because the first thing she had said — *somebody arranged the light* — turned out to be true in a way nobody wanted.

The candles were a clock. One had guttered and drowned in its own wax; the other had burned down clean, which meant nothing had disturbed it, which meant it had burned in still air for a fixed period after the guttering. The coroner put death between half past six and a quarter to seven. The wax said the room had gone still at about half past six. The blood said something else: the long stroke in the neck was still black-red and wet-looking, while the fine flicked spray had dried to the tan of weak tea, and drying spray is slower than drying a loaded stroke by hours, which meant the spray had been thrown first and the neck laid down last, and the whole bird had been made in something under fifteen minutes.

Somebody had painted a heron in blood in eleven minutes, on their knees, in a cold room, while dying.

And the reason the candles had been lit at all, and the reason the chair had been dragged away from the drawing board to the far side of the room, was that a painter needs to stand back. You do not compose a bird at arm's length. You make the mark and then you go and look at it from where it will be seen from, and you decide whether it is finished, and you go back.

There was a smear on the back rail of the chair. A right hand, hauling.

Raval read it as a killer steadying himself. Vance read it as a woman pulling herself up. Neither of them said so.

They had the panel photographed and lifted. They had the wall photographed, and the S measured, and the letter run through something. It was a capital S, neatly formed, the top curve a little open, the way a gilder's S is when the hand is tired. No match in the persons then considered. Vance wrote it up as *a maker's mark or signature of no evident evidentiary value*, and Raval agreed, and the file moved on, because a murder in a studio in a town where a rich collector bought pictureless things had already found its rich collector, and everyone wanted it to be him.

Aurel Fennimore was sixty-eight. He had commissioned the panel: a reproduction of a lost oil sketch by a Flemish master called Abraham Rombouts, *The Standing Heron*, known only from a photograph in a 1963 catalogue, of which Fennimore owned the sole print. He had paid Nell Marrable a great deal of money for the right to make a copy. He had been in the room that afternoon. His fingerprints were on the door, the table, the mirror frame, the panel. His cells were under her fingernails.

And then there was the doubled feather.

The Rombouts bird, in the 1963 photograph, has a doubled second primary — a small fault, an artist's slip, the kind of thing that appears in a drawing made quickly by a hand that did not mean to. The bird on the wall had the doubled feather. So the person who painted it had seen the original, or the sole photograph of the original, and had reproduced the fault.

At the trial, in the witness box, with a court reporter typing everything she said for the future, Vance said:

"To reproduce that fault, the painter had to have held the original in his hand."

She did not say *only* the owner could have done that. She thought about saying it. There was a pause of about two seconds. She was aware of the pause, at the time, in the way you are aware of a step that does not go down.

She did not add the other thing, which was: *or a person who had spent a year copying it, which is what she was paid to do, which is what her assistant did every week of his life, which is what the panel on the floor said in gold leaf.*

Fennimore was convicted. He died in custody four years later, of a kidney infection the doctors called unlucky. The world found the case beautiful. It was beautiful. There is no denying it: it was beautiful, and it was true, and a man went to prison for it.

Vance's book about the case — *Composition: On the Reading of Rooms* — sold ninety thousand copies. The house on Cutler's Row was bought by a charity and opened to the public. Room 3 has the heron reproduced on the wall, life-size, at the correct height; the wax is on the sill; the panel is in a vitrine downstairs, repaired, its snapped wing reattached, the gold still bright under the glass. People queue. They take photographs. They stand at the back of the room, at the distance where a bird resolves.

There was a gift shop.

---

Ama Okafor came into the case in the winter of 2025, through the door the Crown Prosecution Service had left open, because she was a bloodstain pattern analyst who freelanced for defence firms and Fennimore's solicitor had been fighting the conviction for eleven years without a single new fact.

What Ama Okafor did was very small and very stupid and it took eleven years.

She had the scene photographs. Nobody had ever looked at the wall photograph properly, because there was a body in it, and because the wall photograph was famous, and because being famous is a kind of varnish.

She looked at the panel photograph next to the wall photograph. She noticed that the wall bird's head faced right and the panel bird's head faced left.

Then she did the thing that no one in 2016 had thought to do, which was to actually go and stand on the floor.

She had the room's dimensions. She had the position of the panel, the position of the chair, the smear on the chair rail. She put a camera at the height of a prone person's eye — forty centimetres — at the point on the boards where Nell Marrable's hand had put down, and she angled it at the wall.

And there it was. The wall bird was the panel bird, seen from the floor.

Foreshortened. Steep. The raised wing foreshortened into a fan, the head thrown large and close because it was the nearest thing to her, the beak foreshortened to a hard little line, the whole thing resolved onto the vertical plane of the plaster the way a thing resolves when you are lying on your side six inches from it with your eyes at the level of the table.

The wall bird was not a painting by a murderer. It was a drawing of her own panel, made from the floor, by the body.

The doubled feather was in the panel too, because she had been copying the Rombouts for a year, and you cannot copy a bird for a year without learning its faults.

The tremor in the long stroke — which Vance had called, in the book, with some pride, *a stylist's nervous affectation, a mannerism of the hand* — was a blood pressure going down.

The broken mirror was not a killer afraid of his own reflection. She had broken it so that the reflection would not double the composition.

The fifteen minutes of candle were not the fifteen minutes of a killer's theatre. They were how long she had.

And the letter was not a maker's mark.

The bird was painted in blood on lime plaster. A heron, standing, wings half-raised, the head turned back over the shoulder as though something had come up behind it. It was a little under a metre long and it was, without qualification, the most beautiful thing she had ever seen.

"It's a bird made of her blood."

"Yes," said Vance. "It is."

The head was a dense black-brown bloom of contact stain, three centimetres across, the blood so thick in the middle it had come away from the plaster in a shallow curl and lifted like a piece of scab.

The beak was flicked — a hard thin line of spatter, four centimetres, launched from the brush with a snap of the wrist.

The wing was the piece she would spend the rest of her life thinking about. It was not drawn. It was thrown: hundreds of droplets flung off a stiff brush in a single motion, each one with a comma-tail, spreading in a fan that was dense at the shoulder and thinned toward the tip until the wing seemed to come apart into air. Flicked spatter. You could not make that with a brush. You could only make it by throwing something wet and letting physics do the drawing.

And the eye.

The eye was the only place in the entire composition where the wall was allowed to be white. The bird had one eye and it was looking at something out of the room.

The legs were two thin runs of drip, down the plaster and onto the boards, and at the foot of them, where the drips had gathered and stopped, two small clusters of contact stain: the feet.

And below all of it, low on the wall, near the skirting, a small neat mark.

It was about three centimetres tall. It was a capital letter, formed in blood, in the flat unhurried hand of somebody who had spent a life making letters.

S.

She noted it. She wrote it in her notebook, along with a small sketch of the whole thing, and beside the S she wrote the word mark? and underlined it.

Then she looked at the rest of the room, and the rest of the room took over, the way it always did.

The rope creaked once as the man’s weight settled against the branch.

Sheriff Dutch Harlan stood back with his hat low over his eyes. Beside him, Deputy Nicks watched the cattle cross the dry riverbed, as if the hanging were no more remarkable than a rattlesnake in the grass.

“No last words?” Nicks asked.

Harlan looked up. “He already spent ’em.”

The condemned man—thin, sun-blackened, and stripped to a pair of faded trousers—gagged against the rope. His eyes bulged, red-rimmed and wet. His fingers clawed at his throat, then at the hemp, while his boots kicked uselessly against the trunk.

The drop came without ceremony.

His feet left the ground.

For half a second, his body hung straight and rigid. Then came the sound: a wet, dense crack, like a green branch snapping deep inside a dry bundle of wood. It was not a loud noise. That was the worst of it. The sound traveled plainly through the still air, crisp and final.

Nicks looked away.

The man’s head lolled sideways. His mouth opened, but only a dry rasp escaped. His legs began to move—first a hard, involuntary jerk, then a series of shorter kicks that slowly lost their strength. One boot scraped bark. The other swung free and struck the dirt with a dull thud.

His right hand tightened into a fist. The left fingers curled inward, slow and uneven, like the legs of a dying insect folding beneath itself. His jaw worked silently. The muscles in his neck stood taut beneath the bruised skin, and his shoulders twisted as his body tried to pull free from what it could no longer feel.

Harlan stepped forward and lifted the loose end of the rope, keeping the man from choking before the drop finished its work. He did it without hurry.

A breeze moved through the mesquite. The condemned man’s body jerked again, toes dragging, heels scraping a thin furrow in the earth. His fist opened. His hand reached outward—toward nothing, perhaps toward the road or the last pale rim of sky above the horizon—then fell back against his thigh.

The twitching continued in pieces. A shoulder. A knee. The small bounce of his boots against the tree. Each movement grew weaker until his body hung heavy and still, swaying a finger’s width with each breath of wind.

Nicks touched his hat brim.

“That’s done, then,” he said.

Harlan watched the cattle move beyond the riverbed. “Ain’t done till he’s in the ground.”

He reached for the knife at his belt. The condemned man’s head moved gently in the breeze, cheek nearly touching his chest, while the last faint tremor passed through his dangling hands.

# The Thirst

The alley behind the shuttered laundry on Fell Street was narrow enough to touch both walls with an outstretched hand, and it smelled of rain and rust and the sweetish rot of a bin that had not been emptied in a week. Mira had chosen it for that reason. Privacy. A place where screams could be swallowed by the traffic noise on the boulevard, where the dark came down like a lid.

She had not fed in nine days.

That was a mistake. A stupid, sentimental mistake involving a wedding and a toast and a young bride who had looked at her with such uncomplicated happiness over the punch bowl. Mira had let her go. She had walked home the long way, through the park, with her hands shaking inside her gloves, and she had said to herself, *not tonight, not while I can still taste the wine.*

Nine days of that. Nine days of the hunger sitting in her throat like a splinter working deeper.

Now the man was drunk. That was convenient. He came in from the boulevard with his tie loose and his shoes in his hand, and he made the mistake of smiling at her.

"You're pretty," he said, swaying.

"I know," said Mira, and let him follow her in.

---

She took him against the wall, not roughly, almost gently. She set his own hand on her shoulder to steady him, and she leaned in close enough that he could smell the cold iron of her, and she said, "Look at me."

He looked. His pupils were wide, glassy, and he kept trying to focus on her eyes and failing, and she watched the exact moment his body registered the wrongness — the air around her being too cold, the wrong shape of her, the way the streetlight behind her threw her shadow away from her instead of toward him.

"*Run,*" she said.

He didn't. Drunks never believe the first warning. He said something about wanting to see her fangs, which was so darkly comic she nearly laughed, and then his hand was at her waist and his breath was in her ear, sour and warm, and the hunger in her throat became a physical thing, a hook, a fist closing.

She bit him.

There was only *need*, need so complete it obliterated thought, and she drank the way a drowning man drinks air, without dignity, without gratitude.

She felt it hammering, felt it begin to falter, felt the intervals stretch out like a slowing metronome. *Too fast, too fast, he'll burst.* She pulled back just enough to breathe, lips sealed red, and pressed her thumb to the punctures to slow the flow so his heart wouldn't stutter out on her.

His cheeks hollowed. In the yellow wash of the single bulb on the wall he looked like a wax figure of himself, a thing displayed in a shop window.

They tracked her face without seeing it. He tried to say something — she caught the shape of a word, maybe her name, maybe *please* — and his voice came out as a thin exhalation, a breath with consonants in it.

Mira licked the punctures closed, pressed her mouth to the wound one final time and felt the last of it, weak and slow, and then stepped back.

He slid down the wall. His knees folded. He sat there in the rainwater at the base of the bricks with his tie askew and his shoes still in his hand, and he looked up at her with eyes that no longer held anything at all, and he said, "I'm cold."

"I know," she said.

She considered staying. She crouched, and put her hand on his cheek, and she said — because nine days of hunger had made her strange, because the blood was singing in her veins and she was feeling something close to joy — "You're doing fine. You did fine. Stay here."

Then the cold of her own cheek against his skin, and he flinched from it, and something in his face finally went slack in a way that frightened her — not death, not yet, but the absence of the person — and she understood that if she stayed she would take the rest, would drink until there was nothing left to give, and she did not want that. She wanted it. That was the horror of it. She wanted it so much that her teeth ached.

So Mira stood, and stepped over him, and walked out of the alley into the wet street with her gloves on and her mouth warm and her belly full, and she did not look back, and she heard him say, very quietly, to no one:

"Mira?"

---

# Nothing Has Teeth

The power went out at 11:40, and Mara assumed the storm had taken the transformer on Beech Street.

She sat on the floor of her kitchen with a flashlight between her knees and a glass of water going warm in her fist, and she listened to the rain come down hard enough to sound like gravel thrown against glass. Wind worried at the loose sash of the window above the sink. The refrigerator clicked off with a small mournful sigh, and the house settled into its bones.

She counted the seconds until the storm would pass, the way she always did. One, two. Rain. A car passing on the far side of the block, its tires hissing on the wet road. Three, four. The faucet dripping. Her own breathing, which had always been a little ragged since 2019, when she'd been on a call for a man named Petros with a hole in him and no one to hold the other end of the stretcher.

At forty-one seconds, something crossed her forearm.

She felt it as heat first. A thin bright line of heat laid across the inside of her arm, from wrist to elbow, the way you'd feel a finger dragged along a stretched wire. It didn't hurt. Not then. Her skin prickled and rose in a wave, and she looked down at the flashlight's spill and saw nothing there but her own pale arm and the dark smear of a dried-out blood smear from a paper cut she'd made on Saturday.

Then the line opened.

The pain came after the blood, which was wrong, and she knew it was wrong, because she was a paramedic and she had held a hundred wounds in her hands and they always announced themselves with pain first. But the blood came first here. A slow welling, a widening of red along that thin diagonal, as if something invisible had drawn a knife down her arm with the blade held perfectly flat so that it parted the skin without catching. Warmth ran down to her elbow and off her wrist and hit the tile of the kitchen floor with a sound so small and so wet that she could not stop looking at the spot it made.

She pressed the heel of her hand over it. Her heart was doing something ugly and unrhythmic in her chest. There was nothing under her hand but her own arm.

"It's the glass," she said. The window sash. Something came down in the wind, a shard, and it had—

She got up. She went to the sink and pulled the sash closed with her good hand and unbuckled it, and there was nothing on the ledge but rainwater and a dead spider, and the wood was smooth and unbroken. She held her arm up to the flashlight and turned it slowly.

The wound was clean. That was the thing that made her sit down on the floor. A glass cut would have ragged edges, would have had a little crater of grit in it. This was a single clean line, almost surgical, with the edges lying open like lips, and it was bleeding in a steady pulse that matched her heartbeat and not the storm's.

She worked her own fingers. The cut hurt when she flexed. When she pressed it, the pain was deep and specific and traveled up under her arm into her shoulder, and she had to press harder, harder, to make it stop, and when she let go it kept going, a tooth of pain sitting in her forearm like something that had been left there on purpose.

*Shock,* she thought. *You cut yourself. You cut yourself on the window and you don't remember because of the storm and the hour and the—*

The second one came in her throat.

Not a cut. A pressure. A slow, deliberate tightening on the front of her throat, the exact size and shape of a hand, and she felt the separate fingers of it — she felt them distinctly, four points of pressure and a thumb below and a web of tension across her windpipe — and she clawed at her own neck and found nothing, no hand, no cord, no wire, nothing but her own fingers and her own throat and the bruising already coming up under her skin in the unmistakable purple of fingers that were not there.

She couldn't get breath. She got maybe a third of a breath, a thin sip that hissed past the pressure in her larynx, and she dropped the flashlight and crawled for the hall and got her face to the floor and dragged in air that smelled like wet wool and old coffee and, faintly, under all of it, iron.

*It's in the room,* she thought with enormous calm, the calm she got on bad calls, the calm that meant her hands would keep working while the rest of her came apart. *It's in the room and I can't see it and it has hands.*

She held the counter. She made herself say things out loud. "There's nothing in the room. There's nothing in the room and I'm bleeding and there's nothing in the room."

The pressure eased. Her breath came back in a tearing, ugly pull.

On the fourth step down the hall, her calf opened.

This one was worse because she felt it enter. Something blunt and cold pushed into the muscle of her lower leg, slow, a cold blunt pressure sinking in like a finger pushed into wet dough, and her leg buckled and she caught herself on the wall and slid down to the carpet and got her hand on her shin and felt the blood coming up between the fingers of her hand, hot and fast now, faster than it had any right to come from a puncture you could put your thumb over.

She could not find the entry wound. She pressed and pressed with both hands and the blood just kept welling, from somewhere she couldn't localize, from everywhere at once, and the cold thing inside her calf moved.

She screamed. The scream went up through the dark house and came back to her from the stairwell, and in the space between the sound leaving her mouth and the sound arriving there was a space where nothing happened, where nothing made any noise at all, and that silence was so much worse than what had hurt her.

*Am I doing this to myself,* she thought. *Is this what it is. Is this the thing that's happening to me.*

She had a flash — violent, unwanted, complete — of a case in 2019, a woman in a resus bay at St. Agnes, forty years old, saying *it touches me, it touches me and you can't see it*, and the doctors looking at each other over her, and the CAT scan coming back clean, and the woman crying in the corner of the room telling them it was in the walls, that it had been in the walls of her apartment for six months, and they'd given her antipsychotics, and she'd been gone by Thursday, and Mara had thought, *she's crazy, she's so frightened she's crazy*—

Mara got herself onto her knees in the dark hallway with blood running down her leg and pooling in the wool of the carpet and did the only thing she could think of. She said, out loud, in the flat professional voice she used on scene, calm and level and kind:

"I can hear you. I know you're there. I can't see you, but I can hear you."

And the house was quiet.

And in the quiet, something breathed.

That was the moment the terror became total, because it wasn't a monster in a closet, it wasn't a shape in the window — those she could have fought or fled. It was a *presence* in the air beside her, in the space her hand occupied, in the inches between her skin and the air, and it was breathing, and she had no idea how big it was, and no idea whether what she was feeling was its hand or its mouth or its weight, and it was so close that she could feel the damp of it on her face like the damp of a dog's nose.

Her arm was still bleeding. Her throat was already purpling into the shape of a hand that was not there. Her calf was full of something cold and moving.

And then, very gently, at the back of her neck, below the hairline, where the skin is thin and the nerves are a map of everything — the lightest possible pressure. A single fingertip. Just one. Resting there. Not pressing. Just resting, the way you'd rest a finger on a page to hold your place while you read.

She stopped breathing on purpose.

*Don't move,* she thought. *Don't move. It's waiting for something. It's waiting for me to do something. If I can just not do anything, if I can be still, then maybe—*

The fingertip moved. It dragged, barely, a millimeter of pressure, a tiny scratch of its nail, if it had nails, and the line it opened on her neck was thin as a thread and she felt it fill with blood and run down her collarbone into her collar.

Her mind did something she would be ashamed of afterward: it went quiet. All that clinical machinery ground to a halt and what was left was simply the animal in the dark with a wet hand, listening to a thing she could not describe, unable to look at it, unable to look away, unable to be anywhere else.

She never saw it. Not once. Not a shadow, not a shape, not a distortion in the rain on the window. Whatever it was, it did not need to be seen, and that was the last and worst of it — that a thing could be so completely present in a room, could take hold of your throat and press a finger into your spine and slide cold into the meat of your leg, and wear no face at all, and you would go to your grave with the word *it* in your mouth and no picture to go with it.

The rain went on. The storm moved off over the neighborhood. Somewhere far off a siren rose and fell and rose again.

Mara lay on the carpet of her hallway in the dark, and she did not move, and she did not sleep, and the blood went on leaving her body at the rate her heart insisted on, and the thing beside her stayed exactly where it was, close enough to touch, patient as furniture, and content to wait.

She understood, then, with a clarity more horrible than any pain she had taken that night, that it was not hunting her.

It was farming her.

## The Reckoning

The man in the linen coat had a voice like a clerk counting coin.

"In there, you said. Three names. Master Vahl, Mistress Errin, and the boy Otik." He dipped his pen. "We need one. The rest may walk. It's arithmetic, not mercy — the arithmetic is simply done on our side, or on yours."

"If I give you all three—"

"You misunderstand the arithmetic." He did not look up. "You will give us one, and you will watch the other two leave this building with their names struck from our ledger. If you give us three, we will take three, and the courtesy you were hoping to buy will be extended to no one at all, including you." A small, tired shrug. "I have made this offer eleven times. It is never refused."

Berit stood at the window with her back to the room because she could not bear to see him write. Behind her the wall was sweating in the July heat; the street below carried the ordinary sounds of a market day, someone arguing over duck, a cart wheel grinding on cobblestones. It was obscene. Two streets from this cellar, a woman was haggling over turnips.

*Three,* she thought. *He hasn't even said how long.*

"How long do I have until the noon bell?"

"Two hours. Perhaps three, if the magistrate is in a good mood." The pen scratched. "And I will tell you what a good mood buys you, since you are clearly a person who wants to know: it buys nothing. It changes only the order of events. The arithmetic stays."

Eleven times. Eleven families, somewhere in this city, spending eleven long afternoons with the same math: *who do I love least?* Berit had spent the last two days failing to solve it, and failing was its own kind of answer, because in failing she had discovered that she loved all three of them exactly the same amount, which is a thing you can discover about a heart but cannot say aloud to a man with a pen.

That was the true shape of her agony. Not the choosing — the choosing she could have done in a heartbeat, some nights, with a bottle in her. The agony was that there was no smallest love. She had gone through each of them like a woman checking rooms for a candle in a burning house.

Vahl, who had taught her to read, in a cellar in the salt quarter, with a wick floating in a saucer of oil so that the light would not be seen from the street, and who had said, when she was nine and mouthing the shapes of letters like chewing bread: *Sound is cheap. Anything can be loud. Take the quiet one. Take the patient one.* He had been dead eleven minutes in her memory and yet he was the man she most wanted to walk out of this room with, and she knew — with a clarity that felt like a nail driven into the sternum — that she would not lift a finger to save him.

Errin, who had held her hand in the fever ward for six days and had never once, not once, mentioned her mother. Errin, who had laughed at a joke she made in the marketplace once, so that the woman selling pears had laughed too, for no reason, from the warmth of it. Errin had gotten her a scar, or something like a scar; Errin had gotten her a life.

Otik. Nineteen. He had a mother in the tanner's district. He had not been afraid of anything yet, so he did not know what to be afraid of with, and he had made a joke about the gallows that morning — *I'd look well in black, they'd say* — and she had hit him for it, hard, in the shoulder, and he had said *what?* and she had said *nothing,* and had felt her own hand stinging for the rest of the hour.

She had been prepared for the arithmetic. She had not been prepared for the equality of the terms.

---

At the third hour the man in the linen coat brought them.

That was the cruelty, or the honesty, of it — he brought them, so that she could not delegate. She wanted to hate him for it and found she could not; he was a function, and functions cannot be hated, only feared.

They came up the cellar stairs in a file, and the three of them stopped in the doorway of the room and looked at her, and Berit understood that she had become a thing they were now looking *at*.

No one spoke.

Vahl went first, because he was the oldest and slowest, and he stopped in front of her and inclined his head — a small, courteous bow, as if they were meeting in a doorway in the rain — and he said, in his careful, patient voice: "Well."

"Don't," she said.

"Berit."

"Don't say it kindly, you'll make me worse."

Otik behind him, jaw set, trying to look like a man in a story about a man. Errin last, leaning against the wall with her arms crossed, and Errin who was the only one of the three who looked at the man in the coat and *read* him, who had spent a life learning what people wanted and had decided in the space of a second that this man wanted only to be obeyed and could be managed. Errin's eyes went to the window, to the light, to the length of the drop, and came back, and Berit watched her do the arithmetic too and watched her arrive at the same answer, which was that Errin knew. Errin knew that Berit was going to have to say a name.

The man in the linen coat held out a slip of paper and a pen.

"Write the name. I will make it sound like your own decision, in the hearing, because a man's decision is worth less than a woman's and the record must show cooperation." A pause. "That is not a kindness. That is only cheaper for me."

Berit's hand did not want to move. She made it move.

She wrote three names on the edge of the paper, in the order she loved them, which was the order she would have to destroy: *Vahl. Errin. Otik.*

She looked at it for a while.

Then something happened in her that she did not fully understand even later. It was not courage. It was the opposite of courage: it was the recognition, cold and complete, that she was going to do this, that she had already done it, that the writing of the three names was the last moment at which the world still contained the possibility of a different outcome. Everything after this was a slow descent toward a thing already in motion. It was like watching a cart roll toward a child and understanding that calling out would not stop it, only be part of the noise.

She put the pen down.

"Otik," she said.

The boy made a sound. Not a word. He had been ready — he had been ready since the doorway, she thought, he had been *prepared* and had not been allowed to be brave about it — but he made a sound that was not a word.

"No," she said, and her voice was perfectly level, which she had never known she could do. "Not because I love the others more."

"Otik," the man in the linen coat repeated, writing, "and the others walk."

"Wait." She held up her hand. "Wait. I want to say—"

"There is nothing you want to say that carries more weight than the name you have given."

---

They gave her three-quarters of an hour, in the cell, with Otik.

She has forgotten most of what she said and remembered all of it. She knows the exact number of times she said his name. She knows that at some point she told him about the light in the salt quarter, the wick floating in the saucer, and that he asked, *what candle?* and she said, *there was no candle, we had a saucer of oil and a wick and it made no difference at all,* and he said, *that's not what you said was most beautiful,* and she said, *I know what I said,* and then she could not get the rest of it out, and he put his forehead against the wall and let her talk about the arithmetic, the total absence of a smallest love, and the way a heart can hold three people at exactly the same level and no higher.

She told him she would carry it. She used the word *carry*, which is the word people use for things that do not weigh anything.

He said: "Don't. It doesn't help me and it makes you smaller."

She said: "You have a mother in the tanner's district."

"I know."

"I could go to her. After. If you—"

"Don't," Otik said. "Berit. Don't make it a debt. You're not a bank."

The guards came at the eleventh hour of the third hour.

---

The square was full. That was the part she had not allowed herself to imagine: that a crowd would come. Not a mob — a crowd, a *public*, drawn by the notice nailed to the door of the Custom House: *By order of the Tribunal, one sentence of the law will be carried out at noon in the Market Square, the name to be given in the record.* People came because it was a Tuesday and there was nothing else, because executions in a square are a kind of weather, and because a boy of nineteen was a story they could tell afterward.

She was made to stand at the front. They needed her visible: her face, her consent, the shapes of the words *I give him to you freely,* which the man in the linen coat had coached her on the walk over, and which she had said once, out loud, in the market, to test the feel of them, and had felt her stomach turn over at how easily they came.

The block was new. That detail undid her more than anything. New wood, pale, the wood of a cart wheel, and the notch worn in it already from practice, and the straw, and the boy with the axe standing to the side with the axe held down the way you hold a broom until someone tells you what to do.

Otik looked for her in the crowd. He found her — she was the only thing he could have been looking for, the only fixed point — and he looked at her for a long moment, and she thought: *say something. Anything. But for God's sake, if you're going to be brave, be brave now, because I have run out of the ability to hold you.*

He did not say anything. He nodded, once, the way he'd nodded at a threshold. He was still practicing the gesture. He had never in his life been in a room where a nod would have to mean something and he was doing his best.

Then they laid him down and the leather went over his eyes and she could not see his face anymore and that was, in the strange accounting of her mind, the single mercy the day contained.

The man in the linen coat read the sentence. His clerk read it too, because the clerk had a cold and the words had to be exact, and the two voices overlapped in the way that made it sound like one voice with a split in the middle:

*Otik, son of Marek, of the tanner's district, aged nineteen years, found...*

Berit heard none of it after the second clause. She had begun to say the words she would need afterward — *I could not save him, I could not choose, there was no smallest love* — and she discovered they did not fit. They were all true and together they made nothing, a pile of coins that would not buy bread. There was no arrangement of them that made her innocent and there was no arrangement that made her monstrous and the world, it turned out, did not have a third drawer.

The last thing Otik did was move. His feet, under the leather, found a place for themselves. He lined his heels up parallel, the way a man does on a dock when he wants to look like he means it, and Berit saw it happen and had to put her hand over her mouth.

The sound was not what she had expected. She had always, in the private dark of her own imagining, made it a sound — a crack, a report, a meat-and-bone *chunk* of it. It was smaller than that. It was a *thud*, wet, and a short silence after, and then the crowd made a sound that was almost a disappointment, a collective intake, a hundred people remembering to breathe.

The head rolled. The blood came after the head, which she had not known, which she would think about for years afterward — that the body could be so patient about it, that it took a full second to acknowledge what had been done to it, and then let go all at once, and ran downhill across the pale new wood and over the edge and into the straw, and the straw drank it and turned dark at the edges.

The man in the linen coat came to her side and said, mildly, as if discussing freight: "The two others will be struck from the ledger tonight. You will be struck from it as well, unless you would like to stay on it."

She looked at Otik's body, and at his boots, still together.

"Yes," she said. "Strike me."

He made a small note. Then he said, "There will be an inquiry, in three weeks, at which you will be asked again the same question you were asked this morning, and you will be asked it by people who would very much like an answer that suits them. Decide now what your answer will be, so that you don't have to decide it then in front of others."

"I'll answer the same."

"Good. That is the answer that suits everyone." He closed the book. "It's a market day, you know. There's a woman selling pears by the fountain with a bad cough and she gives too much fruit anyway. You've a whole life in front of you. It's genuinely a fine afternoon."

---

Vahl and Errin waited by the Custom House steps, in the shade, like two people who had agreed on nothing and would not discuss it.

They did not embrace her. Errin took her hand and held it, and looked at her a long time, and said, "Say one thing to me and then I'll never ask you again." And Berit said, "He asked me not to make it a debt." And Errin said, "All right," and let go of her hand, and that was the end of the conversation they ever had about it, in any form, for the rest of their lives.

Vahl said only: "We go now. There's nothing to be done at the harbor until dusk."

So they walked home. Along the street where the woman was selling pears and coughing and giving too much fruit. Past the block in the square; a woman was already hosing the platform down, and the straw was being raked into a pile, and the wood was being scrubbed, and someone had put the axe back on its block as if it were a hoe.

Berit stopped there and could not make herself go on, and Errin said, "Wait," and went and got three pears and gave them to her, and Vahl stood with her while she held them, not saying anything, patient, the way he had been patient with a nine-year-old girl learning the shapes of letters by candlelight.

They were, as it turned out, almost inaudible.

That is what she had gone on to tell herself, in the years following: that she had loved them all the same, that the arithmetic had been the same on all three sides, that if the ledger had asked for a fourth name she would have written her own without a moment's hesitation.

But she knew, and she had known since the cellar, in the moment before the pen went down, while her hand hovered over three names written in the order she loved them — she knew that the boy had made a joke that morning, and that she had hit him for it, and that when she said his name she had felt something in her *release*.

She had not chosen the least-loved. She had chosen the one whose death would be bearable.

And she had known that, and had done it anyway, and had stood in the square two hours later while her hand lay open on the front of her coat like a woman waiting to be given something.

*This is what a person is,* she thought, and did not finish the thought, and ate the pear, which was too ripe, and afterward went and found the woman with the cough and bought six more, so that the woman would remember her, or wouldn't.

# The Persimmon Tree

The first thing you should know about Herring Lane is that it is quiet in a way that describes the street's *character*, and the first thing you should know about my neighbor is that he is the most ordinary man in America.

Warren Kress lived in 14 Herring Lane, in the yellow house with the buckled porch and the persimmon tree that had never borne fruit. He was fifty-three or so. He kept a station wagon and a blue panel van with a magnet on the side advertising a plumbing company he didn't seem to work for. He was widowed, or at least he said so, and he had a way of saying it — hands cupped around a coffee cup, eyes on the middle distance — that made you sorry for him without knowing anything at all about the woman.

He was up before six. He swept his stoop every Sunday, though there wasn't a leaf on it. He knew the names of every dog on the block and asked after them. When I had my back go out lifting a doghouse roof in July, he came over with a bottle of ibuprofen and a cylinder of Flex Tape and stayed two hours helping me, and he didn't say a single thing about my sister, or my marriage, or the fact that I'd been drinking too much in that year and everyone on the street could smell it on me — not a *single* thing. He just handed me tools.

"That's a good tree," he said, looking at my side of the property, where the persimmon came up through the fence. "Want me to trim it back? It's hitting your gutter."

I'd had a persimmon tree too, once. It died. The fence between our lots was old gray cedar, five feet, and it had been leaning since before I bought the house.

For six years, Warren Kress was the man next door.

Then, in the second week of September, the smell came.

It came late, at night, in August's last hot spells, when the windows are open and the whole street is a stew of dog and jasmine and hot asphalt. A sweetish smell, chemical, like nail-polish remover or like the tank at the back of a pool, and it came from the direction of 14 Herring Lane and nowhere else. Nobody else smelled it. When I mentioned it to Deirdre across the street she said, "Skunk," and when I said it again to the mail carrier she said, "Skunk," and I believed them, because that's how it works, isn't it — you take the answer you're given.

The other thing was Biscuit.

Biscuit was my dog, a yellow Lab, eleven years old, and for six years his only hobby in this world was screaming at Warren Kress's kitchen window at two in the morning. Every night. Not a bark — a *scream*, that rising strangled yelp dogs make when they want a thing they can't reach. It drove Mrs. Yancey nuts. "Your dog," she'd say, tapping her cane, "is a lunatic."

In August, Biscuit stopped.

He didn't stop all at once. He just got quieter about it, and then one night in late August I heard him make a sound I'd never heard from him — a low, sustained moan, like a child in a nightmare — and he wouldn't go out in the yard for two days after. When I went to the fence to look, Biscuit was standing in the rain up against the boards, hackles up, staring at the house, and when I called him he wouldn't come.

The week before the storm, Mrs. Yancey stopped answering her phone.

She's eighty-two and lives alone at 16 Herring Lane, the house directly across from Kress's. Her grandson calls every Sunday at eight. He called the house instead. No answer. He called the police, and two officers came, and I stood on my porch in my bathrobe and watched them go up 16 Herring Lane's walk, and I watched Kress come out of his front door in his bathrobe, mildly, hands raised, holding his own cell phone, saying *I just got off the phone with the state hospital, she's been forgetting things*.

The grandson came the next day from out of town and found her room empty, her bed made, the TV on with the shopping channel murmuring. Her purse was in the kitchen drawer. Her checkbook was in the kitchen drawer. Her house had been *tended* — the gutters cleared, the hedges cut, the little porch light replaced — and the only thing wrong with it was that she'd been gone for four days.

"Warren's been helping her," the grandson told me, with a strange look. "He does her yard. He fixed her screen door." He paused. "He has a key. He said she gave him a key."

And I remember what I said, because I remember everything I've said for the last eleven weeks and I have wished, every single night, that I'd said something else.

I said, "Well. She's lucky to have a neighbor like that."

The search of 14 Herring Lane took four hours. They went in the house, the garage, the van, and the yard, and they came out and told us that the house was clean. Kress was attentive, cooperative, patient. He had a job — he *had* a job, it turned out; he did maintenance for a school district and he was very good at it, everyone said so, he'd fix boilers and doors and drive a man downtown at four in the morning if you asked him. He offered to help search. He took the officers around and showed them the boiler, and the electrical panel, and the crawlspace, and when they asked about the smell he said *fertilizer*, and they nodded, and everyone went home.

And then the storm came, and the fence came down.

It was the ninth of October. Not a hurricane — a late storm, one of those wet October ones with no wind to speak of, just six hours of hard rain and a sky the color of a bruise. The old cedar fence on our shared property line didn't fall so much as *soften*, and somewhere around midnight a whole section of it went over with a sound like a body going down stairs, and my persimmon tree came down with it, its branches spread across the driveway like something on an operating table.

I went out at half past midnight in the rain with a flashlight to see what I'd lost. The wind wasn't the issue; the weight of the wet branches was dragging the fence posts, and there's a section of my back fence that's been leaning since 2011, and honestly, that's the whole reason I went out.

And that's the only reason I'm alive, or awake, or whatever I am.

Kress's cellar door was open.

It's a steel door at the back of the garage, and I remember noticing it that night because it was *lit*. Not the little bulb on the steps — a warm yellow light spilling up out of the hole in the ground and out across the wet gravel, and the rain falling into it and turning to steam. The door was propped open with a length of two-by-four.

I stood in the rain and I looked at it and every animal part of me said something I couldn't translate into language. *Go inside. Go inside. Go inside.* I had a flashlight in my hand and a bottle of something in my other hand, and I don't remember which one.

I want to be honest about this part, because people want you to be a fool or a genius, and I was neither. I was a man standing in the rain thinking, *he's probably got a generator down there. He's probably got a space heater running* — because it was forty-eight degrees and I'd heard that sound before, that particular sound of a *bigger* space heater through a vent. He had a generator. The house had power during the outage. Everyone on the block knew Kress had power during the outage.

He had a generator, and he had a space heater, and the cellar door was propped open, and I am going to have to live with the rest of my life knowing that I thought about turning around.

I didn't.

I walked over. The gravel was loud. I said, "Mr. Kress? It's me, from next door. Your cellar's open."

Nothing.

I shone the flashlight down the steps. Nine steps, painted, with a handrail. At the bottom, a landing, and a door — an actual door, finished, with a brass knob, which for a *cellar* on that street is unusual, and which at the time I thought was a very nice touch, a man who took pride in his house, he'd fixed it up, he'd made something of it.

The light was coming from under the door. And there was a smell coming out.

I'd been smelling that smell since August. It had a name now that I recognized it, sort of, the back of my brain had filed it and just now my body handed me the file: it was *sweet*, and *faintly ammoniac*, and there was something in it that was worse than both, something organic and low and patient, the smell of a thing that has been warm for a long time in a small room.

And underneath that, another smell. Coffee.

I opened the door.

---

The room beyond was finished — that was the first wrong thing, the thing that snagged in my mind and held. Finished like a *living room*. Drywall and baseboard, a ceiling with a light fixture, a wall-to-wall carpet in the good kind of brown tweed. There was a lamp. A Tiffany lamp, with the glass shade faded to a soft amber, sitting on a end table next to a recliner.

There was a television, small, bolted to a bracket, playing a shopping channel with the sound off. The smell of coffee came from a percolator on a cart. The percolator was *on*. It was still percolating. I watched the little blue flame under it, because for three or four full seconds I watched the little blue flame under it, and my brain was trying to get back into the ordinary world where a percolator sits in a finished basement and someone's *watching TV without the sound on*.

Then I looked at the far wall and the ordinary world went away and did not come back.

It was a corkboard. Six feet by four, maybe, mounted on the far wall, the kind of board you buy at an office supply store. On it, photographs, pushed on brass pins, arranged in loose columns, and around them, hand-drawn lines of red yarn, and beside each one a date and a place name and a *number*, all in the same neat blocky handwriting.

The top row was white women my age or a little older. The second row was older, different faces. There were also things I'd have called *souvenirs* if I'd been looking at them in a shop window — a hardbound ledger on the end table with a rubber band around it; a jar, a big one, on the floor by the corkboard, its glass fogged and its contents turned cloudy and pale, something suspended in the fluid that I could not look at directly; another jar like it, smaller, in the row of shelves along the left wall, and a third, and a fourth, four or five of them in a row, all of them with the same white cloudiness, all with something in them.

I have to be careful here. I want to describe it accurately, because you might think I'm exaggerating, and I need you to know that I am the least exaggerating man you have ever read.

The first jar, the big one: it was a foot and a half tall, the kind of jar you'd get at a restaurant supply store for pickles. The fluid had gone the color of skim milk. Suspended in it, curled, was a *hand*. A human hand, closed, the fingers drawn in tight, the nails dark, the wrist ending in a clean cut just above where the watch would have been. It had been in there long enough that the skin had gone the color of a museum specimen.

The smaller jars were worse, because they were *shaped for display*. In one, a set of teeth arranged in a piece of dental wax, like a smile, with a label below it: a name, and a date. In another, a coil of hair, black, braided, wrapped around a spool. In another, a swatch of skin, tanned dark and cut into a rectangle the size of a playing card, with a hole punched in one corner.

On a shelf, a velvet box, the kind that holds a ring, opened, containing a single yellowed incisor.

On a wooden hanger, a child's shoe. One. Blue canvas, size ten, with a hole worn in the toe.

On the wall next to the corkboard, a small hook in a length of red yarn, and hanging from it, a wedding band.

And at the bottom of the corkboard, on the floor, in a litter box that had been cut down with a reciprocating saw, a great deal of dark dried material that had been cleaned up around the edges but not removed, because why remove it when you'd *cleaned* it, when you'd *swept* it, when you did the work of a person living in and maintaining and *caring for* a thing.

There was a rocking chair by the corkboard. A child-height mark in pencil on the doorframe of the closet. A pair of reading glasses on the arm of the recliner. A shopping list on the fridge in the little kitchen nook, in the same blocky handwriting: *egg, coffee, foil, tape, ammonia.*

And the rectangle in the carpet. That's what took me. There was a clean rectangle in the brown tweed, four feet by six, its edges sharp, and the pile inside it was flattened from years of feet. Something had been standing there. Something had been *held* there, over and over, long enough to wear the nap off the carpet down to the backing.

On the far side of the room, past the recliner, there was a bed. A hospital bed, electric, with the rails up. The sheets were pulled back.

On the bed, in the position of a person lying on their back, was a shape under a blanket, and the blanket rose and fell.

I didn't scream.

I want that on the record. I stood in the doorway with my flashlight in my hand and the rain in my hair and I *did not scream*, because some deep idiot piece of my brain understood that if I made a sound I would be a person making a sound, and if I was a person making a sound in this room then I would be one of the *things on the wall*.

The shape under the blanket was small. It was the size of Mrs. Yancey.

The blanket rose and fell. And then it stopped, and something moved under it, and a voice came out of the pillow — thin, cracked, absurdly *polite*, a voice like a small old lady who has been waiting a long time for company:

"Is that the mail? Is it the mail?"

---

I ran.

There was no door to run *to*. I turned around and the door I came through was shut, and the brass knob turned a quarter-turn and stopped, and I *threw* myself at it and hit it with my shoulder and it did not move, and then I understood: this door opens from the *other* side*.

That was when I heard him.

He was already talking when I heard him, and that was the worst part, because it meant he'd been listening the whole time — to my flashlight, to my weight on the steps, to my breathing. He came down the stairs slowly, one hand on the rail, taking his time, and he was holding a cup. A coffee cup. His house voice. "You shouldn't have come down here, Ed." A pause. "Do you know how much I like you?"

There was a key in the lock. Turning.

I looked left. There was a small coal chute in the wall, an old coal chute, plastered over on the outside, with a heavy iron flap and a hinged grille. I put my flashlight in my teeth and I crawled into it on my hands and knees, in the dark, in the *slickness* of it, and behind me the door opened and the light from the basement flooded the chute and I saw him framed in the doorway, a big man in a white undershirt with his coffee cup, looking down at my feet going into the hole, and he said, quite conversationally, "It's all right. It's all right, Ed. It doesn't have to be like this."

I got out through a hole in the fence that had nothing to do with the persimmon tree.

---

They found me at 4 a.m. on the front steps of 15 Herring Lane, and I was covered in the filth of a coal chute and I was speaking in a voice that wasn't mine. I said *basement, basement, basement, there's a woman in the bed.*

The officers found me convincing. They found me *very* convincing. That's the strange part of what happened next. Two uniforms took me to the hospital and one of them, a young guy named Petrosky, took me seriously enough to take me back to 14 Herring Lane at five in the morning with a flashlight and a sense of duty.

There was no basement light on. The cellar door was closed, padlocked, chained.

He let us in. Warren Kress, in a cardigan, at five in the morning, without a flicker of anything on his face, except *tiredness*, except the tiredness of a man being troubled by a neighbor. He said the cellar was where he kept the old furnace, and the padlock was because of the raccoons, and he'd had problems with raccoons his whole life.

Petrosky went down. The nine steps, and the landing, and the door — the door was just a door, and it opened, and beyond it was a furnace, and an old coal bin, and standing water.

Petrosky came up the steps and looked at me on the walkway and he was very quiet.

"Mr. Bram," he said. "There's nothing down there."

They dug the yard. They took the couch, the workshop, the van, the shed. They took six hundred photographs and a shoebox of receipts and they found nothing. The state police came and were polite to Kress and thorough in a way that a person almost has to admire, and the case died in eleven weeks for a beautifully ordinary reason: no body, no evidence, no *victim*. A woman missing. A neighbor with a key. A basement.

Mrs. Yancey's grandson told me his grandmother had early-stage dementia, and that she'd had episodes before. He said she was probably in a facility in Ohio. He said it like he was apologizing. He had her puffy, kind face, and he was *relieved*, and I wanted to grab him by the lapels and shake him and say *do you know what his handwriting looks like on her shopping list*, but there is no version of that sentence a person can say out loud without sounding exactly like what I was becoming on Herring Lane.

The eleven weeks were the hard part. Not the discovery. The discovery was a *clarity*, a horrible clean clarity, and after it I knew what I knew and I slept fine. What I couldn't sleep through was the eleven weeks of the neighborhood.

Because here's what happens: the woman across the street was *gone*, and everyone on Herring Lane had a theory, and the theory was: *Ed Bram is a drunk, Ed Bram has a history, Ed Bram had an episode, Ed Bram went into Warren Kress's house in the middle of a storm, and what did you expect, Ed Bram has been like this since his wife.*

Deirdre came to my door with a casserole and told me that she hadn't meant anything by it. The mail carrier stopped waving. Somebody took down the little metal mailbox I'd had since 1988 and left it in the yard without a note. Kids I used to let wait for a lost ball wrote their names on the pavement with chalk so I could read them from the window, the way you do when you're not coming in.

And Warren Kress came to my door on the last Sunday in November and brought a bag of ziti and a jar of sauce he'd put up himself, and he stood in my doorway the way he had stood in it a hundred times, with his cap in his hands.

"Ed," he said. "I know what people are saying. I know what you saw. I want to say something to you, and I want to say it once, and then I'm going to leave."

I stood there with the door open and I couldn't get a word out.

"You've seen me at my worst," he said. "Everybody has. But you'd never — you'd never hurt a *person*, Ed. There's a difference between a man who's sick and a man who's bad." He looked at the yard, at the stumps of the persimmon tree, at the fence we still hadn't replaced. "Mrs. Yancey was a wife to me for nine years before she was a stranger. Nine years, and then she was nobody to anybody, and nobody was coming for her, Ed. Nobody was coming for her except me."

"That's insane," I said.

"I know," he said. "Everybody says that." He put the bag of ziti on the table and he stepped back and he said, "I'd take that if I were you. It's better with the basil."

And here's the thing, the thing I have to give him, the thing that took me the longest: he wasn't lying. He believed every word of it. That was the shape of the man. He genuinely believed that what he did was *care-taking*. He had a ledger with the dates in it and a shopping list that said *ammonia* and a Tiffany lamp for the light of a woman in a hospital bed, and somewhere in him, in a room I never saw, there was a version of the story where all of that was love.

I took the ziti. I didn't eat it. I threw it out on Halloween.

---

The case stayed cold. There's no statute of limitations on something that technically didn't happen.

I moved in the spring. Goodacre Arms, a third floor, on a street with no trees and no porches and no neighbors who know when your dog's not eating, and I thought about that more than anything else, more than the jars, more than the blanket going up and down. I missed knowing.

Biscuit died in February. He was fourteen. I don't know why and I have theories I'm not going to write down.

I did not sleep well in the year that followed, and I did not expect to, and I made my peace with the light being on.

Then, in October — a year to the day since the storm — I got a package.

No return address. A padded envelope with my new address written on it in a neat blocky hand. I knew the handwriting before I turned the envelope over. I'd spent six years watching him sign the little card he left my gate with. It was the same. It could have been traced by the same hand in a hundred courtrooms.

Inside the envelope was a Polaroid, and the picture was taken *from above*, printed on the instant film, and I have to explain the angle: it was shot from a second-story window, in the dark, with a long lens, of a parking lot. My parking lot. My car, the blue Civic, in its space, with me coming out of it, mid-stride, a bag of groceries in one hand.

There was a red circle drawn around the car in grease pencil.

And beneath it, on the white border of the Polaroid, in that same handwriting, a date and a time:

**WED · 3:00 A.M.**

It was a Tuesday when it arrived. The Wednesday was the next day.

I called the police. I want that clear too. I called them and I gave them the address of the post office branch I'd gotten it from, and I told them everything, and a very kind detective named Alvarez took a Polaroid of the Polaroid and looked at it a long time and then looked at me a long time and asked me a question I have not been able to answer in a year:

"Mr. Bram," he said. "Why would he take a picture of you *parked*?"

And I sat there in a rented apartment with a dead man's handwriting in my hand, and I understood what he meant. It wasn't a threat picture. A threat picture shows a house. A threat picture shows a *window*. This was a picture of a man arriving home at three in the morning, and it was nice — it was *composed* — and it was the picture of a man who has been taking these many thousands of times, and who has a collection, and who adds one now and then, the way you add a shell to a jar.

A collector doesn't photograph the target. A collector photographs the *acquisition*.

Except that the Wednesday came and went, and nothing happened, and I don't know what that means either. Maybe the collection has a schedule. Maybe the schedule changed. Maybe he was interrupted. Maybe somebody in that house with the good carpet and the shut door heard a knock on the outside of it that I will never know about, in a room I'll never see, in the amber light of a Tiffany lamp.

I still have the Polaroid. It's in a lockbox. It's in a lockbox because on the third of December, exactly at three in the morning, my building lost power for forty minutes, and when the lights came back on, the lockbox was closed and the door was still locked and nothing was disturbed, and I have never in my life been so grateful for a deadbolt.

I don't sleep with the light on anymore, though. I had that backwards.

I sleep with the light off, and I sleep with my shoes on, and every Wednesday at three in the morning, I get up, and I stand in the hall with my face against the cold window, and I watch my parking lot, and I count the cars.

There's always one I don't recognize.
