Drywall and baseboard, a ceiling with a light fixture, a wall-to-wall carpet in the good kind of brown tweed. There was a lamp. A Tiffany lamp, with the glass shade faded to a soft amber, sitting on a end table next to a recliner.

There was a television, small, bolted to a bracket, playing a shopping channel with the sound off. The smell of coffee came from a percolator on a cart. The percolator was on. It was still percolating. I watched the little blue flame under it, because for three or four full seconds I watched the little blue flame under it, and my brain was trying to get back into the ordinary world where a percolator sits in a finished basement and someone's watching TV without the sound on.

Then I looked at the far wall and the ordinary world went away and did not come back.

It was a corkboard. Six feet by four, maybe, mounted on the far wall, the kind of board you buy at an office supply store. On it, photographs, pushed on brass pins, arranged in loose columns, and around them, hand-drawn lines of red yarn, and beside each one a date and a place name and a number, all in the same neat blocky handwriting.

The top row was white women my age or a little older. The second row was older, different faces. There were also things I'd have called souvenirs if I'd been looking at them in a shop window — a hardbound ledger on the end table with a rubber band around it; a jar, a big one, on the floor by the corkboard, its glass fogged and its contents turned cloudy and pale, something suspended in the fluid that I could not look at directly; another jar like it, smaller, in the row of shelves along the left wall, and a third, and a fourth, four or five of them in a row, all of them with the same white cloudiness, all with something in them.

I have to be careful here. I want to describe it accurately, because you might think I'm exaggerating, and I need you to know that I am the least exaggerating man you have ever read.

The first jar, the big one: it was a foot and a half tall, the kind of jar you'd get at a restaurant supply store for pickles. The fluid had gone the color of skim milk. Suspended in it, curled, was a hand. A human hand, closed, the fingers drawn in tight, the nails dark, the wrist ending in a clean cut just above where the watch would have been. It had been in there long enough that the skin had gone the color of a museum specimen.

The smaller jars were worse, because they were shaped for display. In one, a set of teeth arranged in a piece of dental wax, like a smile, with a label below it: a name, and a date. In another, a coil of hair, black, braided, wrapped around a spool. In another, a swatch of skin, tanned dark and cut into a rectangle the size of a playing card, with a hole punched in one corner.

On a shelf, a velvet box, the kind that holds a ring, opened, containing a single yellowed incisor.

On a wooden hanger, a child's shoe. One. Blue canvas, size ten, with a hole worn in the toe.

On the wall next to the corkboard, a small hook in a length of red yarn, and hanging from it, a wedding band.

And at the bottom of the corkboard, on the floor, in a litter box that had been cut down with a reciprocating saw, a great deal of dark dried material that had been cleaned up around the edges but not removed, because why remove it when you'd cleaned it, when you'd swept it, when you did the work of a person living in and maintaining and caring for a thing.

There was a rocking chair by the corkboard. A child-height mark in pencil on the doorframe of the closet. A pair of reading glasses on the arm of the recliner. A shopping list on the fridge in the little kitchen nook, in the same blocky handwriting: egg, coffee, foil, tape, ammonia.

And the rectangle in the carpet. That's what took me. There was a clean rectangle in the brown tweed, four feet by six, its edges sharp, and the pile inside it was flattened from years of feet. Something had been standing there. Something had been held there, over and over, long enough to wear the nap off the carpet down to the backing.

On the far side of the room, past the recliner, there was a bed. A hospital bed, electric, with the rails up. The sheets were pulled back.

On the bed, in the position of a person lying on their back, was a shape under a blanket, and the blanket rose and fell.

I didn't scream.

I want that on the record. I stood in the doorway with my flashlight in my hand and the rain in my hair and I did not scream, because some deep idiot piece of my brain understood that if I made a sound I would be a person making a sound, and if I was a person making a sound in this room then I would be one of the things on the wall.

The shape under the blanket was small. It was the size of Mrs. Yancey.

The blanket rose and fell. And then it stopped, and something moved under it, and a voice came out of the pillow — thin, cracked, absurdly polite, a voice like a small old lady who has been waiting a long time for company:

"Is that the mail? Is it the mail?"

I ran.

There was no door to run to. I turned around and the door I came through was shut, and the brass knob turned a quarter-turn and stopped, and I threw myself at it and hit it with my shoulder and it did not move, and then I understood: this door opens from the other side*.

That was when I heard him.

He was already talking when I heard him, and that was the worst part, because it meant he'd been listening the whole time — to my flashlight, to my weight on the steps, to my breathing. He came down the stairs slowly, one hand on the rail, taking his time, and he was holding a cup. A coffee cup. His house voice. "You shouldn't have come down here, Ed." A pause. "Do you know how much I like you?"

There was a key in the lock. Turning.

I looked left. There was a small coal chute in the wall, an old coal chute, plastered over on the outside, with a heavy iron flap and a hinged grille. I put my flashlight in my teeth and I crawled into it on my hands and knees, in the dark, in the slickness of it, and behind me the door opened and the light from the basement flooded the chute and I saw him framed in the doorway, a big man in a white undershirt with his coffee cup, looking down at my feet going into the hole, and he said, quite conversationally, "It's all right. It's all right, Ed. It doesn't have to be like this."

I got out through a hole in the fence that had nothing to do with the persimmon tree.

They found me at 4 a.m. on the front steps of 15 Herring Lane, and I was covered in the filth of a coal chute and I was speaking in a voice that wasn't mine. I said basement, basement, basement, there's a woman in the bed.

The officers found me convincing. They found me very convincing. That's the strange part of what happened next. Two uniforms took me to the hospital and one of them, a young guy named Petrosky, took me seriously enough to take me back to 14 Herring Lane at five in the morning with a flashlight and a sense of duty.

There was no basement light on. The cellar door was closed, padlocked, chained.

He let us in. Warren Kress, in a cardigan, at five in the morning, without a flicker of anything on his face, except tiredness, except the tiredness of a man being troubled by a neighbor. He said the cellar was where he kept the old furnace, and the padlock was because of the raccoons, and he'd had problems with raccoons his whole life.

Petrosky went down. The nine steps, and the landing, and the door — the door was just a door, and it opened, and beyond it was a furnace, and an old coal bin, and standing water.

Petrosky came up the steps and looked at me on the walkway and he was very quiet.

"Mr. Bram," he said. "There's nothing down there."

They dug the yard. They took the couch, the workshop, the van, the shed. They took six hundred photographs and a shoebox of receipts and they found nothing. The state police came and were polite to Kress and thorough in a way that a person almost has to admire, and the case died in eleven weeks for a beautifully ordinary reason: no body, no evidence, no victim. A woman missing. A neighbor with a key. A basement.

Mrs. Yancey's grandson told me his grandmother had early-stage dementia, and that she'd had episodes before. He said she was probably in a facility in Ohio. He said it like he was apologizing. He had her puffy, kind face, and he was relieved, and I wanted to grab him by the lapels and shake him and say do you know what his handwriting looks like on her shopping list, but there is no version of that sentence a person can say out loud without sounding exactly like what I was becoming on Herring Lane.

The eleven weeks were the hard part. Not the discovery. The discovery was a clarity, a horrible clean clarity, and after it I knew what I knew and I slept fine. What I couldn't sleep through was the eleven weeks of the neighborhood.

Because here's what happens: the woman across the street was gone, and everyone on Herring Lane had a theory, and the theory was: Ed Bram is a drunk, Ed Bram has a history, Ed Bram had an episode, Ed Bram went into Warren Kress's house in the middle of a storm, and what did you expect, Ed Bram has been like this since his wife.

Deirdre came to my door with a casserole and told me that she hadn't meant anything by it. The mail carrier stopped waving. Somebody took down the little metal mailbox I'd had since 1988 and left it in the yard without a note. Kids I used to let wait for a lost ball wrote their names on the pavement with chalk so I could read them from the window, the way you do when you're not coming in.

And Warren Kress came to my door on the last Sunday in November and brought a bag of ziti and a jar of sauce he'd put up himself, and he stood in my doorway the way he had stood in it a hundred times, with his cap in his hands.

"Ed," he said. "I know what people are saying. I know what you saw. I want to say something to you, and I want to say it once, and then I'm going to leave."

I stood there with the door open and I couldn't get a word out.

"You've seen me at my worst," he said. "Everybody has. But you'd never — you'd never hurt a person, Ed. There's a difference between a man who's sick and a man who's bad." He looked at the yard, at the stumps of the persimmon tree, at the fence we still hadn't replaced. "Mrs. Yancey was a wife to me for nine years before she was a stranger. Nine years, and then she was nobody to anybody, and nobody was coming for her, Ed. Nobody was coming for her except me."

"That's insane," I said.

"I know," he said. "Everybody says that." He put the bag of ziti on the table and he stepped back and he said, "I'd take that if I were you. It's better with the basil."

And here's the thing, the thing I have to give him, the thing that took me the longest: he wasn't lying. He believed every word of it. That was the shape of the man. He genuinely believed that what he did was care-taking. He had a ledger with the dates in it and a shopping list that said ammonia and a Tiffany lamp for the light of a woman in a hospital bed, and somewhere in him, in a room I never saw, there was a version of the story where all of that was love.

I took the ziti. I didn't eat it. I threw it out on Halloween.

The case stayed cold. There's no statute of limitations on something that technically didn't happen.

I moved in the spring. Goodacre Arms, a third floor, on a street with no trees and no porches and no neighbors who know when your dog's not eating, and I thought about that more than anything else, more than the jars, more than the blanket going up and down. I missed knowing.

Biscuit died in February. He was fourteen. I don't know why and I have theories I'm not going to write down.

I did not sleep well in the year that followed, and I did not expect to, and I made my peace with the light being on.

Then, in October — a year to the day since the storm — I got a package.

No return address. A padded envelope with my new address written on it in a neat blocky hand. I knew the handwriting before I turned the envelope over. I'd spent six years watching him sign the little card he left my gate with. It was the same. It could have been traced by the same hand in a hundred courtrooms.

Inside the envelope was a Polaroid, and the picture was taken from above, printed on the instant film, and I have to explain the angle: it was shot from a second-story window, in the dark, with a long lens, of a parking lot. My parking lot. My car, the blue Civic, in its space, with me coming out of it, mid-stride, a bag of groceries in one hand.

There was a red circle drawn around the car in grease pencil.

And beneath it, on the white border of the Polaroid, in that same handwriting, a date and a time:

WED · 3:00 A.M.

It was a Tuesday when it arrived. The Wednesday was the next day.

I called the police. I want that clear too. I called them and I gave them the address of the post office branch I'd gotten it from, and I told them everything, and a very kind detective named Alvarez took a Polaroid of the Polaroid and looked at it a long time and then looked at me a long time and asked me a question I have not been able to answer in a year:

"Mr. Bram," he said. "Why would he take a picture of you parked?"

And I sat there in a rented apartment with a dead man's handwriting in my hand, and I understood what he meant. It wasn't a threat picture. A threat picture shows a house. A threat picture shows a window. This was a picture of a man arriving home at three in the morning, and it was nice — it was composed — and it was the picture of a man who has been taking these many thousands of times, and who has a collection, and who adds one now and then, the way you add a shell to a jar.

A collector doesn't photograph the target. A collector photographs the acquisition.

Except that the Wednesday came and went, and nothing happened, and I don't know what that means either. Maybe the collection has a schedule. Maybe the schedule changed. Maybe he was interrupted. Maybe somebody in that house with the good carpet and the shut door heard a knock on the outside of it that I will never know about, in a room I'll never see, in the amber light of a Tiffany lamp.

I still have the Polaroid. It's in a lockbox. It's in a lockbox because on the third of December, exactly at three in the morning, my building lost power for forty minutes, and when the lights came back on, the lockbox was closed and the door was still locked and nothing was disturbed, and I have never in my life been so grateful for a deadbolt.

I don't sleep with the light on anymore, though. I had that backwards.

I sleep with the light off, and I sleep with my shoes on, and every Wednesday at three in the morning, I get up, and I stand in the hall with my face against the cold window, and I watch my parking lot, and I count the cars.

There's always one I don't recognize.

The first alarm didn’t sound so much as tear through the prison—a mechanical scream that shook dust from the ceiling and drowned every other noise beneath it.

Red emergency lights strobed through the corridors. Cell doors hammered open. Somewhere above, a generator failed, and the lights died for three terrible seconds before returning in dim, uneven flashes. In that darkness, the cell block became a blur of bodies: prisoners surging into the hallway, guards charging from the opposite end with shields raised, batons swinging.

“Move! Move! Move!”

No one moved fast enough.

The first guard went down beneath a wave of inmates. His shield cracked against the floor, and a boot caught him in the ribs. The baton in his hand disappeared under a dozen bodies. He vanished beneath kicking heels and swinging fists, his whistle still shrieking uselessly in his throat.

The second line tried to hold. Riot shields came up, forming a trembling wall of black polycarbonate. The inmates hit it like breakers against a sea wall—once, twice, then all at once. A guard’s arm snapped sideways. Another staggered back with blood boiling from a wound above his eye.

Then the line broke.

Batons rose and fell. Fists smashed into helmets. A guard was driven backward into a steel door hard enough to dent the frame. Another found himself face-down on the concrete, shielding his head as boots crashed down again and again. His radio crackled beneath him, dispatch screaming for units that had no path through the chaos.

The prisoners were just as brutal. One man was seized by the collar and slammed face-first into a reinforced observation window. Glass starred outward but held. He hung there, bleeding, while another blow drove him to the floor. Across the corridor, two inmates grappled with a guard who had lost his shield. They beat him with the flat side of it until his arms gave out, then dragged him into the smoke.

The air thickened with dust, sweat, and the bitter smell of smoke. Fire had started near the laundry chute, fed by paper and piles of clothing. Flames licked up the wall as officers withdrew past it, their silhouettes jerking in the red light. A ceiling sprinkler turned, but the water pressure was weak, leaving only a mist that made everything gleam.

In the visitation room, an officer fired his stun gun point-blank into an inmate’s chest. The man convulsed, clothing scorched around the contact points, and collapsed. The officer stepped over him—then took a brick to the side of the head and fell beside him.

No one could tell where the fighting stopped and the panic began. The wounded crawled through the crush of legs. The standing fought over weapons, shields, even shoes. Prisoners who had been rivals moments earlier now stood back-to-back against the guards, hacking and striking at anyone wearing blue. Guards who had been trained to separate fights now swung at anything that moved.

A cell door flew off its hinges. Metal screamed against concrete. The riot spilled into the adjoining block, where more doors were already being broken open. The alarms kept screaming, indifferent to the blood spreading beneath the fluorescent lights.

For a few seconds, the entire prison existed as one violent roar: crashing metal, breaking glass, commands nobody obeyed, and the wet, brutal sounds of impacts landing again and again.

Then, beneath all of it, the radio announced that the west wing was lost.

The corridor filled even faster.

**Hotel Room 814, 11:40 p.m.**

The television played a muted cooking show. Someone onscreen was making pasta with the urgency of a hostage negotiator.

Mara sat cross-legged on the bed, an oily cloth moving slowly along the barrel of her pistol. Beside her, Dain cleaned a knife with a hotel laundry sock, careful not to leave fibers on the edge.

“Okay,” he said, “I need you to settle something.”

Mara did not look up. “You’re going to dislike my answer.”

“That hasn’t stopped you before.”

She inspected the slide, then set the pistol on a white towel. “My favorite is the one nobody notices until later. No drama. They go to bed annoyed about work, and by morning the problem has solved itself.”

Dain sniffed. “Passive. Efficient. Very boring.”

“And clean.”

“Clean is a tool, not a style.”

He held the knife against the lamp, turning it until the blade flashed. “I prefer when they know. Not much, obviously. Just enough for the face to change.”

Mara raised an eyebrow. “You want an audience?”

“I want *recognition*. The mark understands the mistake they made. They understand that the people they crossed were not abstract.” He wiped the blade again. “Then it’s over.”

On the television, the contestant dropped a pan of gnocchi.

“Your favorite,” Mara said, “is fear with a strict serving size.”

“Exactly.”

“Not poisoning. I know you love poisoning.”

“Poisoning is a masterpiece when done well,” Dain said. “But it lacks punctuation. I prefer punctuation.”

Mara laughed softly. “You want the kill to have a sentence structure. Subject, verb, consequence.”

He grinned. “Now you understand me.”

She picked up her pistol again. “I like disappearances. They walk out of one life and never arrive in another. Sometimes it’s an accident. Sometimes a robbery. Sometimes nothing at all.”

“Sometimes the target is placed in a car that will be found at the bottom of a river,” Dain said.

“Exactly. Though I prefer the ones with questions left. Let the police spend years arguing about what happened.”

He tossed the laundry sock into the wastebasket. “So your ideal is confusion.”

“My ideal is consequence without closure.”

The room was quiet except for the soft clink of metal.

Dain began reassembling his knife. “What about mistakes? Not ours—the target’s. A person who thinks they’re protected. Who assumes their money makes them invisible.”

Mara’s hands slowed. “Now that’s a good kill.”

“It isn’t even about the killing. It’s the expression before they understand. The half-second where they realize all their precautions failed.”

“Romantic,” she said.

“Pathetic, maybe.”

“Those are often the same thing.”

Dain glanced toward the adjoining wall. “The target in nine-twelve checked in under a false name. Three phones. No luggage except one red suitcase.”

Mara looked up. “You’ve already started.”

“Professional curiosity.”

“You’ve already started.”

He shrugged. “He keeps checking the hallway. Every thirty seconds. He thinks he’s being discreet.”

“I noticed,” Mara said.

Something in her tone made Dain look over.

She had stopped cleaning the pistol.

“What?” he asked.

“Nothing. Just thinking about how boring your favorite kill would be if he saw us right now.”

Dain’s expression softened into a smile. “He hasn’t seen us.”

Mara placed the pistol beside the knife on the towel. “No,” she said. “Yet.”

The cooking show cut to a commercial.

Neither assassin moved to change the channel.

**The Fire**

The faggots were green—fresh-cut birch and hazel, the sap still wet in them—so they gave up more smoke than flame, and the smoke came on low and slow, crawling along the ground like a thing looking for a way in.

Marguerite had been bound to the stake before dawn, and she had spent the whole grey hour of waiting feeling the cold. Now the cold was over. The heat arrived in waves: first a soft pushing against her shins, the way a hand might test a door. Then it settled, patient, and began to work upward.

She smelled herself before she felt it. Hair went first, always—the smell of it was sharp and sweetish, like a kitchen on a bad day, and it made her think absurdly of the comb she kept in her apron. Then the wool of her dress. Pitch and resin came with a thick, choking bitterness that coated the inside of her nose and throat, and she tasted it, and thought: *this is what burning tastes like.* Not like fire. Like pitch, and grease, and the flat metallic tang of her own skin.

She screamed then, properly, the way a woman screams when the whole world has gone wrong: her name, the name of the child she had cured, the name of the man who had spat in her doorway. *I did it for the boy. I did it for the boy, I only wanted him to live.* The crowd made a low sound. Some of them crossed themselves. One man near the front was eating something.

The first real fire took at her feet, and the scream changed.

That was the strange part, the part no one could hear from where they stood in the muddy square. The first scream was a woman's scream—a cry with a shape to it, rising and falling, carrying. The second was not a cry but a sound pushed out of a body that no longer had a say in it: high, ragged, tearing at the top like cloth ripping. It came out of her in pieces. She had been a strong-lunged woman; she had carried water up the hill for years. But the fire found the moisture in her and took it, and her tongue cracked and thickened in her mouth, and what had been a voice became something hoarse and hammered, a bark, a whistle punched through a wet sleeve.

The smoke was the worst of it, she would say later, if there were a later. Everyone talks about the flame. But flame is visible, and visible things can be waited out. The smoke was inside her. It went down her throat and filled her chest and turned her breath to powder, and each inhalation was a scrape, a hiccupping gulp, a drowning in empty air. It got into her eyes and made them run so she could not look up at the sky she had been watching all morning, the one thin cloud that would not commit to anything.

Heat came in waves, and between the waves there were little mercy-gaps of cold where she could remember what it felt like to be a person with a name and hands. In one of those gaps she thought about the boy. His name was Thomas. She had given him a tea of rue and wormwood and honey, and his fever had broken in the night, and his mother had come to her door with a knife and said *witch* and would not say thank you. It was the only thing she had ever wanted to do that worked, and she had done it out of a kind of stupid, ordinary goodness, and for that she was going to be cooked alive in front of nine hundred people, and the smoke was going to take her voice before the fire took the rest of her.

Then the fire reached the place where her voice lived, and it stopped.

What followed was not a scream. It was a sound like a bellows with a hole in it, a wet mechanical rush, absurd, almost funny if you were far enough away to hear it as anything but human. Her throat was a seam of fire. Every breath she pulled seared, and every breath she pushed out whistled through tissue that was no longer soft enough to close properly. She opened her mouth wide and the wide-open mouth produced nothing at all—just heat, just the smell of cooking meat on the left side of her face—and she understood, with a terrible clarity, that she was screaming into a room where no one could hear her.

The crowd surged forward a step, all of them, the way a crowd does, and someone began to push the faggots closer with a pole and someone else threw something—a rag, an old shoe, a clump of earth from the square. The heat became a single unbroken wall. She stopped pulling against the ropes because there was no longer a body to pull. The last of her was the whistling, thinner and thinner, and then a bubbling at the back of her throat that she could feel but not shape, and then nothing but the enormous roaring of the fire, which went on being loud after she had stopped.

Someone in the front row said, *Lord have mercy,* and meant it. Someone else said nothing and picked up his hat and turned away, and the crowd made room for him, and for a while after that the square smelled of pitch and burnt hair and the sweetish rot of a thing cooking in the open air, and the children cried, and the smoke went up and up and thinned and was gone, and the stake stood in the middle of the marketplace with a shape on it that nobody could look at directly.

There is a kind of quiet that comes after. Not silence—silence is the wrong word, there was still the fire, still the crowd, still the dogs. A quiet inside the witness, a settling, the moment when the world agrees to continue and you find you have joined it without permission.

And that was the part that would have undone her, if she had been able to hear it: not the burning, but how quickly it became ordinary. How fast the smell stopped being a smell and became *the way things are done here.* How the man with the pole wiped his forehead on his sleeve and stepped back into the line to wait for the next one, humming.

## The Ninth Rising at Greymarch

The river had come up in the night and taken the bank.

It happened the way rivers do — without announcement, without hurry — and by morning the low field where Greymarch's soldiers had been buried in a common trench had gone soft at the edges and begun, quietly, to give up its dead. Water runoff had undercut the earth and slumped it in long ugly folds, and where the folds had split, the black air underneath breathed out its cold mineral smell, and the shapes that had lain undisturbed for a hundred and thirteen years were no longer shapes at all but merely suggestions. A boot. A shoulder. The pale buckle of a belt, green with verdigris, holding a fist that had been a fist in a soldier's lifetime and was now a curled thing full of rain.

The village had let the field go. There was nothing in the trench worth keeping, and the Sable Duke's levy had come and gone, and the crows had been down to nothing but hair and boots by the second winter, and so the field was simply a low wet meadow with a long shallow scar in it, and no one in Greymarch ploughed that side of the watercourse.

No one until Vessa.

---

She came in with a lantern that gave no light, only a sort of thin blue argument — a flame the color of a bruise, sitting low in the glass like something sulking.

The people of the upper road heard her later and remembered only the sound, because the sound came first: a tapping, rhythmic, patient, the sound of a woman driving seed into soft ground with the heel of her hand. *Tap. Tap. Tap.* There were no wards in her practice. No circle scratched in the dirt, no candles at the cardinal points, no recitation of any name of power that the folk of the hill had ever heard. The hill folk were farmers, and they knew all the old shapes of the world — the salt line, the iron nail, the church-bell that would not ring — and they said, afterward, that the woman in the black coat did none of those things, and that was why it worked.

She sowed.

The seed was small and black and smelled of a lakebed, and she cast it in handfuls, walking the length of the old trench in a slow diagonal, and where the seed fell into the split earth it did not lie. It sank. It went down into the mud as though the mud were thirsty, and it took the black water with it, and after a while the field began to steam faintly in the cold air, the way a road steams after rain.

Then something began to come up.

It did not come up the way a thing comes up. It came up the way a *crop* comes up — drawn, coaxed, pulled at from below by a root that did not intend to be a root. The first of them broke the surface at the widow's grave end of the trench and rose without any of the usual stages. No bloating. No softening. No slipping. The earth simply opened along the seams of a body that had been lying folded for a century and *released* it, and the thing that stood up was green as a thing in a ditch and had been dead for so long that the rot had finished with it and moved on.

It was a man namedCorr. Everyone in Greymarch knew that; he had been a serjeant of the ninth company and had died of a flux in the year the levy came. He had been buried holding a sprig of bitter rosemary in his teeth, because his mother had put it there, and the sprig was still there, black with age and dry as a whisper, and the muscles of the jaw had set around it like a staple.

He did not look at Vessa.

That was the part that the two woodcutters watching from the fence could not stop telling each other, afterward, over and over, in the years when there was still someone left to tell. He did not look at her. He looked at the place where the seed had gone in. And then he *walked* to it.

He walked well. Better than living men walk. His knees did not creak. His weight shifted without the small collapses that flesh makes when it trusts itself, and the water in the field took his weight and closed over his boots without a sound, and he did not drag his feet. He stood over the spot where he had been sown and he *waited*, like a horse with its head down, and out of the black soil beside his heel came a single pale shoot, and it unfurled at his ankle — a leaf the shape of a grain but thin as onion-skin.

---

They came up all night. That was the thing. The great mass of them did not come in a horror of pushing and clawing and broken fingernails; they came up in ones and twos, and then in tens, and by the fourth hour of the morning the field was full of them standing knee-deep in the mud, waiting, each one with its small pale shoot at its feet, each one turned toward a place in the earth.

Vessa walked the rows and she spoke to them, and her voice was the voice of a woman coaxing a horse over a stile — low, bored, patient, reasonable.

"You'll hold until the harvest," she said. "You'll hold until then and you won't tire. You'll hold because you're *grown* now, and a grown thing doesn't lie down."

The rot on them was not offensive. That should have been the warning, and it was, but nobody took it as one, because there was so little smell — only the cold sweetish breath of turned earth and, under that, the dry skinned-muskiness of old cloth and old hair. Their skin had gone the color of boiled leather and it hung on them in slack folds, and the fold at the wrist would close if you pushed it, like a mouth. The dead of Greymarch had been buried in their coats, and the coats had blackened to a shine, and the hands inside the sleeves had pruned to the color and texture of a drowned person's hands, and the hands were the worst of it, because the fingers had shrunk away on the bone and left three knuckles and a thumb gripping nothing at all, forever, with the perfect grip of a man holding a spear shaft that had rotted out of his hand eleven years before he died.

The lung of the boy at the second grave — nine years old, had died of the same flux — was outside his ribs. It lay against the outside of his chest like a bladder, translucent and veined, and it *moved*. It filled and emptied with nothing. It filled and emptied because the magic had found the shape of breath and copied it without troubling to ask where breath came from, and it made a small wet sound each time, like a mouth working at a crust of bread.

Where the arrow had gone in under the serjeant's collarbone, the wound was still open. That was the second warning: not fresh, not running, but *open*, glazed and quiet, the way a wound closes too early in a living man and never closes at all in the dead. Nothing had taken him. Something had simply held him at the moment of it, and the body had gone on being a body around the injury like a cup around a crack, and would hold there, faithful, until the wheat came in golden.

They did not answer when she spoke. They answered to the *soil*. Vessa would tap a place with her heel and every head in the row would turn, at once, without the flailing jerk of a puppet but with a smooth unified swivel, like a field of corn deciding which way the wind is.

---

By dawn she'd sowed the whole trench, and they were standing in it, and they had begun to do the thing that made the farmers of the upper road leave their houses and not come back.

They were holding hands.

Men who had died in the same year and the same company and the same mud, some of whom had gone into the ground holding each other's wrists in the dark, some of whom had been at each other's throats a half hour before the flux took them, were reaching out and taking hands. A chain of them across the field, wrist to wrist, fingers closing on the pruned knuckles of the next. They did it without sound. And they stood so, in the grey light, shoulder to shoulder, a holding of hands like children at a festival, and their boots were in the furrow and their boots would not come up for a long time.

And they were singing.

Not loudly. Under their breath, if breath were what they had. A hymn — the old marching hymn of the ninth company, the one they had sung up the hills with the levy, the one with the long descant on the *—march, march, march* — and they got it right. Every man of them got it right, in a hundred and thirteen different voices that had been buried in wet ground since before the songs about them were written.

But the hymn was in Vessa's voice.

That was the third warning, and it was the one that broke the woodcutters, because the song came out of the mouths of the dead in the flat unhurried tone of the woman in the black coat, and when she opened her mouth to correct a man near the fence who had slipped the tempo, it was the same sound, the same voice, from two places at once — and Vessa stopped, and put her fingers to her throat, and looked at her own hand with an expression the men could not read and would spend the rest of their lives describing as *puzzled*, which was not the right word, and *grateful*, which was worse.

---

The grain came in nine days.

It came in wrong. It came up white, then the color of ash, then a dull hammered gold, and it came up *fast* — a hand's breadth a day, then a foot, then three feet — and it came up through them. Out of the hollows of their cheeks, where a man's cheekbone would be. Out of the sockets of the eyes, so that each skull wore a soft gray cowl of it like a hood. Between the ribs, at the seams of the coats. Their hair had gone, most of it, and what was left had braided itself into the stalks and held on. The grain rooted in them and drew, and the drawing was what made them stand up straight.

And the army did not march.

She wanted it to march. That was the trick of it, and she understood it by the ninth day, standing in the wet field with her lantern in her hand and the row of them standing patient as fenceposts: she had not made an army. She had made a *crop*. The raising was a sowing, and the harvest was the wheat, and when the wheat came in gold the dead would be *ready* — a field being worked by all the hands that had ever died in it, and the marching would be the harvest-movement, down the row and out, and there would be no stopping it, because you cannot call in a harvest once the sickle is in the field.

She had thought, for eleven years, that she was commanding them.

She found the seed in her own chest, on the ninth night, when she was tired and cold and could not get warm by the fire she had not lit. A small black grain, hard as a seed, lodged under the fourth rib on the left, and it had a root in it, fine as a hair, threaded down into her.

She stood in the dark a long while with her hand over it. The kind woman of the hill had found her on the road with nothing and a fever and a name she would not say, and had fed her, and had asked her once what she was working at, and had not liked the answer.

"Harvest," Vessa said, out loud, to nobody, to the field, to the row of wheat-headed dead standing hand in hand in the furrows. The wind moved and the grain ticked like a hundred small clocks. "It's nearly harvest."

And in the field beyond the watercourse, where the enemy's dead lay in their own long trench — the Sable Duke's men, carried up the same road, buried the same spring, three hundred strong — the ground began to steam.

---

*You cannot sow the wind.*

**The Test**

The room smelled like rust and old cigarettes, and the only light came from a single bulb hanging low on a cord, swinging a little because the door had just been kicked shut behind him.

They took his phone. They took his jacket. They told him to leave his wallet on the table with the pizza boxes and the football he'd watched the whole of last Sunday on. All of it was done in a businesslike way, the way you'd take a coat at a restaurant, and that was the worst part — how ordinary it was. How much of it had already become ordinary for these people.

"Stand here," Bri said. "Don't move till you're told."

She was the one who'd recruited him, six weeks ago now, in the parking lot of a gas station where he worked the graveyard shift. She was small and soft-spoken and never once raised her voice. She'd told him he had a face people trusted. She'd told him the money was easy and the company was better than the company he had. She'd told him the only rule that mattered was that you didn't bring problems in and you didn't back out once you were in.

He'd said he wasn't ready.

He'd said it twice.

The second time, she'd smiled and said, *That's fine. We'll wait.*

They'd waited. That was the thing he'd failed to understand at the time — that waiting was itself a kind of pressure, that the longer he stayed on the outside, the more the inside started to look like the only safe place to be.

Now a man named Russo sat in a folding chair against the wall with his ankles crossed and a phone in his hand, scrolling. He hadn't said a word since Nate came in. He didn't look up. He didn't need to. Every so often he'd make a small sound of amusement at whatever he was reading, and that sound did more work than shouting would have.

Bri carried a length of black pipe to the table and set it down.

"Nate," she said. "Look at me."

He looked.

"You know Coley."

He did. Coley had been in the crew the year before Nate ever heard of it — a wiry older guy with a laugh you could hear from the street, who'd worked the register at the liquor store where Nate's grandmother used to buy lottery tickets. Coley had slipped Nate a sleeve of cigarettes on his sixteenth birthday. Coley had, when things got bad for Nate at home, quietly paid off a debt Nate hadn't told anyone about.

"He's a rat," Bri said. "He was talking. He's been talking for two weeks."

Nate's mouth didn't open.

"He was going to take everything off us. The money, the name, the crew — you." She said *you* like it was a favor Coley had done to him. "Russo wants him handled. And he wants to know who's still standing on our side." She tipped her head toward the pipe. "You don't have to kill him. I want that in your head. Killing's more paper than it's worth. He breathes, he talks to the state, then he goes home to his wife's mother and he takes a plea and he's out in four years doing a little community service and he's still alive to do it again."

*But* — and here she stepped closer, close enough that he could smell the coffee on her breath — *he has to not be able to talk. That's the test. That's all it is.*

"Six swings," Bri said. "Hard ones. You count them out loud so everybody knows you can do it. Then he's done."

And then she did the thing he would think about later, the thing that told him there was no version of this where he was anything but in it.

"You walk out of here without swinging, you're not in the crew. You're not in the crew *and* you've got what we know. So now you have two problems, and I'm only offering to solve one of them."

She put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart, and gave him a little push back, friendly, like she was straightening his collar.

"Make Russo happy. Make Coley quiet. Make your grandmother proud."

Russo still hadn't looked up. He scrolled. Somewhere behind Nate, a man breathed in through his nose — slow, deliberate, the sound of someone trying to control themselves.

Nate turned around.

Coley was on his knees in the middle of the floor, hands behind his back, zip-tied. His lip was split. There was already a dark spread on the front of his shirt that hadn't been there an hour ago, and his eyes were open and rolling toward the light.

He looked at Nate and something went out of his face. It wasn't fear anymore. It was worse than fear. It was recognition, and then it was hope.

"Nate," Coley said. "Nate, kid, you don't have to do this. Look at me — you don't have to do this. Tell them no. Tell them you said no. That's all, that's all you gotta—"

Bri stepped past him and set the pipe in Nate's hand.

The pipe was heavier than he expected. It was cold and slick and it wanted to slip.

"Count," she said.

He raised it.

He brought it down.

The sound was smaller than he'd imagined — a wet, flat *thock* that didn't seem like enough to be doing what it was doing. Coley's head snapped sideways and he made a noise Nate would hear on bad nights for the rest of his life.

"One," Bri said.

He raised it again. His arm was shaking so badly the pipe wobbled in the air.

"Two."

Coley was crying now, not screaming, and he kept saying Nate's name, and each time he said it the name got smaller and more broken, like a word being worn away.

"Three."

*Harder*, he told himself. *Bri said hard ones. Russo is watching. If I can't do it I have two problems and Bri only offered to solve one of them and my grandmother has a hundred and six years left and somewhere out there are men who are worse than Coley and they are also going to want to know.*

"Four."

By the fifth his arm had gone numb and everything had narrowed down to the bulb and the pipe and the shape of Bri's hand on his shoulder, steadying him, guiding him, patient as a woman teaching a child to hold a pen.

"Six."

He swung and then he stood there with the pipe hanging at his side, breathing, and the room was very quiet except for Coley on the floor making a sound like a bag of groceries being unpacked.

Bri took the pipe from him and set it back on the table. She looked down at Coley, then at Russo, and gave a small nod.

Russo finally raised his head. He looked at Nate for a long moment, the way you'd look at a dog you'd just watched drag a rope in a yard — assessing whether it had taken the lesson or whether it needed another one.

"Yeah," he said. "He'll do."

He went back to his phone. That was all. There was no handshake, no embrace, no moment that would have told Nate, if he'd needed one, that something had been won. Bri peeled off three folded hundreds and put them in Nate's hand and closed his fingers over them, and her hands were warm, and her voice was almost kind.

"See," she said. "Wasn't so hard."

Then they let him out, and he stood on the loading dock in the cold with money in his fist and his coat over his arm and the taste of copper in his mouth from where he'd bitten the inside of his cheek.

For eleven weeks afterward, Coley didn't talk. He never gave a statement, never made a deal, never took the plea that Bri had promised him. Nobody ever knew for certain whether it was because he was too broken to speak or because he had decided, in the end, that saying Nate's name one more time in a room with a recording device in it was a worse thing than whatever came next.

What Nate understood — walking to his car, then to his grandmother's kitchen, then to the graveyard shift, where he stood behind a register for eight hours and smiled at every single person who came in — was that the pipe had never been the point.

The point was that they'd found something they could use to keep him. They'd found the one thing he couldn't walk away from, the one door in him that would swing open, and they'd wedged it wide with a man who had once given him cigarettes for free.

And they had. And now the test was over, and there would be another one, and another, each one cheaper to them and more expensive to him, and the terrible arithmetic of it was that every time he passed, they gave him a little more of the thing he wanted.

A name. A cut. A reason to believe he wasn't the kid from the gas station with the dead father and the bad home — but a person somebody would answer for.

He rang up a customer. He bagged the milk. He looked at his own hands the whole time, and they were steady, and that was the thing he couldn't stop thinking about.

They were completely steady.

### The Courtesy of Dinner

He took the first bite before I touched my own.

Across the white tablecloth, Victor smiled as though we were old friends rather than a man and his ruin. The restaurant was quiet enough for us to hear the rain tapping against the windows. Candlelight trembled between us. Silverware chimed softly against porcelain.

“Tell me again,” he said, “how bad is it?”

“Not bad at all,” I said. “Merely inconvenient.”

He laughed. It was the laugh I remembered from board meetings: warm, confident, entirely unconvincing.

Above his plate, the candles bent toward him.

Victor set down his spoon. His fingers lingered on the handle a moment too long.

“Everything tastes strange,” he said.

“How strange?”

He considered the question with the seriousness he gave to contracts and deadlines. “Like coins. Like someone stirred a spoonful of money into the soup.” He took another sip of wine. “And the room has become remarkably warm.”

I knew what that meant. The first warmth came from inside, spreading beneath the skin before any honest flush could explain it.

“Perhaps the fire is too high,” I said.

“Mm.”

He pulled at his collar. A faint shine gathered along his hairline.

“I’ve had a difficult week,” he said. “I barely slept Tuesday.”

“That would do it.”

He smiled again, but the muscles arrived late. He turned toward the window, where the rain wrote thin lines down the glass.

“My daughter starts at the university in September,” he said. “Did I ever tell you that?”

“No.”

“Criminology. She wants to understand why people do terrible things.” He touched the rim of his glass. “I told her it was better not to know. That people are mostly frightened. They do what they believe will make them safe.”

His hand was trembling.

I watched his throat work as he swallowed. A bead of sweat slipped from his temple and vanished into his collar.

“Victor.”

“I’m fine.”

His voice had thickened. Not much. Just enough that the final word arrived late, as if it had crossed a greater distance than it should have.

“No,” he said, suddenly. “No, that isn’t right.”

He looked down at his plate. The food had become interesting to him again. He nudged the vegetables with the edge of his fork, then stopped, staring at them as though they had rearranged themselves.

“The light’s too bright,” he said.

The candles had not changed.

He raised his glass and found it difficult to close his fingers around the stem. Wine trembled against the rim.

“Water,” he said. “Could we have some water?”

The waiter brought it. Victor wrapped both hands around the glass but did not drink. His knuckles were white.

I asked him about Clara—the university, the courses, the little apartment she had found with north-facing windows. I asked because I knew he needed something ordinary to hold onto, and because I wanted to hear how carefully his voice could still form the words.

“North-facing?” I said.

“She says the light is better for studying.”

“She’s right.”

He nodded. His head dipped farther than he intended.

I reached across the table and touched his wrist. His skin was damp and unnervingly warm beneath my fingers. His pulse beat hard and shallow, quickening when I made contact.

He looked at my hand.

“You’re very still,” he said.

“What do you mean?”

“Most people fidget.” His eyes moved toward mine. They seemed to focus a moment late, as though arriving at my face from somewhere far away. “You’ve always been good at waiting.”

There it was—the acknowledgment, tucked between symptoms like a ribbon sewn inside a coat.

His glass slipped from his fingers. I caught it before it spilled.

He whispered, “I can’t taste anything.”

The color had begun to leave his face. What remained was pale and waxy, slick with sweat. His lips parted. His breathing changed, becoming shorter, more deliberate, as if each breath required a small, private decision.

“I think I’m ill,” he said.

“I’m sure it’s nothing.”

“No.” He tried to straighten in his chair. His shoulders rose, but his body followed a fraction too slowly. “No, something’s happening.”

Around us, the restaurant continued its quiet evening. A woman laughed near the window. Silverware rang in another room. No one looked afraid yet.

Victor’s fork clattered against his plate. He flinched at the sound.

“Call the doctor,” he said.

“I would, but—”

“My daughter.” He gripped the table. His fingers dug into the cloth. “If something happens, tell Clara it was an accident.”

“Of course.”

“Don’t promise that.” His gaze sharpened for one bright instant. “Don’t lie to me now.”

“I won’t.”

He searched my face. Behind his eyes, terror was moving faster than his body could express it. His mouth worked around syllables that never became sound.

Then the muscles of his face slackened.

His breathing turned rough. His head bowed toward his plate, and I caught him before he could fall forward. He weighed almost nothing in my arms. The warmth of him was fading already.

“Victor.”

His eyelids fluttered.

“No,” he murmured, so softly that I had to lean close. “Not yet. Not before the—”

He did not finish.

His hand closed weakly around my sleeve. His lips moved once more, forming a name that might have been Clara’s, or mine, or no one’s at all.

I laid him back against his chair and arranged his napkin across his chest. Then I sat opposite him, folded my hands, and watched the rain crawl down the window while the candles burned low.

I had waited years for that dinner.

It had been worth the wait.

# The Sentence of Corvin Ashlock

The tide had gone out three hours ago, and the sea lay flat and oily as the lid of a black pot, breathing through the reefs to the west. Without the tide the water always looked wrong. Too low. Too hungry. The men felt it in their boots and stopped speaking of it.

They had been circling the ship since first light.

Captain Edmund Vahl saw them from the quarterdeck, dark fins nosing the surface off the leeward reef, and he counted seven, then nine, then too many to count, because the shoal ran deep there and the water over the coral shelf was the color of weak tea. He had ordered the gut-tbucket thrown over the side at noon — offal, broken fish, the guts of a sow that had eaten her own pups. The sharks had come in on the offal and stayed, and the crew had watched them and stopped eating.

Now, at the ninth hour, with the sun going down orange and sick over the drowned reef, he had them bring the plank out.

---

Ashlock did not struggle when they brought him.

That was the thing that troubled Vahl most afterward. A man who fights has to be dragged; a man who fights at least proves he thought there was another way. Ashlock came up the companionway with his hands bound behind him and his head shaved, and he walked on his own feet, and his eyes were open.

He was thirty-eight. He had been the ship's bosun for six years and had sailed with Vahl since they were both deckhands on a Baltic brig, and everyone aboard the *Black Fortune* knew that in some room below decks, in some earlier watch, there had been a conversation in German about how a captain who takes a percentage of the prize money while his people eat salted worm is a captain whose head is worth a crown.

"Daarna," said Vahl.

*Afterward.*

They had found the manifest in the sea-chest, altered, with Vahl's name written in as the holder of four shares that belonged to six honest men. Ashlock had not denied it. He had said only: "You'll find the true ledger in the cache on Sorrow Key, when you don't need it anymore."

Vahl had thought about that for six weeks.

---

The plank was laid out from the main deck's quarter port, over the rail, out to the mainmast boom and beyond, and from the end of it there was nothing but nine feet of air and then the water.

Ashlock looked at it. He looked at it a long time.

"How far?" His voice came out strange — high and thin, the voice of a man who has no more moisture in him than the air around him.

"Twenty feet," said Vahl. "Maybe twenty-two. There's a swell tonight."

"And the sharks."

"Are the sharks," said Vahl, "the least of what you should be thinking about."

Ashlock's jaw worked. His eyes went to the water, where the fins moved without hurry, round and black and patient. Somewhere below the surface a heavy weight turned over, and the pale flat of it passed like a shadow of a coffin lid.

"Captain." Ashlock's throat worked. "Captain, I had a son in Nassau."

"I know."

"He's—"

"I know where he is." Vahl was not unkind about it. That was the cruelty of it, and he had known it was the cruelty of it, and had chosen it anyway, because the alternative was to let six men watch a captain's bargain be broken and let him grow afraid of his own crew, and a captain who is afraid of his crew is a corpse who hasn't been informed yet. "He's with a woman named Mbeki in a house near the market. He's nine years old and he thinks his father is a captain of a merchant vessel in the Baltic."

"He'll be told."

"He'll be told whatever you decide to tell him," said Vahl. "That's the last thing you'll ever do, and I'd rather you spent it on something useful." He stepped back. "Walk."

---

The bound man went out onto the plank.

He went as far as the third board from the end, and there he stopped, and the sweat came off him in a shine that the two deck lanterns picked out and made into something like gold, and he stood with his bare feet on the wet wood and his hands behind him and his face turned to the sky.

He did not pray. Vahl had half expected him to. Instead he said, quietly, in German, "*Ich habe es getan,*" — *I did it* — as though finishing an argument he had been having in his own head for six weeks, and then he laughed, one short bark of a laugh with no bottom to it.

Then he started to shake. Not all at once. It began in the knees and moved up, and his shoulders began to judder, and his head went down and came up, and the tendons in his neck stood out like rigging under load. He was a big man. He had held a boat's boom stay in a squall off the Guinea coast single-handed and not lost his footing. Now his feet were working at the wood like a horse trying to find purchase in a slick.

"Steady," said Vahl, though he knew it was useless, and he hated the sound of his own voice more than he hated the shaking.

Ashlock's eyes came to him. In the lantern light they were the eyes of a man who has already arrived somewhere.

"Vahl," he said.

"Lieutenant Harrow. Take his shirt."

They cut the shirt away at the shoulders because the bound arms were useless and the canvas was heavy when wet and would drag a man under before the sharks even came. Ashlock stood there bare to the waist, pale, ribs showing, the bound hands hanging behind him like a union of two things he would never hold again, and the shivering turned into a kind of vibration that Vahl could see in the lantern flame.

Then he went off the end.

He did not scream. That was the worst part for the crew, the men ranged along the rail and watching with the stillness of men watching a man drown: he did not scream at all. He struck the water at an angle, one arm going up, and the splash came up white and green in the lantern light, and the sound it made was small, a wet slap, nothing like the noise the sea made against the reef.

And then the sea closed over him and there was a patch of light where he had been.

---

Nobody moved.

The captain counted. Somebody in the dark behind him was counting, and Vahl could hear the ledger of it: *One. Two. Three.* He had a name for the time between the splash and the first blood, because he had watched two men go into the water in his life and both times he had thought it was an eternity, and it was, in fact, about ninety heartbeats.

At twenty-two a fin broke the surface, close, and swung — not toward the light but toward the scent — and the water boiled up in a long ragged seam of white, and Ashlock's arm came out of it, and the arm was gone from the shoulder before anyone drew breath.

"Jesus Christ," said a boy of fifteen at the rail, and was struck silent by a look from the bosun.

It lasted a long time. Vahl had wanted it to be quick and it was not quick, and there was no way to look away without looking like a man who wished it were quicker and was afraid that wishing had made it slower. The sharks came in from three directions at once and worked with a terrible coordination, as though they had done this before, as though they had rehearsed it, and the water went red in patches and the red spread out thin and did not sink, it stayed where it was, swirled and dispersed and swirled again, a rose window of blood opening and closing under the lanterns.

Ashlock shouted once. A single syllable with a name in it, cut short. The crew's grip on the rail tightened. Then the shouting changed quality — shorter, higher, grunts of effort and impact — and after that the sea did the rest of its business under the surface, and what came up was mostly white belly and a yard of something trailing, and the blood, and the fins.

The sharks did not leave. They stayed in the patch, circling, working, and the crew stood at the rail and watched until the lantern burned down and the crew of the watch were called away, and the last man up was a tall quartermaster namedStyles, who stood there a long time with his arms folded, staring down at the water as though waiting for it to give him something back.

---

Vahl went to his cabin at the fourth hour.

He had a bottle he did not drink from and a chart he did not read, and he sat in the dark with the sea working at the hull below him, and he thought about the ledger in the cache on Sorrow Key, and whether the man had told the truth about it, and about the lying to the boy in Nassau, and about the man walking out on the plank with the bound hands and the German prayer that was not a prayer.

He had done it before. Twice. A mutiny at Port Royal, a quartermaster named Pell who had swum well and gone three miles and was found four days later in pieces on the windward beach, and before that, on a long grey crossing with two dead officers in the lazaretto and no witnesses, when Vahl was twenty-two and had not yet learned what he was.

Both times he had felt the thing afterwards that he felt now: not guilt, exactly. More like the sensation of a man checking his teeth and finding them all present but loose.

He went up on deck an hour before dawn. The water had gone slack and the blood was gone and the sharks had drawn off to the deep water, and the sea lay over the place where Corvin Ashlock had been as if nothing had ever happened at it, and a frigate bird hung on the still air, waiting.

There was one thing he wanted. He wanted the water to have kept the man's face, so that he could say to himself that it had been a decent death, that some part of the man had gone down whole and fast and gone out of the world before the sharks made their claim.

The water had kept nothing. It never did.

---

**Later**, they sailed north with the season, and the *Black Fortune* kept her name and her crew and her captain, and off the Florida Keys in a storm in October, a boy of fifteen named Tobias Rann, who had watched a man walk a plank that August, came to the captain's cabin at the middle watch to ask whether it was true that the sea never gave a man back whole.

Vahl looked at him for a long moment. The boy had a good face and a bad night behind it.

"No," he said. "The sea gives nothing back. That's the lesson in it." He poured the boy a cup of watered rum and made him drink it, and then he said, "But there's no one alive who can say what the lesson is. Not the boy in Nassau. Not the others." He turned the cup in his hand. "That's the mercy in it. Whatever we do here, Lieutenant, the sea keeps it. It's the only partner we have who never sells us out."

And the boy went away, and the ship went on, and the water alongside went on being black and flat and breathing, and somewhere beneath it, in the cold and the dark and the enormous patience of the shoal, the reefs went on keeping the weight of the iron they had taken in.

# What the Quarry Keeps

## I.

The roof was sound. That was the first thing he told himself, each morning, in the grey hour before the light came up over the chalk ridge and the quarry.

The roof was sound and the walls were sound and the well was capped and the pump worked, and therefore nothing was coming in. Not through the roof. Not through the walls.

Not through him.

Marek found the water first in his lungs.

He woke choking, three, four times a week, with the taste of cold pond and the pressure of nine feet of it behind his ribs. No water in the room. No water on the floor. Just the bed and the dark and the taste, and his own hands clawing the sheet as though he could pull it up and let the air back into a body that was already full of it.

*It is the lungs,* the doctor in town said, when Marek finally went. *You breathed in the river as a boy. It's in the tissue. It comes back when you're tired.*

Marek was not tired. He had not slept more than two hours together since the fourteenth of November.

---

## II.

Emil had wanted to leave.

That was the whole of it, the entire sum of the crime, when you laid it out in the light: Emil had wanted to leave, and Marek had wanted him to stay, and on the fourteenth of November there had been a scuffle on the wet clay bank of the flooded quarry at the old tile works, and Emil had gone in.

The coroner wrote *misadventure.* The coroner wrote *the deceased was in the water some considerable time before recovery was attempted.* The coroner did not write that recovery had been attempted for nine minutes, and that the attempt had consisted of a man pressing a spade handle down on the back of his brother's neck, holding him under while the black water closed over his head, while his fingers came up and gripped the wood and scraped at it and finally let go.

Marek had counted. That was the thing he could not put down. He had counted the minutes on his father's old wristwatch, face down in the water where it struck the silt, its ticking muffled to a rumor, and he had counted them the way a man counts sheep to get through the dark.

Nine minutes. He had held his brother under for nine minutes because in the eighth minute Emil had got his hand on the bank, and in the ninth he had stopped.

And the coroner had written *misadventure*, and Marek had signed it, and they had buried Emil in the churchyard on a day of hard frost and blue-white sky, and Marek had stood at the graveside and found that his grief was a relief, and had hated himself for the relief, and had gone home and slept nine hours.

It was the only time since.

---

## III.

The dripping started in the second month.

Not a leak. He went up with a ladder and a lantern and found the attic dry as a bone, the beams clean, no bloom, no stain, no sign of any water at all. But in the hall, in the kitchen, in the room where Emil had slept — the sound of a drop falling into a pool. Patient. Regular. The interval of a man breathing in a chair.

And the smell. Not rot. Cold water and weed. The green-black smell of the quarry in October, when the algae came up and the whole basin stank like a lung.

And the bees.

Emil had kept bees. It was the last thing anyone gave him credit for. Bees do not ask about money or the works or the will. Bees go where the flowers are. Emil had put four hives in the orchard behind the tile yard and had talked about moving them south, and Marek had said nothing at all, because Marek was holding the spade.

There had been no bees in the orchard since November. The hives had been empty and cold and Emil had not known and had gone to the orchard anyway on the last afternoon to check them, and Marek had followed him, because Marek had followed him everywhere that year like a shadow with a grudge.

Now, in January, in a hard frost with the ground iron to the depth of a foot, a hive hummed behind the kitchen wall.

Marek put his hand on the plaster and it buzzed. Not loudly. The way a boy stammers, in threes and fours, catching on the same syllable.

*M-m-marek.*

---

## IV.

The chair was the worst of it, and he could not say why.

Emil had sat in the chair by the hearth. He had sat in it every evening for four years, mending combs, reading the almanac, working his thumbnail along the frames and humming. When the chair was occupied, it was occupied. That was its function.

Now the chair stood pulled out from the hearth at an angle, as though someone had just stood up from it. And Marek, coming in from the cold with his hands numb, would see it, and would stop, and would stand in the doorway for a long moment before he moved it back. Every night. He moved it back in the morning and it was pulled out again by evening, and by the third week he stopped moving it and started sleeping in the kitchen with the lamp on.

He did not want to look at it in the dark.

But he looked at it in the dark.

---

## V.

The hands were the proof he could not hide.

He washed them. That was all. He washed his hands the way other men touched a woman, long and repetitively and without any pleasure in it. The skin went from red to raw to cracked to bleeding at the knuckles, and then the cracks would seal and it would start again, and the water came out of the tap pink and then clear and then pink again. The physician in town looked at them and said *eczema, likely, keep them dry.*

He kept them wet. He kept them under the pump until the cold water numbed his shoulder to the bone and he could not feel his fingers at all, and the water was the right temperature, that was the obscene part — the water was the exact temperature of the quarry in November, forty-four degrees, and when it ran over his wrists he felt it settle into his sleeves like a hand on his shoulder.

He was being *held*.

On the worst nights he washed until he bled and then sat on the kitchen floor with the tap running and his hands in his lap, red, ruined, and he could still feel the wood.

The city had been digesting him long before I got there.

Rain needled the broken windows and pooled around the walls, black water trembling with the building’s breathing. The smell came first: copper and rot, sweet enough to make my teeth ache. Then the body.

He lay where the fire escape had spat him, one arm twisted beneath him, his throat opened in a ragged crimson grin. Someone had carved a message into his chest, but the rain had blurred the letters until they looked like a street map drawn in a dead man’s skin.

I crouched down. My hat brim shadowed his eyes, but they were open. Not empty. Angry. The way a man looks when he knows the end is coming and still tries to spit in its face.

I touched nothing. I never do.

Three days ago he’d been selling secrets downtown. Cheap ones, dirty ones—the kind that make the powerful sweat through their shirts. Now his secrets had been scooped out and spread across the sidewalk, and the city had gone on walking over them, heel to heel, like every other piece of garbage.

Somewhere above us, a window rattled. Somewhere below, a patrol car swept past, blue light crawling over the brick. The rain swallowed the sirens before they reached the alley. That’s how this city works. It devours its dead and calls it weather.

I looked at the wound again. Messy. But the cuts were deliberate. Too deliberate for a mugger, too theatrical for a professional. This wasn’t just murder. It was a sermon. A warning. Somebody wanted the neighborhood to see what happens when the rats start carrying knives.

The victim’s watch had stopped at 2:17. Broken glass glittered beneath his fingers, white and sharp as teeth. A telephone receipt clung to his shoe, softened by the wet. I studied it without touching it.

The city had handed me another puzzle wrapped in its own filth. I’d unwrap it, find the hand that made these cuts, and drag that hand into a room where the lights don’t flicker.

But first I’d let the rain finish washing the blood from the pavement.

In this town, even the blood eventually learns to disappear.

The city had been digesting him long before I got there.

Rain needled the broken windows and pooled around the walls, black water trembling with the building’s breathing. The smell came first: copper and rot, sweet enough to make my teeth ache. Then the body.

He lay where the fire escape had spat him, one arm twisted beneath him, his throat opened in a ragged crimson grin. Someone had carved a message into his chest, but the rain had blurred the letters until they looked like a street map drawn in a dead man’s skin.

I crouched down. My hat brim shadowed his eyes, but they were open. Not empty. Angry. The way a man looks when he knows the end is coming and still tries to spit in its face.

I touched nothing. I never do.

Three days ago he’d been selling secrets downtown. Cheap ones, dirty ones—the kind that make the powerful sweat through their shirts. Now his secrets had been scooped out and spread across the sidewalk, and the city had gone on walking over them, heel to heel, like every other piece of garbage.

Somewhere above us, a window rattled. Somewhere below, a patrol car swept past, blue light crawling over the brick. The rain swallowed the sirens before they reached the alley. That’s how this city works. It devours its dead and calls it weather.

I looked at the wound again. Messy. But the cuts were deliberate. Too deliberate for a mugger, too theatrical for a professional. This wasn’t just murder. It was a sermon. A warning. Somebody wanted the neighborhood to see what happens when the rats start carrying knives.

The victim’s watch had stopped at 2:17. Broken glass glittered beneath his fingers, white and sharp as teeth. A telephone receipt clung to his shoe, softened by the wet. I studied it without touching it.

The city had handed me another puzzle wrapped in its own filth. I’d unwrap it, find the hand that made these cuts, and drag that hand into a room where the lights don’t flicker.

But first I’d let the rain finish washing the blood from the pavement.

In this town, even the blood eventually learns to disappear.
