Not rough stone, but dressed stone, laid in courses, the mortar between them furred with something pale. The ceiling is low. That's the thing I notice first and understand last: how low it is. I could reach up if I were on my feet. Whoever built this did not want me to stand upright, and then later discovered they did not need to stop me doing that at all.

Water is dripping. Somewhere behind me and to the left. A slow, deliberate drip with a little stutter in it, like a heart that isn't well. It falls into a channel in the floor — there's a groove worn into the stone, a gutter, and the drip runs along it and away — and I realize with a lurch that the sweet smell and the rust smell are coming out of that gutter. The room has been washing itself for a very long time and it hasn't managed.

Now the implements.

They hang on the far wall, where a single shuttered lantern throws a weak cone. At the edge of the light they are only outlines, and for a while I convince myself they are kitchen things — hooks, a rack, a line of hanging pans — and that any moment I will turn over and find this is a larder, a cold cellar, a place where my own bad dream has simply dressed itself up. But the light moves, or my eyes do, and the outlines resolve, and they are not kitchen things.

There is a long hook. There are several, of varying length, hung by their eyes so they sway a little when I shift my weight, and they move with a slow, patient rhythm, like things that have been waiting and are still waiting. There is a frame of iron that someone welded into the corner, with a brace of joints along it, and I make myself not understand what that brace is for, and I understand it perfectly. There is a table. That's all it is, a table, wooden, heavy, and I can see the tools laid out on it in a row with a kind of terrible neatness, the way one lays out instruments before an operation: a bowl, a jar, a folded cloth, three things with handles, and something long and thin and bright that I look at for too long and then make myself look away from. A bucket stands underneath the table, and there is a stain on the stone beside the bucket that has been mopped. You can tell it's been mopped. The cloth went over it in arcs. Whoever cleans this room does it by habit, in the dark, without hope.

The walls are wallpapered in nothing. They were once plastered and painted, I think, and the damp has brought the plaster up in long blisters, and the paint has come away in sheets, and there are places where someone has written on the wall in a hand I almost know. Not words. A count. Days. The tallies are very fine and very careful and they go up higher than a standing man could comfortably reach, and they stop, abruptly, in the middle of a blank space, which is somehow the worst thing in the room.

By the door there is a chair. An ordinary chair, wooden, with a straight back, and it is the only thing in this place that looks as though it was bought for a purpose of comfort, and that is what breaks me. Not the hooks. The chair. Somebody sat in it. They sat in it for a long time, with their hands on their knees, and they did not scream, and the wood is polished by that.

I have been in here eleven hours. I know this not because of the count on the wall but because I know my own body, and my body has been folded, and the cold has been entering and leaving my chest all night like a slow tide.

I test the ropes once. I do not test them twice. The ropes hold, and they hold the way things hold when someone else has tested them, over and over, on other people, on me, in a previous life I don't intend to think about yet.

Here's what I have instead, and I hold it very tightly, in the dark, with my wrists screaming:

The bucket is not full.
The hook nearest the door is out of my reach, but the table is a table, and tables have legs, and legs have length, and if I can get to the floor, I can get to the floor.

The dripping goes on. The room breathes. The hooks sway, faintly, in the draft from the door, and somewhere on the other side of it, very far off, I hear a sound I have been waiting all night to hear and had stopped believing in — a footstep, and then another, and then the scrape of a latch.

I stop breathing.

The door begins to open.

And I think, with everything I have left: not the chair. Whatever you do, do not put me in the chair.

# THE THIRTY-EIGHT MINUTES

## 5:52 a.m.

The parking lot behind the Northgate laundromat smelled of bleach, hot grease, and the sour milk of the bakery dumpsters. Five people stood around a white cargo van with its rear doors open, breathing white into the cold, passing a thermos of gas-station coffee between them like a communion.

Ruben Ortiz had the floor plan of Cascade Mutual Bank spread across the hood of the van, weighed down with a box of carpenter's pencils clipped from the hardware store across the street.

"Four minutes," he said. "Teller station, the room behind it, then the vault. Cash carts come out at eleven-ten, we take them at the loading door, we're gone before the ink's dry on the deposit slip."

Nobody asked about the alarm, because Ruben had explained it: the system was on a forty-five-second delay and the monitoring company had been upgraded in June, and the drill was a two-man job with a diamond bit that needed twenty minutes on the plate.

Twenty minutes in a bank with a silent alarm and a camera.

"You said four minutes," said Denny Grady. He was thirty-eight, a warehouse forklift driver with a shaved head and the flat calm of a man who has hit people for money. "Fine. But you didn't say *four minutes of me holding a gun over a woman's head while you're on a ladder with a power tool."

Ruben looked at him for a long moment.

"Nobody fires," he said. "Nobody fires unless somebody fires first. That's the rule and it's not up for discussion."

At the driver's door of the van, Cato Vance rolled his window down and spat. He had a duffel bag in his footwell with a wedding photo in it that wasn't his.

"Unless somebody fires first," he said.

The nineteen-year-old was sitting on an overturned bucket at the back of the lot with his phone, thumbing through it. Marcus Bell, called Marc, called "The Kid," who had filmed a stick-figure robbery in a garage in Bakersfield two years ago and had forty-one thousand subscribers to prove it.

"Hey," he said. "Should I bring the camera?"

"Which camera?"

"The — for the video."

"Bring it," Ruben said, and did not look up from the plan, and that was how the whole morning got decided.

Here is what the money was for, since the money was the reason and the reason was the reason: Ruben Ortiz had spent twenty-two years walking into banks he didn't own, photographing damage, interviewing the tellers about the day the pipes burst. He knew where every bank's cameras were blind because he had stood in that blind spot himself, with a flashlight and a clipboard, in 2009, in a flood.

He had a daughter in Modesto with a tumor.

He also had the money, which was the problem. He had thirty-eight thousand dollars of it and it was not enough, and the difference between thirty-eight thousand and enough was the difference between a man who goes to the door and a man who goes through it.

Lila Ferris was in the blue Civic two rows over, engine running, wipers going, because Oregon in October was a cold damp country that got into your bones. She was twenty-six and she had driven a getaway once before in Yakima and had sworn on her mother's grave she wouldn't do it again, and here she was, doing arithmetic on the gas tank, thinking about a bus ticket to Bend.

"I'll be at the church on Kearney," she said through the van window. "Two minutes. If you're not out in two minutes, I'm not there."

Ruben folded the plan. "Fourteen minutes. You're generous."

---

## 10:41 a.m.

Friday pay period. Cascade Mutual had a line out the door at ten-forty and a coffee cart in the corner and a child somewhere in the building with a crayon.

Marisol Vane was holding her daughter's hand and thinking about the mortgage. Ada, five, had a sheet of paper she was drawing on and had asked twice if they were going to be a "long time." The teller, Pamela Ellis, twenty-two years old and eleven weeks into the job, had already decided about the girl: she would draw a sun. She had a Sun Machine pen in her apron pocket, the glittery kind, and she was going to give it to her, and that was going to be the best part of her week, and in the back of her mind she was also thinking it would be a nice story to tell someday, *I gave a little girl a glitter pen on the day that happened.*

At 10:41 a.m. a man in a canvas jacket came through the double doors and said, "Everybody stay where you are. Don't move. This is not a joke."

He had a gun.

Eleven seconds later the second man came in with a shotgun, and the third with a pistol, and the fourth was a big man with a vest that had plates in it, and the fifth was in the parking lot moving a white cargo van around the corner like a man moving a chess piece.

"Down," said the man in the canvas jacket. "Down on the floor. Hands where I can see them."

Pamela Ellis put her hands on the counter.

"Open the drawer," said the man with the shotgun.

She fumbled with the key. The keys were on a ring and the ring was on a hook and she had to unhook it and her fingers did not want to work, and there were eleven people on the floor in front of a counter and a girl with a glittery pen in the pocket of a teller who was crying.

"Open it," the shotgun man said.

She opened it.

The noise the drawer made was the loudest thing in the room. It went *chk-chk-chk-chk* as the bills riffled, and every person in that lobby heard their own future in it, and then the man in the canvas jacket came around the counter and said something to the manager, Harold Nkemelu, a man of forty-eight who had a tie with a small coffee stain on it, and Nkemelu said, "The vault's on a timed release. I can't — I can't get you in there. It's not me. It's a program. I have a phone call—"

The big man hit him in the face with the butt of the shotgun.

Then everybody was on the floor and the door was locked and a hand was over Pamela Ellis's mouth and she could smell the coffee on the big man's breath, and she thought, absurdly, *I wanted to give her the pen.*

At 10:43 a.m., Marcus Bell, nineteen, stood in the lobby with his phone in his hand and a grin on his face and said, "Yo, do y'all see this? Do y'all SEE this?"

At 10:44 a.m., in the parking lot, Marisol Vane stopped looking for her keys.

---

## 10:44 a.m.

The 911 call came from a woman standing in the drive-through lane, and the dispatcher, a woman named Trudy Beaulieu who would think about that call for the rest of her working life, wrote in the little box: *armed robbery in progress, subject with hostages.*

The first unit was two and a half blocks away.

Officer Zachary Byrd was twenty-four and four months on the job and had wanted this job since he was nine. His partner, Dominic Tessaro, was eleven years out and had a folder of paperwork at his kitchen table he intended to finish that weekend.

"Which way?" Byrd said.

"Cascade."

"Cascade." Tessaro put the car in drive. "Okay. Okay. Let's go."

They came up Kearney at 10:49 with the lights on and no siren, and Byrd saw the white van at the loading dock and the blue Civic idling at the curb in front of the loan center and two men in the driver's seat of the Civic who did not look like people waiting for a mortgage appointment.

That was the whole tell, in the end. It was never anything else. It was always a car that didn't belong.

Tessaro braked. "Zach."

"I see it."

The robbers were still holding the lobby. A man in a canvas jacket was visible through the plate glass, standing by the customer counter with a gun in his hand, and the customers were on the floor, and the branch manager was on his knees with blood coming out of his eyebrow into his coffee stain.

Byrd got out. Tessaro got out. They stood behind the armored truck that had been parked out of habit and never in the way.

"Dispatch, we have a 10-31 in progress, four to six subjects, hostages visible from the north—"

Then the man in the canvas jacket turned his head.

He looked straight at them. He took a step toward the glass. And Officer Zachary Byrd, in front of a bank, in the middle of the day, in a city of two hundred thousand people, made the decision that people make in about a quarter of a second, which is to assume the man with the gun is not going to shoot first, because if he is, everything changes, and you will be the one it changes for.

"Zach—"

Two rounds. The first hit the armored truck's door, a flat *ping* and a puff of dust. The second came through the plate glass of the bank six inches from Byrd's head and went past him into the lobby, and the plate glass did what plate glass does, which is shatter inward in a sheet, and the sound of it was like the top of a chandelier coming down.

Byrd was hit in the throat.

He did not scream. He made a sound like a man answering a question in another room, and then he was sitting on the sidewalk with his hands in his lap, and there was a great deal of blood, and Tessaro had him by the collar and was saying *Zach, Zach, stay with me,* and the blood was coming out between the officer's fingers in a steady pulse, and Tessaro looked at it and then at his partner's face and said something he had never said to another human being and would say again, later, in a dark room, to a board of people in a long room with a flag on the wall.

Byrd was dead in the lobby parking lot at 10:50 a.m.

He had ninety seconds yet of being alive. In the bank, everyone ducked. Six inches of laminated glass between the lobby and the shooting and it saved nothing.

At the transit stop on Kearney, a woman named Alice Trần-Dyer saw the whole thing from the bench and later said, "It was so quiet except for the glass. It was the quietest loud thing I ever heard."

## 10:52 a.m.

Police came from four directions at once, the way it goes in a city that has been through this before: two cruisers from Division Six, a supervisor from the district, an overtime sergeant who happened to be three blocks away and was the best thing that happened to Cascade Mutual that day, and then the green truck.

Detective First Grade Dana Whitlock had been negotiating for eleven years, which meant she had learned that the most useful thing in the world was a boring, slow voice on a telephone.

At 10:52 the command post went up in the parking lot of the elementary school across the street: two card tables, a whiteboard, a bank of radios brought out of a sedan trunk, and a laptop playing the bank's CCTV on a loop, four angles, no audio. Whitlock watched a nineteen-year-old boy walk around a lobby with a phone and a smile, and wrote on the whiteboard in marker: **WHY IS HE SMILING.**

On the screen, the boy walked to the customer counter and crouched down behind it.

Whitlock said, to nobody, "Okay."

At 11:02, the Sheriff's K-9 unit pulled up on the east side of the building. Officer Ira Sandoval had been a dog handler for twelve years and Rex was a seven-year-old German Shepherd with a black saddle of odor-detection tape on his back, and they had done eleven hundred searches together, and Rex could work a hallway that four officers had already said smelled like nothing.

"Sandoval," Whitlock said into the radio. "Sandoval, hold at the corner. Do not approach the door."

Sandoval was already moving. ---

## 11:04 a.m.

The call came in on the bank's main line and Detective Whitlock answered it on the sixth ring.

"Talk to me." Ruben's voice. Flat. Patient, almost bored, the voice of an insurance man who has sat across a table from three thousand people who were about to lie to him.

"Then you know how this goes. You want everybody to walk out. That's fine. That's the whole thing. Get me one vehicle, empty, at the north lot. I'll send two people out with everyone."

The vault was a 12-gauge steel door with a timed release. It had a dry fire-suppression system. The money would be $1.2 million and it was in a room that four people in a van could not open and walk away from in the time they had.

"Talk to me for a minute. Tell me where you're at right now."

## 11:09 a.m.

Grady had put the security guard, Clyde Banks, in front of him as he went to the front windows, and his hand was on the man's belt like a man holding a dog.

"I want to talk to you!" Grady shouted at the parking lot. "I want to talk to you RIGHT NOW! You want to talk? Come in here! One man. No weapons."

## 11:12 a.m.

"Mr. Ortiz—"

"Heard it. Heard it on the radio. Your people are loud." A pause. "That video's going to be on the news by lunch."

"Ron—"

"Don't."

The assault team stacked in the laundry room behind the bank: eight men in black, a dog handler with a dog they did not need, a paramedic, and a woman from the tactical center holding a bullhorn.

Farrow put his hand on the door.

"Flashbang goes at breach. Gas follows. We go through fast, we go through loud, we get him off the hostages, we get our people out. If he's got a gun on somebody, we shoot the gun first and we don't care what's on the other side of it."

Somebody said, "Copy."

"Anyone got a problem with that?"

Nobody said anything about a nine-year-old with a phone.

## 11:13 a.m.

They came into the lobby like weather.

The bang of the flashbang in a marble room is not like a bang anywhere else; it is a bang with a long bright tail, and every camera in that building filmed the ceiling tiles coming down like snow, and for eleven hundredths of a second the entire lobby was a white room with a hundred small suns in it.

Then gas rolled across the terrazzo in a low white cloud.

Ruben Ortiz was behind the counter with three hostages on their knees — Marisol Vane, Ada, five, and Harold Nkemelu — and he had a pistol pressed against the back of the manager's head, and he had twenty-one hours of a plan in his head and no vault, and he said, "What—"

The vault's steel door, thirty feet away, had a hole in it the shape of a quarter and a drill still turning inside the wall with a sound like a wasp in a can, a shriek and a chatter, and then a wounded animal noise: the bit had finally bitten through and the plate had come off the inside.

Marc Bell was at the cash-machine end of the lobby with his back to the wall and his phone in his hand, and he was nineteen, and he had been crying for six minutes without making any sound, and when the flashbang went off he fired four rounds at the ceiling, at the marble, at the windows, at nothing, at anything, all of them going into the tile and the drywall and the crown molding, and the marble counter sprayed dust, and one of them went through a pane of glass above the customer benches and out into the parking lot where its noise brought two officers who were not looking in that direction.

Officer Yusuf Adeyemi took a round in the vest plate and another in the thigh.

Officer Cole Prigmore, twenty-six, three months in the team, took a round high in the shoulder and went down and then came up on one knee with his gun in his hand and a sound Whitlock could hear on the recording afterward, a short syllable, just a sound a person makes.

Grady was dead by the counter. Banks was dead against the glass. The drill was screaming in the wall.

Ruben fired twice at the flashbang and did not hit anyone. He hit the ceiling. He grabbed the manager and put the gun back against his head.

"Shoot him," Farrow said, meaning the manager, meaning *shoot past him.*

They came through the breach.

The lobby became a thing I have never seen described accurately in any film, and I have seen all of them: the noise was layers, the rifle crack and the handgun crack and the ugly flat *snap* of rounds going into tile and the brass hitting marble and bouncing, all of it rolling off the terrazzo and coming back doubled, and the marble counters chipping, and the coffee cart's canvas awning going up in the air, and cold coffee and broken cups, and the ficus in the white planter exploding into a fine mist of dirt and green leaves that hung in the gas.

Marc Bell fired again — six rounds, fast, high, at the ceiling, at the breacher — and then he was in the ATM alcove with his back against the wall and his knees up and his hands over his ears and his right hand still holding the pistol, and Officer Adeyemi came around the corner and said, "Drop it! Drop the gun!"

Marc put his hands over his ears and said, "I don't wanna die. I don't wanna die, man. I don't wanna die—"

and there was a burst, four rounds, and Marc Bell slid down the wall of the ATM alcove with his hands still over his ears, still holding the pistol, in the blue light of a Wells Fargo sign that was still lit in a dead lobby, and Whitlock never learned what he was thinking about in that last second, which is a mercy, because it would have been about his mother.

In the vault anteroom, Ruben Ortiz shot Harold Nkemelu in the chest, not on purpose, because Nkemelu moved, because Nkemelu was forty-eight and had a hole in his own vault and was trying to help; and Ruben said, "No—" and then the assault team was in the anteroom with the gas and the light and the screams, and it took four more seconds.

Ruben Ortiz came out of the vault anteroom at 11:16 with his right thigh opened up to the bone and a pistol in his hand, and kneeling in the lobby on the terrazzo next to the body of a seventeen-year-old customer named Nadia Reyes-Cruz — no, of a customer named Nadiya Farouk, twenty-six, who had been kneeling at the counter since 10:41 and had a scraped knee and a dry eye and had been praying under her breath the entire time — with the gun still in his hand.

Whitlock was in the lobby.

She had crawled in from the breach after Acey's patch pulled back and she was on the marble with her weapon down and her hands open and she was nine feet from a man with a gun and two hostages.

"Mr. Ortiz."

He turned his head. His face was gray.

"You're done," she said. "Look at the room. Everyone who was ever going to help you is dead. You're the last one. Put it down and this ends."

He looked at the gun in his hand like it belonged to someone else.

"The vault," he said. "It opened. I was *going* to—"

"I know. It's over. Put it down."

### The Slow Room

The first thing Ren noticed was the silence.

Not the ordinary silence of an empty room — a *held* silence, the kind that presses against the eardrums like a hand. The building had been silent for six hours now, ever since the door had sealed behind him with that soft, almost polite click. He'd told himself the others were ahead of him, that the evacuation route ran deeper into the foundations, that someone would come.

No one had come.

The second thing he noticed was the smell. Faintly sweet, like burnt sugar and wet grass, threaded under the stale air of a room that hadn't been aired in months. He thought: *cleaning fluid.* Thought: *paint.* Thought nothing at all, and went back to the door and put his shoulder into it again.

It didn't move. The door was not locked. It was simply, absurdly, *painted shut* — some kind of sealant, weeks old, the frame swollen with damp. He'd already done the arithmetic on that. He'd already scraped his fingernails down the seam of the panel, already shouted until his throat went raw, already checked the ceiling for a hatch and the floor for a drain and found, in both cases, smooth concrete.

The third thing he noticed was the fog.

It came in low, a thin grey layer that pooled around his ankles like something alive, and where he walked it swirled up around his knees in slow, lazy curls. It didn't behave like gas. It behaved like *water*, like something with intention. Where it touched his skin through the holes in his shoes, he felt a cold prickling that was almost affectionate.

*This isn't real,* he thought. *This is a ventilation problem. This is a building with a leak. This is—*

The headache arrived without preamble.

It was not the headache of a blow or a hangover. It came in behind both eyes at once, a single hot point of pressure that spread outward like ink through wet paper, and Ren staggered sideways into the wall. The concrete was cold against his cheek. He pressed his palm flat against it and focused on the coolness, on the grain of it, on the fact of *now*, and for a while that was enough.

Then the sweet smell thickened.

---

The panic came in waves, and each wave was worse than the last because each wave took something with it.

The first wave was loud. He was on his feet, pacing, running the circuit of the room — door, window, door, window — twelve steps, turn, twelve steps, turn. He was shouting. He was reasoning aloud in fragments, half-argument, half-prayer: *There's a vent. There's always a vent. High on the wall, behind the shelving. It's a server room, for God's sake, they don't seal server rooms—*

The second wave took his voice. His throat closed to a dry click, and the shouting turned into something higher and more embarrassing, an animal noise he didn't recognize as his own. He found himself biting the collar of his jacket, tearing at the fabric, breathing through his mouth because the air tasted like pennies and warm batteries and something sweeter underneath, like overripe fruit left in a closed car.

The third wave took his hands. They began to shake — not the fine tremor of cold, but a deep, muscular juddering that shook his whole frame and made him drop the piece of shelving he'd pried loose and was using to attack the window. He sat down hard. He noticed, with the terrible clarity of a fever, that his fingers were tingling. Numb. Pins and needles, from the tips down.

The window. The window was the only thing in the room that wasn't painted shut — the glass was intact, the frame was real, and beyond it was eight stories of nothing. He got up and put his shoulder against the sash and pushed with everything he had, and the window moved, actually moved, an inch, and he heard something in the frame shift, and he thought *yes, yes, yes*—

The gas was thicker at the top of the room. He felt it go across his face like a warm hand when he leaned in, and the taste in his mouth became a taste of *rot*, of a copper coin held against the tongue, and his stomach turned over and he was sick on the floor, kneeling, retching, and when he looked down at the puddle it had a faint iridescent sheen, like oil on water, and he thought, with a calmness that scared him more than anything else that had happened yet:

*Oh. So that's what it is.*

---

The confusion was the worst part. Not the pain — he could have borne the pain. The confusion was the sense of his mind coming apart at the seams, thoughts sliding off each other like wet tiles.

He knew the room. He knew it was a sub-basement archive, four floors down, no windows except the one that didn't open, walls poured in 1974. He knew this because he'd read the plaque. Twenty minutes ago he'd read the plaque and thought it was boring. Now he couldn't remember the year, and the not-remembering made him laugh, a horrible wet sound, because what else do you do.

The fog was at his chest now. It lay in a perfect horizontal plane, moving with him, and he noticed — and this detail would follow him for the rest of his life, however long that was — that the layer *rippled* when he breathed. It came toward him. It was being drawn toward him, gently, patiently, the way water finds a drain.

*It's carbon monoxide,* he thought, and then: *No. Carbon monoxide is odorless. Carbon monoxide doesn't have a smell. Carbon monoxide doesn't pool. This is something else.*

*Doesn't matter. Doesn't matter what it is. Doesn't matter—*

The dizziness hit and he went sideways into the shelving, which toppled, and he fell with it, and lying on his side on the concrete with his cheek against the cold he could feel his heart going too fast, too light, skipping. His vision had a soft grey vignette around it now, like looking down a tube. The headache had become a bright, precise needle between his eyebrows.

He tried to get up. He got an elbow under him. He got one knee up.

And then the room began to narrow.

It was gradual, which was the cruelty of it — the grey at the edges crept in slow enough that he kept thinking it had held, kept thinking *I can still see, I can still see, the light's still there.* But the light was going yellow, then amber, then a muddy brown, and the shapes in the room — the shelving, the fallen chair, the door with its sealed frame — grew soft and distant and enormous all at once, as if the walls were breathing outward.

His lungs stopped working properly somewhere in there. He couldn't say when. One breath was a rattling, wet, tearing thing in his chest, and the next breath was nothing at all, and his body — his poor obedient body, which had carried him forty-one years — simply *refused*, the diaphragm locking, the throat closing around air that wasn't there anymore.

He thought, very clearly, in a voice that sounded like it belonged to someone reading a weather report:

*I would like to get up.*

He got up. He made it onto his hands and knees, and then onto one knee, and then his arms gave and he went down onto the concrete face-first, and the impact was distant, muffled, unimportant. The fog settled over him. It was warm. It smelled like the sweet thing again, cut grass and burnt sugar, and he thought of a summer evening twenty years ago, a field, someone's hand in his hair, and he was crying without knowing it, and the yellow light came down around him like a lid.

The last clear thing he had was the sound of his own breathing, ragged and shallow, slowing.

Then the room went quiet, and the fog came in after him, patient and sweet, and the light in the room — the only light, the little emergency strip above the sealed door — burned on, indifferent, for a long time.

## The Arithmetic

She did the math first.

That was the thing people never understood about her — the thing the second husband had brought up the night he found the cash in the garage and she'd said *not yet, wait*, and he'd looked at her with the first faint shape of an understanding she'd respected him more for. You did the math first, because the math was the only part of it that was true.

The math said eleven days.

Eleven days, give or take, before联邦 — no.

Eleven days before the search protocol reached the property room in the courthouse annex and somebody with a badge from a different alphabet opened Box 61 and found the notebook in it. Federal agents kept notebooks. Charles Okonjo had kept one for twenty-two years, and in the last page of the 2019 section there were four lines in a careful clerical hand, and two of them were hers.

The math had said eleven days for a while now. The math had said six days in March and had been right about the six days, mostly. The math was always right. It was a machine. It did not have a body attached to it, and that was the whole of her religion.

---

Here is what had happened, in the order it had happened, which was not the order it would be told in.

Four years ago a courier named Ward Peale had seen a car in a driveway on Runyon and had described the car to a federal agent named Okonjo, who had written down the plate and the hour and the description of the woman behind the wheel. Peale had been twenty-three and had liked the sound of his own name in a courtroom someday, and it had cost him his life on the embankment at Frankford in the third week of October, which Kellan did not regret, because regret was a sensation and sensations were for people who could afford them.

Then Okonjo had noticed. Okonjo had begun the slow, patient, unforgivable work of a man building a file, and six weeks ago he had come to the 12th District in a rented gray coat with a photograph in his breast pocket.

And then Okonjo had been shot in the hallway of his own building, at 11:40 on a Thursday night, and nineteen separate witnesses had heard gunfire and nobody had called it in for nine minutes.

So: two counts. Peale. Okonjo. One of them federal the moment somebody read the notebook, which was a thing that had been sitting in Box 61 since February, in a Ziplock bag, in a box with forty other boxes, because nobody had any reason to look at the notebook of a dead federal agent in any particular hurry.

Captain Danner had come to her office on the second of March and had stood in the doorway with his hat in his hands and said, *How would you like to handle the file, Sarge.*

That was all. That was the entire conversation. A hat, a doorway, a question, and Danner looking at the middle distance the way men do when they have made a decision and would prefer not to have it acknowledged. Danner had been twenty-two years in the Bureau and had the administrative constitution of a paper bag, and he had put the bag over his own head years ago, and he had put it there because of her, and now he was asking her how she'd like to handle the file.

*Cleanly,* she'd said.

*There's a young man in the file,* Danner had said. *Bell. Bell's the one from the bicycle shop, the one across from the laundromat? His cousin's truck was in that alley.*

And Kellan had said, *I know him.*

Which was true. She had bought batteries from him in the spring of last year. He had asked her about the traffic court thing, the thing with the registration, and she had told him the truth, which was that the clerk's office was a swamp and his cousin should file the appeal, and he'd said *thank you, ma'am,* and she had thought, *there's a nice kid,* and then she'd thought nothing else at all, because the case was six weeks old and there was a file with eleven days left in it.

---

Marcus Bell was nineteen years old and had been awake since four, and Kellan could see it in the way he held his shoulders, and she did not find it moving. She found the whole interview, in fact, professionally pleasant. She was a courteous woman. She had a way of asking questions that made people feel like they were helping her, and this was not manipulation, exactly; it was closer to craft, the way a good carpenter doesn't *manipulate* a joint.

She gave him water from the machine in the hallway. She gave it to him in the paper cup with the crack in the rim, and she took it back and put it in the trash herself rather than have him hold it, so his hands were free, so his hands would be free later.

She started him at the beginning and let him run, because a nineteen-year-old who hasn't slept will tell you everything if you simply don't interrupt.

The car had been towed from the lot on Berks. Eleven-fifty dollars. He'd had eleven dollars and a bus transfer, and the truck was his cousin Teresa's, and the truck had a heater that worked and a toolbox in the back seat that had belonged to their grandfather, and he'd stopped behind the building because he had to piss and the gas station wanted two dollars and his cousin's truck wouldn't start without letting it warm up ten minutes, and he'd parked it in the alley because the alley was free, and he'd been there maybe six, eight minutes, and he'd seen a white man come out of the side door and go up the street fast.

*Did he see you?*

*No. No, he was inside. He came out after I left. I left before.*

*Kellie.* He was from Erie and he still called her Kellie and she had let it happen, which had cost her something and bought her more. *Marcus, I need you to think really carefully. Is there any chance he saw you?*

And here was the part she had waited nine days for, the whole reason she was in a room with a boy who had been awake since four: at this point, the shape of the story began to change in him. She watched it happen. It was almost beautiful. The shoulders came down half an inch. The eyes stopped moving.

*…I don't know,* he said. *I parked back there. What if he saw me?*

*Would that be a problem?*

*No,* said Marcus Bell. *No, no, I didn't do anything.*

*Nobody said you did.*

*But if he saw me, then—*

She let the silence do it. She had a lot of silence. She had once spent four hours in a room with a man who wanted to put his own wife in the river and had gotten exactly what she wanted out of it, and she had learned that people will build their own conviction if you simply decline to build one for them.

*Marcus,* she said, gently. *Tell me about the jacket.*

*The green one? The Carhartt?* He laughed. *That thing's rank. It still smells like Danny's fire in '19 and my mom won't let me throw it out. It's in the closet.*

*You're sure the whole night? Green jacket?*

*The whole night. It was cold. It's in the closet, I told you—*

*That's fine,* she said. *That's fine. I'm just writing things down.*

She wrote things down. She had already been in his apartment twice, with a consent form and a courtesy and a young partner beside her who thought she was the finest boss he'd ever had in his life, and both times she had stood in that closet and looked at the green jacket hanging on the doorknob with its pockets sagging, and she had made herself look at it the way she looked at everything else, which was without any feeling whatever, which was the part that would have frightened people, if they ever found out. Fear requires an imagination. Hers had been packed away in a Ziplock bag in a freezer in February and it had been there since February, and she had kept the frozen peas because they were the reason she didn't look at the bag twice.

---

The gun was not the case. The gun would be a problem — ballistics, the property room, the inventory sheet countersigned by Fielding, who had died of a heart attack in the hallway on the eleventh of March and who had initialed the sheet on the ninth of February and had never initialed the bottom.

The knife was simpler. The knife was a five-inch blade with a buck-stab handle that she had carried in the shoulder holster on the ninth of February and had put in the freezer in a Ziplock bag inside a bag of peas, and the freezer had kept it, and the freezer had not asked her a single question.

She had the knife in the bag from the hardware store on Kensington with her when she walked into his building at 7:40 on a Wednesday evening in July, and she had gone up the stairs behind Detective Renteria, who was carrying the warrant in a brown envelope and who had no idea what was in the brown envelope, because there was nothing in the brown envelope, because that was the point of the brown envelope.

Renteria had been on the job eleven months. He had a haircut that cost too much. He thought of her as a mentor, and she was letting him think that, because a man who thinks he's a witness is not a man who looks.

*Marcus,* she said, on the landing, with the old intensity coming up in her voice. *Marcus, I have to be honest with you.*

He was standing in his own doorway with his socks on and the television on behind him.

*Do you have anything in the apartment that you've touched since that Thursday? Anything that might have blood on it?*

And here's the beautiful arithmetic of it: she had spent nine days teaching him the shape of his own guilt by never once contradicting him, and now the boy was going to do her the favor of handing her the thread.

*The jacket,* he said. *Jesus. The jacket. It's in the closet, it was in my pocket, I had a lighter and a—*

*Which pocket?*

*Left. It's in the left pocket, there's a shirt wrapped around it, my cousin gave me the shirt, it's—*

*Marcus.* She put a hand on his arm, and Renteria saw her do it, and Renteria remembered it later as the moment the case broke open. *We're going to go in and look. Okay? I'm not going to make this harder than it has to be.*

*I didn't do it.*

*I know,* she said. And she said it the way she said everything: as information.

They went in. The closet was small, and the jacket was on the doorknob, and she lifted the left pocket and there was the shirt, and under the shirt there was the frozen peas bag still half-full with the Ziplock inside it, and she said, *Don't touch that,* in a voice like a door slamming, and Renteria jumped, and Marcus Bell put his hand over his mouth.

Then she called the unit, and the unit came, and there was a photograph, and there were two uniforms, and after a while a man in a van took the whole thing away in a plastic bag with a number on the tape, and she watched it go down the stairs past her in its plastic bag with her own groceries' frost still on the outside of it.

---

The arraignment was in September. He took eleven minutes to decline. His cousin Teresa stood up behind the rail and said, *He was in my truck, but he wasn't—* and the bailiff told her to be quiet, and Kellan stood at the far end of the room with her hands loose in front of her like a woman at a funeral, and she did not look at her shoes.

The county's offer was seven to eleven. His priors made the trial a formality; the priors made it worse than a formality, made it a coroner's diagram of a life. She went through the file after the plea and did the last of the math, because she always finished the math.

He would be thirty-four or thirty-five when he came out. If he did the full run with good behavior, which he would, because he was a quiet kid, he would be forty-one. He would be forty-one and he would have a record that put him on every list for the rest of his life, and there would be a job he could not have and a sister in Erie who would be forty-four by then and who had a daughter who would be nineteen, and none of it would be because of him. It would be because a man in a rented gray coat had written down a plate number.

Kellan put the file in the drawer and shut it and thought: *that's the cost.* Not *that is terrible.* Not *what have I done.* Just the cost, tallied and set against the other column, which was eleven days, of which nine were gone.

She had one moment. In the hallway of his building on the ninth of July she had put her hand flat on the banister and thought about Peale on the embankment and about Okonjo's careful handwriting and about the number of pages in the notebook that were hers, and it had lasted about two seconds, and what had ended it was not mercy and not guilt but the observation that she was tired and that eleven days did not get longer because she stood in hallways.

*Fifteen hours,* she'd said to herself, in the stairwell, to nobody. *I've got fifteen hours of feeling left in the whole year. Better spend it on something.*

---

The card came in October. It was from a man named Arturo Bellows of the845 who had watched a homicide documentary on a Tuesday night, and it said:

# The Cache

The wind came down the overpass in a long, patient exhalation, carrying dust and the faint sweet stink of rot from the drainage channel below. Nothing grew out here anymore. The asphalt had cracked into puzzle pieces, and between the cracks there was only gray powder, boot-scraped smooth in places where people had walked the same desperate line a thousand times.

Three of them had come for the bag.

Marisol saw them first. She was crouched behind the crumpled husk of a delivery van, forty yards back, and she counted heads the way her father had taught her to count ammunition: *one, two, three.*

The old man. The one they called Hook, because of the thing he wore where his right hand used to be. The teenager with the tire iron. And the girl— no, not a girl. Sixteen, maybe, with a face like a wet paper bag and a length of blue pipe taped to a wooden handle.

And they were all watching the same thing: a canvas grocery bag, sitting on the hood of a burned-out sedan in the middle of the road, holding what the kid had called last night, in a whisper, like a prayer, *the food.*

The cache had been found that morning by the boy, nobody knew whose boy. But the flood had come up through the cellar, and the cans had swollen, their seams pushed out into soft pregnant curves. Two of them had burst and begun to ooze. One, a tin of peach slices in syrup, sat at the bottom of the bag with a bulge in its lid like a small, patient bomb.

*Still,* Marisol thought. *Still, they might—*

"It won't keep," said the boy. He was maybe nine. He had the bag in both arms and he had not let go of it since he'd dragged it out of the cellar, and his arms were shaking so hard the cans knocked together. *A sound like bones.* "My mom said, if it's bulging, you throw it out, you don't—"

"Shut up," said the teenager.

He had the tire iron held low, not raised. Twenty, maybe. Boots that had been somebody else's. He was standing six feet from the bag with his weight on his back foot, and Marisol knew that stance, had seen it in the parking lot at the Food Depot two winters ago, when the crowd had first gone quiet and the managers had started swinging baseball bats at each other's shoulders.

Hook came out from behind a concrete barrier, moving like a man whose knees hurt. He had a screwdriver in his good hand, the tip ground down to a flat wedge, and he had the loose hand stuffed inside his coat, and he wasn't going to be able to swing it worth a damn, and everybody knew it, which was presumably why he had come anyway.

"You know what's in there," he said. His voice was a gravel thing dragged over gravel. "Peaches."

The teenager said nothing.

"You know what's in there," Hook said again, and now there was something ugly and hopeful in it, the way a man talks when he has nothing left. "I can *smell* it. From here, I can smell the sugar."

Then he came forward.

Everything happened fast and very slowly, the way it does.

Marisol came up out of the van's shadow with the chain whipping out behind her—it had been a porch swing chain, once, in a world where porch swings existed—and the loop of it cracked across the teenager's raised forearm just as the tire iron came down. She heard the sound the bone made. It was smaller than people expect. It sounds like a green branch stepped on.

The boy ran. Of course he ran, and the bag came apart in his arms, and the cans went rolling out across the hood of the sedan and onto the asphalt, and that was the moment the fight actually began, because now there was no single thing to hold.

They went for the cans.

Hook got the peaches. He got them because he was closest and because he didn't care anymore, and he sat down right there on the road with the tin clutched to his chest like a sleeping infant, and the teenager hit him in the back of the head with the iron, and Hook's forehead opened up in a long red seam that didn't bleed so much as *spread*, dark and slow, the blood going into the dust and becoming brown paste.

Marisol got a hand on the peaches too. They wrestled for it on the ground, in the dust, and the can came apart between them—the lid peeled back with a hiss of pressure, and the smell was so thick and sweet and rotten that both of them gagged, and out of the can came the ugly gray-pink slick of spoiled fruit and thin syrup, running across the asphalt and into the cracks, and it was *all* of it, the whole cache, gone in a smell.

The teenager was on his knees holding his ruined forearm, screaming into the dirt. Hook was on his side, his good hand still hooked around the crumpled tin, and his breathing had gone to a bubbling whistle. Marisol sat back on her heels with the chain in her lap and blood on her hands that wasn't hers, and she looked at what she had done, and at what she had, and understanding arrived all at once in her stomach.

Nine cans. Four of them burst. One was dog food. One had beans in it, green and dull and safe, and the boy had it—had been holding it against his chest with both arms, silent, while the two of them tore each other apart over the peaches.

"Mister," the boy said. He was crying, but he wasn't running. He held out the can of beans. "Here. You can have it. I don't want it, I want my mom."

Hook's good hand opened. His fingers uncurled like something dying in the heat. The tin rolled a few inches and stopped against the teenager's knee, which the boy had to reach across to touch, and the boy did it, and the teenager shoved him away with his good elbow and then, after a moment, didn't.

Marisol stood up. Her chain was still swinging. She wanted— she did not know what she wanted. She wanted the peaches. She wanted to not have wanted them.

Then she picked up the burst can of beans with the leaking edge, the one nobody wanted because it was split and the sauce had gone gray, and she crouched down beside Hook, and she put it into his good hand, the way you'd give a man a cup of water.

Hook drank from it. She looked up at the teenager, still kneeling there with his arm bent wrong and the peaches in his lap.

And he looked at her with all that hate and terror and hunger still in his face, and then at the boy, and he spat, and said, "There's a clinic. Two blocks..If there's a clinic."

"Walk with me," Marisol said, to Hook, to the boy, to whoever was listening. "We'll walk with you."

Nobody took the peaches. They lay there in the road all night, and by morning the wasps had found them, and the wasps were the only living thing in nine square blocks that still had a reason to come back.

That was the whole spring. That was the whole year.

*The ones who cache the food,* Marisol thought, dragging Hook's arm across her shoulders, *are the ones who starve. It's never the ones who fight for it.* But she didn't say it out loud, because by then she wasn't sure it was true anymore, and because saying it would have meant the boy had been right about the bulging cans, and then there'd have been no point in any of them being there at all.

## Nine Minutes

The fog came off the bog in long grey ropes and settled in the hollow by the birches, so that the twenty-four paces between the two of us were only faintly marked out — a scuffed place on the frozen grass, two dark hollows where the hooves had gone through the crust the night before.

Cholera had been in Riga since June. There was no second shot. There was one shot, and it was mine, and I made it, and he was on the ground for nine minutes.

Nobody has ever told his sister the truth, because there is no truth there that would fit in a sentence. I go to Sõmerpalu twice a year. It was the best I ever saw. I have never once been able to make that sentence do any work at all.

### The Appointment

The room above the shuttered tailor's shop had been rented for eleven days, paid in cash, under a name that was not his. It contained a bed, a chair, a window, and a table. He had swept it twice. He had done that because the landlord swept once and he could not bear the thought of another man's broom marks on the same floor — not out of cleanliness, exactly, but because a clean room is a room with no history, and he wanted no history between himself and the four walls.

Outside the window, across nine hundred meters of tram line and old brick, the Civic Hall had put up its flags. They hung limp in the afternoon. There was a crowd gathering at the doors: pensioners in their good coats, students, a knot of press photographers with the look of animals waiting for grain. A banner over the entrance read WELCOME MINISTER KOLARIC. The minister was expected at four. It was three-forty.

He laid the case on the table and opened the latches. They made no sound, which he had checked, twice, on the first day.

The rifle came in three pieces and had lived in a foam-lined coffin longer than most marriages. He knew the assembly the way a pianist knows a chord — not by thinking of it but by the body's own arithmetic, the weight of one part announcing the correct place for the next. The barrel blank went into the stock first. Then the bolt carrier, seated with a soft definitive *chk* that he felt more than heard, the way you feel a door close in another room. The rings, the glass, the reticle. He turned the scope by hand and watched the room's far wall swing through the field of view, and he set the parallax and did not check it again.

He worked without music. He had once been told that he was strange about this, and had stopped explaining. The absence of sound made the work cleaner. It also made the room feel like a held breath.

His hands did not shake. That was not discipline, exactly; the shaking had been trained out of him years ago, in a basin of cold water and a young instructor's disappointment. He had been twenty-two and had thrown up behind a building after his first job and then gone back and done it again. Now there was a place in him where a thing like remorse should have lived, and he had looked for it once, seriously, the way you look in a drawer you know is empty. There was nothing there but a kind of tidiness. The world was divided into things he had been paid to do and things he had not. Anything else was clutter. Anything else was a man he'd once been, taking up space in a chair, worrying about things that had already happened and could not be un-happened.

His daughter had called on Sunday. He had let it ring and then turned the phone face-down, and there was a voicemail, and he had listened to it twice, and the content of it was: *Are you eating? You look thin in that picture.* He had not deleted it. He would not delete it, later, when they came to see him — when they came to see him if they came, if there was anything left to see. He kept it because it was hers. He was not sentimental about her. He was simply organized. There was a place for her, in the filing, and it was not the same place as the work, and the two did not touch.

The clock on the wall of the Civic Hall changed to three-fifty. On his table, beside the rifle, a slice of bread sat on a folded paper napkin with a knife beside it. He had brought it from the bakery on the corner, and he ate it now, methodically, and drank water from a bottle with a straw, and looked out the window at the flags.

Two hundred meters down the street, a woman came out of a doorway and stood with a cigarette and a phone pressed to her ear, laughing at something. He watched her for a moment with real interest. There was no calculation in it. He liked the way she pushed her hair back with the hand that held the phone. There were people in the world who were still, in the middle of their lives, that easy about their bodies, that careless with themselves. He had known one, once. He didn't think about it. He was not a man who thought about things; he was a man who did them and then, if there was time, slept.

The bolt was chambered. He laid the rifle across two folded towels on the sill so the barrel rested on the frame, not the muzzle, and he brought his eye to the glass.

The world narrowed.

Nine hundred meters out, the Civic Hall's stone facade filled the circle of the scope: the fluting of the columns, the banner, the shallow steps. Crosshairs floated over it, thin and unmoving, waiting the way a question waits to be asked. He settled his breathing. He did not hurry it. There was a rhythm to it — in, out, hold — and between the third and fourth breath the sights came alive.

He found the podium. Empty. A glass of water on it, catching the light. A microphone cable coiled like a dropped rope. He centered on the podium's front edge and waited.

Below, the crowd made its small sounds. It had the sound of a crowd and not of a mass; individual voices, a child's complaint, a camera's mechanical stutter. From up here the noise arrived flattened, like the sound of rain on a roof two rooms away. He had never once, in nine years, been able to hear it as a sound. Only as data.

At four o'clock the doors at the side of the hall gave, and there was a movement in the press, a shift of weight, the way a field shifts when wind crosses it.

Vera Kolaric came out onto the steps.

She was smaller than her photographs. That always surprised him. Sixty-one years old, gray-haired, in a blue coat that was probably a compromise — the thing she wore because it photographed well and because she had stopped thinking about clothes. She was not a beautiful woman. She was a serious one, and there was a tiredness at the corners of her mouth that no camera had ever quite hidden, and it was that, more than anything, that he had spent three weeks with: the plain human fatigue of a person who has held a difficult job for a very long time and has stopped pretending the job is not difficult.

He had read her speeches. He had read them the way other men read train timetables — thoroughly, without interest, because the details contained information. The steel tariffs. The port contracts. A clause about the northern mines, section nine, that would put four thousand men back at work and cost her the coalition. There was a photograph in the file of her at a factory gate in the rain, shaking hands. He had looked at it a long time. He had looked at it the way you look at a picture of a bridge you are going to be under.

She reached the podium. She took the glass of water and did not drink from it, just held it, and adjusted the microphone a half-inch closer, and then she looked up at the square and gave them a small smile that was not performative at all, that cost her something, that was for the crowd and not for the cameras.

Two men in grey suits came up the steps behind her and took positions at the edges of the platform, and he found them with the crosshairs without meaning to, and moved off them. Irrelevant. They were in the file. They were furniture.

*Cold*, the shot would be. He knew what the report would say afterward: an entry wound to the left temple, angled slightly downward, the round having passed through the frontal bone and out through the base of the skull, the trajectory consistent with a shooter positioned above and to the northeast. The word the newspapers would use was *precision*. He had always found that word strange. Precision implied care. It implied that he cared very much about where the bullet went. He did not. Precision was simply what happened when a thing was done correctly, and doing it correctly was the whole of his moral life now. There was no room left over for anything else in the man. He had made the room.

The reticle settled.

He put the crosshairs on her forehead, just below the hairline, where the bone was thick and the path to the brain was short and the round would do its work fast — for her, which was a thought he allowed the word *for* but did not allow to become *mercy*. There was no mercy in it. Mercy was a kindness and kindness was a thing that cost something, and he had nothing left to spend, and she would be dead in a fifth of a second either way and would not know a thing about it, which was, if he was honest with himself — and he was not in the habit — the part of the job he actually liked. Not the politics. Not the money. The fact that it was quick. The fact that people were allowed to be, in the end, uninterrupted.

The wind came off the roof tiles at a slight angle. The Appointment

The room above the shuttered tailor's shop had been rented for eleven days, paid in cash, under a name that was not his. It contained a bed, a chair, a window, and a table. He had swept it twice. He had done that because the landlord swept once and he could not bear the thought of another man's broom marks on the same floor — not out of cleanliness, exactly, but because a clean room is a room with no history, and he wanted no history between himself and the four walls.

Outside the window, across nine hundred meters of tram line and old brick, the Civic Hall had put up its flags. They hung limp in the afternoon. There was a crowd gathering at the doors: pensioners in their good coats, students, a knot of press photographers with the look of animals waiting for grain. A banner over the entrance read WELCOME MINISTER KOLARIC. The minister was expected at four. It was three-forty.

He laid the case on the table and opened the latches. They made no sound, which he had checked, twice, on the first day.

The rifle came in three pieces and had lived in a foam-lined coffin longer than most marriages. He knew the assembly the way a pianist knows a chord — not by thinking of it but by the body's own arithmetic, the weight of one part announcing the correct place for the next. The barrel blank went into the stock first. Then the bolt carrier, seated with a soft definitive chk that he felt more than heard, the way you feel a door close in another room. The rings, the glass, the reticle. He turned the scope by hand and watched the room's far wall swing through the field of view, and he set the parallax and did not check it again.

He worked without music. He had once been told that he was strange about this, and had stopped explaining. The absence of sound made the work cleaner. It also made the room feel like a held breath.

His hands did not shake. That was not discipline, exactly; the shaking had been trained out of him years ago, in a basin of cold water and a young instructor's disappointment. He had been twenty-two and had thrown up behind a building after his first job and then gone back and done it again. Now there was a place in him where a thing like remorse should have lived, and he had looked for it once, seriously, the way you look in a drawer you know is empty. There was nothing there but a kind of tidiness. The world was divided into things he had been paid to do and things he had not. Anything else was clutter. Anything else was a man he'd once been, taking up space in a chair, worrying about things that had already happened and could not be un-happened.

His daughter had called on Sunday. He had let it ring and then turned the phone face-down, and there was a voicemail, and he had listened to it twice, and the content of it was: Are you eating? You look thin in that picture. He had not deleted it. He would not delete it, later, when they came to see him — when they came to see him if they came, if there was anything left to see. He kept it because it was hers. He was not sentimental about her. He was simply organized. There was a place for her, in the filing, and it was not the same place as the work, and the two did not touch.

The clock on the wall of the Civic Hall changed to three-fifty. On his table, beside the rifle, a slice of bread sat on a folded paper napkin with a knife beside it. He had brought it from the bakery on the corner, and he ate it now, methodically, and drank water from a bottle with a straw, and looked out the window at the flags.

Two hundred meters down the street, a woman came out of a doorway and stood with a cigarette and a phone pressed to her ear, laughing at something. He watched her for a moment with real interest. There was no calculation in it. He liked the way she pushed her hair back with the hand that held the phone. There were people in the world who were still, in the middle of their lives, that easy about their bodies, that careless with themselves. He had known one, once. He didn't think about it. He was not a man who thought about things; he was a man who did them and then, if there was time, slept.

The bolt was chambered. He laid the rifle across two folded towels on the sill so the barrel rested on the frame, not the muzzle, and he brought his eye to the glass.

The world narrowed.

Nine hundred meters out, the Civic Hall's stone facade filled the circle of the scope: the fluting of the columns, the banner, the shallow steps. Crosshairs floated over it, thin and unmoving, waiting the way a question waits to be asked. He settled his breathing. He did not hurry it. There was a rhythm to it — in, out, hold — and between the third and fourth breath the sights came alive.

He found the podium. Empty. A glass of water on it, catching the light. A microphone cable coiled like a dropped rope. He centered on the podium's front edge and waited.

Below, the crowd made its small sounds. It had the sound of a crowd and not of a mass; individual voices, a child's complaint, a camera's mechanical stutter. From up here the noise arrived flattened, like the sound of rain on a roof two rooms away. He had never once, in nine years, been able to hear it as a sound. Only as data.

At four o'clock the doors at the side of the hall gave, and there was a movement in the press, a shift of weight, the way a field shifts when wind crosses it.

Vera Kolaric came out onto the steps.

She was smaller than her photographs. That always surprised him. Sixty-one years old, gray-haired, in a blue coat that was probably a compromise — the thing she wore because it photographed well and because she had stopped thinking about clothes. She was not a beautiful woman. She was a serious one, and there was a tiredness at the corners of her mouth that no camera had ever quite hidden, and it was that, more than anything, that he had spent three weeks with: the plain human fatigue of a person who has held a difficult job for a very long time and has stopped pretending the job is not difficult.

He had read her speeches. He had read them the way other men read train timetables — thoroughly, without interest, because the details contained information. The steel tariffs. The port contracts. A clause about the northern mines, section nine, that would put four thousand men back at work and cost her the coalition. There was a photograph in the file of her at a factory gate in the rain, shaking hands. He had looked at it a long time. He had looked at it the way you look at a picture of a bridge you are going to be under.

She reached the podium. She took the glass of water and did not drink from it, just held it, and adjusted the microphone a half-inch closer, and then she looked up at the square and gave them a small smile that was not performative at all, that cost her something, that was for the crowd and not for the cameras.

Two men in grey suits came up the steps behind her and took positions at the edges of the platform, and he found them with the crosshairs without meaning to, and moved off them. Irrelevant. They were in the file. They were furniture.

He knew what the report would say afterward: an entry wound to the left temple, angled slightly downward, the round having passed through the frontal bone and out through the base of the skull, the trajectory consistent with a shooter positioned above and to the northeast. The word the newspapers would use was precision. He had always found that word strange. Precision implied care. It implied that he cared very much about where the bullet went. He did not. # Room 14

The motel had a name like a postcard nobody sent: the *Sundowner*, its neon sign missing the S, so it read UND OWNER in cold pink letters from the parking lot. Ray had made his peace with the room in the first ten minutes. Bedspread the color of a bruise gone yellow. Cigarette burns on the nightstand's fake laminate, one of them still tacky, somebody's gin. A wall unit of air conditioning that kicked and groaned every four minutes like an old man turning in his sleep. Stained ceiling tiles. Under the sink in the bathroom, a travel sewing kit meant for pillowcases and nylon hems, and a laminated card listing numbers for the front desk that nobody would answer.

He had laid everything out on the bedspread in a row, the way you saw it in the movies, and the row was so absurd it made him laugh, and then the laugh turned into something with a crack in the middle of it.

On the left: a folding pocketknife he'd bought at a gas station outside Barstow, the blade still faintly greasy from the plastic wrapper. Beside it, a straight razor from the shaving kit, chrome and cheap. A pair of motel sewing needles, sizes 4 and 4½, no thread, no suture. A ball of black nylon thread, meant for hemming a blouse, and he understood that his thigh was not a blouse and that this distinction was going to cost him.

On the right: a bottle of peroxide from the first-aid box in the desk drawer, half-full and brown from age, the cap crusted shut. A glass from the bathroom, rinsed, half full of water. A folded bath towel. A second towel for the floor. The phone, propped against the lamp, flashlight on, because the overhead bulb threw more shadow than light and he wanted to see, God help him, he wanted to see.

And the belt. He'd cut the strap off his own belt with the pocketknife because a belt was the thing you'd grab. He had it looped through the bed's brass headboard, doubled over, and he'd test it twice already, hauling his full weight against it with both hands until his arms shook. It held. It was, in the whole stupid arithmetic of the night, the only thing in the room that had passed a test.

Shirt off. Jeans cut off at the knee with the razor because he couldn't bend far enough, and when the denim parted he saw his own thigh and the hole in it and made a sound he'd never made before, high up in his chest, a little bird noise.

*Don't look. Look. Look. You have to look.*

The bullet had gone in low and left and had not done anything dramatic. That was the thing nobody tells you: no cleanly punched hole, no tidy little pink mouth. There was a ragged tear an inch and a half long, the skin around it already purpling and swelling, the wound still open and grudging, weeping that thin pink fluid that wasn't quite blood yet. Below the hole, halfway down the muscle, a hard little knob of something under the skin. A copper slug, maybe three hundred grains, sitting against the femur.

Twenty-two feet from the door. Eighteen from the window. Across two parking spaces and a strip of gravel, the trooper had stood in the road with his flashlight sweeping and told him to keep his hands where he could see them, and Ray had kept his hands where he could see them and had watched his own blood go into the gravel and turn it black.

So. Nineteen hours and a stolen Chevy and a Sundowner with a broken S, and here he was, on a bedspread the color of a bruise, with a pocketknife and a blouse needle.

*Okay.*

He took a swig from the glass. Tastes like chlorine and the shower faucet. He pours the peroxide over the wound, and it happens all at once, a bright white fizzing that eats into the flesh and burrows, and the sound that comes out of him is not a scream, exactly, it's more structural, more like a beam giving way. His spine arches off the bed. The leg kicks, hard, and the heel slams into the nightstand and knocks the glass off the edge.

It doesn't break. He watches it fall in slow motion and land on the carpet and thinks, with terrible clarity, *that is the last clean water in the world.*

"Fine," he says. "Fine. Fine. Fine."

He grips the belt. Pulls until the leather bites into his palms and the knuckles go white, and he can feel the tooth of the buckle against his hip with every breath. Then he picks up the pocketknife with the other hand, and the hand is shaking so badly that he has to put the knife down and breathe through his nose, four counts in, six counts out, the way he'd been taught in a class he almost failed, some first-aid course in a vocational high school, a lifetime ago.

The pain is the part he will remember. Not the cut, not the digging. There is a difference between pain and *agony*, and the difference is that agony is pain that has opinions about you. Agony argues. Agony makes a place for itself and expands, presses outward along the nerve, takes the leg and the hip and the small of his back and the base of his skull and squeezes them all at once like a hand closing. There is iron in it. There is a taste like a copper coin held between the teeth, and a cold sweat breaking out over his whole body in a sheet, so that the hair on his chest stands up and the sheets are soaked through beneath him in minutes.

And then there's the *sound*. He makes a sound. It is animal. It is not him. It is the body's own distress call, rising out of him without permission, and it is so loud in the cheap room that he hears it bouncing off the window glass, and somewhere out in the parking lot a dog starts up and answers.

He stops cutting.

Twenty seconds. He lies there with the belt in both fists and his chest heaving and the cold sweat running down his ribs, and he thinks about a hospital bed. White sheets. An anesthesiologist with a mask that smelled like sweet rubber and someone else's childhood, and a bright room with the right kind of light, and a doctor saying the word *exploration*, meaning they're allowed to open him up and search him for the thing, meaning there's a professional in the world whose entire job is knowing which way the femoral runs and how much blood a man is allowed to lose before he stops being a man.

He gets up on his elbows. He picks up the knife.

The entry opens. He widens it with the blade and there is a moment — a half-second of total silence in his head, no bird, no nothing — where the pain drops away entirely, and he understands it isn't gone, it's just filed itself so far back that it can't reach him, and that this is the body's mercy, and that the bill will come due later, all at once, with interest.

Then it opens the skin and the muscle at the same time, and the blood comes.

It comes differently than he'd expected. He'd imagined pouring. Instead it *pumps* — a thick, dark, arterial gout that wells up and pushes out of the wound in a rhythm he can count, one-two, one-two, matching a heart he can't slow down, so the wound keeps beating like a second heart hanging off his leg. It runs down his thigh and pools in the crook of his knee and runs off the edge of the bed onto the carpet, and he watches it go, this red going into the ugly carpet, and thinks about the gravel, about the black becoming black.

He has to tie off. He has to pull the nylon thread tight around a vessel with a shaking hand and a button of a needle from a hotel sewing kit, and when the needle punctures skin it is a bright, specific, absurd pain, nothing like the pain of the cut — the pain of the cut is weather, the pain of the needle is a pin, a tiny sharp detail, and he screams at that one too, because he is past caring.

The vessel stops. The bleeding thins to a seep. Good. That part, at least, that part, the part he was most afraid of — that part is survivable.

Now the bullet.

He can feel it. He turns the knife sideways and slides the edge of the blade down into the wound, blunt end first, groping, and there is a hard flat scrape against bone, and the sound of his own breathing going high and thin and fast, and his body finally understanding what it's been asked to do begins to fight him — the thigh locks, the muscles clamp down around the blade like a fist, and he has to work through that, has to pry, has to talk to it in a low furious whisper, *relax, relax, come on, relax, you stupid son of a bitch, relax* —

And then the bullet slides free.

He cannot see it. He is looking at the ceiling, at the water stain on the ceiling tile shaped like a bird, and he feels the slug come up through the meat and out over the blade, and a piece of him rides up with it, and the leg convulses, and his heel hits the nightstand again, and the glass on the carpet breaks.

He reaches under the bedding. He pulls out the slug and holds it up in the phone's flashlight.

It's smaller than he thought. Copper-colored, dull, one end flattened, one end rounded, a little smear of red on it, and he looks at that little smear for a long time.

*That was inside me. That was inside me for nineteen hours while I drove and slept and thought about how my mother would say it.*

And then the pain comes back. All of it. Every bit of it, plus the interest, plus the bill — a white-hot flood from the thigh up through the hip and into his backbone, and the room goes gray at the edges, and the ceiling tile bird swims, and he lies there in the wet sheets with the slug in his fist and his teeth sunk into the towel, and he presses the folded bath towel into the open wound with a hand that has stopped obeying him and binds it with the other end of the nylon thread and thinks, with the last clear thought he'll have for a while:

*Sixty miles to the hospital. Sixty miles. Stay awake. Stay awake, and don't stop on the highway, don't you dare stop on the highway—*

Out in the parking lot, the trooper's cruiser is still sitting under the sign with its lights off, where nobody had thought to move it.

The broken S buzzes and hums. UND OWNER.

Somewhere around three in the morning the air conditioner clicks off, and in the sudden silence Ray Delacroix, who had wanted to be somebody, lies on his side on a bedspread the color of a bruise with the window open and his leg throbbing in time with his pulse, and does not sleep at all.
