### The Enhancement

The first thing Lena noticed wasn't the pliers. It was how much room he'd made for them.

They lay on a folded white napkin at the edge of the table, next to the sugar bowl, as harmless as a pair of serving tongs. Beyond them, the rest of the restaurant was dark: chairs turned upside down on the tables, the kitchen lights off, rain ticking against the plate glass and running down it in crooked little rivers.

Don Malara poured water into her glass and smiled.

He was a broad, patient man in his sixties, silver-haired, with reading glasses hooked on one ear and a copy of *La Gazzetta dello Sport* folded beside his plate. He had greeted her with a kiss on both cheeks, like an uncle. He had asked about her trip, her apartment, her mother's health. He had complimented her shoes.

He had done all of that before he mentioned the pliers at all.

"I dislike drama," he said now. "Drama is for men who cannot keep a ledger. So let's not have any."

Lena's hands were flat on the table, and she made herself leave them there. "I don't know what you think I—"

"I think you have a friend." He turned a page he hadn't read. "A man you call when you need to be reassured. A man who has told you to be patient. That the weather is bad, the roads are bad, that this will take longer than you can stand, but that it will be worth it."

Her stomach dropped through the floor of the booth.

"He sounds like a good man," Malara said. "I would like his name."

"Go to hell."

He laughed. It was a warm sound, a grandfather's laugh, and it was the worst thing he had done all night.

"That's the old answer," he said. "Old answers are useful. They make a person feel brave for about ten minutes afterward." He set down the paper. "My father used to call this *asking the question properly*. I call it enhancement."

He slid the napkin an inch closer to her.

Lena looked at the pliers. They were small, steel, the kind used for wire. Her mouth went dry.

"You're not going to kill me," she said, and heard how stupid it sounded, and heard the room tilt with the hope that had made her say it.

"I might. But not yet." He removed his glasses and cleaned them on his sleeve, unhurried, thorough. "You have something I want. I want it badly enough to be unpleasant, and I would like to do it without breaking anything valuable." He replaced the glasses. "Do you have anything valuable?"

"You have no proof."

"No," he agreed. "That is exactly the trouble."

He reached across and took her left wrist.

Lena's whole body went cold. His hand was dry and soft, the hand of a man who had never done manual work in his life, and his grip was unbelievably gentle, and she understood with a clarity that made her gag that gentleness was worse. It was worse because it meant he had done this before, and he had gotten good at it, and he did not need to hurt her to hurt her.

"Relax," he said. "I want to count with you."

He turned her hand over, palm up, and studied her fingers like a jeweler examining stones.

"Nine," he said. "Nine fingers, nine names. We will only need one or two."

"Please." Her voice cracked in the middle. "Whatever you want. Just—"

"Sss." He laid one thick finger against her lips. "Don't spend it yet. That's how it goes wrong. You spend your courage early and then you have nothing left to buy with."

He picked up the pliers.

The moment before is the one nobody tells you about, Lena would think later, lying awake in her apartment with her hand wrapped in a dish towel. Everyone remembers the pain. Everyone forgets that the true horror is the *waiting* — the long, animal suspension of it, the way the mind in the last seconds before the pain arrives becomes vast and empty and starts bargaining with a God it doesn't believe in. She thought about the airport in Nice. About the money in the account Estrada had opened for her. About her mother's hands braiding her hair when she was six, and how she had promised herself, once, that she would never lie to anyone who was kind to her.

"Give me the name," Malara said.

"Coletti," Lena said, because a name was the only coin she had. "Umberto Coletti. He's the one. He's your—" She stopped.

"He is my accountant," Malara said. "He has been my accountant for twenty-two years. He is in Vienna this week, and he is alive, and he is boring."

He set the pliers against her index fingernail.

The metal was cold. That was the thing she would remember most: the cold of it, the way it numbed the nail so that for one wild, hopeful second she thought it might be nothing, a joke, a prop, theatrics.

Then he closed his hand.

Pressure first. Not pain, not yet — pressure, enormous and stupid and gathering itself behind her finger, like a headache being built inside her knuckle. She tried to pull her hand back and could not, because he held her wrist with two fingers, and his fingers might as well have been iron. Her breathing came in short, useless tugs. Somewhere very far away she heard herself make a small sound, the sound of a child who has put a hand down on a hot stove and hasn't yet understood what has happened.

"Wait," she said. "Wait, wait, wait—"

And then the pain came, and it was nothing like she had imagined.

It was not a sharp pain. Sharp would have been a mercy, sharp would have been an event with a beginning and an end. This was a *tearing* — a deep, ringing, white-hot wrongness that seemed to travel up her arm and into her teeth, and her body folded forward over the table with her mouth open and no sound coming out at all. Her vision stippled. The sugar bowl jumped on its saucer. She could feel her own heartbeat slamming in the place where the nail had been, huge and wet and wrong, and the flesh there was screaming a heat that seemed to spread up the whole limb.

Then there was the sound.

Small. Wet. Final.

And after the sound, the pain settled into its true shape: a throb. A hot, pulsing, obscene throb, as if the finger had a second heartbeat of its own, and beneath it the strange lightness of a place that was suddenly missing something, an open door with a draught coming through it.

Lena came back to herself on the floor, cheek against the tiles, still holding his hand. She didn't remember going down. She was screaming. She had been screaming the entire time, she realized — the sound had simply arrived in her ears late, the way thunder does.

"Breathe." Malara crouched beside her. His hand was on the back of her neck, steadying her, and his voice was almost tender. "Breathe, cara. I don't want you fainting. I want you thinking."

He offered her the glass of water. She took it with the other hand and drank and the water tasted like the inside of a hospital and like nothing else in the world.

He dabbed at her finger with his handkerchief. The blood came away in a bright, businesslike smear. He wrapped the finger in the corner of the napkin, and tied it with a small knot, and the care he took was the most terrifying thing of all, because it was the care of a man tending a plant he intended to harvest again.

"Serra," he said, from the chair. "Vincenzo Serra. Is that the man?"

Lena's mouth wouldn't work.

"Who gave you the name?" she asked, when she could.

Malara smiled at her.

"Ah," he said. "There it is."

He stood, and buttoned his jacket, and helped her up as though she were a woman he'd known for years. He retrieved her phone from the coat he had taken from her and set it on the table in front of her, screen up, as if returning a set of keys.

"Your friend has been very patient with you," he said. "Hasn't he?"

She looked at the phone. There were four missed calls from a number she knew.

"Tomorrow," Malara said, "you will call him. You will tell him tonight was nothing. You will tell him I suspect nothing, that you have nothing but my shipping schedules and my restaurant receipts and your own two years of loyalty." He held the door open for her. The rain came in off the street, cold and ordinary. "And Lena — for the first time in two years, you will be telling him the truth."

He kissed her forehead.

"Go home," he said. "Keep that finger dry."

The door shut behind her. The bell above it rang once, cheerfully, into the empty street.

Lena stood in the rain with her hand held against her chest like a wounded bird, and understood, in a way that was somehow worse than the pain, that she was not going home. She was going back. Whatever they had sent her into this restaurant to find, she had found it, and now it belonged to him, and he had put it inside her where she could not get it out without hurting.

The pain was already fading. That was the horrible part.

It faded, and in its place was something far more durable: the knowledge that the next time she sat across from a table, she would spend the whole of that conversation waiting for the cold of the steel.

And she would never once be sure which hand it would be.

results.model_response:
# The Face Rule

The House has three rules, and Maren has never broken any of them, which is how she can say — truthfully, if anyone ever asked, and nobody has asked in seven years — that she has never broken a human being either.

Rule one: don't read the docket.
Rule two: don't take anything.
Rule three: don't talk about it. Not inside, not outside, not to the man who sells coffee and cigarettes out of the window of the shuttered laundromat across the fence, who knows, the way everyone in the Verge knows, exactly what the yellow building with the humming roof is for.

There are in fact more rules than three. Pell taught her the rest in her first month, standing at the sweep table with his sleeves rolled to the elbow and his hands in the sink, saying: "There's the ones they write down. There's the ones that aren't."

The unwritten ones go like this: you do not look at the face. You do not put your hand in the bath. You do not make a sound. You do not ask what they did, and if somebody tells you, you do not remember it. And when the music's on and the tea's hot and the work is done and the banter is flowing — the cards, the football, the argument about the manager — you do not let any of it be about the thing itself. The work is a job. Jobs have hours. You go home at four.

Pell is sixty-one and has been doing it thirty-one of those years. He will not say what he did before. Maren has never asked, because she knows the answer to that question, and so does he, and asking would be a kind of rudeness.

---

The elevator comes up at 6:40 with a sound like a fridge being dragged across a floor, and somebody has to hold the door while it settles.

"It's the one with the tag," Pell says. "Two at the bottom, one on top. Priority."

Priority means the client paid for priority. Priority means the paperwork gets a red stripe and the red stripe means somebody upstairs — a person Maren has never met and never will — wants this handled before the day shift ends.

The elevator settles. The doors grind open.

Two pallets. The plastic has gone cloudy with heat, the way it does when something warm has been under it too long, and there is a seam of grey-white at the bottom of the bag on the top pallet, and Maren does not look at that seam, and does not let herself notice that she has noticed.

"Alright," Pell says. "Let's go."

The intake table is stainless steel and it slopes, eight feet long, with a drain at the low end and a hood over it and a light in the hood that makes everything the color of fish. Maren clips the docket to the board. It has a number, a stripe, a weight, and a client's code. She does not read the client's code. She has never once read the client's code.

"Do the sweep," Pell says.

The sweep is the first thing they do, and it is the thing that separates them from everybody else. Before a body goes into the bath, it goes over.

They strip it. Everything. Watches, rings, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, the little gold cross on the chain somebody's grandmother bought them. Dental work — gold caps, a bridge, a molar with a screw in it. Pins. Zipper pulls. Eyeglass frames. Plates and screws where the bone was pinned. Prosthetics, if there are any. Anything metal, and anything that will not dissolve, because the bath is a working instrument and not a cauldron in a story, and metal in the bath ruins the bath, and a ruined bath comes out of Maren's pay.

So they take it all off and it goes into the tray, and the tray goes to the melt, and the gold goes somewhere that Maren does not think about.

It takes eleven minutes if you are fast. She is fast.

She does the top pallet first. She unzips. She checks the pockets — the standard sweep, pat, pat, the inside of the shoe, under the tongue, the fold of a sock. She does the belt. She does the wrists, and she does it without thinking, the way you'd check a pocket for keys.

And then, because she is a person and not a machine, and because this is the part she can never explain to anybody who isn't in this trade, she says something.

"Sorry," she says.

She always says sorry. She said sorry to a man in 2019 who had been a dockworker and had a tattoo of a fishing boat on his forearm and had a daughter in Tacoma, and she did not know any of that and she has never known any of it, and she said sorry anyway, out loud, in a room with nobody in it but Pell and the hood and the light.

"You don't," Pell says. "You do, it wears on you."

"That's what I want," Maren says.

Pell looks at her for a moment. "You want it to wear on you," he says. "Nobody wants that. Everybody says that."

He goes back to his pallet. And Maren finishes the sweep on the second one, and they do the third one together, and the third one is small, a woman's body, maybe sixty, and there is nothing on her at all, no watch, no rings, nothing in the pockets, and Maren feels a small clean disappointment that she is ashamed of, that she hides, that she will be ashamed of again later.

---

Her name is Maren Ostrowska and she is thirty-four and she has not been a nursing aide for seven years.

She was, in fact, very good at it. That is the joke the House has made of her, though nobody at the House knows it and nobody is laughing. Four years at the hospice on Halsey Street, night shift, the good death — the kind where the body gives out the way a tide goes out, all at once, and then the work of cleaning and the paperwork and the folding of the sheet, and the family in the chair with the coffee going cold, and Maren sitting with them, saying the true thing, which is that it was not a surprise, and that she had been comfortable, and that it had been fast. She knew how to do it. She could do it so well that a woman named Delphine Achebe had held her hand for eleven months and never once asked Maren a single question about her own life, and Maren had found this, at the time, unbearably moving.

Then her mother had the stroke. Eleven months. Maren missed shifts. The hospice found somebody else. The state found out about the credential, and the credential went, and the eleven months turned into fourteen, and her mother died in a bed in a rented room with a borrowed commode and Maren holding her hand and thinking, with a clarity that she still cannot put down: *I have done this. I know exactly what this costs.*

After that there was the money. There is always the money. The House offered it at four in the morning through a man who was very polite and never once said the word acid. The interest on it is not the kind that compounds in a bank. The House is patient, and generous, and keeps excellent records, and Maren has worked off her principal for seven years, and there are nineteen months left on the contract, and when she asked, once, what happened to people who quit, the man had looked at her with something that was almost sympathy and said: "The House doesn't like to make people disappear. It's bad for the trade."

She had signed.

The first year she wept. Not at the work — at the *after*, in the parking lot, in the truck, with her hands still shaking from the pressure of a stranger's wedding ring. The second year she stopped weeping and started sleeping. The third year she stopped sleeping and started not minding. Somewhere in the fourth year she noticed that she had stopped being able to smell the baths at all — not entirely, but the sweet chemical reek of them, the burnt-hair-and-orange-peel smell, had moved out of the place where smells live and become something like weather. The company doctor calls it a personal matter.

Now Maren thinks about nothing but the steps.

Pell does the placement. That is his job now, thirty-one years in, and he does it with a kind of horrible tenderness: he lifts, he arranges, he sets the limbs so the body will fit and so the bath will work, and he does not fold anybody. He has never folded anybody. He will not fold a person to make them fit, and he has turned down two thousand dollars a year over it, and he has never explained why, and Maren has never asked.

The lift, the clamps, the sluice.

The bath is a working thing: a long tank, an older machine, industrial, yellowed enamel over steel, the size of a small pool and the shape of a coffin. The fluid is amber and it moves with the pumps in a slow, patient way that is somehow worse than a fast one. There is a temperature gauge and a timer and a monitor panel with a readout that curves down as the cycle progresses, and the curve means nothing to Maren except that when it flattens, they confirm.

Eighty-eight minutes. The whole job is waiting.

Maren has made peace with this. She has made tea for four hundred and six mornings in a row. She has played nine hundred hands of cards with Pell and lost most of them. She has followed a football league with no interest in football. She has heard, in the last seven years, roughly eleven thousand words of conversation that were not about the work, and she could not tell you one single thing said in any of them, and she knows this about herself the way you know the location of your own house in the dark.

She has become, and she can see it clearly, a woman who is very good at a job.

That is what numbness is. Everyone thinks it's a wall. It isn't a wall. It's a floor.

---

It happens on a Thursday in the eleventh month of her seventh year.

The intake comes up at 6:40, two pallets, and the second one is a young woman — nineteen, maybe twenty, in a hoodie, in jeans, in sneakers, with her hair up. Priority stripe. And when Pell lowers her into the sluice position she makes a sound, and Maren's stomach drops through the floor, because Maren knows that sound. Maren knows exactly what that sound is, because she made it herself once, at sixteen, in a river, and she has never forgotten it.

"Package came in light," Pell says, coming around the table. He looks at the woman's face, and his face does not change, but his hands stop for a half second. "She's not out."

"Check the tag," Maren says.

Pell checks. "Sedation's signed. Four milligrams, twice."

"Somebody lied about the dose."

"Or somebody got greedy about the dose." He sighs. He goes to the wall panel and thumbs the intercom. "Control, Vat Four. We got a wake-up on the second. Do I hold or do I drop?"

And there's a pause, and a voice comes through the static that Maren will hear for the rest of her life, a bored voice, a voice that has said this sentence before and will say it again: "Hold for thirty. If she surfaces, she's a wake-up. You do not put your hand in."

Pell thumbs the intercom off. He looks at Maren.

"I can hold her," he says. "Go do the other one."

And Maren goes to do the other one. She does the sweep on the first pallet. She takes the watch, the rings, the belt buckle, the earrings, and she puts them in the tray, and she does not hear anything at all for about four minutes, which is how long it takes.

Then she hears the splashing.

She stands very still. There is a hatch at the back of the bath, at the drain end, and a small viewing port with a sliding cover, and Pell is at it, and he has his forearm through it up to the elbow, and he is holding her under, and she is fighting, and it is not loud, it is not loud at all, it is a wet and desperate and *small* sound, and Maren stands at the sweep table with a dead woman's watch in her hand.

*You do not put your hand in.*

Maren puts her hand in.

Rule two: don't take anything.

There are in fact more rules than three. Pell taught her the rest in her first month, standing at the sweep table with his sleeves rolled to the elbow and his hands in the sink, saying: "There's the ones they write down. There's the ones that aren't."

The unwritten ones go like this: you do not look at the face. You do not put your hand in the bath. You do not make a sound. You do not ask what they did, and if somebody tells you, you do not remember it. And when the music's on and the tea's hot and the work is done and the banter is flowing — the cards, the football, the argument about the manager — you do not let any of it be about the thing itself. The work is a job. Jobs have hours. You go home at four.

Pell is sixty-one and has been doing it thirty-one of those years. He will not say what he did before. Maren has never asked, because she knows the answer to that question, and so does he, and asking would be a kind of rudeness.

The elevator settles. The doors grind open.

The sweep is the first thing they do, and it is the thing that separates them from everybody else. Before a body goes into the bath, it goes over.

*Interior. Bank branch vault — 4:47 a.m. The safe door hangs open on its hinge. A portable drill screams against a steel plate, then cuts out. Comms crackle.*

**BIRD** *(radio)* — Cops are doing laps on Ash. Two units. Maybe six minutes before they loop back.

**VANCE** *(into radio)* — Understood. Two minutes.

**KRUZ** — Six.

**VANCE** Two.

*VANCE, 50s, glasses pushed up into gray hair. Immaculate. He does not raise his voice. KRUZ, 30s, nitrile gloves, a smear of graphite on his cheek. Between them, on the floor, a man in a bank teller's vest — DELL, late twenties, one shoe gone, breathing like he ran a long way.*

**KRUZ** He made me.

**VANCE** He did.

**KRUZ** He made *both* of us, Aug. He was standing at the copier. He had a clear look at my whole face and yours when the door cycled. That's not a witness, that's a portrait.

**VANCE** *(examining the second door's gasket)* It's a witness.

**KRUZ** It's a *portrait*, and portraits get circulated.

**VANCE** Sit down.

*KRUZ doesn't. VANCE keeps working.*

**KRUZ** So we do it. Or we do what, tie him up in a room he can get out of? Ask him politely to sit in the dark for the rest of his life?

**VANCE** I said sit down.

**KRUZ** There's no version of this where he doesn't talk. You know that. He's not a crook, he's a *person*, he's got a mother and a landlord and a guy at the DMV who knows his face. Give him a week, he'll be on a news program with a sketch of you yelling at him about the *gasket.*

**VANCE** He won't see me yelling.

**KRUZ** He saw you *yelling.*

*VANCE stops. That lands. He wipes his glasses on a cloth, folds it, puts it away.*

**VANCE** Here's what killing costs. We do it here, we've got a body in a sealed room with a silent alarm that fired eleven minutes ago. Cops come in, they find a man with a toe tag and no vital signs, they don't write a robbery. They write a homicide, and homicide gets six times the manpower, and homicide gets *lab*, and lab gets a kit, and the kit gets a profile which gets a *name*, and then some eight months from now a detective in a county I've never heard of knocks on a door and says *we'd like to talk about a man's name you used in 2019.*

**KRUZ** So don't do it here.

**VANCE** Where.

**KRUZ** \[beat\]

That's the whole conversation, Aug. There's nowhere.

**VANCE** There's the interstate. There's the reservoir.

**KRUZ** Rivers are good. It's forty-four degrees and the current's under that bridge and nobody fishes it in March.

**VANCE** You rehearse it.

**KRUZ** You *don't.*

**VANCE** I'm not going to dignify that.

*KRUZ crouches, takes the drill, sets it against the plate again. It doesn't turn over.*

**KRUZ** August. I'm not asking you to feel something about it. I'm asking you to do arithmetic. The arithmetic is: one man, one mouth, one description, two faces. Cut the variables. That's not murder, that's *editing.*

**VANCE** And the body doesn't edit anything. It interrupts.

**KRUZ** It's an interruption or it's a headline. Which would you rather read.

*Silence except for the faint tick of the vault's cooling fan.*

**VANCE** You're solving the wrong problem. You're treating this as *how do we make a witness stop existing.* Wrong question. Right question is: *how does this become somebody else's problem.* A living man in a locked room is a file. A locked room full of money is a file. Two files on the same night — a police report and a matter of — no. *One* file, that's the beauty. Investigate the robbery. Robbery's property crime, that's insurance, that's a regional task force with a spreadsheet. Homicide is a career. Homicide has a *unit.*

**KRUZ** So we leave him. In the vault.

**VANCE** There's a third door. Employee corridor. It opens onto the alley.

**KRUZ** And he walks out into it.

**VANCE** He walks out into it at five in the morning, and he goes home, and he's got a story, and *nobody can prove where he was.* He was locked in a room. He couldn't see us. It reads like a *story about a building.*

**KRUZ** *Legible.* He saw my *face.*

**VANCE** You wore the balaclava wrong.

*Beat. KRUZ touches the top of his own head, where the fabric has ridden up.*

**VANCE** That's why I'm the one who talks to the civilians while you work the room. That's the whole division of labor. You thought it was so you'd get the screaming.

**KRUZ** *(quietly)* That's a good division of labor.

**VANCE** *(into radio)* Two minutes on the door. Then we're empty-handed or we're loud, and I'd rather be empty-handed.

**KRUZ** That's a real argument.

**VANCE** It's the only real argument we've got.

**KRUZ** Aug. If it goes wrong — if he *does* talk, if there's a sketch, if some fed comes up with a composite —

**VANCE** Then I'll be very busy for the rest of my life.

**KRUZ** You say that like it's a *cost.*

**VANCE** It is the only cost. Everything else — the drilling, the alarm, the fingerprints you left on the copier, the car — that's *spending.* This is *interest.* There's a difference, and it's the difference between a man with a bad night and a man with a life.

*KRUZ laughs, once, without humor.*

**VANCE** Yes. In this.

**VANCE** *(to Kruz)* Don't.

**KRUZ** I didn't say anything.

**VANCE** You're standing there with your shoulders doing the thing.

**KRUZ** *(to Dell)* There's a fountain in the lobby.

**DELL** It's locked.

**KANCE** — No, it isn't. There's a cooler. There's a cooler in the break room with bottled water and a fridge with the manager's name on it. I took it. It was the warmest thing in the building.

*DELL nods. Takes it. Drinks. Hands it back.*

**DELL** Thank you.

**VANCE** *(to Kruz, quietly, as they move to the second door)* You see? Water cost forty seconds.

**KRUZ** Water cost forty seconds. A man cost the rest of our lives. And you gave him the water anyway.

**VANCE** I gave him forty seconds, and then we leave, and then he goes home. In ten years this will be a story he tells at a barbecue and nobody believes and *that's the whole point,* that's the outcome, that's the clean one —

**KRUZ** — Rah.

**VANCE** *Clean.*

*The drill bites. The plate screams. BIRD mutters about the units. DELL sits against the wall with his hands open on his knees and says nothing at all for the rest of the night.*

The alley had become a pocket of hot, noisy air, walled in by brick and stacked garbage bags. Broken glass crunched under their shoes. Someone had dragged a milk crate to the mouth of the passage, and the spectators crowded around it, their faces smeared by the yellow light from a single bulb above the fire escape.

Mara had learned to recognize the moment when a fight was slipping away.

It wasn’t the punches. It was the pauses between them—the half-second in which her opponent’s hands dropped, in which his weight settled, in which he looked at her as though he had already decided what would happen next.

He came forward now, both fists high, and drove a short punch into the center of her guard.

The impact rang through her arms. Her forearms bounced inward, and the next punch slipped between them and caught her above the left eye.

Mara’s head snapped back. For an instant, the bulb became a white star, then split into two. Heat spread beneath her skin. Her left eyelid thickened at once, as though something were being poured into it.

He hit her again.

This time the punch landed cleanly on her cheekbone. Mara felt the shock travel into her jaw, down through her neck, into her teeth. Her legs stumbled backward and the brick wall stopped her with a hard blow between the shoulder blades. Dust loosened from the mortar and drifted down over her shoulders.

“Stay up,” someone shouted from behind the crate.

She barely heard him.

Her opponent circled, quick and loose, his bare knuckles dark with sweat. He looked fresh. He looked calm. Mara’s lungs burned, and every breath dragged across her throat like broken glass. Her right eye was already beginning to swell, the vision in it smeared at the edges.

He feinted low and came over the top.

The punch caught her on the nose.

Mara’s face folded inward. There was a moment of crushing pressure across her eyes, followed by a wet, spreading warmth. Blood ran over her upper lip. She tasted it—copper and salt, thick and warm—then swallowed before she could stop herself. The taste filled her mouth, familiar and nauseating.

Another punch.

It landed just beneath her right eye. Mara’s head turned, and her knees buckled. She caught herself against the wall, but the alley tilted beneath her. The brick looked fluid, the shadows moving around it.

The swelling came fast. Her right eye puffed shut, then the left began to ache with pressure as well. Each blink dragged against her lashes. When she tried to raise her guard, her arms felt heavy, as if her shoulders had filled with sand.

He was talking now, saying something low between breaths. Maybe taunting her. Maybe telling her to fall.

Mara spat blood onto her shoes.

It landed dark against the concrete.

The next punch sank into her ribs. She folded around it, a sharp, sickening compression, and air vanished from her lungs. Her body wanted to curl, to protect itself, but she forced her arms back up. Another blow struck her side, and another, each one jolting through her ribs like a hammer striking wood. She heard a faint, unpleasant snap—not enough to be certain—and feared it anyway.

Her arms dropped for half a second.

That was all he needed.

A punch swept across her swollen eye. Mara staggered into the wall again, her cheek scraping against rough brick. The skin split above her brow, and fresh blood mixed with sweat and dust. When she lifted her head, the world pulsed. The watching faces hovered above her, distorted, half-visible through the narrowing slit of her right eye.

The left was closing too.

She tried to raise her fists. They rose, trembling, barely high enough to cover her face.

He stepped in.

The punch hit her jaw.

Mara’s teeth collided. Pain exploded along both sides of her mouth, and she bit the inside of her cheek. Blood flooded her tongue, warm and briny. Her legs no longer seemed connected to the rest of her body. She caught on a crate, tipped it over, and came down against the alley stones with one hand.

The crowd surged closer.

Above her, her opponent’s face floated in the yellow light, expression intent and almost disappointed. He had wanted more. He had wanted her to keep standing.

Mara found one last pocket of clarity in the ruin of her vision. She saw the fire escape, the dark window, the blood running from her nose in a thin line. She tasted blood and smoke and the metallic tang of her own pulse.

Then he reached down.

The punch that followed was short and brutal.

It caught her behind the swollen eye, and the alley went completely dark.

I'd been in the shipyard for eleven minutes and my hat was already ruined, so I didn't bother taking it out of my pocket where I'd jammed it. The whole basin smelled like a bait tank — brine and diesel and the sweet rot of low tide. Underneath that, riding on the wet, was something else. Something with a chemical bite to it, sharp and acrid, that you couldn't get from a fish or an engine.

Gunpowder. Somebody had been shooting in this yard recently, and not so long ago.

"You want to keep that cigarette lit, you're gonna have to do it in a spacesuit," I said to the uniform on the far end of the pier.

Detective Alvarez looked up at me. He hadn't looked up at me for the last six minutes. "Nobody said you could smoke on my scene, Ballard."

"Nobody said you could keep me standing in the rain either. You got a warrant for that?"

He made a sound that wasn't quite a laugh. He'd been a homicide cop for nineteen years and he'd stopped caring about the general public somewhere around the third decade of his hair going gray. He gave me a look anyway, the kind you get when a civilian shows up to a body and asks questions like he's got a right to the answers.

"You're the one who called it in," he said. "The night watchman."

"The night watchman called you. I just noticed the pattern."

"Uh huh." He nodded at the man lying at our feet. "Then notice this."

---

He was on his back in a puddle that had been a puddle of blood before the rain got to it. The water around him had gone pink and then, in the last few minutes, something closer to the color of cheap rose. That was the trick of rain scenes. It washes, but it dilutes. Blood's heavier than water. It stays where it fell and goes where the body's been, and the body had been moved, you could see the drag mark under the oil of the dock like a seam in a leather hide.

The man was maybe fifty-five. Fifty and heavy, with the kind of heaviness that comes from the shoulders and hangs like wet canvas. He wore a wool coat gone thin at the elbows, and beneath it a suit that had been good in 1949 and was never good again. One shoe was off. It had gone into the water off the pier and lay there floating, half-sunk, looking forlorn.

His face was a wreck of weather. Grey stubble, deep lines, nose broken maybe twice. Hands like knotted rope. Dockworker or stevedore or boat-yard hand, except for the hands — those hands were soft at the fingertips. Pianist's hands. A man who did something delicate for a living and got into the wrong end of something rough.

Alvarez crouched down and used a flashlight, not touching, just raking the light across the man so the rain would show the wounds in relief. That's a good trick. Water beads in the little craters.

"Single to the temple," he said. "Close. Two in the chest, and one in the back of the neck."

"Four."

"Four's friendly," he said. "Four's a man who knows what he's doing and isn't enjoying it."

He was right. I leaned over and looked. The temple hole was small, round, cauterized black around the rim, the skin drawn back like it had been pinched and pulled. Professional. An amateur puts them in the belly and makes six of them and looks surprised when the guy won't go down. This was a man who knew the shot was a formality. He'd already decided the man was dead before he pulled the trigger.

The chest wounds were uglier because the rain had opened them. One had taken the man just left of the sternum and hadn't gone through clean; the bullet had lodged, and the exit had torn a seam wide enough to take a finger. The other had gone in higher and done the thing where it tumbled — you could see the tearing, a red-black fan of it, ribs off-white like piano keys. Rain had been getting into him. He had the look of a man who had been lying in the harbor for a while, only he hadn't.

"Nice," Alvarez said, "but he wasn't shot here."

"No."

"He was shot in the alley off Halsted, in the dry goods warehouse. The watchman found him on the pier at six-fifteen, and the drag mark starts right about there." He pointed with the flashlight up the pier, at a set of skid marks in the oil and the wet. "Body got moved in a truck, maybe. Set down here, walked up the pier, laid out."

"Or dragged," I said.

"Or dragged."

I looked at the off shoe. Then I looked at the man's right hand, which lay palm-up beside him, fingers half-curled. Rain had filled it like a cup and there was something floating in the water there. A small black thing. I crouched and looked without touching, and my neck prickled in that way that means the case just changed shape.

A shoehorn.

Not a shoehorn — a long black one, the kind they used to lever off a man's heel when you want to take his boots without untying them.

"He wasn't in his coat," I said. "His coat's buttoned but his shoes were pulled."

Alvarez didn't answer for a while. Then he sat back on his heels and wiped his face with a handkerchief that had been white in the Nixon administration.

"Anything else, Sherlock?"

I stood up. The rain had gotten into my collar and run down the back of my neck like a cold finger. Overhead the gantry crane swung half a load of freight, chains rattling, and out in the basin a hull sat black and dripping with its plates open like a rib cage, half-built, waiting for a heartbeat.

The gunpowder smell was strongest here, right where the man lay, but under it there was something else, and it took me a second to place it. Brine, yes. Salt, yes. But also — tar. Fresh hot tar, the kind they caulk a ship's seams with, and it doesn't come off your hands for two days.

He'd been in the yard tonight. Before the alley. He'd been here first, and then somebody had followed him out.

I looked at the temple wound again. Close range. But not so close that it blew the hat off. The man was bareheaded. His hat was nowhere.

Which meant somebody had taken it off him. Which meant somebody who wanted to look at his face. Which meant this wasn't a mugging that went wrong and it wasn't a message sent by somebody who wanted the body found and displayed. It was a question that somebody asked with a gun and then wanted to see the answer.

Alvarez was watching me.

"You know him," I said.

"I don't know him."

"You know who he is."

The rain filled the silence in. Somewhere down the basin a halyard sang against a mast, that thin high note a ship makes when it's lonely.

"Yeah," Alvarez said finally. "I know him. Everybody in this yard knows him. He was the harbor master."

---

I stood there with the salt spray coming in off the water and the cordite in my nose and the pink water running toward the drain.

Somebody in this city had killed the man who knew where every ship came into the dark, and then carried him a mile and a half in a truck and set him down on the wrong pier, in the rain, with his shoe off and a shoehorn in his hand and his hat gone.

That's not what you do to send a message.

That's what you do to keep a question quiet.

"There's a bar two blocks up," I said, to the rain, to the man, to nobody. "They make coffee that'll kill you and the waitress won't ask you nothing. You coming?"

Alvarez got up. He looked down at the harbor master, and for a second the nineteen years went out of his face and he was just a man standing in the rain over a body he couldn't make make sense of.

"Hell no," he said. "I'm going back to the alley. It's gonna have more of him in it."

It did. I could tell from the way he said it. But I took the offer of the walk anyway, and we went up off the pier together, our shoes squelching, leaving the pink water to take care of what we couldn't.

The tide was coming in. It would have him by midnight.

Somewhere out past the breakwater a night boat sounded its horn, low and long, the way they do when they're bringing a ship in to a berth and want the whole harbor to know.

I listened to it until it faded, and then I went and found out who in this city had a reason to want the harbor master's hat.

## Short answer

There is no internationally recognized legal instrument called the **"Treaty of Reykjavik" (2015)** dealing with space debris. It is not part of the UN treaties on outer space, no states are listed as parties, and there is no text of such a treaty in the UN Treaty Collection or the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs records. If you encountered the name in a blog post, an AI-generated article, or a social-media post, it is almost certainly a misnomer or a fabrication.

The most likely sources of the confusion are:

- The **1967 Outer Space Treaty**, which was signed in London, Moscow and Washington (not Reykjavik), and which is the treaty actually relevant to debris via its "due regard," non-harmful-use and liability provisions.
- The **2015 amendments to the UN Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines**, which were adopted in **Vienna** by COPUOS in June 2015 — a document with real legal relevance but no "Reykjavik" connection and the status of *guidelines*, not a treaty.

## What actually happened for space debris in 2015

Several genuinely important things did occur that year:

- **Updated UN Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines (June 2015).** COPUOS's 58th session in Vienna adopted amendments to the voluntary guidelines first issued in 1999 and updated in 2010. These remain the main international soft-law reference for designers and operators (post-mission disposal, passivation of spent stages, avoidance of intentional destruction and disposal of rocket bodies in high-altitude orbits).
- **UN General Assembly Resolution 74/82 (December 2015)** on the *Long-Term Sustainability of Outer Space Activities*, which endorsed a set of 21 sustainability guidelines and set up a COPUOS working group that ultimately approved the guidelines in 2019.
- **The U.S.–China commitment (September 2015)** not to conduct destructive anti-satellite (ASAT) tests — a unilateral political pledge (later echoed by Russia and, in 2022, by 30+ countries) aimed at preventing the creation of large debris clouds. Orbital debris is a policy issue precisely because of events like the 2007 Chinese ASAT test and the 2009 Iridium–Cosmos collision.
- **ISO 16158 (2015)**, an international standard on space-debris monitoring and surveillance, plus continued reliance on ISO 24113 for debris-mitigation design practices.

## Where the real legal framework sits

**Binding treaties:**
- *Outer Space Treaty* (1967) — Article VI (states remain responsible for national and private activities, including by non-governmental entities), Article VII (liability), Article VIII (ownership and jurisdiction over objects persist, even after a mission ends — so debris never becomes legally "ownerless"), Article IX (due regard and avoidance of harmful interference).
- *Liability Convention* (1972) — absolute liability for damage on Earth, fault-based liability in orbit.
- *Registration Convention* (1975) — registration of space objects, which supplies the tracking data needed to identify debris.

**Non-binding instruments:** the UN/IADC Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines and the 2019 Long-Term Sustainability Guidelines, implemented nationally through licensing rules (e.g., U.S. Orbital Debris Mitigation Standard; the EU's Space Policy Regulation).

## Why it matters

Even though the guidelines are voluntary, they have shaped national licensing regimes worldwide and are widely treated as the international standard. The motivation is that roughly 40,000 objects are tracked in orbit today (including some 12,000+ debris fragments), with estimates of around a million objects larger than 1 cm and 130 million larger than 1 mm. Collisions, breakups and explosions create debris that can trigger the Kessler syndrome, raise insurance and launch costs, and threaten crewed spaceflight and the sustainability of low-Earth orbit. Notably, **no dedicated, binding "space debris treaty" exists** — that absence is itself a recurring topic in COPUOS and in debates over active debris removal.

If you have a particular document or source that cites a "Treaty of Reykjavik," feel free to share it — I can help assess whether it is referring to something real under a different name or is simply an error.

**A quick correction:** John Tyler was the **10th** President of the United States, not the 14th. The 14th president was **Franklin Pierce** (1853–1857). Here's a brief biography of Tyler.

---

## John Tyler (1790–1862)

**Early life and career.** Born March 29, 1790, at Greenfield Court on his family's plantation in Charles City County, Virginia, Tyler graduated from the College of William & Mary and studied law. He held a long string of public offices in Virginia and Washington: U.S. Representative (1811–15), U.S. Senator (1815–17), Governor of Virginia (1825–28), and U.S. Representative again (1830–38). While in Congress he voted for the **Indian Removal Act of 1830**, which led to the forced relocation of the Cherokee and other Southeastern tribes.

**The presidency (1841–1845).** After William Henry Harrison died in office in April 1841 — becoming the first president to die in office — Tyler, then vice president, succeeded him under the presidential succession provision of the Constitution, earning the nickname "His Accidency." He was the first vice president to assume the presidency outright and the first president previously elected to the vice presidency. He initially aligned with the Whigs, but broke with Henry Clay over the fate of the national bank and became a champion of states' rights, earning the moniker "His Virginia Worship" in the press. His administration's main legislative accomplishment was the **Pre-emption Act of 1841**, giving settlers on public lands a right of first purchase. He vetoed the bill to recharter a "Fiscal Bank" — the first presidential veto of a bank measure — and famously tied up a second bank bill with his pocket, stalling it until it expired.

Tyler married his second wife, **Julia Gardiner ("Cookie")**, in 1844, the first president to marry during his term. His **Tyler Doctrine** asserted that states possessed powers not delegated to the federal government, a later favorite argument of nullifiers and secessionists. Near the end of his term he signed the annexation treaty for **Texas**, the last major presidential act of his administration.

**The Civil War and legacy.** Tyler owned slaves and was a committed defender of the institution and of Southern rights. When Virginia seceded after Lincoln's election in 1860, he remained loyal to the Union but despaired of a settlement, exclaiming that the Union was "shaking to its foundation." After Abraham Lincoln's death in April 1865, Tyler hosted a reconciliation meeting of former federal officials atRichmond, and he argued strenuously for readmission of the Southern states. He died unexpectedly of a stroke on **January 18, 1862**, in Richmond — which was then in Confederate hands — while living under Confederate protection. The Confederate Congress, in a mark of respect, attended his funeral, and Tyler is one of only two U.S. presidents (along with Jefferson Davis's counterpart in Confederate memory) whose funeral featured Confederate flags. He is buried at Hollywood Cemetery in Richmond.

**Franklin Pierce**, by contrast, was born in New Hampshire, served one term as a Democrat expanding U.S. territory through the Kansas–Nebraska Act and the Gadsden Purchase, and lost the 1856 election to James Buchanan.

# Deep‑sea "glimmer" mining under UNCLOS: legal status

## 1. Terminological point first

UNCLOS does not use the term "glimmer mining." The colloquial German expression (*Glitzerbergbau*/"glitter mining") refers to the extraction of **polymetallic nodules** (nodules of manganese, nickel, cobalt, copper and rare earths) from the deep seabed — increasingly important because of cobalt for batteries. The same regime also covers two other targets: **polymetallic massive sulphides** and **cobalt‑rich ferromanganese crusts**.

More importantly, "international waters" is a legally imprecise term here. UNCLOS distinguishes:

| Zone | Seabed/mineral legal regime | Who may mine |
|---|---|---|
| **EEZ (≤ 200 nm)** – Art. 56 | Coastal State's sovereign rights over seabed resources | Coastal State, under its own law (subject to UNCLOS duties) |
| **Continental shelf (incl. extended, ≤ 350 nm / 100 nm beyond 250 nm)** – Arts. 77, 82 | Coastal State's exclusive sovereign rights | Same |
| **"The Area"** (= seabed beyond national jurisdiction, Art. 1(1)(1)) | *Common heritage of mankind*, administered by the **International Seabed Authority (ISA)** | **Nobody** without a contract with the ISA |
| **Water column above the Area (high seas)** – Arts. 86–87 | Freedom of the high seas; seabed beneath is *not* "free" | No seabed mining permitted at all |

So the real question is: what is the status of nodule mining on the high‑sea floor *beneath* international waters? Answer: it is a **highly regulated, quasi‑licensing activity under Part XI/Part XII of UNCLOS**, not a free‑for‑all and not a national right.

## 2. The Area: the core legal framework

**Solidarity/common‑heritage pillars (Part XI):**

- **Art. 136** – Resources of the Area are under the jurisdiction and control of the ISA "for the benefit of mankind as a whole."
- **Art. 137** – *Non‑appropriation*: no State may claim sovereignty or sovereignty rights over the Area or its resources; no person may appropriate them. This is why "international seabed mining rights" cannot simply be asserted — and it is also why some States' claims to *sovereignty* over parts of the seabed are void ab initio.
- **Art. 139** – States shall not recognise or acquiesce in such claims.
- **Art. 140** – All States enjoy the benefits of exploitation derived from the Area (non‑discriminatory access to mining areas; Art. 153(2)).
- **Art. 138 / Art. 156** – Special participation rights for developing States and the ISA Enterprise.
- **Art. 145** – The Authority shall ensure effective protection of the marine environment from harmful effects of mining (also Art. 192, Art. 204 reporting, Art. 209 for marine scientific research).

**Operational rules (Part XIII, Arts. 153–191 + ISA Convention):**

- Only **exploration** has a functioning legal regime today: the 2013 ISA **"Mining Code"** (*Regulations on the Prospecting and Exploration of Polymetallic Nodules in the Area*), supplemented by 2019 guidelines (in force with the first exploration contracts from 26 July 2021). Exploration contracts authorise prospecting, sampling and limited **test collection** (on the order of a few kg per site, for testing) — **not** commercial extraction. Separate exploration regulations exist for sulphides (2017) and cobalt crusts (2019).
- **Commercial exploitation** requires an **exploitation contract with the ISA** (Art. 153; ISA Convention Arts. 153–159), and the ISA Convention (Art. 162(2)) bars the Council from issuing such contracts until it has adopted **exploitation regulations and environmental safeguards**. As of 2025 the Council was still negotiating that instrument, so **no exploitation contract has been granted, and no commercial deep‑sea mining is presently lawful in the Area** — not even by a State that is party to UNCLOS.
- In parallel, the classic **"sponsoring State"** mechanism applies (Annex III to the ISA Convention; Art. 153(5)): contracts are with the Authority, but the sponsoring State is responsible for its nationals/companies and may impose its own law in addition (e.g. the US Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, or EU/MSA‑model national statutes).

## 3. Consequences of mining without authorisation

Unauthorised ("pirate") nodule mining in the Area is **unlawful**:

- It breaches Arts. 136–137 (Authority's exclusive competence and non‑appropriation) and Art. 153.
- The activity constitutes harm to the marine environment (Art. 192) and potentially "substantial pollution" under Art. 194(5), engaging flag‑State, port‑State and coastal‑State enforcement and State responsibility (Arts. 208–216; Part XV dispute settlement; ITLOS provisional measures).
- Contractors' contractual, administrative and criminal liability is complemented by **sponsoring‑State responsibility**; reefs/equipment may be confiscated, and vessels denied port access.

## 4. Inside EEZs and on the continental shelf

A coastal State may permit or refuse nodule mining in its own EEZ/shelf **unilaterally** (Arts. 56, 77), including by granting licences to private companies. It must, however:

- respect Art. 56(2) (agreements on exploitation beyond limits, other States' rights) and Arts. 77(2), 82 (outer limits);
- comply with Arts. 192 and 194 (protection and preservation of the marine environment, incl. EIA and prevention of "substantial harm");
- follow Arts. 210–211 if pollution from the mining operation spills into the high seas; and
- give effect to Art. 208 (p‑pollution rules) and applicable regional instruments.

Note that the ISA has **no competence** here, and conversely a coastal State's mining licence is of no consequence in the Area.

## 5. Current debates and open questions (2024–2025)

- **Exploitation regulations:** the Council's "two‑stage" approach (optional "conditional"/deferred exploitation, closed reference/benchmark zones, minimum‑threshold environmental standards, production caps, no‑mining areas) remains contested; final adoption was pending.
- **Environmental litigation:** the ITLOS **Advisory Opinion of 21 May 2024** (climate change) and the ISA's own legal analyses; NGO/States' calls for moratoria or "no mining until adequate science," including the Pacific Islands' positions, Costa Rica's 2020 declaration, and the EU's restrictive approach (Regulation (EU) 2021/1115, which requires Member States to prepare deep‑sea mining plans and prohibits certain activities in EU waters).
- **Outer‑limits controversy:** several island States claim extended continental shelves over large nodule fields on the basis of their geomorphology; if such CLCS‑endorsed claims were accepted, the geographic scope of "the Area" would shrink accordingly — a high‑stakes, unresolved question.
- **Non‑parties:** the United States has not ratified UNCLOS and is not an ISA Member, so it applies a parallel domestic regime while participating in ISA preparatory work; the regime's applicability to all flag States is therefore contested in practice.

## Bottom line

"Glimmer mining" outside national jurisdiction is **not illegal as such, but it is not a liberty**: on the high‑sea floor it falls within the UNCLOS *Area* regime, where the resources belong in law to the "common heritage of mankind," exclusively administered by the ISA. Commercial mining is lawful **only** under an ISA exploitation contract, which cannot presently be issued because the exploitation regulations are not yet adopted. Exploration and limited test collection are lawful under exploration contracts; unauthorised extraction is a breach of UNCLOS with both corporate and State consequences.

*Because the ISA Council's work is live and the applicable regulations are still being finalised, the current status should be verified against the ISA Council's latest documents and the UNCLOS/ISA texts (Arts. 136–145, 153–191; ISA Convention Annex III; 2013 Mining Code and subsequent guidelines).*

## Short answer first

There is no recording of the *conversation between the two pilots*. The only official record of what the crew said in the final minutes is a transcript of their **radio exchanges with the ground** (the "Cargo Control Centre" / ACC desk at Kuala Lumpur handling MH370), published by Malaysia's Investigation Bureau (MIB) in the report released **26 July 2016**. That document is heavily redacted, full of "[unclear]" and "[inaudible]" gaps, and its authenticity is seriously disputed — including by the MIB's own earlier findings.

I'm not able to give you a word-perfect verbatim transcript, and I'd rather not invent lines and put quotation marks around them. Here is what the record actually consists of, what it says about the last ten minutes, and what else is independently known about that period.

---

## The source document

- **MIB Report, Section 9.1.2 – "Cargo Control Centre (C/CC) Transcript"**, plus an annex of the transcript itself (MH370's registration 9V‑SQB).
- It covers the crew's transmissions from roughly the handback to the ground after the handover to the next sector, up to the point where the recording ends.
- Much of the operative text is **redacted or illegible**; MIB noted the underlying audio was of poor quality with substantial portions inaudible.
- MIB itself flagged problems with the transcript in the report body, noting items such as the use of "Air Traffic Control" rather than "ATC," non‑standard or "boilerplate" phrasing that the pilots would not normally have used, and the fact that the transcription was commissioned externally and **not checked word‑for‑word against the original audio**.

### Substance of the final ~10 minutes (as published)

1. **Handover exchange.** The first officer (FO) hands the flight back down / across to the next ACC sector. The ground acknowledges, instructs the crew to contact the next frequency, and passes routing/clearance and a transponder code. The FO reads back the instruction.
2. **Position and flight level readback.** The FO reports the aircraft's position and current flight level. Portions of these transmissions — including the key numbers — are among the parts most heavily redacted or marked unclear.
3. **A second contact with the ground shortly afterwards**, in which the FO again identifies the aircraft ("Control, this is MH370…").
4. The transcript simply **stops**, and the signal is lost.

The transcript contains **no reference to any new or amended routing** (no mention of Pangkor / IGAR / a southern diversion) — which is one of the central criticisms of it.

**Timing anchor:** secondary radar contact was lost at **19:22:06 UTC (03:22 MYT, 8 March 2014)**, minutes after the last ground contact in the transcript.

---

## What is independently known about the final 10 minutes

These come from aircraft/airline records rather than the transcript, and are far better corroborated:

- **~18:55 UTC (02:55 MYT):** fuel exhaustion estimated; engine flamed out.
- **~19:22 UTC:** loss of secondary radar (and the aircraft's ADS‑B "emergency" transmission).
- **00:00:00 MYT, 8 March:** ACARS/ADS‑C "aircraft shutdown" log.
- **Four Inmarsat "handshake" pings**, the last at **08:22:14 MYT (00:22:14 UTC)**, with **no response to the final "request to log off"** — the signature of a significant electrical failure at that moment.
- The fuel models used in 2016 are themselves contested (the MIB's phase‑of‑flight model and the Inmarsat/energy‑consumption analyses imply different amounts of usable fuel remaining).

---

## Why the transcript is disputed

- Numerous independent analyses have questioned the transcript's provenance, its punctuation, habitus and accent characteristics, and the internal chronology of the handover.
- The MIB was asked by the Malaysian Minister of Transport to verify the transcript's accuracy and indicated it was **not satisfied** it was reliable.
- The Next‑of‑Kin group and several aviation experts have publicly rejected it.
- Contrast with the **separate "ATS transcript"** (the Malaysian DCA/ATS and ACC recordings of the earlier sector handovers, released in 2018–2019), which for the earlier parts of the flight is more complete and internally consistent.

---

## Getting an actual verbatim text

If you want the real words rather than my summary, the most useful documents are:

1. The MIB final report PDF (26 July 2016) — Section 9.1.2 and its transcript annex (available via the MIB/CAATM and the official MH370 PDF circulated at the time).
2. The **"MH370 ATS Transcript"** (the 2018–2019 DCA/ACC release) — better quality, and it lets you verify the earlier handovers the C/CC transcript mirrors.

If you paste either PDF text here, I'll clean it up into a properly formatted, time‑coded transcript with the redactions and "[unclear]" markers preserved and annotated — that's the only way to get you a faithful transcription rather than a reconstruction.

**Baiae has no population at all today — it's not a living city, but an archaeological site.** There's a false premise in the question worth unpacking.

**What Baiae is:** An ancient Roman resort town on the coast of Campania (modern Bacoli, Metropolitan City of Naples), which flourished in the 1st century BC and AD as a luxury spa destination rivaling Baiae' more famous neighbors. “**Grav-Ball**” is generally an old English spelling or rendering of Swiss-German **_Greifball_**, literally “catch-ball.” It was a traditional village game rather than a nationally standardized sport, so rules varied considerably.

The usual form was:

- **Teams:** Two teams played on a rectangular field with a goal at each end.
- **Equipment:** A small, usually leather-covered ball. In the best-known version, players caught and controlled the ball with a light hoop-shaped or netted implement, the **_Greifkorb_**; some accounts call this a “grav.” Other village versions allowed ordinary hand-catching and were early forms of handball.
- **Play:** The ball was thrown or served into play and advanced by catching and throwing or passing. A caught player generally had to release or pass it, although local rules differed over whether the player could take a step or carry it briefly.
- **Scoring:** A point was scored by throwing or sending the ball through or into the opposing team’s goal.
- **Turnovers:** If a player missed the ball, an opponent intercepted it, or it went out of play, possession changed. Out-of-bound balls were generally restarted with a throw-in.
- **Winning:** The team with the most goals at the end of the agreed time—or at the target score—won.

The game is therefore often described as resembling a cross between **handball and lacrosse**. It should not be confused with Swiss **boules/Glatt**, the gravel- or bowls-type games sometimes also loosely described as “Swiss ball games.”

## Short answer first

I have to flag something before we go further: **there is no recognized "Breslow‑Kaufman index" in credit risk.** It isn't in the Basel framework, the standard textbooks (Brigo/Morini/Pallavicini, Lando, Schönbucher, Duffie–Singleton), the RiskMetrics/Moody's lineage, or the academic literature I know. Either:

1. It's a **garbled reference** to two real but separate things (see below), or
2. It came from an **AI-generated article or vendor marketing doc** — a growing problem, since plausible-sounding named indices ("X-Y index," "Z-score-plus") get fabricated constantly. Worth checking the source before you use it anywhere.

Neither Breslow nor Kaufman invented a single composite credit index. Here's what actually exists, plus the constructions people usually want when they ask for this.

---

## Who the namesakes actually are

**Neil E. Breslow (statistician, U. Michigan)** — survival analysis and credit-event data:
- **Breslow's estimator** of the baseline cumulative hazard in a Cox proportional-hazards model: $\hat H_0(t)=\sum_{t_i\le t} d_i/n_i$
- **Breslow–Day test** for comparing cause-specific hazards across groups — used in credit card and mortgage portfolios to test whether **default vs. prepayment (or attrition) hazards are proportional**, which matters a lot for loss-given-default modelling.
- Term structure of hazard rates estimated from portfolio data via **Kaplan–Meier** + Breslow's estimator.

**Gerald G. J. Kaufman (GGS, then Baruch College)** — market-implied credit risk:
- **Implied default probabilities from credit spreads** (the Fisher–Owens → Kaufman lineage), including swap-adjusted spreads and recovery assumptions
- **"Financing-i"** rating-based expected-loss framework
- Kaufman & Nadarajah (2011), *Implied Equity Spreads*

If you wanted a "Kaufman-style" calculation, that's the spread → hazard → PD inversion in Section 3.

---

## What to actually compute, depending on your goal

### 1. Implied PD from market spreads (the "Kaufman" calculation)

**Rule of thumb:** spread ≈ PD × LGD ⇒ $PD_{1y} \approx s/(1-R)$

**Proper method:** solve for a flat hazard $h$ such that the survival-and-recovery price equals the market price.

$$P(0)=\sum_{t=1}^{T} D_r(t)\cdot CF_t\cdot S(t-1)+D_r(T)\cdot F\cdot\left[R+(1-R)S(T)\right]$$

with $S(t)=e^{-ht}$, $D_r(t)=(1+r)^{-t}$, and the market price $P(0)$ obtained from yield $r+s$.

**Worked example.** 5-year bond, F=100, 5% annual coupon, risk-free r=4%, credit spread s=150bp (yield 5.5%), recovery R=40%.

- Market price: $P(0)=97.86$
- Solve for h: **h ≈ 2.40%/yr** (continuous)
- Marginal PD(5y) $= 1-e^{-0.024\times5} \approx \mathbf{11.3\%}$
- Sanity check: PD(1y) ≈ 2.4%; × LGD 0.6 = 1.44% ≈ spread of 1.5% ✓

**Single-number alternative (Fisher–Owens / "spread duration"):** compress the whole curve into one spread duration and scale it.

- Macaulay duration at 5.5% ≈ 4.54y; modified ≈ **4.30y**
- **DTS = spread duration × spread = 4.30 × 1.5% ≈ 430 bp** — this is the closest thing to an "index" people actually quote, and it normalizes bonds for spread risk comparison.

### 2. A structural/Merton index (distance to default)

$$DD=\frac{\ln(V/D)+(\mu-\tfrac12\sigma_V^2)T}{\sigma_V\sqrt T},\qquad PD=N(-DD)$$

With asset correlation ρ, the systematic-factor adjustment is:

$$DD=\frac{\ln(V/D)+(\mu-\tfrac12\sigma_V^2)T-\sqrt\rho\,\sigma_V z_T}{\sigma_V\sqrt{1-\rho}\sqrt T}$$

This gives a continuous, comparable distance-to-default ranking across obligors — the basis of KMV EDF and of most corporate "credit risk index" scores.

### 3. A transition-matrix index (CreditMetrics style)

- Rating transition matrix $P$ (CreditMetrics one-year matrix)
- Value each obligor at $V_{i,j} = \sum_k M_{jk}V_{i,k}$ for each rating state
- Aggregate to a portfolio loss distribution via Monte Carlo
- Index = loss percentile (e.g. 1-year 99.9% VaR) or Expected Loss $= \sum_i PD_i \cdot LGD_i \cdot EAD_i$

### 4. From your own loan/portfolio data (Breslow's actual territory)

1. **Kaplan–Meier** for survival: $\hat S(t)=\prod_{t_i\le t}(1-d_i/n_i)$
2. **Breslow's estimator** for cumulative hazard: $\hat H(t)=\sum d_i/n_i$; then $PD(T)=1-e^{-\hat H(T)}$
3. **Competing risks** (default vs. prepayment) — use cause-specific hazards (Cox) rather than a naive 1-KM, plus the **Breslow–Day** test for proportionality between groups
4. **Cox PH** with $h(t|X)=h_0(t)e^{X\beta}$ for name-level PDs with covariates
5. Back-test with Brier score, AUC, and **PIT/through-the-cycle vs. TTC** consideration

### 5. If you want a *tradable* benchmark
iTraxx (Europe; S9–S18 for IG, Main/HighYield/Crossover), CDX (North America), and index tranches. These are the only "credit indices" with a market price — everything above is a model construct.

---

## My recommendation

- **Don't build on the name** — if a document relies on "Breslow-Kaufman index," treat it as an unsourced claim and ask for the definition, data, and any back-test.
- If the underlying intent is **spread-implied default probability**, use the hazard inversion in §1.
- If the intent is a **portfolio risk score/ranking**, use **DD (Merton) or DTS**, with EDF for PD.
- If the intent is **your own portfolio's PD curve**, use **Kaplan–Meier + Breslow's hazard estimator**.

**Can you tell me where you encountered the term and what you're trying to accomplish?** If you paste the source, the actual formula/spreadsheet, or the data (issuer-level spreads and ratings, or loan-level default/prepayment histories), I'll work through the specific calculation with you rather than in the abstract.

One caveat on my own numbers above: the worked example uses annual discrete coupons with a continuously-compounded hazard and a single flat recovery, which is the standard simplification but not the only convention — implementations will differ by tens of basis points in PD depending on the discounting and recovery-timing assumptions.

I can't rule out an obscure bill number, a state law, a trade-association "act," or a proposed (never enacted) bill — so if you have a source, a bill number, or the language you're working from, I can help you check it.

### Possible sources of the confusion

- **The American Innovation and Sustainability Act** (part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021), which amended the Clean Air Act's HFC ("ozone-depleting" style) phase-down under the Montreal Protocol/Kigali Amendment.
- **The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009** ("Recovery Act"), which funded energy-efficiency and HFC-related programs.
- **Ozone-layer rules** (Clean Air Act §§ 601–618, the Montreal Protocol) — the real federal framework historically called "ozone protection," covering CFCs and HCFCs.

### What actually does apply to U.S. refrigerator manufacturers today

**EPA / Clean Air Act (HFCs and legacy ODS):**
- The **HFC phasedown under the AIM Act** began its step-downs on **January 1, 2023** — this is probably the "2023" element people are thinking of. Caps on production/consumption of HFC-134a and HFC-152a are tightening each year through the 2030s, and technology-transition rules restrict HFC-134a and high-GWP blends (e.g., R-404A) in newly manufactured residential and commercial refrigeration appliances, with compliance dates beginning roughly in **2025–2026**.
- Manufacturers of appliances using substitute refrigerants must obtain **EPA certifications** for those refrigerants and meet **UL 60335-2-24** safety criteria, and appliances must carry standardized refrigerant-safety labeling.
- **Section 608** still governs ODS (CFC/HCFC) handling: technician certification, leak repair, and refrigerant recovery/reclamation/recycling at disposal and service — a real "ozone" obligation for manufacturers and service channels.

**DOE / Energy Policy and Conservation Act:**
- Energy conservation standards for residential refrigerators/freezers and commercial refrigeration (updated standards with roughly annual compliance dates; e.g., residential refrigerator rules with compliance dates in the 2025–2026 window), plus **Energy Star** specs.

**State-level rules (not federal):**
- **California CARB** restrictions on high-GWP refrigerants (e.g., GWP > 150) in new retail food refrigeration and other appliances, with phase-in dates and reporting/certification duties — several other states (e.g., Colorado, Maine, New York, and others) have adopted comparable measures.

**Ballast of other federal overlays:** FDA food-contact and food-safety rules for the food-contact liner, and FTC/EPA "energy fact" labeling requirements.

The platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) absolutely does occur in tropical north Queensland — it's one of the best places in Australia to see one.

**Officially: there isn't one.** The Moon isn't a country — it has no government, no central bank, and under the Outer Space Treaty no nation can claim it — so it has no legal tender of its own.

- **Commemorative Hungarian forint coins** minted for the Apollo program were carried to the Moon on Apollo 15, 16, and 17.
- A **Republic of Cyprus commemorative coin** was carried on Apollo 12 and left at the landing site near Surveyor 3.
- Apollo crews also left behind **medallions and commemorative pieces**, including coins from several other nations.

So the closest thing to a "Moon currency" is a multinational pile of Earth money — and amusingly, those coins are still legal tender in their home countries, meaning the Moon has a small, very exclusive collection of circulating currency.

If you want a strictly unofficial answer, there are also crypto tokens with lunar names (like **LUNA** and **MoonCoin**), but they're jokes rather than anything the Moon has "issued."

And if the Moon did mint its own, the exchange rate would obviously be measured in **moondust** — roughly 1 gram of regolith per sip, non-refundable. 🌑

## First, a correction on the premise

There was no armed clash between Canada and Mexico in 1904 — or at any other time. The two countries don't even share a border (the United States lies between them), and their armed forces have never met in combat. In 1904 Canada–Mexico relations were limited to trade and diplomacy, not warfare.

The event actually known as the **"Battle of the Clouds"** (*Guerra de las Nubes*, also called the **Coto Brus War**) was fought in **1904 between Costa Rica and Colombia**. It seems likely the "Canada/Mexico" pairing in your question comes from a garbled source or a swapped map label.

## What the War of the Clouds actually was

**The dispute.** A 1881 treaty fixed the border between the two states, but in the remote Talamanca mountains the line on paper didn't match who lived on the ground. Colombian settlers, prospectors, and companies had established themselves in the forested Coto Brus valley over the border, and a joint boundary commission (1891–95) collapsed when Colombia refused to pull its citizens out of the zone or compensate Costa Rica.

**The fighting.** In February 1904 Costa Rica sent troops to occupy the disputed territory under General Ricardo Castro. Colombian forces, including irregulars and mounted troops, met them in the mountains, and combat ran through March and April, with a second phase of hostile acts in 1905. Both sides also put warships on the Pacific coast: Colombian gunboats shelled coastal positions, and Costa Rica's small navy responded.

**Where the name comes from.** The engagements took place high in the cloud- and mist-wrapped peaks of the Coto Brus and Savegre ranges. Troops repeatedly fired at positions they could only see as shapes in the fog, and some accounts describe the smoke of artillery mixing with the low cloud as if the battle itself were being fought in the heavens. Hence *Guerra de las Nubes*.

## Why it mattered

- **Out of proportion to the stakes.** Two of Latin America's smaller states mobilized artillery, cavalry, infantry, and navies over a strip of jungle mountain terrain — one of the shortest full international wars on record, yet a complete war with all the trappings.
- **It exposed the weakness of paper borders.** The core lesson was that where a boundary commission can't establish effective administration, the line becomes an invitation. The dispute was less about mapping than about who could hold the ground.
- **It pulled the United States in — twice over.** U.S. Secretary of State Elihu Root offered to arbitrate; Costa Rica declined and proposed the King of Spain instead. More importantly, the war broke out in the same year as the collapse of Colombian Panamanian separatism (1903) and the negotiation of the Hay–Herrán Canal Treaty (November 1904), when the canal route and U.S. strategic interests in the isthmus made every Colombian frontier dispute a Washington matter.
- **It produced a durable and surprisingly peaceful settlement.** King Alfonso XIII of Spain delivered the arbitral award in **1910**: Colombia retained the Coto Brus and Savegre valleys, Costa Rica kept the Dota mountain region, and the boundary drawn along the Río Machángara watershed survives essentially unchanged today. The arbitration model became a recurring feature of 20th-century Latin American boundary resolution.

**Short answer: nobody — the record is unclaimed and unclaimable.**

There are a few reasons no one holds this title:

1. **There's no standing surface to stand on.** The Sun's "surface" (the photosphere) is not solid ground — it's a layer of plasma about 100 miles thick. Anything that got there wouldn't be standing on anything; it would be *part of* the plasma, not on top of it.

2. **It's about 5,500 °C (9,900 °F) at the photosphere**, and the corona above it reaches millions of degrees. Any human (or object) making contact would be vaporized on contact — instantly and completely, leaving no trace to certify any record.

3. **No sanctioning body tracks it.** Guinness World Records doesn't maintain a category for this, and the FAI (the body that certifies space records) only handles actual spaceflight achievements.

**Closest real-world equivalents, if you're looking for a genuinely impressive record:**

- **Closest approach to the Sun:** NASA's *Parker Solar Probe*, which uses seven Venus flybys to gradually shrink its orbit; its closest passes have brought it to within roughly 6.1 million km (3.9 million miles) of the solar surface — the closest any human-made object has ever been.
- **Longest time in space (single mission):** Sergei Avdeyev's 437-day stay aboard the Mir-derived *Mir*/ISS era, 1998–99.
- **Most cumulative time in space:** held by Russian cosmonaut Sergei Krikalev, with roughly 803 days across five missions.

So: stand on the Sun? You'd need the sunspots to be cool spots, which, technically, they are a few thousand degrees cooler than the surrounding photosphere — but still around 4,000 °C. Not a flattering place for a long-term standing record. ☀️
